items.author: Anirudh Trivedi
items.content:
For India’s D2C brands, quick commerce has opened up another route to millions of consumers. But turning that access into profitable growth remains a challenge. Platform commissions, advertising expenses, inventory requirements and frequent discounting can quickly erode the margins brands earn from the channel.
For Gurugram-based personal hygiene brand Pee Safe, however, quick commerce has become one of its most profitable distribution channels, accounting for nearly 40% of domestic revenue and delivering double-digit contribution margins, compared with single-digit margins on traditional ecommerce.
Getting there was far from straightforward.
Pee Safe spent nearly two years struggling to keep its products consistently available on quick commerce platforms. Its existing distributor network could not meet the channel’s replenishment requirements, while products and pack sizes that performed well on ecommerce did not necessarily find buyers on 10-minute delivery apps.
The company eventually overhauled its supply chain, changed how it managed its product assortment and used the consumer awareness it had built over the years to limit its dependence on paid advertising.
The result is a distribution mix in which quick commerce now contributes 40% of domestic revenue, followed by D2C and ecommerce at 35% and offline retail at 25%.
But the significance of Pee Safe’s experience goes beyond this revenue split. It shows how quick commerce economics can differ considerably depending on whether a brand uses the channel to create consumer demand or fulfil demand that already exists.
In an exclusive conversation for The Quick Commerce Code by Inc42 and Nitro Commerce, Pee Safe cofounder Rithish Kumar discussed how the brand built its quick commerce operations, the changes that improved its margins and the challenges of extending that growth into new markets.
From An Early Bet On Instant Delivery To Fixing A Broken Supply Chain
Pee Safe’s origins predate India’s quick commerce boom.
The idea emerged in 2013 after cofounder Srijana Bagaria developed a urinary tract infection following a road trip. The experience prompted Srijana and Vikas Bagaria to explore products that could address hygiene concerns associated with public washrooms.
After several months of product development, they created a portable, alcohol-based toilet seat sanitiser spray that dried quickly after application. The product became the foundation of Pee Safe, which formally launched in 2017 and subsequently expanded into feminine hygiene, intimate care, personal care and wellness.
The brand was entering categories where consumer education and trust were particularly important. Alongside established multinational companies, newer brands such as Sirona, Nua and Plush were also competing for a share of India’s evolving feminine hygiene market.
For Pee Safe, building distribution was central to taking its products beyond the consumers who were already familiar with the brand.
That also explains why the company began experimenting with faster delivery relatively early.
In 2018, Pee Safe listed its products on Grofers, the grocery delivery platform subsequently rebranded as Blinkit. The proposition was different from conventional ecommerce, where consumers often waited a day or more for delivery.
The pandemic-driven acceleration of doorstep deliveries made the channel increasingly relevant. As Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart expanded, Pee Safe saw an opportunity to make products such as sanitary pads, toilet seat sanitisers and other personal care essentials available closer to the time of purchase.
However, the operating model behind its early quick commerce expansion was not designed for the channel.
Pee Safe initially relied on the same distributors that serviced neighbourhood retailers and modern trade outlets to supply quick-commerce platforms.
For distributors accustomed to servicing established retail relationships, managing a much wider assortment, holding inventory and frequently replenishing platform warehouses presented a different set of demands.
Consequently, Pee Safe frequently struggled with stock availability.
The problem wasn’t necessarily a lack of consumer demand. Products that customers wanted were not always available when they searched for them.
By late 2023 and early 2024, the company began changing its approach.
Instead of depending on traditional distributors to manage quick commerce supplies, Pee Safe moved to a model of supplying platform warehouses through third-party warehousing partners, gaining greater control over inventory planning and replenishment.
According to Kumar, the restructuring materially improved fulfilment.
The company reported fill rates of 97-98% during a recent quarter, while on-shelf availability for its core products exceeded 90%. It targets availability above 80% for products outside its core assortment.
These metrics capture different aspects of fulfilment: fill rate measures how much of a platform’s order a brand supplies, whereas on-shelf availability indicates whether customers can actually purchase the product.
The distinction matters because products that remain unavailable on an app cannot generate sales, regardless of the demand for them.
Pee Safe now has a dedicated team of seven to eight people managing quick commerce operations. Kumar monitors performance dashboards daily and, at times, hourly.
The channel has also changed the company’s working-capital cycle. According to Kumar, quick commerce platforms typically settle payments within 30 days, sometimes sooner, compared with longer cycles in traditional and modern trade.
Faster collections offer an advantage, although they do not eliminate the investment required to maintain inventory across warehouses and fulfilment centres.
The operational improvements are also reflected in third-party availability data.
An analysis by Zodiac AI by Nitro Commerce found that Pee Safe maintained average on-shelf availability of 94.7% on Blinkit during 1-25 August 2026, although availability differed across cities.
For Pee Safe, fixing product availability was only the first part of making quick commerce work. The next challenge was understanding which products consumers wanted to buy through the channel and at what price points.
Why Pee Safe Had To Rethink Its Products For Quick Commerce
When Pee Safe began expanding on quick commerce, it had roughly five to six SKUs on the channel. Today, its assortment has grown to more than 60 products across platforms.
But expanding the catalogue did not mean transferring the same packs and pricing that worked on Amazon or in offline retail.
One of the clearest examples came from acne patches.
Pee Safe initially offered a 60-piece pack priced at ₹499, but the product struggled to gain traction. The company subsequently introduced a smaller 12-piece pack at ₹99, which became one of its leading SKUs in the category.
The smaller pack reduced the upfront commitment and suited consumers looking for a quick solution or trying the product for the first time.
Sanitary pads presented a different pattern.
Rather than gravitating towards smaller packs, customers were frequently purchasing larger quantities. Pee Safe responded by moving from a 12-pad pack priced at approximately ₹199 to a 30-pad pack costing around ₹399.
The contrasting experiences highlighted an important distinction: consumers were not necessarily looking for smaller or cheaper products on quick commerce. Their preferred pack sizes depended on the category and the reason for purchasing.
According to Kumar, the ₹100-₹150 price bracket can work well as an entry point across several categories, but the company uses platform-level demand data to adjust its assortment.
The wider beauty and personal care market shows similar differences in purchasing behaviour.
Redseer’s Quick Commerce BPC Brand Index for January-March 2026 found that 50 gm/ml sunscreen packs accounted for 78% of quick-commerce sales for a leading brand, compared with roughly 50% of its ecommerce sales. Larger 80 gm/ml packs accounted for just 2% of the brand’s quick-commerce sales.
Large FMCG companies, including Parle, ITC and Hindustan Unilever, have also developed channel-specific packs and price points to cater to quick-commerce consumers while differentiating their online and offline assortments.
For Pee Safe, the lesson was to approach quick commerce as a distinct retail channel rather than another outlet for its existing inventory.
The brand uses consumer demand, product movement and regional purchasing patterns to determine which SKUs deserve more inventory and where new products should be introduced.
However, the company did not disclose SKU-level sales uplifts or contribution margins, making it difficult to quantify precisely how much the assortment changes contributed to overall revenue or profitability.
That leaves another important part of the story: why Pee Safe is able to generate stronger margins on quick commerce despite the additional costs associated with the channel.
Why Quick Commerce Is More Profitable For Pee Safe Than Ecommerce
One of the biggest challenges for consumer brands on quick commerce is the cost of getting discovered.
A brand entering Blinkit, Zepto or Swiggy Instamart may need to spend on advertising, discounting and promotional visibility while also absorbing platform and fulfilment costs.
For products priced at ₹150-₹200, those expenses can quickly make the economics unattractive.
Kumar estimates that advertising costs in some categories can reach ₹8,000-₹10,000 per thousand impressions, while additional discounts of 10-15% can further reduce the amount brands retain from each sale.
Pee Safe, however, had an advantage when it expanded on quick commerce: a consumer base that had already discovered the brand elsewhere.
After years of building awareness and repeat consumption through Amazon and other channels, Pee Safe found that many quick commerce customers already knew which products they wanted.
Rather than relying entirely on advertisements to generate discovery, consumers were searching for Pee Safe directly.
That distinction has been central to its profitability.
According to Kumar, a substantial share of the brand’s quick commerce revenue comes from organic demand, helping it limit advertising expenditure and avoid excessive discounting.
The company estimates repeat-purchase rates ranging from 20% to 60%, depending on the product category.
Together, existing brand recognition, repeat purchasing and tighter control over promotions have helped Pee Safe generate double-digit contribution margins on quick commerce, compared with single-digit contribution margins on traditional ecommerce.
There is, however, an important distinction between channel-level contribution margins and company-wide profitability.
Contribution margins measure what remains from sales after the costs included in the company’s calculation. They do not necessarily account for every corporate expense, brand-building investment or other cost incurred by the business.
Pee Safe has not disclosed a detailed like-for-like breakdown of platform commissions, advertising, logistics and warehousing expenses across its sales channels.
Nor has it quantified how much of the demand generated on quick commerce is genuinely incremental, rather than shifting purchases from its existing ecommerce channels.
This matters because the profitability of an individual channel can partly reflect brand-building expenditure incurred elsewhere.
Pee Safe’s experience nevertheless points to a potentially important distinction for emerging D2C businesses: quick commerce may be more effective at profitably fulfilling established demand than at creating demand for an unfamiliar brand from scratch.
For Pee Safe, the next test is whether those economics can hold as the company expands its product portfolio and reaches consumers in markets where brand recognition may be weaker.
Why Expansion Beyond Metros Requires Another Playbook
Pee Safe’s quick commerce footprint now extends to more than 6,500 dark stores across 250 cities through quick commerce platforms, according to Kumar.
But distribution has not translated into uniform demand across markets.
Nearly 50% of the company’s quick commerce sales now come from Tier II cities and smaller markets, while southern and western India together contribute approximately 60% of the channel’s revenue.
The expansion has brought the brand into 25+ markets such as Ahmedabad, Jaipur, Lucknow, Dehradun, Indore, Nagpur, Bhopal, Guwahati and Patna.
These markets have required Pee Safe to rethink which products it launches and how it markets them.
Instead of making its entire catalogue available immediately, the company typically enters newer cities with familiar categories such as sanitary pads, where consumer demand is already established.
Products that require more education, such as menstrual cups, are introduced more selectively. Local purchasing patterns also influence these decisions.
Kumar cited stronger demand for menstrual cups in Kerala and panty liners in Maharashtra and Gujarat, illustrating how category preferences can differ across geographies.
The company uses regional and pin code-level data to identify products underperforming relative to national benchmarks and direct advertising spend toward specific markets.
Content is another part of this approach.
Approximately 80% of Pee Safe’s influencer content is produced in regional languages, allowing the brand to communicate with consumers beyond its initial metropolitan customer base.
The company combines this content with geographically targeted marketing to encourage consumers to purchase its products through quick commerce platforms.
Such spending also highlights the limitations of a purely organic-demand model. While existing brand recognition has supported Pee Safe’s margins, reaching new customers and developing unfamiliar product categories may require additional investment.
Interestingly, Pee Safe is now applying elements of its Indian quick commerce strategy abroad.
Can Pee Safe Sustain Its Quick Commerce Advantage?
Pee Safe’s overall financial performance provides useful context for its quick-commerce ambitions.
According to Inc42’s financial data, the company generated ₹82.5 Cr in revenue in FY25, up approximately 44% from ₹57.3 Cr in FY24. It reported a net loss of around ₹4 Cr in FY25.
Kumar said the company’s revenue grew by approximately 60% in FY26, although the financial statements were still being audited at the time of the conversation.
For FY27, he expects revenue growth to exceed 100%. The quick commerce business forms a major part of that ambition.
According to Kumar, Pee Safe’s quick commerce revenue reached an annualised run rate of ₹150 Cr in September 2026. The figure represents the annualised pace of sales at that point, rather than revenue recognised over a completed financial year.
In January 2026, Pee Safe also secured $32 Mn in a Series C round led by OrbiMed, comprising a combination of primary capital and secondary share sales. Its investor base has also included Alkemi Venture Partners and Venture Catalysts.
The funding is intended to support expansion across offline retail, quick commerce, ecommerce and brand marketing.
However, pursuing growth across multiple channels will also require Pee Safe to manage inventory investments, advertising expenditure and competition from both established consumer companies and emerging brands.
Private labels are another potential challenge.
As quick-commerce platforms expand their own product portfolios, they could compete more directly with brands selling through their marketplaces.
Kumar believes Pee Safe’s position in intimate and feminine hygiene offers some protection because consumers place considerable importance on trust when purchasing these products.
“Private labels can be threatening when you don’t have high defensibility. A platform building a private label in women’s hygiene faces a high trust deficit as it takes years to build, and Pee Safe has a head start on that,” he said.
That confidence will be tested as competition increases and platforms develop their own capabilities in categories currently served by third-party brands.
Pee Safe is also looking beyond quick commerce for its next phase of expansion.
While offline retail already contributes a quarter of domestic revenue, the company intends to deepen its presence in the channel. Kumar also sees scope to improve its performance on traditional ecommerce, where he believes the brand remains underrepresented.
The strategy is to expand the categories already demonstrating traction and capture a larger share of those markets, rather than relying exclusively on new product launches.
For Pee Safe, quick commerce has evolved from a difficult distribution experiment into a major revenue contributor. But its experience also shows that getting listed on a platform is only a starting point.
The harder work lies in making products consistently available, matching assortments to buying behaviour and ensuring that the cost of selling does not exceed the value of the demand a brand captures.
Whether Pee Safe can preserve that balance as it expands across categories and geographies will determine how much of its next phase of growth quick commerce can profitably support.
[Edited By Shishir Parasher]

OPPO has launched its most-awaited flagship lineup, the OPPO Find X10 Series, at a global launch event in Mallorca, Spain. OPPO is preparing to bring its latest flagship innovation to Pakistan, with the OPPO Find X10 Pro Max set to arrive in the market soon. At the top of the lineup, the OPPO Find X10 Pro Max introduces the industry’s first Triple 200MP Camera System and will soon be available in Pakistan, bringing the country its first Hasselblad flagship phone.
Beyond its technology, the Find X10 Pro Max’s upcoming arrival raises expectations for OPPO’s next move in Pakistan’s premium smartphone market. With its advanced imaging system and flagship specifications, the device could reshape consumer expectations of what a high-end Android smartphone can offer. Its arrival is expected to add fresh momentum to the flagship category, encouraging greater competition around flagship innovation and the value consumers expect from premium devices.
The arrival of the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max also reflects how far OPPO has progressed as a technology brand in Pakistan. With its emphasis on imaging, design, and performance, the Find X10 Pro Max is poised to generate interest among photography enthusiasts, content creators, and technology users seeking a premium smartphone experience.
Developed in collaboration with Hasselblad, the series combines advanced camera hardware with OPPO’s next-generation LUMO True Image Engine to deliver authentic detail, natural colors, and lifelike tones. Beyond its camera system, the Find X10 Pro Max combines a premium Borderless Design with the flagship MediaTek Dimensity 9600 Pro, an 8,000mAh battery, and the latest ColorOS 17. Together, these features contribute to a flagship experience designed to meet the demands of users who want one of the best cameras on an Android flagship, along with powerful performance.
As anticipation builds ahead of its Pakistan debut, questions around the device’s local pricing and its place among established premium smartphones are likely to add to the market interest. While official pricing and availability details remain under wraps, the Find X10 Pro Max’s arrival presents an opportunity for OPPO to further challenge perceptions of its flagship capabilities and strengthen its position in Pakistan’s evolving smartphone landscape.
The global unveiling marks the beginning of the Find X10 Series’ next chapter, with Pakistan set to be part of the conversation as OPPO brings its latest flagship innovations closer to local consumers. Further details regarding the official Pakistan launch and local availability of the OPPO Find X10 Pro Max will be announced in due course.

items.author: Asif Mehmood
items.content:
The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) on Wednesday expressed concern over the alleged murder of 15-year-old Waseem Abbas in Multan and the subsequent death of the primary suspect in an alleged police encounter, calling for an independent and transparent investigation into the case.
The suspect, Tauqeer Nazir, had allegedly chased Abbas in his car after a dispute over work and run him over in a private housing society in Multan on October 19. He was arrested and handed over to police on a four-day physical remand by a judicial magistrate the following day. Later today, police said the suspect fled custody and was then killed by his accomplices when a police party tried to re-arrest him.
According to the HRCP, Abbas was reportedly chased and run over by his employer. The subsequent death of the suspect in an alleged police encounter has raised serious questions about the state’s approach to protecting human life and upholding legal safeguards.
The commission said extrajudicial killings violate the right to due process and deprive victims and their families of the opportunity to establish the truth and seek justice.
It added that the perception that such killings are an acceptable means of controlling crime suggests that vengeance without accountability is being prioritised over justice.
The HRCP called for an independent and transparent investigation into the case and urged the authorities to bring an end to extrajudicial killings in all forms.
Bonded Labour Liberation Front seeks probe into orphanages
Separately, the Bonded Labour Liberation Front Pakistan demanded an investigation into Abbas's death and action against unregistered orphanages allegedly involved in the exploitation of children.
Read: Man accused of running over Multan teenager killed in CCD encounter
According to a press release issued by the organisation’s president, Syeda Ghulam Fatima Gilani, Abbas was living at an orphanage in Multan and had been sent to work at a workshop, where he died after being run over by a vehicle. The organisation termed the incident a killing rather than an accident and called for legal action against those responsible.
The organisation alleged that more than 52 unregistered orphanages across Punjab were sending children to brick kilns and workshops for labour. It also accused the relevant labour officer in Multan and an official of the Child Protection and Welfare Bureau (CPWB) of negligence and demanded action against them.
The organisation called for strict action against unregistered orphanages and registered institutions involved in child exploitation, monthly surprise inspections of all orphanages, and the creation of an online record of children residing in these facilities.
It also urged the Lahore High Court to take notice of the incident.
“Wasim should have been in school, not at a workshop,” Gilani said, warning that the organisation would approach the High Court if no action was taken within seven days.
The case
The first information report (FIR), registered on Monday named Nazir and Amjad Ali as suspects and invoked Sections 302 and 34 of the Pakistan Penal Code, relating to murder and acts done by several persons in furtherance of their common intention. It alleged that the two men pursued Abbas in a car and deliberately ran him over, causing fatal head injuries.
According to the FIR, Sub-Inspector Liaquat Ali Bhatti was on patrol with police personnel in Royal Orchard when a man identified as Mukhtiar Ahmed approached them at around 4:35pm. Mukhtiar told police that his cousin, Abbas, had been working as an electrician for the suspects and that they had allegedly subjected him to violence and threatened to kill him. The report stated that Abbas had fled to a neighbouring street to escape the alleged abuse, while the two suspects pursued him in a vehicle. Police said they saw Abbas running in fear, followed by a Honda vehicle bearing registration number BVE-474.
The FIR alleged that the suspects ran the vehicle over Abbas with the intention of killing him. His head struck a pillar at the gate of house 3-A, crushing his skull and causing severe injuries. He died at the scene.
Two residents, Saqlain Raza and Syed Naseem Abbas, were named as witnesses in the FIR. According to the report, they told police that Abbas had passed by shortly before the incident, saying that the suspects wanted to kill him and that he was running to save his life.
The FIR further stated that the vehicle stopped after the incident and the suspects attempted to flee. Nazir was apprehended at the scene, while Ali escaped. Police took the vehicle into custody as evidence.
Mukhtiar told police that Abbas wanted to leave the job because of the alleged violence and feared for his safety. The FIR alleged that the suspects pursued him over his decision to leave and acted in concert to kill him.

items.author: Amiya Johar
items.content:
Jio Platforms’ $3.2 billion IPO was reportedly fully subscribed within around 100 minutes of opening on Wednesday (21 October), as investors rushed to take part in India’s largest share sale.
Sources told Reuters institutional investors covered their allocated portion within 10 minutes of bidding opening, although demand from retail investors was slower. Around a third of the shares are reserved for retail buyers.
“It’s the fastest in the history of India,” a source said.
Reliance Industries’ telecoms unit is offering 270 million shares priced at between INR1,065 ($11.28) and INR1,119 apiece, with the offer closing on Friday (23 October). The IPO values the business at up to $108.3 billion and marks the first public offering from billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance conglomerate in two decades.
The company plans to use most of the IPO proceeds to repay or prepay borrowings at Reliance Jio Infocomm, its telecoms subsidiary, with the remainder earmarked for general corporate purposes, including capital expenditure.
Jio Platforms reported a profit of around $3.2 billion on revenue of $15.5 billion in the year to March.
The offering also comes despite a weak domestic equity market, after the country’s Nifty 50 benchmark index of 50 leading Indian companies slumped this year.
However, Indian wealth management firm SMIFS Limited noted “the long-term outlook for Jio Platforms Limited remains highly favourable, driven by sustained growth in India’s digital economy”.
According to the company, Jio Platforms will “benefit from rising 5G adoption, increasing smartphone penetration, accelerating broadband penetration, growing enterprise digitalisation and expanding demand for cloud and AI-enabled services”.
Jio’s telecoms business has more than 500 million subscribers, making it the world’s second largest telecoms operator in a single country after China Mobile. It disrupted India’s telecoms market after launching in 2016 with low-cost data plans, putting pressure on rivals Bharti Airtel and Vodafone Idea.
However, the company continues to face regulatory uncertainty and growing competition in satellite connectivity, as billionaire Elon Musk’s Starlink prepares to enter India’s market.

PKR 100,000 is a line many buyers hesitate to cross. Spend less and you expect compromises, spend more and you expect everything. The TECNO POVA Curve 2 5G, launched in Pakistan on October 15 at PKR 99,999, sits just under that line, and TECNO’s pitch is that it asks for no compromises: a 5G processor, an 8000mAh battery and what it calls the slimmest design among phones with a battery that size.
Here is what the phone offers, in the order most buyers care about, and what to weigh before you decide.
Performance and 5G: fast now, fast later
The phone runs on a MediaTek Dimensity 7100 5G processor, with 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. At this price, the question is less how fast it is on day one and more whether it stays that way. TECNO says it holds 90 minutes of smooth Free Fire at 60fps, helped by Ice Cooling 3.0, and that it is TÜV Rheinland certified to stay lag-free for six years. The software promise backs that up, with 2 Android version updates and 3 years of security patches.
Battery: the reason to look twice
Battery is where the POVA Curve 2 5G aims hardest. Its 8000mAh cell is meant to take you two days between charges, with more than 15 days of standby, according to TECNO. When you do need a charger, 45W fast charging takes it from empty to full in 82 minutes, and 10W reverse charging lets it power other devices.
The part buyers tend to overlook is longevity. TECNO says the battery is built for 2,000 cycles, which it describes as six years of safe use, so it shouldn’t need replacing in the time you’re likely to own the phone.
Design: the slimmest 8000mAh phone
At 7.42mm and 195g, TECNO says the POVA Curve 2 5G is the slimmest phone among those with an 8000mAh battery. That matters because a big battery usually means a bulky phone, and this one is meant to slip into a pocket and sit comfortably in the hand.
The look is inspired by interstellar spaceships, with bold, flowing lines and a minimalist finish, in Melting Silver, Mystic Purple or Storm Titanium. Corning Gorilla Glass 7i and SGS-certified 1.5m drop resistance cover everyday knocks.
Display: smooth, bright and responsive
The 6.78-inch curved AMOLED display runs at 144Hz, so scrolling and games stay smooth, and peak brightness of up to 4,500 nits keeps it readable outdoors. A 2160Hz touch sampling rate keeps touch responsive, and anti-mistouch means wet or oily hands shouldn’t cost you a tap.
The camera and extras
The camera isn’t the headline here. It’s a 50MP primary camera, a 2MP macro camera and a 13MP front camera, backed by AI tools including AI Eraser 2.0 and AI Flare Remover. The Ella voice assistant adds call translation and WhatsApp summaries, and FreeLink 2.0 keeps calls and messages going between phones within 1.5km without network coverage. If photography is your top priority, compare samples before you buy.
Price and who it suits
The POVA Curve 2 5G is available across Pakistan in 8GB RAM + 256GB ROM at PKR 99,999. It suits people who use their phone hard and are tired of chasing a charger: gamers, heavy multitaskers and anyone whose day runs longer than a typical battery.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
Government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline on Wednesday after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent ‌website operators scrambling to protect their systems.
Developers of the PHP programming language said Tuesday they had identified two critical vulnerabilities, and urged users to update their sites as soon as a fix was released. They said around 1345 GMT on Wednesday that a new version fixing the vulnerabilities was live.
But with reports that hackers were exploiting the flaws to break into websites, government agencies in the Netherlands and Finland were among those that took sites offline ahead of ​the fix as a precaution.
PHP underpins large parts of the internet, raising concerns that a significant number of websites could be vulnerable to attack.
"PHP is everywhere. It quietly powers WordPress, ​Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under ⁠the hood," cybersecurity company Huntress said in a blog post.
Read: US judge orders Saudi engineer held in OpenAI case
Dane Knecht, the chief technology officer of Web and cloud security firm Cloudflare, said that attacks were emerging and Cloudflare was updating its ​firewall rules as a stopgap measure.
"We are seeing early attacks emerging and are updating mitigations as new vectors show up. This is a STOPGAP only. Patch as soon as PHP releases the update," he ​said on X.
Wordfence, a security plugin that protects WordPress websites, said all WordPress sites run on a PHP-installed server. It warned that automatic updates would not apply the fix and advised site owners to find out who is responsible for updating PHP on their sites.
Cybersecurity agencies in Europe, Australia, Japan and Britain have urged PHP users to update immediately or take websites offline until patches can be applied. The Dutch cybersecurity agency itself went offline, saying ​it had done so as a precaution because of the vulnerabilities.
Officials have said that all PHP versions from PHP 5 onward could be affected, although PHP has not yet disclosed which versions are ​vulnerable.
Critical software
PHP is a programming language used to run websites. When a visitor loads a page, a server running PHP assembles the content and sends it to the browser. It is free, open-source software maintained by ‌volunteers.
It is also ⁠among the most widely used software on the internet. PHP runs roughly 75% of websites whose programming language can be identified, according to web technology tracker W3Techs. It is the engine behind WordPress, which powers about 43% of all websites, from blogs and small business pages to government portals, online stores and news sites.
Automattic, the company behind WordPress.com, said: "We don't comment on the details of security issues, but our team is prepared and has been working with the PHP security team to ensure a smooth update."
Security experts said the vulnerabilities could potentially open the door to millions of servers because so ​many websites rely on the same underlying software. ​Rather than target victims individually, attackers could scan ⁠the internet for systems running vulnerable versions of PHP.
Read more: Israeli firm used online ads to run vast spy operation, researchers say
AI-assisted hacking campaigns, which have proliferated in recent weeks, could magnify the threat, said Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow at King's College London.
"The scale is huge," Olejnik said. "And with AI, exploitation may happen instantly, on a large scale."
The risk is particularly ​acute for small websites run by individuals or organisations with limited technical resources, often on shared hosting services where customers do not directly ​manage the underlying servers. Security ⁠experts said such sites could take longer to patch and remain exposed well after fixes become available.
Mass outages
In the Netherlands, several organisations followed the example of the National Cyber Security Centre and took public-facing websites offline, including the Port of Rotterdam, government portal Overheid.nl, the national soccer association KNVB, the websites of the country's five largest political parties and several hospital websites.
Danish municipal IT company Kombit said it had shut down several ⁠services, including ​the national school communication platform, a spokesperson told Reuters.
Disruption was even more widespread in Finland, where state IT services provider ​Valtori said government public network services had been taken offline "as a precautionary measure."
France's Interior Ministry said it had temporarily taken local government administrative websites offline while awaiting a security fix.
The US cybersecurity agency CISA did not respond to emails seeking comment.

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
Zomato and Blinkit parent Eternal has unveiled Dark, a privacy-focused AI platform that founder Deepinder Goyal hopes to launch globally within 2026.
In Eternal’s Q2 FY27 shareholder letter, Goyal said the platform is aimed at power users, including founders, researchers, scientists, enterprises, and governments, who want to keep their conversations and research private.
Dark has been in internal use for a few months, he said, adding that its privacy features had encouraged him to share more information and explore questions he would hesitate to ask other AI assistants.
The platform uses fine-tuned frontier open-weight models running on Eternal’s own infrastructure. Unlike building a model from scratch, this approach involves adapting existing models whose trained parameters are available for developers to use and modify.
According to Goyal, Dark uses end-to-end encryption, alongside an encrypted memory management layer controlled by users, to retain context across sessions.
“We cannot read your conversations, even if we are forced to,” he said.
He positioned Dark around concerns that users’ interactions with mainstream AI assistants could be retained or accessed by others, discouraging them from sharing sensitive information.
He argued that disabling the use of conversations for model training does not, by itself, address questions around data retention, legal holds, human reviews, or third-party logging.
Eternal’s AI Ambitions
Goyal said concerns around data retention, human reviews, legal holds and third-party logging on mainstream AI platforms could limit the extent to which people use AI for sensitive or commercially valuable work.
He argued that founders, researchers and scientists may hesitate to share breakthrough ideas with AI tools over fears that their information could be accessed by others. Similarly, individuals may avoid asking AI assistants sensitive questions about their health, finances or relationships because of privacy concerns.
Dark aims to address these concerns by combining data privacy with what Eternal describes as high-quality AI responses. The company said it has fine-tuned its models to deliver answers that prioritise truth over user approval, adding that benchmark results would be disclosed later.
Goyal also highlighted the potential risks associated with AI companies retaining user conversations, questioning whether such data could eventually be used to influence consumer behaviour or shape users’ beliefs.
However, not many details about the platform are available yet. “Dark will launch globally, hopefully within 2026,” Goyal said in the letter.
With Dark, Eternal has doubled down on its strategy to commercialise AI capabilities developed for its own operations. In February last year, it launched AI-native customer support platform Nugget after building it as an internal tool over three years to handle millions of customer support interactions per month across Zomato, Blinkit and Hyperpure.
Nugget offers businesses conversational chatbots and co-pilots, alongside voice AI, image classification and workflow automation to businesses.
These disclosures came as Eternal reported a 92% surge in its net profit to ₹125 Cr in the quarter ended September 30, 2026 (Q2 FY27), from ₹65 Cr in the previous year’s quarter. On a sequential basis, profit rose 36% from ₹92 Cr.
Operating revenue for the quarter zoomed 78% YoY and 19% QoQ to ₹24,138 Cr. Including other income of ₹351 Cr, total income stood at ₹24,489 Cr.
District Faces Higher Risk From Agentic Commerce
Apart from outlining its own AI ambitions, Eternal also raised concerns about the impact of agentic commerce on its group companies. Notably, it said its going-out vertical District faces the highest potential disruption from AI agents as they could bypass the platform to discover restaurants, book tables and purchase event tickets, reducing the platform’s role as an intermediary.
Goyal classified District as being in the medium-to-high risk zone, warning that AI agents could weaken content-led competitive advantages, including reviews, ratings and curated listings, by synthesising information from across the internet. However, he believes competition could increasingly favour platforms with stronger execution capabilities.
Meanwhile, he said that Zomato and Blinkit are relatively insulated from agentic commerce because their businesses rely on complex fulfillment infrastructure rather than discovery alone.
According to consumer surveys cited by Goyal, over 65% of Zomato app openings are exploratory, with users browsing an average of 12 menus and more than 100 food images before ordering. He argued that food discovery is an enjoyable activity that conversational AI may not easily replace.
While repeat orders and restocking could shift to AI agents, Eternal said reordered carts account for only a low-single-digit share of activity on both Zomato and Blinkit. It also believes in-app AI assistants could cater to these use cases.
More importantly, food delivery and quick commerce require real-time coordination between restaurants, delivery partners, inventory systems, pickers and dispatch operations. He argued that agents could initiate transactions, but the platforms managing fulfillment would remain responsible for delivering orders and resolving issues.
This comes as consumer companies are increasingly exploring agent-led shopping and payments. In February 2026, Razorpay and NPCI demonstrated agentic payments through Anthropic’s Claude, enabling users in a pilot to order food and groceries from platforms including Zomato, Swiggy and Zepto within AI conversations.
Meanwhile, Meesho has developed Vaani, a voice-first, multi-agent commerce system designed to help users discover and compare products conversationally.

items.author: Akshit Pushkarna
items.content:
Eternal, the parent company of Blinkit and Zomato, reported a consolidated net profit of ₹125 Cr for the second quarter of FY27, up 92% YoY from ₹65 Cr in the previous year quarter. On a sequential basis, profit surged 36% from ₹92 Cr in Q1 FY27.
Operating revenue for the quarter zoomed 78% YoY and 19% QoQ to ₹24,138 Cr. Including other income of ₹351 Cr, total income stood at ₹24,489 Cr. Eternal’s adjusted revenue increased 76% YoY and 19% QoQ to ₹24,621 Cr. On a like-for-like (LFL) basis, adjusted revenue grew 58% YoY.
The difference reflects Blinkit’s shift towards an inventory-led model, under which revenue includes the full value of goods sold directly to customers rather than only marketplace commissions. The like-for-like calculation excludes the cost of goods sold from Blinkit’s own inventory and Hyperpure’s non-restaurant revenue.
Total expenses for the quarter rose 75% YoY to ₹24,166 Cr, while tax expenses came in at ₹198 Cr. Consolidated Adjusted EBITDA almost tripled YoY, surging 197% to ₹666 Cr.
However, the company’s cash balance at the end of September dipped by ₹1,813 Cr to ₹16,475 Cr.
The decline was driven by seasonal net working capital requirements, including building Blinkit’s inventory ahead of the festive season and quarter-end timing in Zomato’s weekly restaurant settlement cycle that temporarily lowered payables.
Besides, Eternal’s board also approved exchanging its entire stake in adtech startup AdOnMo for shares in Mygate ahead of a proposed merger between the two startups. Eternal will eventually own around 4.4% of the merged entity, with the holding currently valued at ₹156 Cr.
The board also approved transferring the India going-out business housed directly in Eternal to wholly owned subsidiary Zomato Entertainment Pvt Ltd for around ₹130.76 Cr, subject to adjustments, through a slump sale. The business housed in two other subsidiaries will subsequently be consolidated into the same entity to streamline operations.
Here’s how Eternal’s key businesses performed during the quarter:
Blinkit Accelerates Store Expansion
Blinkit remained Eternal’s largest revenue contributor, with operating revenue increasing 94% YoY and 22% QoQ to ₹19,152 Cr. On an LFL basis, revenue grew 84% YoY.
The quick commerce business reported a segment profit of ₹488 Cr. Its adjusted EBITDA stood at ₹184 Cr, compared with a ₹156 Cr loss in the year-ago quarter.
Blinkit’s net order value (NOV) rose 79.3% YoY and 22.2% QoQ to ₹20,940 Cr. Its adjusted EBITDA margin improved for the sixth consecutive quarter to 0.9% of NOV.
The company added 308 net new stores in Q2 FY27, taking its network to 2,751. Eternal now expects Blinkit to cross 3,500 stores by March 2027, raising its earlier target of 3,000, and reach around 5,000 stores by March 2028.
CFO Akshant Goyal said the accelerated expansion was supported by improving performance in smaller cities and newer categories, with new stores meeting the company’s margin and payback expectations.
Eternal expects Blinkit’s adjusted EBITDA margin to continue improving through the expansion, with profitability gains at mature stores and cities offsetting the initial drag from new outlets. Its mature cities already report adjusted EBITDA margins exceeding 5%, while cities contributing around 70% of NOV are adjusted EBITDA positive.
Although annual NOV growth moderated to around 79% owing to a higher base, management expects growth to pick up as new stores open and scale. Blinkit is tracking ahead of its three-year guidance of 60% NOV compound annual growth, but Eternal said it was too early to revise the target upwards.
Zomato’s Growth Regains Pace
Eternal founder Deepinder Goyal reiterated the company’s long-term expectation of more than 20% annual growth in food delivery, following a recovery over the past two quarters.
Zomato’s food delivery NOV increased 21.5% YoY to ₹11,445 Cr. Operating revenue rose 37% YoY to ₹3,396 Cr.
Adjusted EBITDA increased 25% YoY to ₹627 Cr, although its margin declined marginally to 5.5% of NOV. Average monthly transacting customers grew 16% YoY to 28 Mn.
Goyal attributed part of the previous year’s slowdown to some ordering occasions shifting to quick commerce as the segment expanded. That shift now appears to have stabilised, he said.
Recent growth has been driven by more customers ordering food online and placing orders more frequently. A growing share of new users are ordering food online for the first time, including many outside Zomato’s top eight cities.
“There is still a lot of headroom. Restaurant food is a small part of how India eats. As cities grow, incomes rise and more young people live away from home, we think the food delivery market can keep compounding at 20%+ for many years,” Goyal said.
District Retains Breakeven Timeline
District’s NOV increased 58% YoY and 1.3% QoQ to ₹3,259 Cr. Operating revenue grew 61% YoY to ₹304 Cr, although it declined 4% sequentially.
Its segment loss narrowed to ₹55 Cr from ₹61 Cr in the preceding quarter. Adjusted EBITDA loss remained broadly flat QoQ at ₹64 Cr, while its adjusted EBITDA margin improved to -2% of NOV from -3.1% a year ago. CFO Goyal said District remained on track to achieve adjusted EBITDA breakeven within the four-to-six-quarter timeline outlined in January 2026.
Annual NOV growth is running above 50%, ahead of the 30%+ compound annual growth assumption built into its FY30 plan. Eternal retained its FY30 targets of ₹28,000 Cr in NOV and ₹1,400 Cr in adjusted EBITDA.
However, management flagged AI agents that transact on consumers’ behalf as a potential longer-term disruption to parts of the business. Eternal said it is building physical infrastructure and operations that could help District deliver a differentiated customer experience.
Hyperpure Turns EBITDA Positive
Restaurant supplies business Hyperpure reported operating revenue of ₹1,154 Cr, up 13% YoY. On an LFL basis, revenue increased 22.7%.
Its segment profit stood at ₹19 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA turned positive at ₹10 Cr, as against a loss of ₹5 Cr a year ago.
Hyperpure now serves around 85,000 restaurants, up from 62,000 a year ago.
Management said two-hour deliveries, greater adoption of organised procurement, and services such as kitchen setup were supporting growth. Around 25% of its orders are delivered within two hours.
The others segment, which includes Bistro and Nugget, reported revenue of ₹132 Cr, up 39% from ₹95 Cr in the preceding quarter. Its adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed to ₹91 Cr from ₹94 Cr sequentially.
Shares of Eternal ended Wednesday’s trading session 2.71% lower at ₹311.75.

items.author: Sponsored Post
items.content:
Bitcoin for treasury, stablecoins for payments. That rule fits most of what a business does with either asset, and it fails in two places. It treats Bitcoin’s volatility as a one-way risk, and it treats a stablecoin as a permanent hedge against the naira.
Bitcoin swings in both directions, and the naira has gained about 9% on the dollar over the past 12 months. Below are the four differences that matter, the job each asset fits, and a way to skip the choice.
Bitcoin vs stablecoins: 4 differences that matter to a business
The comparison runs on four dimensions: price stability, accountability, settlement, and risk. Each is easier to judge with numbers than with adjectives.
Bitcoin
Fiat-backed stablecoin (USDT, USDC)
Price
Set by open-market supply and demand
Designed to track $1, can briefly lose the peg
Accountability
No issuer, rules enforced by the network
Named issuer, reserves, redemption terms
Settlement
One chain, a block about every 10 minutes
Minutes, around the clock, several networks
Main risk
Market risk
Counterparty and reserve risk
Price stability, and what “stable” costs
Bitcoin’s price moves a lot. It peaked near $126,000 in October 2025 and traded at about $81,400 on October 20, 2026, a fall of roughly 35%.
The same swing shows up at day scale. A poster on a Nigerian Bitcointalk thread said an employee paid in Bitcoin “could lose 3-5% of its value within a day.” A second poster replied that the payment “could also gain extra 2 to 5%.” Neither figure is measured data, but both describe the mechanism: you don’t know what the payment is worth until you convert it.
A fiat-backed stablecoin such as USDT or USDC is designed to track the US dollar at roughly 1:1. Circle says USDC’s reserves are cash and short-duration US Treasuries. For a business choosing between the two, USDC or USDT is its own decision.
Stable does not mean risk-free. In March 2023, Circle disclosed that $3.3 billion of USDC reserves, about 8% of the total, sat at the failed Silicon Valley Bank, and USDC briefly lost its dollar peg. Stable means lower volatility, not zero risk.
Who’s accountable: no one, or a named company
Bitcoin has no issuer. A decentralized network of nodes and miners enforces its rules through proof of work, which is the mechanism behind the Bitcointalk line that “Bitcoin is trusted.” For stablecoins, the same poster wrote, “that trust is placed [on]the people that introduced it.”
A stablecoin’s soundness depends on its issuer, reserves, reporting, and redemption terms. In the US, the GENIUS Act requires covered issuers to publish a monthly reserve report, examined by a registered accounting firm and certified by the CEO and CFO. That is an attestation, which is narrower than a full audit.
Control is the other difference. On April 23, 2026, Tether froze $344 million in USDT across two addresses, in coordination with OFAC and US law enforcement. OFAC sanctioned the same two wallets the next day as property of Iran’s central bank. Bitcoin has no issuer to flip that switch.
With a stablecoin, a business trusts both the blockchain and the company running it. With Bitcoin, trust sits with the network. These are different dependencies, and neither is lighter.
Settlement speed and what it does to reconciliation
Bitcoin payments can appear almost instantly, but they are final only once included in a block, and blocks arrive about every 10 minutes. Businesses often wait for several confirmations on large payments. Lightning is faster, but most counterparties don’t use it by default.
Stablecoins settle in minutes, including weekends and bank holidays, across several networks. Breet’s crypto payment API, for example, accepts USDT and USDC on TRC20, ERC20, Solana, BNB Smart Chain, Polygon, Arbitrum, and Base.
Tax reconciliation differs too. In Nigeria, individuals pay income tax of 0% to 25% on crypto gains, measured in dollars between purchase and sale. A dollar-pegged stablecoin usually produces little or no dollar gain, and sales of USDT and USDC are exempt from the 1% withholding that applies to Bitcoin and Ether.
A Bitcoin payment can create a taxable gain between the day you receive it and the day you sell. Companies follow separate corporate rules, so confirm treatment with your accountant.
Risk profile: market risk vs counterparty risk, not “risky vs safe”
Bitcoin’s main risk here is market risk. The payment’s value can rise or fall before you sell, and the same move produces either a loss or a gain.
A stablecoin moves the risk instead of removing it. The concerns become counterparty and reserve risk: whether the issuer holds what it claims, how transparent the reserves are, how fast holders can redeem, and whether the issuer can freeze an address.
Stablecoins also come up for paying teams. Payroll brings legal, tax, and labor questions outside this comparison.
When your own currency is the one gaining
A stablecoin protects a business from local-currency depreciation only while the local currency is depreciating. Over the past year, the naira has not been.
USD/NGN traded at ₦1,330.43 on October 20, 2026, and the naira has strengthened 9.23% against the dollar over 12 months. It has been flat for the last month (0.02%). Trading Economics’ model expects ₦1,308.80 in 12 months, so treat further gains as a forecast.
A Bitcointalk poster flagged the mechanism in September, when the rate sat near ₦1,370. Holding 500 USDT loses naira value if the rate falls to ₦1,200, and “the only time that the USDT will be preferable is when the rate of naira is [depreciating].”
Run the numbers on a business that converts ₦13.3 million into $10,000 of USDT at ₦1,330 and holds it. At the forecast ₦1,308.80, the position is worth ₦13,088,000, about ₦212,000 less before fees. If the naira slid back to ₦1,500 instead, the same $10,000 would be worth ₦15 million, ₦1.7 million more. Both outcomes are a bet on direction.
This leaves the case for stablecoins as a payment rail intact. If a customer pays in USDT and the business converts right away, the naira’s direction tomorrow barely matters. The exposure appears when stablecoins sit as a standing treasury position.
Which one, for which job
“Bitcoin or stablecoin?” is four separate decisions.
Paying a supplier abroad: stablecoin, in most cases. If the supplier invoices in dollars, a dollar-pegged stablecoin removes the exchange-rate gap between invoice and payment, and it settles outside banking hours.
Holding treasury float: depends on currency direction. If your currency is depreciating, dollars preserve purchasing power. If it is strengthening, holding dollars costs you, as the ₦212,000 example above shows. Check the direction before defaulting to “hold stablecoins for safety.”
Accepting a customer’s payment: either works. What matters is the next step. If you convert on arrival, the asset the customer sent never becomes treasury.
Wanting long-term Bitcoin exposure: Bitcoin, on purpose. The price of that upside is drawdowns like the 35% fall above, which can land when you need cash. Hold only money you can leave untouched through one.
You don’t have to pick a side to settle the transaction
None of those four jobs requires holding either asset, as long as the payment converts to fiat when it lands. For many businesses, the need is simple: the customer wants to pay in Bitcoin or a stablecoin, and the business wants naira, cedis, or dollars in its account.
Settle automatically, in fiat, the moment either asset lands
With our Crypto and Stablecoin Payment API, a customer’s deposit of Bitcoin, USDT, USDC, or another supported asset is detected on-chain and converted. With auto-settlement on, it is paid to a linked bank account. With it off, it sits as a USD, NGN, or GHS balance until you withdraw. You can set this per wallet address or business-wide.
A webhook fires the moment a transaction is detected on-chain, so your system can fulfill the order without anyone checking a dashboard. The platform has 100+ verified businesses, 3M+ transactions settled programmatically, and a 99.9% uptime SLA.
Access dollars through stablecoins without carrying a treasury position
A business that needs dollars for a supplier does not have to hold USDT or USDC in between. The API gives import and export teams an interface to convert NGN, USD, or GHS to USDT or USDC and back for supplier payments, bypassing dollar scarcity and the parallel market.
For large trades, our OTC desk locks the rate before execution, so the market can’t move against you mid-trade. Settlement lands the same hour in NGN, GHS, USD, USDT, or USDC. Settling in USDT or USDC is the option for businesses that want dollar-denominated float. The desk is built for large volumes, not routine top-ups, and minimum sizes depend on the asset and currency.
Reconcile the same way no matter which asset shows up
If one customer pays in Bitcoin and another in USDT, finance should not need two processes. The API generates a wallet address per customer or per transaction, with bank details and a label attached at creation. Deposits to that address auto-settle to the right account.
That means no manual matching and no guessing which invoice a payment belongs to, whichever asset landed.
Check the direction, then convert
Bitcoin carries market risk. A stablecoin carries issuer and reserve risk, plus currency-direction risk when you hold it against a strengthening naira. Neither label, “risky” or “safe,” tells you what to do with a payment.
Start with this today: pull your last 90 days of crypto payments. For each one, note how long it sat before conversion and what the rate did in that window. If the gap is days and the rate moved against you, turn on auto-settlement.
Two limits apply. We convert crypto and don’t custody it, so Bitcoin you want to hold for years belongs in your own wallet or with a custodian. And Breet is not a payroll platform.

Nigerian startups Solarcorp, Bravoo and Zendtrax have been selected for the 14th cohort of MARL’s global accelerator programme, with each receiving US$50,000 in funding.
MARL is a US-based early-stage venture capital firm that runs an accelerator programme for tech startups around the world. Alongside funds, it gives founders hands-on help with product development, business strategy and fundraising, and connects them with its network of mentors and investors.
Three Nigerian startups have been selected for the 14th cohort. They are Solarcorp, a climate-tech company replacing diesel generators in malls and commercial clusters with shared solar-and-storage systems; Bravoo, which is building a consumer platform built around rewards and gamified experiences; and Zendtrax, which offers enterprise software for procurement, inventory and supply-chain management.
“At MARL, we believe great technology companies can emerge from anywhere. The selection of Solarcorp, Bravoo and Zendtrax into our 14th global cohort reflects the quality of innovation we’re seeing from African founders,” said Prakash Goswami, managing partner at MARL.
MARL’s vohort 14 Demo Day takes place on November 12.

items.author: Press Release
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Zong has won four prestigious awards in the Telecommunication category at the Asian Innovation Excellence Awards 2026, held in Singapore on 20th Oct. The recognition underscores Zong’s position as Pakistan’s Leading Technology Services Enterprise and its ability to translate advanced technologies, artificial intelligence (AI), and home-grown engineering expertise into meaningful outcomes for customers, business partners, and Pakistan’s digital ecosystem. Across brand, network, consumer services, and business operations, Zong continues to demonstrate how innovation can strengthen customer experience, create differentiated value, and enable a more intelligent and connected digital future.
Zong won the Pakistan Brand Innovation of the Year award for its AI-powered 5G launch campaign, “AIsa Hai Future”. Blending artificial and augmented intelligence with Pakistani creativity, the campaign reimagined the nation’s digital future through a distinctive, customer-focused brand narrative. Challenging conventional telecom advertising, it positioned AI as both the creative medium and the central message, bringing the promise of future-ready technology closer to consumers. The campaign helped narrow the brand equity gap, achieve parity in unaided 5G brand association, and strengthen brand differentiation through enhanced uniqueness and memorability.
Extending this innovation from brand promise to network performance, Zong received Pakistan Technology Innovation of the Year for its AI-driven Self-Intelligent Radio Access Network (RAN) Optimization platform, reiterating the advancement toward autonomous, AI-enabled network operations. Developed in-house, the platform autonomously detects network congestion, identifies and implements corrective actions, and verifies outcomes. By enabling faster issue resolution and intelligent network optimization, the solution enhances network responsiveness and performance, particularly during periods of high demand, supporting delivering a more consistent and reliable customer experience.
Translating customer needs into practical service innovation, Zong won Pakistan Consumer Service Innovation of the Year award for its “My5 – Family Sharing Package.” Designed around the evolving connectivity needs of households, My5 offers a flexible family connectivity solution complemented by value added benefits, including embedded insurance coverage, lifestyle perks and digital streaming access. By bringing connectivity and lifestyle benefits together in one offering, the package provides families with greater flexibility, convenience, and value, including an alternative to traditional home broadband services. The award recognizes Zong’s customer-first approach to developing relevant, accessible, and future-ready solutions that address everyday needs and enrich connected living.
Complementing these customer-facing innovations, DI-CAPE, Zong’s digital commission governance engine, won Pakistan Financial Innovation of the Year. Through intelligent automation, the platform strengthen business governance, improves process efficiency and transparency, and enhances partner enablement across Zong’s distribution ecosystem. This recognition highlights how digital innovation can create value beyond the customer interface by enabling more efficient, transparent, and reliable business processes for partners.
Commenting on this international recognition, Zong’s Head of Strategy & Company Spokesperson, Nabila Yazdani said:
“Winning four prestigious honors at the Asian Innovation Excellence Awards 2026 validates Zong’s technology leadership and commitment to translating 5G, AI, and home-grown digital innovation into meaningful impact. From AI-driven network intelligence and customer-centric connectivity to transparent business processes and a distinctive 5G brand promise, we are turning innovation into tangible value for customers, partners, and society. These wins reflect our strategic focus on delivering an ultimate customer experience while advancing Pakistan’s digital transformation toward a more connected and future-ready digital ecosystem.”
Aligned with its “Aisa Hai Future” brand promise, Zong continues to advance its strategic priorities of Ultimate Customer Experience, Diversified Products & Services Portfolio, and AI Enablement. Through sustained investment in 5G, AI, digital platforms, and in-house technical capabilities, the company is translating technology leadership into smarter networks, more efficient operations, and innovative digital experiences that deliver meaningful value to customers and partners while contributing to a more connected, inclusive, and future-ready Digital Pakistan.

items.author: Rizwana Omer
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
BYD Pakistan will lean on imported cars when it begins selling and plans to build up domestic production over time. The Chinese electric vehicle maker’s long-term aim, according to partner Hub Power Company Limited (HUBCO), is a local share of 80 percent in vehicle production.
The two statements describe a long road. Imports come first, localisation later, and the second step is not guaranteed.
What HUBCO says
HUBCO, BYD’s partner in its Pakistan business plan, says the goal is to reduce reliance on imports, bring down production costs and strengthen the domestic side of the auto industry.
It also sees spill-over effects. Higher local production could create investment openings in parts manufacturing, supply chains and related industrial sectors.
The target comes with conditions. HUBCO says progress will be phased and will depend on investment, production capacity and the industrial and policy environment.
Imports have a job in the meantime. Continued sales of imported vehicles in the early stage, HUBCO says, will help BYD stay available to buyers and move its business expansion forward.
Where BYD already stands
BYD is not starting from zero. Its Pakistan business is nearing local production at a $150 million assembly plant in Gharo, Sindh, which is expected to assemble about 25,000 vehicles a year once operational. The plant is undergoing equipment installation and commissioning.
BYD Pakistan also received its largest shipment so far, more than 2,000 vehicles, on a roll-on/roll-off vessel. Imported vehicles are meant to support deliveries and dealer stock until local production starts.
On infrastructure, HUBCO Green Private Limited and BYD Pakistan have set up 19 public DC fast-charging stations along a 1,300-kilometre corridor between Karachi and Peshawar.
Stage
What has been reported
Now
Imported vehicles continue to be sold.
Next
Gharo plant, 25,000 vehicles a year at full capacity
Later
80 percent local share in production (HUBCO target, conditional)
Why localisation matters for price
Assembly at home changes the cost equation. Fully imported vehicles face relatively high import duties, so local assembly gives a cost advantage and may improve affordability.
That is also why 80 percent is a bigger commitment than assembly alone. Duties apply to the car as a whole, but a high local share requires batteries, motors and components to be made or sourced in Pakistan, which takes much more investment than putting vehicles together from kits.
How far the gap is
In July 2025, a company executive said the plant would begin by assembling imported parts, with some non-electric components produced locally. A plant that starts this way sits well below 80 percent.
HUBCO’s statement gives no year for reaching the target, no figures for the local share at the start and no investment amount tied to it. Those are the numbers that would show how steep the climb is.
The Pakistan angle
The statement lands as the government talks up EV adoption. Haroon Akhtar Khan, Advisor to the Prime Minister for Industries and Production, said on October 13 that Pakistan aims for a 30 percent EV share by 2030 and that the forthcoming Auto Policy would give electric vehicles particular weight.
The policy’s content will matter to BYD. HUBCO ties its localisation goal to industrial and policy conditions, so incentives, duty structure and support for suppliers could decide whether 80 percent is reachable.
Bottom Line
Starting with imports is a sensible way to test demand while a plant comes online. The real test is whether Pakistani suppliers can meet the quality and volume a global EV maker requires.
Parts makers need orders large enough to justify new lines, and orders depend on vehicle volumes that, for now, remain modest. That circular problem has limited localisation in Pakistan’s car industry before.
The 80 percent figure is best read as an aspiration with conditions, not a commitment with a date. A published timetable, interim local-content milestones and named supplier agreements would turn it into something readers can measure.

items.author: Rizwana Omer
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
A trip to a NADRA office has long meant arriving early and joining a queue. The National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) now wants citizens to book a NADRA appointment through the Pak ID mobile app before they leave home.
The authority has urged people to use the facility to choose a registration centre and a time that suits them. Once the slot is booked, they can reach the centre shortly before it and get the service they need without waiting in a long line, NADRA says.
How the booking works
Citizens select their preferred NADRA registration centre in the Pak ID app, then pick an appointment time. According to NADRA, they should arrive a little ahead of that time and observe the schedule.
Earlier reporting described the steps as downloading or updating the app, logging in, then choosing a centre and time slot. The Pak ID app was already in use for online CNIC applications and biometric login, so most users will not need a new application.
A rollout that started small
The idea is not new. NADRA first announced it in July 2025, when the feature was slated for 43 designated registration centres in a first phase. Those included mega centres in Islamabad, Rawalpindi, Karachi, Lahore, Faisalabad, Peshawar and Quetta.
More recently, NADRA released an updated version of the app that covers online complaints and digital identity services alongside appointments. The announcement this week reads as a push to get citizens to use what already exists.
Why queues are the target
Crowded registration centres are a daily problem for people applying for or renewing identity documents. Long waits cost a working day, particularly for those travelling from outside a city.
NADRA says the facility is meant to make services easier to reach, save time and reduce crowding. An appointment system helps because it spreads demand through the day instead of concentrating it at opening time.
Earlier NADRA messaging also asked people to arrive about ten minutes early. That guidance came with the aim of improving crowd management.
What the statement leaves open
The announcement does not say what happens to people who arrive without an appointment. It does not report how many bookings have been made, how many slots a centre releases per day, or whether waiting times have fallen at centres already using the system.
Access is another question. Booking requires a smartphone, a working internet connection and some comfort with apps. Many of the people who queue longest at NADRA offices may be those least likely to have all three.
Bottom Line
An appointment system only reduces queues if two things hold: enough slots, and a clear rule for people without bookings. If slots fill within hours, the line moves from the pavement to the app. If walk-ins are still served first come, first served, the benefit for those who booked disappears.
For now, the advice is practical: update the app, check that your centre offers bookings, and arrive on time.

items.author: Usama Anjum
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Supreme Court of Pakistan has quashed a Rs. 4.79 billion tax demand against the Universal Service Fund (USF), ruling that payments made to telecom operators for expanding connectivity in underserved areas are not subject to tax deduction under Section 153(2)(b) of the Income Tax Ordinance.
The decision marks a significant legal victory for USF, which plays a key role in extending broadband and telecommunication services to remote and underserved regions of Pakistan.
According to official USF sources, the Fund presented detailed facts, supporting evidence, and legal arguments during the proceedings to establish its position regarding the tax treatment of payments made to telecom companies.
After considering the case, the Supreme Court ruled in favour of USF and annulled the tax order issued by the revenue authorities.
The judgment provides clarity on the application of the relevant tax provision to USF payments made to telecom operators for connectivity projects in underserved areas.
What Does the Supreme Court’s Decision Mean for Digital Connectivity?
The ruling is particularly important for USF’s ongoing efforts to improve telecom infrastructure in areas where commercial operators may find network deployment financially challenging.
USF supports projects aimed at extending mobile coverage, broadband connectivity, and digital infrastructure to communities that remain outside reliable telecommunication networks.
With the Rs. 4.79 billion tax demand set aside, the Fund intends to focus on accelerating network deployment activities across unserved and underserved regions.
According to USF sources, the judgment represents an important milestone toward achieving the government’s Digital Pakistan and Digital Nation objectives.
The Fund reiterated its commitment to improving access to high-speed broadband and telecom services in remote parts of the country, where connectivity remains essential for education, business opportunities, and access to digital services.
USF also acknowledged the support of the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication (MoITT) and the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) throughout the legal proceedings.
The decision removes a significant tax dispute for USF and could provide greater certainty for its connectivity initiatives. However, the pace of future network expansion will continue to depend on project approvals, available funding, and implementation by telecom operators.

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Her Startup, an accelerator for women-led technology startups in Africa, has opened applications for the second cohort of its programme.
The Her Startup initiative, a partnership between the KSH Foundation, Tomorrow Foundation and EHA Impact Ventures, will select 10 early-stage women founders and help them build investment-ready tech businesses. The training component will be delivered by Founder Institute, which bills itself as the world’s largest pre-seed startup accelerator.
Women-founded startups continue to struggle for funding in Africa. According to Disrupt Africa’s latest Diversity Dividend report, only 9.6 per cent of ventures funded in 2025 were led by a female CEO.
Her Startup was set up to tackle that gap by giving women entrepreneurs training, capital and networks through a single, integrated programme.
Selected founders will take part in a 12-week intensive training programme with Founder Institute, with fees covered by Her Startup, and will receive a monthly stipend so they can commit to the programme full-time.
They will also get the chance to pitch to Her Startup’s investment committee for funding through convertible revenue-based financing, as well as 12 months of sector-matched mentoring and access to Founder Institute’s global network.
The programme is open to women founders or CEOs aged between 18 and 35 who run a tech-enabled business that has been operating for at least six months and generates at least US$500 in monthly gross revenue. Founders from Francophone Africa are strongly encouraged to apply for the 2026/2027 cohort.
The second cohort follows a 2024/2025 pilot that drew more than 200 applications from 18 African countries. Ten founders were selected for training, and three ventures won funding at the programme’s Pitch Day in Lagos in April 2025. Alumni have since gone on to win grants and awards and attract investor interest.
One of them is Nigerian healthtech startup Dynalimb Technologies, which makes affordable 3D-printed prosthetics.
“Since Her Startup, we’ve seen a steady rise in customer adoption and product sales, as more amputees experience the comfort and mobility that Dynalimb’s affordable 3D-printed prosthetics provide,” said Blessing Aniefiok, the startup’s COO.
Her Startup’s funding model sets it apart, with repayments on its convertible, revenue-based financing linked to each company’s revenue.
“It’s not enough to just give these companies financing. It’s about giving them financing that will truly help them succeed. We chose a convertible, revenue-based loan, an innovative financing mechanism that is just starting to enter the market. It is incredibly founder-friendly, and it will help the women in this programme succeed,” said Evelyn Castle, co-founder of Her Startup and co-founder of EHA Impact Ventures.
Applications are open here until October 26.

items.author: Usama Anjum
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
vivo appears to be preparing another major addition to its premium smartphone lineup, with fresh leaks revealing key specifications of the upcoming vivo X500 Ultra. The device is tipped to feature a next-generation Snapdragon processor, a 144Hz AMOLED display, and an ambitious camera setup.
While the company has not officially announced the device, reports suggest that the vivo X500 Ultra could debut in March or April 2027. For Pakistani consumers, the bigger question is whether this premium flagship will reach the local market and how much it might cost.
The latest information, attributed to Chinese tipster Digital Chat Station, suggests that the handset could feature Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset. The processor is reportedly based on a 2nm process, with leaks pointing to CPU clock speeds of up to 5.01GHz and an Adreno 850 GPU.
If these specifications prove accurate, the device could deliver substantial performance improvements for demanding applications, gaming, and AI-powered features. However, its configuration and performance have not been officially confirmed.
On the front, the vivo X500 Ultra is tipped to feature a large 6.85-inch flat AMOLED display supplied by BOE. The panel could offer 2K resolution and a 144 Hz refresh rate, slim bezels, and an ultrasonic fingerprint sensor.
Triple 200MP Cameras and a Larger Battery Expected
Photography could remain the biggest selling point of the upcoming Ultra model. Earlier leaks have suggested a triple-camera configuration featuring 200MP sensors for the primary, periscope telephoto, and ultrawide cameras.
Such a setup would represent a significant hardware upgrade, particularly for ultrawide photography. However, these camera details remain speculative, and there is no confirmation that all three 200MP sensors will appear in the final commercial device.
Battery capacity could also increase to around 7,000mAh, according to reports. Fast charging is expected, although the company has not confirmed charging specifications. The previous X300 Ultra’s reported 100W charging is a reference point, not a guarantee for the successor.
vivo X500 Ultra Expected Price and Release Timeline in Pakistan
The vivo X500 Ultra is currently tipped for an international debut around March or April 2027, although its official release schedule and market availability remain uncertain.
Preliminary unofficial market listings indicate an expected Pakistan price of approximately Rs. 364,999 for a possible 12GB RAM and 256GB storage version. Considering the Ultra series’ premium positioning, an indicative editorial estimate of Rs. 350,000 to Rs. 420,000 could be plausible if the model officially launches in Pakistan.
These are unofficial estimates, not announced prices. Final pricing would depend on variants, currency movements, applicable taxes, and vivo’s local distribution strategy.
Availability outside China is also uncertain. Pakistani buyers should treat the pricing and launch window cautiously until vivo makes an official announcement.
If the reported specifications materialize, the vivo X500 Ultra could become a notable camera-focused Android flagship in 2027. Its appeal will depend on real-world camera performance, software, pricing, and local availability.
