items.author: Reuters
items.content:
Over the past couple of weeks, a cybersecurity researcher watched as a Chinese-speaking hacker broke into websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including farm equipment maker Deere, home appliance ​company SharkNinja and engine manufacturer Cummins.
Yet the hacker did almost none of the work.
The cybercriminal instead outsourced the hacking spree almost entirely to artificial intelligence, tasking AI agents ‌with spending hours autonomously probing and breaking into targeted sites, according to Snorre Fagerland, principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity company NorForge.
Read: OpenAI agents obscured hacking activity targeting government websites: security firm
In a report provided to Reuters ahead of publication on Monday, Fagerland said the hacker was one of several he discovered while scanning the web for inadvertently exposed instances of Cairn, an open-source AI problem-solving platform popular with hackers. Beginning around October 2, Fagerland said he found about two dozen instances of Cairn being used for malicious activity, which allowed him ​to quietly peer over the cybercriminals' shoulders as they set their AI tools loose on the world.
Fagerland's report on the Chinese-speaking hacker did not name the victims, but Reuters was able ​to establish the victims' identities by independently reviewing the hacker's Cairn activity.
At a time of rising anxiety over the power of autonomous AI tools, Fagerland said ⁠his find was real-life evidence that commercially available AI agents could pull off complex intrusions from start to finish without human intervention, a dramatic boost to the power of a single malicious actor.
"It's ​a new world now," said Fagerland.
Reuters could not ascertain the degree to which the breaches resulted in unauthorised extraction of data.
Deere told Reuters it had taken "necessary remediation actions" following the incident and had "no indication that ​sensitive information was accessed." SharkNinja said the hack had hit a standalone site carrying only product support information and that the threat had been contained. Cummins said it was "investigating the report of a potential cyber-attack on a website operated by one of our third-party vendors."
Read More: Rogue AI agents broke into Indian firms' live systems, government says
Two smaller businesses also acknowledged being compromised. Other victims listed in the Cairn data did not return messages.
Few instructions, many hacks
One of the hackers that Fagerland observed stole a trove of credit card data. Another ​tried to get AI agents to rob a cryptocurrency exchange. The Chinese-speaking hacker was the most prolific. Beginning on September 25, they set their AI army loose against US, Canadian, Australian and Japanese ​e-commerce websites.
Their instructions were terse, sketching out their preferred intrusion tactics in fewer than 100 Chinese characters. As of late last week, their agents had attempted to break into more than 1,200 sites. Successful intrusions typically took around ‌23 hours ⁠of poking and prodding for vulnerabilities. Fagerland estimated that the campaign, which appeared to be using a mixture of China's DeepSeek and Anthropic's Claude Code, had chewed up roughly $5,000 worth of tokens, or about $50 per successful hack.
Fagerland — who has worked in cybersecurity for nearly three decades — said he was impressed by some of the techniques the agents used to compromise their victims. In one case, after failing to find any weaknesses in a big company's public-facing application, the AI agents pored through digital records to find associated infrastructure, located a public-facing control panel, discovered a subtle weakness in the way it processed data, and after ​hours of trial and error, reported leveraging it ​to trick the server into executing malicious commands.
"It's ⁠not straightforward to come up with solutions like that," Fagerland said. "It's not script kiddie stuff."
Cairn's author, whose social media handle is "le1xia0", acknowledged receipt of a Reuters message but did not immediately answer a list of questions. In a recent post on X, they said their platform was "an innovative type of multi-agent architecture and was ​not designed for hacking attacks. If it is used to carry out harmful hacking attacks, that is not my intention."
No supervision needed
The ability of ​agentic AI systems to autonomously ⁠discover vulnerabilities, conduct intrusions, and steal data is a source of increasing anxiety around the world. Rogue agents inadvertently unleashed by major AI companies have hacked their way out of computer labs, broken into government websites, and engaged in unsanctioned social engineering attempts. South Korea and Japan have in recent weeks been buffeted by a series of well-publicised hacks attributed to AI-using cybercriminals.
AI agents are increasingly becoming staples of the cybercriminal underground. In August, the Israeli firm ⁠Gambit Security found ​that Russian-speaking extortionists had leveraged SpaceX's Cursor AI tool to break into seven organisations. In September, Gambit documented an AI agent-driven spree that resulted in breaches at 25 companies and the theft of at least 600,000 credit card records. Last week, the cyber intelligence company Bitsight said that discussions about how to use autonomous agents were surging across cybercriminal forums.
Fagerland said he had previously assumed ​hacker-agents would need at least some supervision. He said it was now obvious that the technology had moved past that.
"The development in this field is astounding," he said.

Hiring thousands of frontline workers (employees who directly provide goods and services to communities) across multiple cities is a coordination-heavy cumbersome task for HR managers. Recruiters have to call prospective employees, follow up on applications, schedule interviews and keep workers informed through onboarding and training.
When hiring volumes spike during festive seasons or business expansion, these tasks can quickly become more difficult to solve manually. Bengaluru-based conversational AI startup Hunar.AI is building AI agents to automate these HR workflows.
The startup today announced the raise of ₹40 Cr ($4.2 Mn) in its Series A funding round led by Blume Ventures. Other investors like Hyderabad Angels Fund, Together Fund, Seedstars, AVNM Ventures, PhysicsWallah cofounders Prateek Maheshwari and Alakh Pandey, and MediaMint cofounder Aditya Vuchi also participated in the round.
Founded in 2022 by Krishna Khandelwal and Shantanu Bhattacharyya, Hunar.AI automates frontline workforce management via its conversational AI agents. These agents help ease various frontline workforce management issues — including hiring, onboarding, training and retention.
It is targeting businesses that need to recruit and manage large numbers of workers, often across several locations and regional languages.
The startup offers voice AI capabilities in more than 20 languages, including Tamil, Telugu and Kannada. This allows enterprises to communicate with workers in their preferred languages while automating workflows that would otherwise require repeated calls and manual follow-ups.
The startup intends to use the fresh capital to strengthen its AI infrastructure, develop its products and bolster its go-to-market strategy.
“Frontline workforce management is one of the largest yet most underserved opportunities in enterprise AI. Solving it requires more than applying general-purpose models to existing processes. It demands a deep understanding of industry workflows, multilingual capabilities and technology that can reliably execute tasks at scale,” said cofounder and CEO Krishna Khandelwal.
The startup claims its AI agents handled more than 1.5 Cr conversations till September 2026, with volumes doubling quarter-on-quarter. Its customers include Swiggy, Zepto, Aditya Birla Capital, Bajaj Finserv, Croma, Dr Lal PathLabs, 1mg and Starbucks.
AI Targets India’s Growing Frontline Workforce
The startup is targeting a workforce segment that spans quick commerce, ecommerce, logistics, mobility, retail and financial services. These businesses often need to recruit workers quickly across multiple cities, while keeping communication and onboarding processes running at scale.
The market size is also expanding. According to NITI Aayog projections, India’s gig workforce is expected to grow from approximately 1 Cr workers in FY25 to 2.35 Cr by 2029-30.
While more workforce helps in finding the right candidates, keeping applicants engaged, coordinating onboarding and ensuring workers receive the necessary information requires manual effort. This is more relevant when recruitment is spread across regions with different languages.
The startup’s approach is to automate these interactions through conversational agents designed around specific enterprise workflows, rather than offer a general-purpose chatbot. Its ability to handle regional languages and integrate into existing workforce processes will be central to how effectively it can serve large employers.
The latest funding will help the startup build out that technology and expand its reach among enterprises.

items.author: Our Correspondent
items.content:
Sindh Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon on Monday stated that the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) was the “last party” to support governor’s rule and the imposition of an emergency in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P), further adding that the party had advocated political dialogue and engagement as the first course of action.
The emergency and governor’s rule were declared on October 11 after negotiations between the government and opposition failed, culminating in a PTI long march towards Islamabad that began on October 4.
“PPP was the last party that was in favour of the governor’s rule. We tried to engage them, not once but ten times, and PPP told the federal government that it wanted to resolve issues through political dialogue, but after multiple attempts, if the K-P chief minister himself had an inclination towards the Taliban and terrorists and was not willing to agree, then the government could not let the people of K-P be left on their own at the mercy of the terrorists”.
 
Memon made these remarks during a visit to the Green Line BRT Operations Command and Control Centre, where he received a briefing on the system’s operations, integration with other transport projects, ridership and overall performance.
Transport Secretary Asad Zamin, TransKarachi CEO Zubair Channa, Yellow Line BRT Project Director Kamal Dayo and Sindh Mass Transit Authority Managing Director Behzad Memon accompanied him.
Memon said it was important to connect the Green Line with other BRT projects. The Red and Yellow lines were also being linked, with plans to connect the Orange Line to the Green Line, the Green Line to the Red Line, and the Yellow Line to the Red Line. The links would make it easier for passengers to transfer between services and reach their destinations.
Read: BRT Red Line picks up steam
He added that work was continuing on sections of the Yellow Line, including bridges and other construction, further saying that the Sindh government aimed to complete the projects as soon as possible and establish effective connections between them, creating an integrated and modern transport network in the metropolis.
Memon said that Sindh had made significant progress in public transport over the past four to five years, including electric scooters, Pakistan’s first electric buses and Pink Buses for women.
He said the Green Line had been built before Sindh assumed responsibility for it, but it had not included buses reserved for women. Women faced difficulties when using public transport, he said, and better travel facilities could encourage them to travel and help parents feel satisfied about sending their daughters out for education and work. He said the Sindh government had taken several steps to empower women and improve their access to transport.
Asked about Green Line ridership, Memon said that when the service was under the federal government, it carried around 50,000 passengers a day, further noting that since Sindh took over the transport department had worked to improve its performance and the service now carried around 90,000 passengers daily.
The senior minister said the Sindh government aimed to begin road construction in every district across the province within the next six to eight months to improve travel facilities.
Read More: University Road mixed lane to open soon: Sharjeel
Memon said that in Sindh, the government had worked with the Rangers and other law-enforcement agencies to tackle terrorism in Karachi. When conditions worsened in the riverine areas, the government and relevant agencies also conducted operations against bandits. He said kidnapping-for-ransom incidents in Sindh had since declined significantly.
Recalling Karachi’s past, the senior minister said the city had once seen 30 to 40 people killed each day, frequent strikes, closures of businesses and educational institutions, and industries relocating elsewhere. Memon said cooperation between the government and the establishment had helped restore peace, adding that Karachi no longer faced daily strikes on the same scale, and terrorist incidents had declined.
Memon recalled the bombing at the October 18, 2007 homecoming rally for former prime minister Benazir Bhutto, in which hundreds of PPP supporters were killed or injured, and her assassination in Rawalpindi later that year. He said the party’s position against terrorism had always been clear.
He said Benazir had pledged in her final speeches that Pakistan’s flag would again fly in Swat, where Taliban and extremist groups had expanded their influence.
Memon reiterated that the PPP would not remain silent when citizens were suffering from terrorism, innocent people were being killed, and businesses were operating in fear.
He described the recent visit to China as successful and said the chief minister would brief the provincial cabinet on it, further stating that the visit aimed to identify opportunities to benefit Pakistan, particularly Sindh and its people.
Memon said the Sindh government was working democratically across sectors, including health, education, transport, irrigation and local government, to improve people’s lives.

items.author: Inc42 Staff
items.content:
A high click rate cannot tell a fintech company whether a user will complete the KYC. Similarly, downloading an app does not promise a purchase. Yet these remain the metrics that digital advertising has traditionally been built around.
For brands, the real challenge is understanding whether a click or app download will actually translate into a business outcome. As advertisers demand clearer links between media spending and business outcomes, adtech is moving towards systems that can predict intent, learn from downstream behaviour and optimise for what happens beyond the click or install.
This is the shift Mobavenue is targeting. The company processes more than 1.25 Bn data signals a day and has built its technology stack around real-time decisioning and continuous feedback from campaign outcomes. In FY26, it delivered 42.72 Mn outcomes, giving its models a growing base of data to learn from.
At the centre of this is Mobavenue’s Neural Engine, which connects signals, intent and outcomes. Rather than treating a bid, click or install as the endpoint, the system is designed to learn from what happens after that decision and use those outcomes to inform future audience, bidding and budget decisions.
For Tejas Rathod, founder and CTO of Mobavenue, this marks a broader shift in advertising — from AI as an optimisation tool to AI as a decisioning layer across the marketing lifecycle.
In a conversation with Inc42, Rathod explains the technology behind Mobavenue’s platform, how the company approaches privacy and invalid traffic, and why it is building towards an advertising ecosystem that connects awareness, acquisition and activation.
Here are the edited excerpts…
Inc42: What has been the biggest shift in the Digital advertising industry, and what is driving it?
Tejas Rathod: The biggest shift is the movement from automation towards predictive intelligence and AI autonomy. Earlier, technology helped advertisers execute decisions faster. Today, AI is increasingly being used to anticipate intent, learn from outcomes and make decisions dynamically.
This is being driven by the growing complexity of digital ecosystems, the volume of signals available and the pressure to deliver measurable business outcomes. The next phase is moving from AI as an optimisation tool to AI as an increasingly autonomous decision-making layer.
Inc42: With privacy regulations tightening and invalid traffic remaining a challenge, how has Mobavenue prepared its tech to maintain targeting accuracy and campaign efficiency?
Tejas Rathod: Privacy has been a foundational consideration in how we have built our tech. Our platforms operate within the requirements of applicable privacy frameworks and regulations across the markets we serve, including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) and India’s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) framework. We also use privacy-conscious approaches to identity, including ID masking and hashing, to derive intelligence without unnecessarily exposing identifiable information.
Our models rely on aggregated, consented signals and behavioural patterns. This lets the system understand user intent and quality while maintaining data safeguards. The objective is to make privacy and targeting intelligence work together, rather than treating them as competing priorities.
Invalid traffic needs to be addressed at multiple points in the advertising lifecycle. Filtering it only after a campaign has run can still result in wasted spend. We therefore use internal invalid traffic detection capabilities at both the pre-bid and post-bid stages.
At the pre-bid stage, the system evaluates available signals and supply characteristics before deciding whether to participate in an auction. This helps reduce exposure to questionable inventory. Post-bid, we analyse delivery and campaign signals to identify patterns that may indicate invalid activity and use these learnings to improve subsequent optimisation.
Fraud detection is also part of our broader machine learning capabilities, alongside audience segmentation, bid optimisation and real-time learning. The objective is to protect both media efficiency and the quality of outcomes.
Inc42: What problem do advertisers still struggle with, and how has Mobavenue built its platform to solve it differently? When did you realise you needed to build more tech in-house?
Tejas Rathod: The fundamental problem advertisers face is not simply acquiring users, but acquiring the right users at the right customer acquisition cost, with a clear path to business value.
We realised early that existing solutions could help us execute media, but they did not give us the level of control and intelligence required to consistently optimise towards the right customer acquisition cost (CAC). That led us to build our tech stack in-house, layer by layer.
Our AI systems analyse billions of signals to identify users with a higher likelihood of conversion, while enabling budgets to be dynamically allocated based on those signals. The objective is not to optimise for media metrics in isolation, but to continuously improve the efficiency and quality of user acquisition. That shift, from media execution to technology-driven outcome optimisation, has been central to how we have built Mobavenue.
Inc42: As brands shift from clicks and installs to outcome-based ROI, how does your engineering team build predictability into the platform? What tech decisions have helped Mobavenue operate at the scale of 1.25 Bn data signals a day?
Tejas Rathod: Predictability starts with the quality and depth of the signals available to the system. Our engineering stack looks at large volumes of consented data signals and combines them with audience segments, behavioural patterns and relevant user attributes to understand intent.
The objective is not simply to identify a user who may click or install, but to predict the probability of completing the business outcome that the advertiser values.
For example, in a fintech journey, that could extend beyond an app install to KYC completion, investment or loan conversion. Our Neural Network continuously feeds outcomes back into the system, allowing models to learn which signals correlate with quality conversions and improve subsequent decisions.
Adtech is a fast-moving environment where the value of a decision can change within milliseconds, while expectations around accuracy and outcomes continue to increase. So, from the beginning, we made a few deliberate technology choices: real-time decisioning, proprietary intelligence and a common data layer rather than multiple disconnected systems.
The other important decision was to build a closed feedback loop into the platform. Every campaign outcome generates a new learning signal that feeds back into our models, helping improve subsequent decisions around audiences, bidding and budget allocation.
In FY26, we delivered 42.72 Mn outcomes, and this scale of execution gives our models a continually expanding base of learning. For us, maintaining performance at scale means combining speed with continuous learning, so that every decision becomes more informed by the outcomes that came before it.
Inc42: Mobavenue recently formalised its focus on AI infrastructure. How does its Neural Engine think differently from traditional programmatic advertising, and what led you to build an intelligence layer across the marketing lifecycle?
Tejas Rathod: Traditional programmatic advertising is largely designed to make the best decision for the immediate media event, such as whether to bid, how much to bid, or which audience to target. Our Neural Engine is designed to learn from what happens after that decision. We have moved our core decisioning from rule-based and traditional ML systems to a unified neural network architecture built around three stages: process signals, predict intent and produce outcomes.
It continuously processes signals, predicts intent and evaluates downstream outcomes, creating a closed feedback loop where every outcome becomes a new signal for the next decision. So, intelligence does not simply optimise a campaign; it continuously learns what drives quality outcomes and adapts its decisions accordingly.
The adtech ecosystem has become good at automating individual parts of advertising, but intelligence is still fragmented across the marketing lifecycle. Planning, audience selection, campaign execution, creative and reporting often sit across different systems, which means marketers still have to connect the dots and move decisions from one stage to another.
We saw that the next opportunity was not simply to automate another task, but to create an intelligence layer that could continuously connect signals, decisions and outcomes. That thinking led to the Mobavenue Neural Engine. It brings together our proprietary advertising intelligence, first-party platform intelligence and real-time business context to make recommendations that become more relevant as the system learns.
The larger shift is from AI as an optimisation tool to AI as a decisioning layer across awareness, acquisition and activation. Our Neural Engine is designed to connect planning, execution, optimisation and reporting, while keeping the marketer in control. For us, the future is not just about making advertising faster. It is about making the entire marketing lifecycle more intelligent, connected and outcome-driven.
Inc42: The company closed FY26 with ₹218 Cr+ in revenue and roughly a 20.8% EBITDA margin. How closely do you tie your product roadmap to these metrics, and which products drove the growth?
Tejas Rathod: For us, the product roadmap is primarily driven by the opportunity we see in the market. Financial performance is an important validation, but we do not build products simply around a revenue or EBITDA target. We look at where consumer behaviour, technology and advertiser demand are moving, and then build around those opportunities.
FY26 is a good example of this approach. Our existing platforms, particularly PrsmX and the Neural Engine across all products, were significant contributors to our revenue momentum during the year. These products continued to evolve as we saw greater demand for AI-driven optimisation and outcome-based advertising.
PiiX is the next example of that product philosophy. We identified a significant opportunity in the Apple Search Ads ecosystem and launched PiiX in Q1 FY27 as a dedicated intelligence platform for that high-intent environment. So, the roadmap is driven by market opportunity, while revenue and profitability validate whether we are creating meaningful value from those investments.
Inc42: Over 73% of your revenue now comes directly from brands. What did you change about the platform and reporting to make enterprise clients comfortable managing campaigns directly?
Tejas Rathod: Direct advertiser relationships required us to rethink the platform experience end to end. We undertook a significant overhaul of the interface, underlying infrastructure and reporting capabilities to make the system more robust, intuitive and user-friendly for enterprise teams.
We also expanded the platform’s functionality across campaign planning, execution, creative intelligence and measurement. A key focus was making reporting easier to understand while providing the level of granularity that enterprise advertisers need to evaluate performance, understand where their budgets are being deployed and make informed decisions.
The objective was to create greater transparency without adding unnecessary complexity. And the larger goal is to make sophisticated technology accessible without requiring the user to deal with the complexity underneath it.
Inc42: How has Mobavenue grown over the past year? Can you share any numbers around campaign performance, advertiser ROI or CAC that highlight the platform’s impact?
Tejas Rathod: Over the past year, our growth has been closely tied to how effectively our technology can improve measurable outcomes for clients. We operate on an outcome-as-a-service model, which means we grow when our clients grow. Revenue per outcome (RPO) is an important business metric for us because it reflects the value generated from every measurable outcome.
Our RPO increased from ₹44.99 in Q1 FY26 to ₹48.44 in Q4 FY26, while quarterly outcomes grew from 9 Mn to 12.61 Mn.
At the campaign level, this translates into measurable performance. Snabbit achieved 5X growth in installs and 10X growth in first-time purchases through precision programmatic optimisation.
For boAt, our PrsmX platform delivered a 91% view-through rate (VTR), along with a 14% increase in aided awareness, a 20% increase in brand favourability and a 19% increase in purchase intent.
Inc42: Where do you see the next big opportunities for adtech?
Tejas Rathod: I see opportunities across three fundamental areas of brand growth: awareness, acquisition and activation. These are not isolated businesses anymore. A brand may need to create awareness, acquire a user and then activate or retain that user, with intelligence from each stage informing the next.
That is the direction in which we are building Mobavenue. Our products address these stages, but they are increasingly connected through a common intelligence layer that allows data and learnings to move across the consumer journey.
Inc42: Five years from now, what do you want Mobavenue to be known for?
Tejas Rathod: Five years from now, I would like Mobavenue to be recognised as a technology company that covers the broader digital growth ecosystem, not just advertising. We see significant opportunities across adtech, martech and monetisation technology, and our ambition is to build proprietary platforms across these areas that work together intelligently.
The post Mobavenue’s Tejas Rathod On The Shift From Ad Optimisation To AI Decisioning appeared first on Inc42 Media.

Days after William, and millions of others, took the test on May 3, authorities discovered that the paper had likely been leaked and circulated on social media platforms like Telegram. The results were voided.
Around the same time, the Chief Justice of India’s Supreme Court compared young people “who don’t get any employment and don’t have any place in a profession” to cockroaches and parasites. In a country with the largest population of 15- to 29-year-olds in the world (nearly 370 million people) and high levels of youth unemployment, particularly amongst the educated, the judge’s remarks struck a raw nerve.
It led to the formation of the Cockroach Janta Party — a mocking reference to India’s governing Bharatiya Janata Party, led by prime minister Narendra Modi — initially as a satirical meme. But the cancellation of NEET gave the Cockroach Janta Party real-life relevance and made it an outlet to channel the extensive frustration and anger of India’s youth. 
In neighboring Nepal, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, so-called Gen Z protests between 2022 and 2025 had toppled governments. 
In June, William joined tens of thousands of students in Jantar Mantar, an iconic venue for public protest in the Indian capital Delhi, to call for the resignation of Minister of Education Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET debacle. The demonstrations lasted for weeks, even as the Delhi Police resorted to tear gas, pellet guns, electric shock devices, and lathis (nearly six-foot-long bamboo sticks) to disperse the crowds. William was a regular.
“I always felt watched,” he told us. At metro stations, on his way to the protests, he said he repeatedly encountered the police. “They made sure that we saw them and that we should feel intimidated by their presence and their numbers.”
As journalists, we covered the June-July protests, including on July 20 when the police brutality reached an ugly peak as protesters marched towards the Indian parliament. Artificial intelligence-enabled CCTV cameras installed under Delhi’s “Safe City” project lined the streets in and around Jantar Mantar. A permanent surveillance tower stood at the center of the protest site, recording around the clock. Multiple drones circled overhead. Photographers hired by the police moved through the crowd. Some officers carried body cameras, and at least one police officer was seen wearing Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses.
Two police surveillance vehicles were parked just outside the entrance to Jantar Mantar. One was Ikshana (the Sanskrit for, literally, the act of seeing), an AI-powered police van with eight cameras that used facial recognition technology to match faces to police databases in real time. The other was a mobile command center. 
According to William, the surveillance was not limited to the protest site. “I saw police detaining students at the metro station,” he said. “They were recognizing students from footage, identifying them by their bags, or style of mask or sunglasses.”
Even after the protests stopped, with the July 25 resignation of Pradhan, the education minister, William said the police paid visits to students in their neighborhoods. They were tracking down protesters. On August 3, he said, two police officers showed up at his lodgings. He was alone. “We have photos of you,” the police told him, “in colour. You’ve been seen going to the protest site on multiple days and also seen at the metro station.” Insisting that attending protests was a democratic right, William refused to let the police into his room without a warrant.
According to the Indian Express, the Delhi Police used surveillance footage accrued during the NEET protests in the summer to identify at least “2,800 people with a criminal background” who would be be prevented from protesting against Gyanesh Kumar. 
Aishe Ghosh, a prominent student activist and national office holder at the left-wing Students’ Federation of India, has challenged the Indian government and the Delhi Police in court over the indiscriminate use of surveillance technology. Not only were the authorities documenting the protests, she alleges, they were using the footage to threaten protesters with public exposure.
Long an object of surveillance, Ghosh, who was a leader of the NEET protests, said the police entered the Communist Party of India (Marxist) headquarters in Delhi to arrest her in August on the basis of protests she had attended five years earlier in 2021. Describing the attempt to arrest Ghosh as a “continuing witch hunt against student protesters,” the CPI(M) added that it was evidence of “the Modi government’s escalating assault on democratic rights.”
Ishan Tankha
Modi’s surveillance state   
Hearing Ghosh’s litigation, the Delhi High Court appeared to suggest that the urgency to examine her specific allegations had dissipated since the NEET protests had concluded. The judges suggested that she file a more general petition.
The NEET protests proved only to be the start of the Cockroach Janta Party’s precipitous rise as serious, youth-led opposition to the Modi government, in power since 2014 and seemingly determined to use every arrow in its quiver, from opaque sources of funds to the takeover of independent institutions to the use of surveillance technology, to stifle dissent. In October, the “cockroaches” poured into Delhi’s streets again. 
This time, they wanted the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, India’s Chief Election Commissioner, a constitutional role meant to be entirely independent, apolitical and focused on maintaining the integrity of the Indian electoral process. An investigation by the Indian Express newspaper revealed that despite 14 objections in the last 10 months from the two other members of the election commission, Kumar had allegedly illegally taken unilateral decisions that resulted in voters being left off electoral rolls. India is currently undertaking an extensive revision of its voter lists that has controversially already disenfranchised 130 million people and potentially swayed state elections in favour of the governing BJP.
Kumar has not directly addressed the Indian Express’s findings. And while Modi too has remained typically silent — in his 12 years as prime minister, he has yet to call a single press conference — the Delhi Police has once again used violence and arbitrary arrests to crack down on still ongoing protests. Jantar Mantar, the de facto site of protests in Delhi since 1993, has been officially shut down. Prominent protesters, including Aishe Ghosh and the founders of the Cockroach Janta Party, have been detained. The opposition led by Congress Party scion Rahul Gandhi — the son, grandson and great-grandson of former Indian prime ministers — has been galvanized. 
But India’s next general election is not until 2029 and the next major state legislative election is not until February 2027 at the earliest. Maintaining momentum is a task Gandhi has yet to show he can manage. 
Meanwhile, the BJP continues to use friendly mainstream television media, alongside its heavy-handed policing, to argue that the protests are marginal, paid for by foreign sources and disliked by the large majority of Indians.
Fallible facial recognition tech
Technology researcher Srinivas Kodali told Coda that India’s efforts to modernise its policing system were stepped up after terrorist attacks in Mumbai in November 2008. Police stations across the country were connected, with access to criminal records and a tracking database. If someone attends a protest somewhere in India, Kodali explained, and has a police report filed against them, that information will be available to every police department in the country. He described the approach as “360-degree profiling,” pulling data together from facial recognition technology, surveillance towers, phone records, social media activity, and government databases including electoral records.
Delhi Police has said its use of technology and AI is meant to maintain law and order and identify people who already have a criminal record and not to randomly profile protesters. However, privacy researchers and lawyers warn that sophisticated surveillance systems can make participation in protests traceable long after the crowds have dispersed. 
Much of the technology for this work is supplied by a growing group of private companies. Ikshana, the AI-powered police van used to monitor protesters in Jantar Mantar back in July, is one example. Rahul Bhardwaj, the Chief Growth Officer at analytics firm Intozi based in Gurugram, a tech hub on the outskirts of Delhi, said the company provides the software layer behind Ikshana’s system. Intozi processes video feeds through AI applications designed for tasks including crowd monitoring, detecting weapons and identifying people against police databases.
Intozi has previously deployed its facial-recognition technology for government security operations at high profile international summits in Delhi. Asked specifically whether its technology was used at Jantar Mantar this summer, though, Bhardwaj cited confidentiality obligations.
The company said that its role ends after its system is installed on police infrastructure, and that it does not retain the database or continue to access the system once it has been handed over to the police. “Images of people who are not in the police database,” Bhardwaj said, “are automatically blurred within seconds, while records associated with people already registered in police databases are retained by the police.”
That places responsibility for the technology and its subsequent use with the police. 
Innefu Labs, whose AI Vision facial-recognition software has been used by Delhi Police in criminal investigations, declined to answer questions about data retention, legal safeguards or its operational relationship with police.
Another company, AjnaLens, confirmed its direct role in live policing. Kuldeep Pathak, Associate Director at AjnaLens said the company had supplied AI-enabled smart glasses to Delhi Police, first used in January 2026 in security operations during India’s Republic Day celebrations. The company confirmed that its glasses were used again during the NEET protests in Jantar Mantar. According to Pathak, their system was given access to a police database containing around 65,000 people with criminal records. He said 14 people were arrested after being recognized through the glasses.
Experts we spoke to questioned what authorises private vendors to access and process police databases, or whether an independent authority audits the system.
Ishan Tankha
Surveillance without accountability
“What statutory regime operates in this context?” asked Menaka Guruswamy, a senior lawyer who is involved in litigation in the Supreme Court over the use of facial recognition technology at Jantar Mantar. “Where is this information hosted? Is it hosted by the private vendor, the state or the police? We know nothing.”
Guruswamy said tenders and contracts between the state and private companies should make it possible to establish what data each party is permitted to access and retain.
Disha Verma, AI researcher at Tech Global Institute and Ashoka University, claims these private vendors get access to police datasets that help them train their AI systems. “They (vendors) did not need to buy training datasets from anywhere,” she says. “They didn’t need to test their product anywhere else. They ended up with a curated, very accurate facial-recognition system.” The data provided by the police, she added, would help vendors sell their product for profit to other companies that want to make use of surveillance technology.
“What I am most concerned about is how much impunity and data and power this gives the private vendors,” Verma said, calling it a “parallel police state.” 
And then there’s the accuracy of the technology, little of which has been subject to question or scrutiny.
In response to Right to Information requests made by the digital rights group Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) in 2022, the police said it considered facial-recognition results with an accuracy score of 80 percent or above as a positive match. Only results below the 80 percent threshold were “subject to further verification using corroborative evidence.”
But the distinction between technical facial recognition matches and actual verified identifications became harder to ignore after the NEET protests in Jantar Mantar in the summer. Delhi Police said its facial recognition system identified 2,873 people with previous criminal records at the protest between July 20 and 26. But at least 25 of those people were actually in jail at the time they were supposed to be protesting.
Intozi’s own description shows why that distinction is not always straightforward. Bhardwaj told us that the company’s recognition threshold is “generally kept above 70 to 80%” and once that threshold is crossed, “it is a 100 percent match for us.” This is why, argues Guruswamy, the Supreme Court lawyer, a statutory framework is necessary. “There is no foolproof system,” she said. “That is why you need accountability, a legal regime, data protection and safeguards governing how these interactions take place.”
Nearly six years ago, Ahmed* (name changed on request) experienced the pitfalls of the Delhi Police’s then fledgling facial recognition technology and surveillance system. He was identified by AI-assisted video analysis as being present during deadly communal violence in northeast Delhi in 2020. Ahmed spent around 18 months in jail, accused of killing a police official during the riots. He insisted that the man seen in the footage used as clinching evidence was someone else.
“My hair was cropped short, and I had different shoes. Only the white shirt and dark trousers matched. But that does not make anyone wearing those clothes me,” Ahmed told us. He said he had shut his shop around noon on the day of the violence and gone home. Footage from one security camera showed him near the lane where he lived. But police later said it had used Amped FIVE, a video and image analysis tool, and AI Vision, facial recognition software made by Indian company Innefu Labs, to place Ahmed at the scene of the crime.
In September 2021, Ahmed was released on bail. The court noted that several people in the area wore similar clothes to those shown in the footage and that the video analysis identifying Ahmed across different recordings would have to be tested at trial.
By then, though, the damage to Ahmed’s life had already been done. Before his arrest, Ahmed ran a garments shop and employed a couple of workers. The shop did not survive his incarceration and, while on bail, he now works at a street stall, barely surviving on his meagre income.
Facial recognition systems turn facial features into numerical data and compare them with stored images, producing a similarity score or a list of possible matches. In a one-to-many search, a single face from a protest can be compared against an entire database.
“It's able to recognize a face the way an iPhone camera might,” Disha Verma, the Ashoka University researcher said. An iPhone's front camera works because everyone looks at it from roughly the same angle in consistent light, she added; but a police station is often dimly lit, angles vary, and the camera used to take the photo might be old and pixelated. "The system the police are using usually has a very large error rate, just inherently," Verma said.
Katie Kinsey, Chief of Staff and Tech Policy Counsel at the New York University School of Law’s Policing Project, told us that broad accuracy claims tell little about how a facial recognition system might work once it leaves controlled testing conditions. “A model tested on one dataset may behave differently when the cameras, lighting, image quality and population change,” she said. 
Live video presents an additional difficulty because the images are less controlled and officers may be acting on alerts as events unfold. Kinsey said systems should be tested under the actual conditions in which police intend to use them.
Verma also raised concerns about biases affecting facial recognition systems. “If the police think a criminal looks like a dark-skinned bearded young man,” Verma said, “that is the data they will collect and that is what will train the AI.” It would, she added, create a feedback loop in which technology does not remove police prejudice but reproduce and legitimise it instead. 
India has constitutional privacy protections and general data protection legislation, but no dedicated law for the use of facial recognition technology. Basically, “you won’t know you are on a watch list,” researcher Srinivas Kodali told us.
We reached out to the Delhi Police Cyber Cell with questions about the use of live facial recognition technology and other surveillance systems during protests, but did not receive a response. 
Some jurisdictions have tried to place clearer limits on this type of power. For example, under the European Union’s AI Act, real-time remote biometric identification by law enforcement in public spaces is generally prohibited, with narrow exceptions. Even then, its exceptional use is subject to necessity and proportionality requirements and generally requires prior judicial or independent authorization.
Police in India have long maintained categories of people they consider suspects or potential troublemakers. For instance, in the south Indian state of Telangana, police have a category called “rowdy sheets” for people considered habitual offenders or threats to public order.  With facial recognition technology, these categories have only widened.  
Lawyer Menaka Guruswamy wondered what might happen when someone photographed at one protest is then seen at another protest. “Are we being criminalized simply for attending protests?” 
Verma said that one of the significant shifts that she has witnessed over the years is how the technologies once associated with borders and the military have moved to civilian policing. The militarization of the Delhi Police has been evident as paramilitary personnel dressed in camouflage have been assaulting and detaining protesters.
Still, the protesters come. 
William Tharien told us that despite being a known face to the Delhi police, despite his fears and struggles with his mental health, despite the monitoring of his social media, he is not going to stop protesting. 
And with Delhi’s cockroaches still calling for the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, still warning of the danger posed to Indian democracy by the Modi government’s authoritarian tendencies, how, William said, could he give up the fight now?

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry on Monday rubbished linking governor's rule and the imposition of an emergency in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa (K-P) to mineral extraction in the province.
The emergency and governor’s rule were declared on October 11 after negotiations between the government and opposition failed, culminating in a PTI long march towards Islamabad that began on October 4. Last week, a joint session of parliament adopted two separate resolutions ratifying the presidential proclamations imposing a state of emergency and governor’s rule in K-P for two months, amid protests from the opposition. Before that, both houses of parliament had separately approved the emergency in the province by majority vote under Clause 1 of Article 232 of the Constitution, despite objections from opposition lawmakers.
The opposition has decried the move as an attempt to encroach on the province's mineral wealth and vowed to resist what it has said is the forcible occupation of Pakhtun lands and the appropriation of their natural resources.
Speaking on the private television programme Capital Talk, Chaudhry said political parties were trying to link the emergency to the debate over minerals because they thought the emergency was imposed to gain power as part of a "power game".
"It’s not a power game but a peace game, because of which an emergency has been imposed".
Read: K-P is rich in minerals; we will 'extract and sell them', says Kundi
The minister noted it was unfortunate that attempts were being made to link the emergency in K-P with things other than terrorism, further adding that the emergency had been imposed in extraordinary circumstances and a constitutional option has been used for that purpose.
Chaudhry further said that the "expectations of certain political parties have not been met, including people in my own party who wanted a share of the authority in the new political setup. It was explained to them that the people selected in the advisory council were done so on merit and were experts in their respective fields."
While explaining the reasons for the imposition of an emergency in K-P, the minister underlined that there were differences of opinion between the former provincial government and the federal government on the issue of counterterrorism, further adding that the former chief minister was not even willing to condemn terrorism and the TTP.
On the security situation in K-P, Chaudhry stated that Dera Ismail Khan was among the 12 districts in which operations would be conducted in the first phase. "There is no writ of the government there in DI Khan, and I can provide you the names of parliamentarians who give protection money to safely return to their home."
Talking about US Chargé d'Affaires Natalie Baker’s statement in which she claimed that Pakistan possessed seven trillion dollars of mineral wealth, Chaudhry noted that Pakistan’s partnership with the US was old, further adding that Natalie took the names of both Balochistan and K-P.
Read More: Govt seeks US investment in minerals
“Mines and minerals that have been buried for the past 80 years, should they not be extracted to pay off Pakistan’s loans? The federal government has stressed that people from K-P and Balochistan will have the first right to the mineral wealth of their province, and the money will be spent on provincial development”.
The minister stated that the federal government would provide figures on how much money had been given to K-P and how much of it was actually spent, adding that numbers would also be shared for Balochistan.
On October 17, K-P Governor Faisal Karim Kundi said the province’s mineral resources would be extracted and sold to promote economic prosperity, urging domestic and foreign companies to invest in the sector through joint ventures to generate employment and support local businesses.
The governor defended the proposed exploitation of the province’s mineral resources, arguing that investment in the sector could generate employment, support local businesses and improve economic conditions.
Pakistan's mineral reserves are estimated at around $8 trillion and spread over 600,000 square kilometres, according to the Institute of Cost and Management Accountants (ICMA). The vast mineral resources highlight the massive economic potential of the mining sector. The sector has historically contributed less than 3% to the gross domestic product (GDP). With strong governance and security, annual mineral exports could rise from about $3 billion to $8 billion, and GDP growth could climb from roughly 3% to 6%.
The challenge, however, is to turn the geological potential into bankable projects, exports, jobs and industrial capacity. This requires more than mining and greater focus on exploration, geological data, modern technology, infrastructure, financing, predictable regulation, environmental safeguards and partnerships with international companies.

items.author: Usama Anjum
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
WhatsApp is working on a new feature for iPhone users that could make opening shared links much more convenient. Instead of switching to Safari or another browser every time someone shares a website in a chat, users may soon be able to browse webpages directly within WhatsApp.
The upcoming functionality has been spotted in WhatsApp beta version 26.41.10.72 for iOS through Apple’s TestFlight program. According to WABetaInfo, the company is developing an improved in-app browser that would support regular web links, allowing users to move between conversations and webpages without constantly switching applications.
WhatsApp previously experimented with a similar feature for iPhone users in 2025. However, that version primarily supported eligible business links and came with technical restrictions, including HTTPS requirements. The new implementation aims to offer broader support for links shared through chats.
Users Will Have More Control Over How Links Open
One of the more useful aspects of the upcoming feature is that WhatsApp reportedly plans to make the in-app browser optional.
Users will be able to enable it through a dedicated setting within WhatsApp. When activated for the first time, the app will display an explanation informing users that supported links will open inside WhatsApp rather than their default browser.
Those who prefer Safari, Chrome, or another browser will still have the option to disable the feature. Users may also be able to open individual links externally through the three-dot menu.
This flexibility could be particularly useful for people who regularly receive news articles, shopping links, documents, and other web content through WhatsApp. Instead of repeatedly switching between applications, users could open a webpage, read its contents, and return to their conversation more conveniently.
WhatsApp Is Also Adding Browser Privacy Controls
Beyond convenience, WhatsApp is reportedly developing a dedicated option for clearing browsing data.
The feature would allow users to remove cookies and cached website data stored by WhatsApp’s in-app browser. This could be helpful for people who want greater control over the information websites save during browsing sessions.
According to WABetaInfo, browsing information is expected to be stored locally on the device. However, users should remember that opening links within an app does not automatically make every website safe or eliminate normal online tracking risks.
The feature remains under development, and there is currently no confirmed release date for all iPhone users.
If introduced more widely, the updated browser could make WhatsApp a more convenient place to access shared web content while allowing users to retain control over their preferred browsing experience.

items.author: Life And Style Desk
items.content:
Actor Mehwish Hayat has explained why she maintains a relatively low-key presence on social media, revealing that she prefers to post occasionally rather than share frequent updates with her followers.
During an interview, the Jawani Phir Nahi Ani star said she does not post on social media frequently. “I post every two to three weeks because I feel like people get bored. They should always be wanting more,” Mehwish said.
She added that her approach also stemmed from her personal preference for privacy. While social media allows celebrities to stay connected with their fans, she does not believe in sharing every aspect of her life online.
“It also comes from the fact that I don’t like to overshare,” she said, highlighting her desire to maintain a distinction between her public persona and private life.
Her comments reflect a deliberate approach to managing her online presence. Rather than posting simply to remain visible, the actress prefers to share content selectively, allowing her followers to anticipate her next update.
Beyond maintaining audience interest, Mehwish also emphasised the importance of personal time and preserving space for herself away from work and social media.
She noted that her professional commitments and the time she dedicates to her fans already occupy a substantial part of her life. “Also, I really love my own time because I give so much time to my work and my fans. If I give the rest of my time to social media, what’s left for me?” she said.
Her remarks underline the importance she places on balancing professional responsibilities, engagement with fans and personal time. For Mehwish, being connected with her audience does not mean documenting every moment or remaining constantly active online.
While celebrities increasingly use social media to share professional updates and glimpses into their personal lives, Mehwish’s comments highlight a more selective approach. She appears keen to maintain a connection with her followers without allowing online engagement to dominate her daily routine.
Her perspective also echoes concerns raised by other Pakistani celebrities about privacy and safety on social media.
Actor Kinza Hashmi recently urged women to be cautious about whom they trust, discussing the importance of trusting one’s instincts and avoiding sharing every detail of one’s life in real time. She noted that fans did not need to know where someone was eating or spending time at every moment, particularly given safety concerns in Pakistan.
Mehwish is one of Pakistan’s best-known film and television actresses, recognised for her performances in productions including Punjab Nahi Jaungi, Load Wedding, London Nahi Jaunga and Jawani Phir Nahi Ani.

Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Punjab is stepping up its efforts to prepare students for a technology-driven future as Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz moves ahead with the second phase of the province’s laptop and scholarship schemes. The latest expansion places renewed emphasis on digital education, artificial intelligence (AI), and skills development to help young people compete in an increasingly technology-focused job market.
Punjab Information Minister Azma Bokhari confirmed the development in a statement, highlighting the provincial government’s commitment to improving educational opportunities for young people.
Want to apply for the Punjab Laptop Scheme? Click here for our complete application guide to learn about the process and eligibility requirements.
According to Bokhari, access to modern technology and relevant skills has become essential for students looking to build successful careers. She stressed that the future of Pakistan’s youth lies in education, artificial intelligence, and practical training rather than political confrontation.
The announcement signals the provincial government’s continued focus on providing students with resources that could support their academic development and digital learning.
Why Laptops and AI Skills Matter for Students
Access to a personal laptop can make a significant difference for students, particularly those pursuing degrees in computer science, software development, engineering, and other technology-related fields.
From learning programming languages and exploring AI tools to attending online classes and developing freelance skills, having the right digital resources can help students participate more effectively in modern education.
Scholarship support, meanwhile, can ease financial pressure on deserving students and help them continue their studies.
With AI and digital skills becoming increasingly important across industries, initiatives that combine educational assistance with access to technology could help more young people explore opportunities in Pakistan’s growing digital economy.
Second Phase Announced, But Application Details Awaited
While the government has announced the second phase of both schemes, the statement did not provide specific details about the number of laptops to be distributed, scholarship allocations, eligibility requirements, or application deadlines.
Students interested in the programs should therefore wait for official notifications before submitting applications or sharing personal information with websites claiming to offer registrations.
The latest announcement reflects Punjab’s broader emphasis on technology and education as tools for youth development. However, the practical impact of the expanded schemes will depend on how effectively they reach eligible students and support their long-term educational needs.

National Bank of Pakistan (NBP) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with PowerChina|Integrity Energy Storage (Shanghai) Technology Co. Ltd. (I²-ESS), China, at NBP Head Office (HO) on October 12, 2026. The MoU aims to establish a framework for collaboration in SME, commercial and corporate financing, lead generation, cross-selling of banking products and services and the exploration of future opportunities in green financing.
The signing ceremony was attended by Mr. Imran Sarwar, President of National Bank of Pakistan, Ms. Naushaba Shahzad, Group Chief IDG , Mr. Usman Shahid, Group Chief CIBG , Mr. Hamad Rasool, RE-ID Faisalabad and Mr. Si Min Zhou, Global Chairman and Mr. Chengyang Yao, Chairman South Asia, representing PowerChina|I²-ESS.
The MoU reflects a shared interest in exploring business opportunities by connecting prospective borrowers, particularly businesses operating in renewable energy, energy storage and allied sectors, with NBP’s banking and financing solutions. Through this collaboration, both organizations aim to identify commercially viable opportunities that support business growth and contribute to the development of sustainable energy-related industries. The arrangement also envisages positioning NBP as a preferred banking partner for financing opportunities referred by PowerChina|I²-ESS. The collaboration is further expected to create opportunities for cross-selling NBP’s products and services, enabling the Bank to strengthen customer relationships and expand its business outreach. In addition, both parties will explore potential collaboration in green financing and other commercially viable projects aligned with NBP’s strategic priorities and business objectives.
The MoU marks a step towards strengthening institutional collaboration between NBP and PowerChina|I²-ESS with a focus on developing mutually beneficial business opportunities and exploring financing solutions for enterprises operating in emerging and sustainability-oriented sectors.

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
Pakistan and Saudi Arabia expressed satisfaction on Monday over progress under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement and stressed the need to strengthen defence cooperation, institutional linkages and strategic coordination.
The understanding was reached during a meeting between Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir and Saudi Ambassador to Pakistan Dr Rajeh Tami Albugamy at General Headquarters in Rawalpindi, according to a statement issued by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR).
The two sides discussed matters of mutual interest and regional security dynamics, with a focus on further strengthening defence collaboration between the two countries.
Field Marshal Munir congratulated Dr Albugamy on his appointment as Saudi ambassador to Pakistan and expressed confidence that his tenure would contribute to further strengthening the longstanding fraternal ties between Pakistan and Saudi Arabia rooted in shared faith, mutual trust and strategic partnership.
Read: PM vows unwavering support for KSA
The ambassador arrived in Islamabad on September 26 and since then has conducted several meetings with the country’s top civilian and military leadership as Islamabad and Riyadh seek to deepen ties.
On October 14, President Asif Ali Zardari received Dr Albugamy’s credentials at Aiwan-e-Sadr, reaffirming Pakistan’s commitment to Saudi Arabia’s security and defence. The president also called for stronger economic ties, highlighted opportunities for greater cooperation and acknowledged Saudi Arabia’s financial assistance and support for oil supplies.
Two days later, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met the Saudi envoy and reiterated Pakistan’s commitment towards the kingdom’s sovereignty, security and territorial integrity amid escalating Houthi attacks. During the meeting, PM Shehbaz described the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement and the Makkah Joint Defence framework as significant milestones in bilateral relations. He also pledged to strengthen institutional mechanisms and expand cooperation across various sectors.
On the same day, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar also met Dr Albugamy. He also highlighted the countries’ longstanding fraternal ties and shared commitment to closer bilateral cooperation.
Read more: President Zardari receives credentials of French, Saudi ambassadors-designate
These diplomatic engagements follow the September 2025 Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement between Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, which established a framework for joint defence, and the subsequent trilateral Makkah Joint Defence Agreement signed on August 7 involving Türkiye.
According to the Makkah agreement, an armed attack against any one of the three signatory states would be regarded as an attack against all three, establishing a framework for collective deterrence and expanded defence cooperation.
The agreement has since been followed by efforts to translate its commitments into closer military coordination. In September, senior military commanders from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye met in Riyadh to review the regional security situation and discuss intelligence sharing, military coordination and the integration of defence capabilities.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Artificial intelligence is making it increasingly difficult to distinguish real people from digital creations, and a recent incident in Brazil highlights how serious the consequences can be. A 49-year-old man reportedly sold his belongings and travelled nearly 2,000 kilometres to meet a woman he hoped to marry, only to discover that she was an AI-generated character.
Edimar Martins, a bricklayer from Brazil’s Maranhão state, told TV Mirante that he first encountered a social media account using the name Jéssica Oliveira in 2020. He said he had not realized the woman was artificial.
On October 9, Martins sold possessions to fund a bus journey to Belo Horizonte, arriving on October 11. He hoped to meet the woman, but his search ended in disappointment. According to his account, a radio station told him the woman did not exist.
After running out of money, he approached Belo Horizonte City Hall for assistance. He reportedly told a social worker that loneliness had motivated his journey and received help to return home.
When AI-Generated Content Has Real-World Consequences
The online persona, also known as Jessica Fazendeira, reportedly attracted around 300,000 followers on TikTok. In a subsequently deleted video, the fictional character offered financial support to a man willing to join her on a farm.
The person running the account later acknowledged that the character was AI-generated but denied ever having direct contact with Martins. There is therefore no confirmed evidence that the account operator personally persuaded him to travel.
Nevertheless, the episode raises questions about how realistic AI-generated people can shape expectations and emotional connections, especially when their artificial nature is not immediately apparent to viewers.
AI tools can now produce convincing images and videos that appear to show real individuals. While virtual influencers can be used for entertainment and marketing, accounts that do not clearly disclose their fictional nature can confuse audiences.
For social media users, this story is a reminder to verify online identities before making major personal or financial decisions. Attractive videos, large follower counts, and a seemingly believable profile do not prove that the person shown is real.
The incident also underscores the importance of transparent AI-content labeling and digital awareness as virtual personalities become increasingly lifelike.

items.author: Nasir Butt
items.content:
The Sindh High Court (SHC) on Monday dismissed a provincial government appeal challenging the acquittal of Baloch Yakjehti Committee (BYC) leader Mahrang Baloch in an incitement case, declaring the appeal not maintainable.
The case against Mahrang and others was registered in Karachi on Oct 11, 2024, on the complaint of a citizen, Asad Ali, under the country's terror law. The complainant stated that Mahrang was a facilitator of terrorist organisations that were enticing educated youth from Balochistan and arranging a movement of terrorists under the guise of processions and rallies. A year later, an anti-terrorism court (ATC) acquitted Mahrang, ruling that the prosecution had failed to present credible evidence. Subsequently, the acting prosecutor general Sindh challenged the acquittal before the SHC in December 2025.
During today's hearing, the high court questioned the prosecution's authority to challenge the acquittal, observing that the original complainant in the case was a private individual. The bench questioned how the prosecution could independently file an appeal against the acquittal when the case had been lodged by a private complainant.
The prosecution argued that the ATC had overlooked material facts while allowing Mahrang's application for acquittal. The state counsel maintained that clear evidence existed against her and argued that the prosecution should have been allowed to present its evidence during the trial.
The prosecutor further contended that acquitting her before the formal framing of charges was inappropriate, as the prosecution had not yet presented its case before the trial court. However, the high court declared the appeal not maintainable and dismissed it, leaving the ATC's acquittal decision undisturbed.
The BYC, known for its activism against enforced disappearances in Balochistan since 2018, has been under increasing scrutiny by law enforcement agencies.
Mahrang has been in custody since March 22, 2025, following her arrest during protests in Quetta over alleged enforced disappearances and other human rights violations in Balochistan. Her lawyer, Imaan Mazari, is also facing different charges, including those of terrorism and is also currently detained along with her husband.
On June 22, 2026, an ATC in Quetta sentenced her to life imprisonment in a separate case involving the killing of a security officer during a protest in Gwadar in July 2024. The conviction drew criticism from human rights organisations, including Amnesty International, which raised concerns over due process and the fairness of the trial.
With additional input from Reuters.

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Ten African startups have been named semifinalists for the Milken-Motsepe Prize in Circular Economy, and will share US$500,000 in unrestricted funding as they compete for the US$1 million grand prize.
The Milken-Motsepe Prize is aimed at companies in Africa revolutionising using different technologies to revolutionise the circular economy on the continent. Run by the Milken Institute and the Motsepe Foundation, the prize will distribute a total of US$2 million in non-dilutive capital to companies using technology to scale circular economy solutions across Africa. Alongside funding, participants receive mentorship, investor connections and global exposure.
The 10 semi-finalists have now been announced, who will be whittled down to five finalists by judges assessing them on commercial viability, scalability, workforce and social impact, and environmental impact. The grand prize winner will be announced at the 2027 Milken Institute Global Conference in Los Angeles, with a US$250,000 runner-up prize also on offer.
Kenya leads the way with three semi-finalists. Bottle Logistics East Africa combines digital reverse logistics with industrial glass recovery to turn discarded glass into returnable packaging, cullet and other products; Sanergy converts urban sanitation and organic waste into organic fertiliser, biochar and other agricultural inputs; and Safi Organics turns rice husks and sugarcane bagasse into a carbon-negative organic fertiliser.
Ethiopia, Tanzania and Egypt each have two startups in the running. From Ethiopia, EKT Trade and Investment manufactures products from plastic waste, and Zafree makes tree-free pulp and paper for the packaging industry using banana farm waste. Tanzania’s Country Materials uses AI to identify, trace and recover scrap metal for the continent’s steel industry, while SafeSip recycles plastic waste into pressure-rated resin and drip irrigation equipment.
The Egyptian contingent comprises Papyrus Egypt, which converts banana plantation waste into biodegradable packaging and liquid fertiliser, and Triple M Electrical and Electronic Contracting, which extends the lifespan of power infrastructure by purifying transformer oil and refurbishing transformers, switchgear and panels.
Nigeria’s Cold Hubs, which builds and runs solar-powered cold rooms, refrigerated trucks and reusable crates for food markets and farm clusters, completes the list.
“Africa is uniquely positioned to lead in this transition,” said Emily Musil, managing director at the Milken Institute, who added that the prize backs entrepreneurs turning resource efficiency into competitive, job-creating businesses.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
Bengaluru-based managed care startup Even Healthcare has raised $50 Mn (about ₹475 Cr) in a Series B funding round led by existing investor Khosla Ventures, with participation from Alpha Wave.
The all-equity primary round takes its total funding to over $120 Mn, the startup said in a statement.
Even will use the proceeds primarily to expand its hospital network in Bengaluru. It plans to open another hospital by the end of 2026, followed by three more by the end of FY27. It currently operates two multispeciality hospitals on Race Course Road and in HBR Layout.
The startup plans to enter other cities after strengthening its Bengaluru presence. “We want to make sure that Bengaluru patients and members are pretty well served,” cofounder Mayank Banerjee told Inc42.
Even said its valuation had tripled since its previous fundraise 18 months ago, without disclosing its latest valuation. The startup last raised $20 Mn earlier this year to expand its hospital network and launch new facilities.
Founded in 2020 by Banerjee, Matilde Giglio, and Alessandro Ialongo, Even offers an integrated managed care model combining preventive care, outpatient consultations, diagnostics, insurance access, hospitalisation, and post-discharge recovery.
The startup aims to reduce healthcare costs by managing patients’ health beyond individual hospital visits. Its services include telemedicine, at-home blood tests, and medical guidance, alongside cashless hospitalisation through insurance partners.
Even employs salaried doctors whose compensation is not linked to the number of procedures performed or revenue generated. The startup said it assesses doctors on patient outcomes, recovery timelines, and re-admissions.
Banerjee said around 85-90% of Even members living near one of its Bengaluru hospitals choose the startup for their healthcare needs.
Even also uses an AI-based quality system to review cases against clinical protocols in real time. It recently launched Even Spotlight, a dashboard tracking clinical outcomes and patient-reported metrics.
The startup said unplanned re-admissions in programmes run with insurance partners remained below 1%, compared with an industry range of 8-15%. It also claimed average hospital stays were 40% shorter, while proactive care helped more than 200 members avoid hospitalisation, saving an estimated ₹15 Cr to ₹16 Cr.
Even claims to serve more than 2.5 Lakh members across 10 cities, having tripled its membership over the past year.
The hospital expansion follows reports in August that Even laid off around 350 employees as it scaled down its insurance business and shifted resources towards a hospital-led healthcare model. The cuts affected 30-35% of its workforce across multiple teams.

Shares of Urban Company ended today’s trading session 9.92% lower at ₹142.6 apiece on the BSE.
Original| October 19, 12:28 IST

Update| October 19, 17:48
Shares of Urban Company ended today’s trading session 9.92% lower at ₹142.6 apiece on the BSE.
Original| October 19, 12:28 IST
Shares of home services company Urban Company slumped 9.5% to ₹143.30 apiece on the BSE during early trading today, following its Q2 FY27 results and board approval for a fundraise of up to ₹2,500 Cr.
At 12:10 IST, the stock was trading 8.56% lower at ₹144.75 on the BSE. The company’s market capitalisation stood at ₹22,323 Cr (about $2.7 Bn) at the time.
Urban Company reported a consolidated net loss of ₹182.5 Cr for Q2 FY27 on Friday (October 16) as against a loss of ₹59.3 Cr a year earlier and ₹92.1 Cr in the preceding quarter.
Operating revenue rose 41% to ₹537.3 Cr from ₹380 Cr in Q2 FY26. However, total expenses increased 61.5% to ₹745.7 Cr, driven largely by higher spending on its quick household help business, InstaHelp.
The company reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹144 Cr, including what it described as a “deliberate” ₹174 Cr investment in InstaHelp. Excluding the vertical, adjusted EBITDA stood at ₹30 Cr.
The company’s board also approved a proposal to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr through equity shares and/or convertible securities via preferential allotment or private placement.
Urban Company said the proceeds would strengthen InstaHelp’s market leadership, support investment across its three businesses, and fund potential acquisitions.
It is also exploring entry into the residential air conditioner market under its consumer appliances brand ‘Native’, which currently sells water purifiers and smart locks. Management said it could meet its profitability targets without additional capital, although InstaHelp’s losses limited its financial flexibility.
Despite the rise in its loss, Emkay Global Financial Services maintained its ‘Buy’ rating for Urban Company and raised its target price to ₹200 from ₹190, citing growth opportunities across its segments and the strength of its core business.
The brokerage highlighted low penetration of its core services, expansion into Tier II cities, improving international profitability, and the Saudi Arabia business’ progress towards breakeven. It also identified Native as a growth opportunity and said InstaHelp was driving higher customer engagement.
