items.content:
*Accuses FG of enriching few to starve citizens *Say workers, masses under siege *N70,000 minimum wage now a cruel joke
By Victor Ahiuma-Young & Henry Obetta
Labour leaders and pro-democracy activists weekend called on Nigerians to unite against rising fuel prices, worsening economic hardship and government policies that have impoverished workers and the masses while enriching a privileged few.
Read Also: Buhari saw Tinubu as ‘Bad News’ for Nigeria — Baba-Ahmed
They warned that the continued increase in the pump price of Premium Motor Spirit, PMS, popularly known as petrol, has eroded workers’ purchasing power, intensified poverty and pushed millions of Nigerians into a daily struggle for survival.
The Nigeria Labour Congress, NLC, human rights lawyer, Femi Falana, SAN, members of the Joint Action Front, JAF, among others, made the call at the first memorial celebration and symposium in honour of late activist Abiodun Aremu in Lagos.
President of the NLC, Joe Ajaero, who was represented by the union’s Acting General Secretary, Benson Upah, said the removal of  petrol subsidy had inflicted devastating consequences on the working class and the wider population, insisting that organised labour would continue to demand relief from the federal government.
In the address delivered on behalf of the NLC President, the labour movement described the prevailing economic situation as a crisis of survival, arguing that workers could no longer cope with the combined effects of rising transport fares, food prices, electricity tariffs and the depreciation of the naira.
“The removal of fuel subsidy has devastated Nigeria’s working class and masses,” NLC President stated.
According to him, transport costs have risen sharply, forcing many workers to choose between paying exorbitant fares and walking long distances to their workplaces.
NLC President also cited the increase in the price of essential commodities, noting that a bag of rice, which previously sold for about ₦30,000, now costs more than ₦80,000, while the price of a loaf of bread had risen from approximately ₦500 to ₦1,500.
He argued further that escalating electricity tariffs had forced some small businesses to shut down, while the depreciation of the naira had increased the cost of imported medicines, industrial inputs and other essential goods.
Ajaero attributed the worsening conditions to what it described as anti-people economic policies implemented without adequate consultation with Nigerians or effective measures to cushion their impact.
“The government has effectively declared war on its own people, pushing the majority to the fringes of survival,” he declared.
The NLC President noted that the crisis was not accidental but reflected economic policies that   enriched the ruling class while deepening the hardship experienced by ordinary citizens.
NLC’s ultimatum over fuel prices
He disclosed that NLC had on October 9, issued a two-week ultimatum to the federal government, demanding an immediate reduction in the price of petrol.
According to him, the ultimatum is intended to compel the government to address the growing disconnect between workers’ earnings and the cost of living.
Ajaero said: “Most recently, the NLC issued a two-week ultimatum to the Federal Government, demanding an immediate reduction in the price of Premium Motor Spirit (PMS), also known as petrol.
“This ultimatum is not a mere bargaining chip but a solemn warning. If the government does not act within the stipulated timeframe, the NLC will have no choice but to seek remedial steps with all of us in this hall today.”
He argued  that fuel  prices should be reduced to a level consistent with the purchasing power of workers earning the national minimum wage of ₦70,000 monthly.
NLC recalled that when the minimum wage was set at ₦70,000 in July 2024, petrol sold for approximately ₦668.30 per litre, compared with prices exceeding ₦1,400 per litre in many parts of the country at the time covered by the address.
“A worker earning ₦70,000 a month cannot afford to buy petrol at ₦1,400 per litre. The government has effectively rendered the minimum wage meaningless.
“The ₦70,000 minimum wage was inadequate when it was announced. It is now a cruel joke. The NLC will not accept a situation where Nigerian workers are expected to survive on starvation wages while the cost of living continues to rise,” the NLC President declared.Beyond the demand for a reduction in petrol prices, the NLC urged the “government to take concrete measures to stabilise the naira, reduce inflation and strengthen domestic refining capacity.
“The removal of the subsidy was justified on the grounds that it would attract investment in local refining. Where is that investment?
Falana questions government’s approach to fuel pricing
Falana, who was the Chairman of the event, challenged the argument that withdrawing petrol subsidy was the only viable option available to the government, pointing to the continued use of subsidies in other countries.
He said “As you are all aware, countries across the world, including major capitalist economies, such as the United States, Germany and France, subsidise not only fuel but also education, healthcare and other essential services.
“That is the reality today. A simple internet search will reveal announcements of various subsidies in different countries.”
The senior advocate argued that governments should be prepared to consider different policy options to protect citizens from economic shocks, rather than treating the withdrawal of subsidies as an unavoidable solution.
He also referred to international developments concerning energy supplies and sanctions against Russia, and argued that countries routinely reconsidered their economic positions in response to changing circumstances.
Falana criticised the federal government’s position on fuel prices, saying Nigerians continued to face high costs, despite official discussions about reducing the landing cost of the commodity.
He said:  “Here in Nigeria, with elections approaching, the government is telling us that the best it can offer is that the landing cost of fuel will be ₦1,350 per litre.
“When the government talks about landing cost, we must consider what that means for Nigerians in Abuja, Jos, Maiduguri and other parts of the country, where additional transportation and distribution costs may apply. That is what this administration has offered the Nigerian people.
“Among those seeking to take over power, only a few, including Omoyele Sowore and Donald Duke, have reportedly stated that, if given the opportunity, they would ensure that fuel sells for less than ₦500 per litre,” he said.
₦70,000 wage can buy only 50 litres of petrol — JAF
Among other speakers, Rashidat Adesina of the Joint Action Front (JAF) highlighted the dramatic increase in fuel prices since the announcement of subsidy removal in 2023, arguing that the consequences had been particularly severe for low-income earners.
She recalled that petrol sold for approximately ₦165 per litre before subsidy was removed, after which the price rose to about ₦500 and subsequently ₦600 per litre.
“We are now discussing prices of ₦1,350 to ₦1,400 per litre, depending on the location and filling station,” she said.
Adesina challenged Nigerians to consider what the increase meant for workers whose monthly earnings remained far below the cost of maintaining a household.
“What does this mean for workers and poor Nigerians?” she queried.
She illustrated the situation by comparing the minimum wage with the prevailing petrol price, noting that a worker earning ₦70,000 monthly could purchase only 50 litres of petrol at ₦1,400 per litre.
“The national minimum wage is ₦70,000 per month. At ₦1,400 per litre, an entire month’s minimum wage can purchase only 50 litres of petrol. That calculation does not include rent, school fees, food, transportation or other essential expenses,’’ she said.
For Adesina, the calculation demonstrated the extent to which rising energy costs had undermined the ability of workers to meet basic needs, even before accounting for other expenses required to sustain a family.
She referred to figures attributed to the National Bureau of Statistics, NBS, that placed the national poverty threshold at approximately ₦345 per person per day, although the specific figures and their reference periods required independent verification.
She argued that the reported poverty levels reflected the vulnerability of households already struggling with rising prices and stagnant incomes.
“The consequences for ordinary Nigerians are severe. While workers and poor households struggle, sections of the business community continue to accumulate enormous wealth,” she said.
Her remarks reinforced the central argument advanced at the symposium that the burden of economic adjustment was falling disproportionately on workers, traders, artisans, young people and other low-income groups.
Activists demand a change in economic priorities
The speakers’ interventions converged on a demand for the federal government to review policies they said had increased the cost of living without providing adequate protection for vulnerable citizens.
They argued that reducing petrol prices, reviewing the minimum wage, stabilising the naira and investing in domestic refining should form part of a broader response to the economic crisis.
Vanguard News
The post NLC, Falana, activists rally Nigerians against petrol price hike, hardship appeared first on Vanguard News.

…says party no better than APC
By Luminous Jannamike
ABUJA – Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, vice-presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, has ruled out withdrawing from the 2027 presidential race in favour of the African Democratic Congress, ADC, declaring that the opposition party offers no better alternative to the ruling All Progressives Congress, APC.
Kwankwaso’s declaration comes amid opposition manoeuvres ahead of the election, with the NDC chieftain accusing the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, PCC, of promoting claims that his ticket with Peter Obi is working for the APC or may step down for the ADC candidate at the last minute.
In a statement on Sunday, Kwankwaso accused the ADC campaign team of directing unnecessary attacks at him, Obi and the NDC instead of selling its own candidate to Nigerians.
“We will not withdraw our candidature for the ADC or any other party,” he declared.
Kwankwaso also dismissed suggestions that the NDC ticket was acting on behalf of the ruling party, insisting that it remained committed to contesting the election.
“The OK ticket is neither working for nor acting on behalf of the APC or any of its candidates. We see no possibility or reason to withdraw from the presidential race in favour of the ADC candidate or any other,” he said.
Turning his attention to the ADC campaign council, Kwankwaso urged it to address allegations levelled against its presidential candidate by Vice-President Kashim Shettima rather than attack the NDC ticket.
He also rejected the ADC’s claim to being an alternative to the APC-led government, which he accused of failing Nigerians.
“The APC-led government has failed Nigerians. The ADC offers no better alternative,” Kwankwaso declared.
Presenting the NDC as a stronger opposition platform, he said his ticket with Obi had the credibility, capacity and nationwide support to unite the country and tackle insecurity, education, agriculture, infrastructure, healthcare and economic challenges.
Kwankwaso urged supporters and well-meaning Nigerians to remain committed to the party’s electoral victory, describing the NDC as the country’s most formidable opposition party.
“I therefore urge all our supporters and well-meaning Nigerians to continue working toward the victory of our great party,” he said.

items.author: Akinbayo Wahab
items.content:
By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief
The Federal Government has disagreed with the World Bank on the latter’s debt servicing/revenue ratio for the first half of 2026, put at 124 percent.
The bank in its recent Nigeria Development Update (NDU) reported that federal government debt servicing was 124 percent above its revenue.
However, the Federal Ministry of Finance, in a statement, yesterday, faulted the bank’s analysis, explaining that the debt servicing figure included those of the state governments and that it was, therefore, wrong to analyse it against the federal government revenue for the period under consideration.
The statement read in part, “This conclusion is misleading, for three reasons, the government said.
“The interest figure includes debt the Federal Government services on behalf of other tiers of government, including external loans to states.
“Measuring this against federal revenue alone overstates the ratio which is only meaningful when debt and revenue cover the same level of government.
“The reported revenue is also incomplete. It excludes independent revenue already earned by government agencies and enterprises but not yet remitted to the Treasury.
” In addition, more revenue is typically earned in the second half of the year than in the first due to the statutory timing of certain tax payments. This is why the ratio stood at 156% in H1 2025, while the full-year 2025 debt-service-to-revenue ratio was below 60%, down from 97% before the reforms.
” This is a clear sign of the progress delivered by the current administration’s reforms.
“Between the first half of 2025 and the first half of 2026, federal revenue rose by 72%, from ₦3.6 trillion to ₦6.2 trillion. Interest payments rose by a much slower 38%, from ₦5.6 trillion to ₦7.7 trillion.
” Revenue is therefore growing almost twice as fast as interest costs. As a result, the interest-to-revenue ratio fell by 32 percentage points in a single year, from 156% to 124%, and the gap between interest and revenue narrowed from ₦2.0 trillion to ₦1.5 trillion. This is the result of reforms working, not a sign of fiscal distress.
“Debt sustainability is assessed on a full-year basis, not over six months. The same World Bank report projects Nigeria’s full-year 2026 debt service, covering both interest and principal, at 46% of revenue.
“This is the appropriate benchmark, and a guide to avoid the invalid conclusions being drawn.
“Every naira borrowed by the Federal Government falls within the limits approved by the National Assembly under the 2026 Appropriation Act and the approved borrowing plan.
“All borrowing is conducted in full compliance with the Fiscal Responsibility Act 2007 and the Debt Management Office (Establishment) Act 2003, and is published regularly by the Debt Management Office.
“The Ministry welcomes informed scrutiny of public finances. We encourage analysts and commentators to apply the same rigour they seek to hold the government to: compare like with like, read figures in context, and seek clarification where the data is unclear.”

items.author: Emmanuel Okogba
items.content:
By Peter Duru, Makurdi
The Benue State Emergency Management Agency (SEMA) says it has spent more than N160 million on the treatment of snakebite victims between March and September as part of efforts to provide healthcare services to Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) and the vulnerable in the state.
The Executive Secretary of SEMA, James Iorpuu, disclosed this while outlining the agency’s interventions in healthcare, food distribution, protection, education, resettlement and livelihood support for displaced persons, despite funding and logistical constraints.
Iorpuu also disclosed that 248 community reporters had been trained to monitor and report incidents in IDP camps and host communities, while 163 displaced children had enrolled in a federal government exchange programme.
He said the agency was also working with humanitarian partners, including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), to facilitate resettlement and help displaced families rebuild their livelihoods.
“We have been spending money on healthcare for our displaced persons. Between March and September, we spent more than N160 million on snakebites alone,” he said.
According to him,”the agency has also made arrangements for IDPs who require medical attention to receive treatment at the Benue State University Teaching Hospital, BSUTH. We have medical personnel coordinating the process, including two nurses working with the hospital to assess patients, stabilise them and refer them to specialists where necessary.”
“One of our major challenges is transportation. We do not have sufficient mobility resources to convey patients to medical facilities promptly, but we continue to make arrangements to ensure that those who need medical attention receive assistance.”
“Food distribution is only one aspect of our responsibility. We have continued to distribute food to displaced persons despite the reduction in available supplies, but our interventions also cover healthcare, education, protection, resettlement and livelihood support,” Iorpuu said.
“On protection, we have trained 248 community reporters who provide real-time information about incidents in IDP camps and surrounding communities. Where cases of sexual and gender-based violence are reported, we refer them to the police for appropriate action. We are also working to expand the reporting mechanism to more communities while protecting the identities of the reporters.”
“On education, 163 displaced children have enrolled in the Secondary School exchange programme. We want to ensure that displacement does not permanently deprive these children of schooling. We are also working to provide support that will enable them to access educational opportunities despite their circumstances,” he said.
“Regarding resettlement, we have moved displaced persons out of school buildings in Naka to a designated location. We are also working with partners, including UNHCR, on resettlement interventions involving shelters, healthcare facilities and other basic infrastructure to improve the living conditions of displaced families.”
“At Akile in Makurdi Local Government Area, we have moved about 110 displaced persons to an area where they can begin rebuilding their lives through farming and other productive activities. The idea is to provide them with opportunities to cultivate crops, harvest their produce, sell them and keep the proceeds rather than depend indefinitely on humanitarian assistance,” Iorpuu said.
“These challenges cannot be addressed by SEMA alone. We need coordinated efforts involving the state and federal governments, local authorities, humanitarian organisations and affected communities. Our ultimate objective is to ensure that displaced persons can return to their ancestral homes when it is safe, while those who cannot return immediately have access to decent shelter, healthcare, education and sustainable livelihoods,” the Executive Secretary said.

The Austrian Airlines crew decided to make an emergency landing in Sofia after reportedly receiving a bomb threat as they neared Romania, Bulgaria’s transport ministry said in a statement, adding that the passengers were evacuated from the aircraft after landing.
The Bulgarian air force scrambled a MiG-29 fighter jet to escort the airliner as part of established procedures, the transport ministry said.
The airline told AFP that 51 passengers and six crew were aboard the flight, and that a security search of the aircraft — an Airbus A320 — was launched after it safely landed in Sofia about a half hour after the threat.
“Once the search of the aircraft is complete, the passengers will be rebooked onto alternative flights as quickly as possible,” the airline said.
According to Flightradar24 data, the aircraft, registered OE-LZE, entered Romanian airspace at around 9:10pm before turning south and heading back towards Bulgaria, where it landed in Sofia.
Data from another flight-tracking platform, ADS-B Exchange, indicates that the aircraft was transmitting squawk code 7700 — a signal for a general emergency — at around the same time.
The transport ministry said that a crisis response team has been set up and the relevant authorities have launched an investigation into the incident.
In a separate incident late last month, the co-pilot aboard a flybubai airline flight headed to Tel Aviv from Dubai attacked the captain and allegedly planned to intentionally crash the plane but was stopped by the captain, passengers and crew.
Last week, Croatia and Germany both scrambled fighter jets after a commercial flight from the Greek holiday island of Corfu to the German city of Nuremberg accidentally sent out a hijacking alert.

items.author: efosataiwo@vanguardngr.com
items.content:
Kylian Mbappe scored twice including one brilliant individual goal as Real Madrid thrashed Sevilla 4-1 on Sunday to climb into third in La Liga.
Arda Guler netted a spectacular opener before Mbappe’s double and a rocket from Yan Diomande as Jose Mourinho side moved above Real Betis, who lost 5-2 to league leaders Barcelona on Saturday.
Mbappe’s first was a sensational strike, involving a roulette on the edge of Sevilla’s box, and his second a chipped Panenka penalty.
Champions Barca are six points ahead of Real Madrid before next weekend’s Clasico at Camp Nou, with Atletico Madrid second, sandwiched between Spain’s giants.
Mourinho lined up with Diomande on the left in place of suspended Brazilian winger Vinicius Junior, and brought Guler in as part of the midfield pivot.
Vinicius’s red card for hair-pulling last weekend provoked ire in the Spanish capital at officiating in Spain.
Madrid fans at their Santiago Bernabeu stadium chanted and held up banners against La Liga president Javier Tebas, after he said the club’s strategy of trying to discredit referees was similar to the techniques of Nazi propaganda chief Joseph Goebbels.
Los Blancos and their new coach Mourinho have complained bitterly about Spanish refereeing in recent weeks, and more generally over the past two seasons, in which they have failed to win a major trophy.
On this occasion it was Sevilla who had more to complain about in terms of officiating as Madrid eased to victory.
A quiet start was disrupted when Madrid midfielder Guler appeared to elbow Sevilla’s Peque, which went unpunished midway through the first half.
Sevilla had resisted the probing of Madrid’s attacking stars early on, but were undone by a moment of magic from Guler himself after 30 minutes.
Jude Bellingham played the ball out to the flank where record signing Diomande received it and fed Guler on the edge of the box.
The Turkish playmaker lofted a superb strike across Sevilla goalkeeper Odysseas Vlachodimos and into the top corner.
– Mbappe skill –
Mbappe came close to adding a second with a lightning-quick burst down the pitch, but his low effort was saved.
The French superstar soon got his goal, one of the best of the season.
Bellingham backheeled the ball into Mbappe’s path and the forward produced a dazzling roulette turn into the area, before showing more skill to rapidly sidestep the goalkeeper and roll home.
Mbappe extended the lead from the penalty spot after he went down under a light touch from Andres Castrin in the area.
The forward, who hopes to be crowned the best player in the world at the Ballon d’Or ceremony later in October, dinked home his ninth league goal of the season.
Sevilla pulled one back with a neat strike from Manuel Bueno, but there was no fightback on the cards.
Ivorian winger Diomande thumped home from outside of the box for his second goal since joining this summer from RB Leipzig, Madrid’s next opponents in the Champions League.
Earlier, Real Sociedad rose to fifth with a thumping 5-2 win at bottom side Malaga, Celta Vigo defeated Alaves 2-1 and Osasuna beat Racing Santander 2-0.

items.content:
Angry youths booed the Deputy Governor of Zamfara State, Malam Mani Mummuni, and attacked his convoy in Gwashi community, Bukkuyum Local Government Area of Zamfara State, on Sunday.
The incident occurred when the deputy governor visited the community on a condolence visit following last week’s attack that led to the killing of nine security personnel and civilians.
A resident who spoke to Daily Trust on condition of anonymity said the community was angry with the deputy governor and the state government over the security challenges in the area said to be one of the largest political wards in the local government.
“The last time they visited us was more than three years ago; they visited us during the 2023 election campaign. Since then, neither the deputy governor nor any state government delegation has visited us to show concern about our growing security challenges.”
Father, son burnt to death as bus, tricycle collide in Plateau
2027: Despite Rift, AbdulRazaq Says Wike Will Give APC 100% in Kwara
“Today, we have shown the world the situation we are in. We have expressed our grievances on several occasions, but no action has been taken to address insecurity and the lack of development projects,” he said.
The resident added that following the bandits’ attacks, members of the community spent six consecutive days without going out to purchase essential items.
“We spent six to seven days without leaving our community. Security personnel stopped escorting people, and nobody could risk his life by going out. If we spend more days like that, believe me, even salt will become unavailable,” he said.
He also lamented the lack of basic amenities in the community.
“We do not have an access road, a good hospital or portable drinking water. Our school buildings are dilapidated,” he said.
Another resident, who also spoke to Daily Trust on condition of anonymity, said the secondary school in the community had deteriorated to the extent that animals now use the premises for shelter.
He said women, children, youths and elderly residents came out to express their grievances to the deputy governor and demonstrate their dissatisfaction with the administration.
“We came out in large numbers, with women, children, youths and elderly people booing the deputy governor and chanting ‘Bamayi, Bamayi’ [we will not]. We know he came to canvass for votes, and we will not vote for them,” he said.
The resident further alleged that the angry youths attacked the deputy governor’s convoy.
“Even the deputy governor narrowly escaped, and a vehicle was destroyed,” he claimed.
However, a member of the deputy governor’s entourage, who also spoke on condition of anonymity, denied that the convoy was attacked.
He said the protesters were around the market area while the deputy governor’s gathering took place near the community’s hospital.
“What they are saying is not true. We were in an entirely different location, and the car they claimed was destroyed was a security vehicle that developed a mechanical fault. It was later towed away,” he said.
Another source told Daily Trust that the deputy governor was accompanied by many security personnel who blocked people from accessing the venue where he addressed some persons on the issue of insecurity.
“Massive deployment of security personnel prevented people from getting close enough to register their grievances. However, we booed the deputy governor and stoned the convoy,” he said.
“Even the deputy governor narrowly escaped because the youths were angry over the lack of government concern and intervention.”
‘Gwashi incident a dangerous warning signal’
Reacting to the development, a commentator, Dahiru Samaila Mafara, described the incident as a dangerous warning signal that the Zamfara State Government and the Federal Government must not ignore.
Mafara said the anger that erupted in Gwashi reflected years of accumulated frustration among residents who had struggled to access their farmlands, markets and neighbouring communities because of banditry.
He said residents in several parts of Zamfara had suffered repeated attacks and kidnappings and faced restrictions on movement, while some were allegedly forced to pay levies to bandits to access their farms.
According to him, the incident involving the deputy governor’s convoy exposed the depth of public dissatisfaction with the government’s handling of insecurity.
“If a Deputy Governor cannot enter his immediate community without his convoy being attacked by angry residents, what is the fate of ordinary politicians, councillors and candidates?” he asked.
Mafara warned that the incident could have serious political implications ahead of the 2027 general elections, particularly in communities where residents felt abandoned because of persistent attacks.
He expressed concern over the security situation on major highways across the state, including the Gusau-Anka, Gusau-Talata Mafara, Gusau-Kaura Namoda, Kaura Namoda-Shinkafi and Kaura Namoda-Zurmi roads.
He also cited the Mayanchi-Gummi route as one of the areas where travellers faced security concerns.
Mafara said the inability of residents to move freely, cultivate their farms and conduct business without fear had contributed to growing distrust of government. He added that some communities had reportedly resorted to negotiating with bandits to survive.
He called on the Zamfara State Government, the Federal Government and the All Progressives Congress (APC) to take urgent steps to address the security challenges.
He urged the authorities to establish a permanent security presence in Bukkuyum, Anka, Maru, Maradun, Tsafe, Kaura Namoda, Zurmi, Shinkafi and other affected communities.
While acknowledging the reported donation of N500,000 to each affected family, Mafara said financial assistance could not replace the need for lasting security.
He said residents wanted to return to their farms, travel without fear and sleep peacefully in their homes.
Mafara warned that failure to address the grievances that triggered the anger in Gwashi could lead to further confrontations between residents and government officials.

Former Delta State Governor, Chief James Ibori, has mourned prominent Niger Delta leader Patrick Dele Cole, praising his commitment to the struggle for true federalism and resource control.

He said Cole played a significant role in the region’s struggle for true federalism and resource control, adding that his commitment to the aspirations of the Niger Delta people remained firm even while he served as a special adviser in the administration of former President Olusegun Obasanjo.
According to Ibori, Cole’s dedication to the region demonstrated his willingness to stand with his people at a time when doing so could carry considerable political costs.
He added that the late leader’s political choices were guided by his commitment to the interests and legitimate aspirations of the Niger Delta people.
“He was a prominent leader in the Niger Delta who stood firmly with us in our struggle for true federalism and resource control. Even while serving as a special adviser in President Olusegun Obasanjo’s administration, he remained committed to his people and their legitimate aspirations,” Ibori said.
He added that Cole’s actions reflected deep loyalty to his roots and an unwavering commitment to the Niger Delta cause.
“At a time when such a stance could carry significant political costs, he chose to stand with his people,” he said.
Ibori urged the family of the late statesman to take solace in God, saying Cole’s contributions to Nigeria’s development, particularly in the Niger Delta, would remain cherished.

By Dayo Johnson, Akure
Ondo State Governor, Lucky Aiyedatiwa, has renamed The Dome International Event and Cultural Centre after former governor Olusegun Mimiko in recognition of his contributions to the state.
The facility will now be known as the Dr Olusegun Mimiko Cultural and Event Centre.
Aiyedatiwa announced the decision on Saturday in Abuja at an event tagged “An Evening of Celebration and Conversation with Mimiko”, organised by young professionals to mark the former governor’s 72nd birthday.
In his goodwill message, Aiyedatiwa commended Mimiko’s contributions to healthcare, education and other sectors, highlighting initiatives such as the free shuttle bus scheme for students.
He also praised the organisers of the event and urged them to remain worthy ambassadors of Ondo State and Nigeria.
Speaking during a fireside chat, Mimiko urged young professionals to prioritise hard work, personal development and preparation for leadership.
He said effective leadership required capacity building, stressing that young people must first develop themselves and build strong personal character before aspiring to lead others.
On national issues, the former governor described the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), introduced by President Bola Tinubu’s administration, as a major intervention capable of widening access to higher education.
He urged young people to support Tinubu’s re-election bid to sustain and expand the initiative.
“You are bustling with energy and zeal and have access to readily available, knowledge-enhancing information. You therefore have to make the best of the opportunities available and maximise your chances,” Mimiko said.
Earlier, the coordinator of the event and former Speaker of the Nigeria Youth Parliament, Ayo Obe, said the celebration was inspired by Mimiko’s moral, intellectual, political and material support for young people over the years.
The Minister of Interior, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, described the young people mentored by Mimiko as his most enduring legacy.
“The best of all the achievements of Dr Olusegun Mimiko are the young people he built through mentorship,” Tunji-Ojo said.
He urged political leaders to invest in mentoring the next generation, stressing that their legacy should include people equipped to sustain their contributions after they leave office.
“For every entry, one day, there will be an exit. But when the exit comes, who will be there to hold your hands?” he asked.
Representing the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Tolu Adegbie commended Mimiko for his achievements despite the limited resources available to his administration.
Adegbie noted that states now had access to more resources following the economic policies of the Tinubu administration.
The Olowo of Owo and Chairman of the Ondo State Council of Obas, Oba Ajibade Gbadegesin Ogunoye III, and Otunba Bademosi, who represented the Osemawe of Ondo, also praised Mimiko’s contributions to healthcare, education and infrastructure.
Other dignitaries at the event included former Kogi State Governor, Capt. Idris Wada; Senator representing Ondo South, Dayo Faduyile; member of the House of Representatives, Fessy West Adediranye; Joseph Akinlaja; and other serving and former federal lawmakers from Ondo State.

Peter Obi, presidential candidate of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), has urged Nigerians at home and abroad to take collective responsibility for building a better country, blaming corruption and leadership failures for Nigeria’s slow pace of development.
Obi made the call in a statement posted on his X account on Sunday after an impromptu meeting with Nigerians in Manchester, United Kingdom.
He said the interaction provided an opportunity to listen to the concerns of Nigerians in the diaspora and discuss their hopes for the country’s future.
Obi said he was encouraged by their passion and determination to contribute to building a Nigeria that works for all citizens.
“The task of building a New Nigeria remains our collective responsibility, and there is no better time to roll up our sleeves and get to work than now,” he said.
The former Anambra State governor warned that the country faced serious challenges that required urgent and collective action.
“Our nation is standing on the brink of a precipice, and we must not shrink from the arduous task ahead of us,” he added.
Obi identified corruption and years of leadership failures as major obstacles to Nigeria’s progress, arguing that the country’s abundant resources should have placed it among the world’s most developed nations.
He maintained that Nigeria’s development depended largely on the character, competence, capacity and commitment of those entrusted with political leadership.
According to him, the forthcoming general elections should be approached as a defining moment for the country rather than a routine political exercise.
“No nation, as I have always maintained, can rise above the character, competence, capacity and commitment of those entrusted with its leadership,” he said.
Obi described the task of rescuing the country as a collective struggle and called on Nigerians to work towards what he termed the birth of a “New Nigeria” that is possible.

items.content:
Former United States President Barack Obama has accused President Donald Trump’s administration of using federal power to intimidate Democratic Congresswoman Ilhan Omar over her criticism of the president.
Obama, in a statement posted on his X account on Sunday, condemned the investigation into Omar’s immigration history, describing it as an alarming departure from democratic principles.
He said the government should not selectively target individuals because of their political beliefs or public statements.
Omar, who represents Minnesota in the US House of Representatives, was born in Somalia and arrived in the United States with her family at the age of 12. She became a naturalised US citizen in 2000 and was elected to Congress in 2018. <Cite refs={[“turn679951search0″,”turn679951search11”]}/>
Obama said Omar had built a career in public service, first as a community organiser and later as a legislator, before becoming one of the Trump administration’s most outspoken critics.
He argued that the administration’s scrutiny of her citizenship was politically motivated, pointing to what he described as an unsubstantiated theory that she was older than officially recorded when her father became a naturalised citizen.
Federal agents searched Omar’s Washington, DC, residence on October 12 as part of a criminal investigation into possible irregularities in her decades-old immigration paperwork. Authorities also seized her phone, according to reports, while the investigation’s full scope remains unclear. <Cite refs={[“turn679951search1″,”turn679951search2″,”turn679951search5”]}/>
Obama questioned the basis for the investigation, arguing that the federal government was bringing its full weight to bear on an elected official because she had criticised the president.
He also cited previous investigations and prosecutions involving individuals viewed as political opponents of Trump, including New York Attorney General Letitia James and former FBI Director James Comey, arguing that such actions raised concerns about the independence of law enforcement.
Obama said the investigation could impose significant financial and personal costs on Omar, including legal expenses and time diverted from her responsibilities to constituents.
He warned that the use of government institutions to intimidate political critics could have consequences beyond Omar’s case.
“The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar’s political views,” Obama said.
He cautioned that allowing such practices to become normal could expose other Americans to similar treatment under future administrations, regardless of which political party holds power.
Omar has denied wrongdoing and described the search of her home as an attempt to intimidate her. The Justice Department has said the search was authorised by a court warrant and formed part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation. <Cite refs={[“turn679951search4″,”turn679951search9”]}/>
The investigation has drawn criticism from Democrats, who have questioned its timing ahead of the November midterm elections. The administration has not publicly established that Omar committed immigration fraud.

items.content:
LASCOPA urges consumers to remain vigilant
By Olasunkanmi Akoni
The Lagos State Government has intensified efforts to protect consumers from counterfeit, expired, adulterated and substandard products, warning that premises found violating consumer protection laws risk being sealed.
The General Manager of the Lagos State Consumer Protection Agency (LASCOPA), Afolabi Solebo, gave the warning during media appearances on the AskLagos programme aired on Lagos Traffic Radio 96.1 FM and Lagos Television (LTV).
Solebo said the agency had continued to identify supermarkets and retail outlets selling unwholesome products, adding that sustained monitoring and enforcement had helped reduce the practice.
He said enforcement actions would be publicised to raise public awareness, encourage compliance and deter businesses from violating consumer protection regulations.
On price transparency, Solebo urged consumers to report supermarkets and shops that failed to display the prices of goods.
He explained that visible price tags enabled consumers to make informed purchasing decisions and helped prevent discrepancies between displayed prices and amounts charged at checkout.
Addressing the “No Refund, No Return” policy adopted by some businesses, the LASCOPA boss clarified that blanket disclaimers did not automatically override consumers’ rights to seek redress.
He encouraged residents who purchased defective, counterfeit or misrepresented products to lodge complaints with the agency.
Solebo also advised consumers to check product labels, verify registration details, examine expiry dates and retain receipts as evidence in the event of disputes.
For online transactions, he urged residents to verify sellers, confirm payment terms, use secure payment channels and inspect goods before payment where payment on delivery was available.
He urged consumers not to remain silent when their rights were violated but to use the agency’s complaint channels, stressing that effective consumer protection required the collective responsibility of consumers, businesses and regulators.
Solebo reiterated LASCOPA’s commitment to protecting consumers’ interests, promoting fair business practices and ensuring a safe and transparent marketplace.
Residents can report complaints through LASCOPA’s social media platforms on Facebook, Instagram and X via @lasgcopa, by email at lasgcopa@gmail.com, or through its toll-free helpline, 080 0005 2726.

items.content:
Michael Carrick said Manchester United’s hard-fought 1-1 draw at bitter rivals Leeds on Sunday felt like a “fresh start” even though their long wait for a win goes on.
Leeds forward Dominic Calvert-Lewin cancelled out Bryan Mbeumo’s first-half opener at Elland Road, extending United’s winless run to six matches in all competitions.
But Carrick saw positive signs five days after the 2-0 Champions League loss at Atletico Madrid, which sparked Lisandro Martinez’s criticism of the club hierarchy over a lack of summer investment.
“We’re not getting too carried away because we haven’t won the game,” said the Red Devils boss, who started the Argentina defender at Leeds but had to replace him at the break due to a thigh problem.
“I think if you keep doing the right things for the right reasons then you get what you deserve in the end.
“It felt like a bit of a fresh start, if I’m honest, today in where we’re at and accepting it and doing something about it.
“It definitely shows that the boys are desperate to do well for each other as much as anything else and how much they appreciate playing for this football club, because there was a real purpose to the group over the last couple of days.”
United head to Como on Wednesday looking for a first victory since last month’s Champions League opener against Sabah before attempting to kickstart their Premier League campaign at home to Bournemouth.
The Red Devils, in 13th spot, have their fewest wins at this stage of a top-flight campaign since 1986/87.
“We’re not accepting it as everything’s great by any stretch,” said the under-pressure Carrick. “I’m realistic with that.
“But sometimes you do struggle, sometimes there’s a bit of where you have to find a way through it.”
He added: “I understand the situation doesn’t look too good if you look at it from a certain way, but I’ve got no doubts that we can go on a good run.”

items.content: Dubai: Trying to correct the rupee to a level that does not reflect economic fundamentals through costly, distortionary short-term measures will ultimately prove futile, former Reserve Bank of India governor D Subbarao said."The RBI should allow the rupee to find its level while managing the trajectory, rather than trying to control it at a particular level...(which) would be distortionary and costly, and it will eventually return to its fundamental level," Subbarao told ET in an interview.Also Read: Looking to ride India boom over next decade with IDBI Bank, says Fairfax chief Prem WatsaThe rupee will strengthen when the country attracts durable capital flows based on fundamentals rather than "borrowed resources," he said. His remarks come as the rupee recovered nearly 2% from near-record lows of 96-97 per dollar last week after the central bank introduced measures to curb dollar demand and speculative bets against the currency.The package included a special USD window for public-sector oil marketing companies (OMCs), a Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve (FERR), tighter forex-derivative restrictions, an OMO (open market operation) sale and higher daily CRR (cash reserve ratio) maintenance requirements.Also Read: Fairfax gets 15 years to reduce stake in IDBI Bank to 26%"The RBI's macroprudential measures last week helped the rupee recover a bit, but the most important question is, why is the rupee falling?" Subbarao said. "Ultimately the exchange rate is a function of market expectations and demand and supply. Correcting the rupee against fundamentals will be ultimately futile."On the special Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) (FCNR(B)) dollar deposits scheme, which mobilised about $133 billion by the window close on August 31, he said, "The market knows that these are borrowed resources and it is a costly proposition." Need for tax reforms to attract foreign investment.Subbarao, who served as RBI governor from 2008 to 2013, rejected the perception that the rupee is falling only because of current account pressures coming from oil prices and high import bills. That is the proximate cause, but there are deeper structural issues, he said. "Capital outflows have been a structural cause of the rupee's depreciation," he added."One of the complaints I hear from international investors who look at opportunities across the world is that India is less predictable and more arbitrary in its regulation and interpretation of tax laws," Subbarao said.

items.author: JEHANZEB ABBASI
items.content:
The Punjab prosecution department has told the Supreme Court that sentences should not routinely run concurrently in every criminal case, including cases involving multiple murders.
It has argued that consecutive sentences should be imposed in exceptional cases involving extremely brutal, inhuman and heinous crimes that shock the public conscience, particularly murder, kidnapping, sexual assault and terrorism.
In a written response submitted through Punjab Additional Prosecutor General Tariq Siddique, the provincial government argued that consecutive sentences for multiple murders would reflect the gravity of each offence, reinforce public confidence in the criminal justice system and serve the deterrent and retributive purposes of punishment.
A seven-member larger bench, headed by Justice Jamal Khan Mandokhail, is examining two questions: whether a person convicted of multiple murders should serve life sentences concurrently or consecutively, and how the term of life imprisonment should be determined under Pakistani law.
The next hearing is scheduled for November 10.
The Punjab government maintained that courts should issue reasoned and explicit orders when directing sentences to run consecutively, particularly in exceptional cases involving crimes committed in an exceptionally cruel, barbaric or inhuman manner.
Referring to Section 4 of the Punjab Sentencing Act, 2019, the written response said the objectives of sentencing included punishing offenders, preventing and reducing crime, deterring criminal conduct, rehabilitating offenders and protecting the public.
The government argued that automatically ordering concurrent sentences in cases involving multiple victims could diminish the seriousness of additional offences and create an artificial equivalence between killing one person and murdering several.
"If courts continue to order different sentences to run concurrently in an unguarded and casual manner, a message will be conveyed to society that our criminal justice system makes no distinction between the murder of one person and the murder of several persons," the response stated.
It added that every unlawful taking of a human life should attract a distinct and meaningful legal consequence. Merging multiple sentences into a single concurrent term, the government argued, could undermine the gravity of additional murders.
The response also raised concerns about the practical duration of life imprisonment in Pakistan. It stated that, after accounting for government remissions and sentence reductions, a life sentence could effectively be reduced to around 15 years.

items.author: AFP
items.content:
With China's economy still struggling to recover from the pandemic, even global fashion icons are beginning to feel the pinch as consumers turn instead to the second-hand market or buy upstart new homegrown brands.
Chinese were once massive buyers of luxury Western brands, accounting for around a third of worldwide spending and earning firms such as LVMH and Hermes billions of dollars.
But consumers' belt-tightening has forced them to rethink their strategies, with Louis Vuitton closing five stores in mainland China in the past two years -- including a chocolate boutique in Shanghai -- while Galeries Lafayette shut its Beijing flagship in May.
"People used to compare who had spent more," dance teacher Yuan told AFP at a new retail space in central Shanghai filled with luxury handbags, belts and jewellery items -- all second hand.
"But now everyone compares who got a better deal and spent less," the 24-year-old said at the two-storey warehouse-style store in the centre of the Chinese financial hub.
After plunging as much as 19 percent in 2024, mainland China's personal luxury market contracted another three to five percent in 2025, according to consultancy Bain & Company.
LVMH recently blamed a "slowdown in demand in China" for a drop in organic sales in the third quarter in its fashion and leather goods unit, a slump expected to be mirrored in its peers' results.
China's second-hand luxury market meanwhile exploded 15-20 percent in 2025, according to Bain & Company.
And domestic industry consultancy Insight & Info Consulting estimates total sales reached 38.4 billion yuan ($5.7 billion) in 2025, while forecasting it could top 100 billion yuan by 2030.
At the new Shanghai store Super Zhuanzhuan, shoppers have to wear black gloves to avoid their greasy fingers touching the products.
Customer Phoebe Ma, 24, said that when her mother's generation was young, China "wasn't so developed" and people were initially familiar with only a handful of luxury brands.
"Consequently, they formed a deep-seated impression that, OK, Louis Vuitton was the absolute best and most prestigious," the freelancer told AFP.
"I just feel that the [LV] monogram is dated. It suits my mother's generation, but Gen Z would rather buy trendy Korean brands," she said.
'Work hard to stay relevant'
Chen Luo, head of China consumer research at Bank of America, said shoppers were moving away from associating luxury solely with social status and towards "self-identity, distinction, experience, quality, emotional value (and) cultural relevance".
"Apart from that, China's retail landscape is very digital/social media driven, and China's digital ecosystem is also very unique," Luo told AFP. "Foreign brands should work very hard to stay relevant in this context."
Adding to the headwinds for Western brands is growing cultural and legal friction.
LVMH recently successfully sued Chinese beverage chain Molly Tea for trademark infringement over a four-petal floral pattern resembling the French firm's monogram.
But the lawsuit sparked an online backlash after Chinese internet users and state media pointed out that the motif shares roots with ancient Chinese traditional patterns.
"It feels a bit absurd," said shopper Echo Wang, 31, who works in marketing.
"Molly Tea may be doing well in China, but it's nowhere near Louis Vuitton's global profile... I think some people feel the lawsuit was inappropriate," she told AFP.
LVMH management called its intellectual property "an absolute key asset", but admitted the furore had "had a negative impact".
Analysts emphasise that China remains vital for the global luxury industry.
"In our view, China will still be an important market, although it may not be a growth engine in two to three years," said Luo.
"Luxury spending is normally rebounding in sync with the economy, as usually the wealthy class will be among the first to benefit from economic recovery."

items.content:
Five security operatives, including four soldiers and a Forest Guard, are feared killed in a suspected Boko Haram attack on Tela-Bala and Guyaku communities in Gombi Local Government Area of Adamawa State.
The insurgents reportedly stormed the two communities around 11:20pm on Saturday and opened fire, forcing residents to flee in different directions.
A resident, Bala Guyaku, who spoke with our correspondent by telephone on Sunday morning, said the incident occurred when he and some of his friends were about to retire for the night.
He said they noticed unusual movements before gunshots were heard from a bush path leading into the community.
Gunmen shoot MACBAN leader in Plateau
Four Police officers arrested for allegedly assaulting man in Ogun
Guyaku said, knowing how the insurgents operated, he and his friends remained calm before sneaking out through a little-known footpath.
“The terrorists came on foot and rounded up our villages around past 11pm and started shooting sporadically while most of our people were asleep. Few of us managed to sneak out unhurt through an unpopular footpath to the nearby bush,” he said.
He said the insurgents operated throughout the night and attempted to advance towards Gombi, the headquarters of the local government area, early Sunday morning but were repelled by troops deployed to reinforce security in the area.
“They took the villages through the night until Sunday morning when they attempted to go to Gombi local government headquarters, but the troops repelled them forcefully. We learnt they killed scores, including soldiers and one Forest Guard,” he said.
According to him, the insurgents also attacked a military armoured personnel carrier (APC) stationed at a checkpoint in Guyaku.
He said the attackers attempted to take the APC away but were unsuccessful, adding that they also tried to set it ablaze but failed, before shooting at it at close range, causing severe damage to the vehicle.
Guyaku expressed concern that residents were now afraid to return to their farms to harvest their crops and called on the authorities to deploy more security personnel to the area.
He said the proximity of the communities to the Sambisa Forest in neighbouring Borno State made increased security presence necessary.
Confirming the attack, member representing Gombi Constituency in the Adamawa State House of Assembly, Rufa’i Umar Gombi, said Tela-Bala and Guyaku were attacked by suspected insurgents.
Rufa’i, who spoke by telephone, said he was on his way to the affected communities to assess the situation.
He said he had been informed that scores of people were killed, including four soldiers and a Forest Guard, but stressed that the figures were yet to be officially confirmed by the relevant authorities.
Efforts to speak with the Chairman of Gombi Local Government Area, Mark Ishaya, were unsuccessful, as text message sent to his phone number received a reply saying “Later”, while calls to the same number were not answered or returned as of the time of filing this report.
Attempts to obtain a reaction from the information unit of the Joint Task Force, Operation Hadin Kai, in Maiduguri were also unsuccessful, as the head of the information unit was said to be on leave.
A security analyst, who spoke on condition of anonymity, described the attack as a possible reprisal following a recent military operation in Garaha-Lar, Dugwaba District of Hong Local Government Area, where troops reportedly killed six insurgents about two weeks ago.
The analyst said several other insurgents were believed to have escaped the operation with gunshot injuries.
Meanwhile, the Kumu Gombi I, the traditional ruler of Gombi, His Royal Highness Aggrey Danjuma Ali, blamed unpatriotic informants for aiding criminal groups and insurgents in carrying out attacks in the area.
The monarch spoke on Saturday when he received the new District Head of Garkida, Andrawus Tarfa Fulani, and his entourage during a thank-you visit to his palace in Gombi.
He said individuals who provide support and information to criminal groups were frustrating efforts to restore lasting peace in communities across Gombi Chiefdom.
The monarch also commended the people of Garkida for their contributions to the development of the chiefdom, particularly Architect John Shallangwa and Dr Bala Usman Borkono.
Similarly, Governor Ahmadu Umaru Fintiri has called on the Federal Government to upgrade and modernise Nigeria’s international land borders with technology-driven equipment, including drones, to improve surveillance and combat criminal groups such as Boko Haram and the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP).
Fintiri made the call at the Federal and State Security Administrators Meeting (FSSAM), organised by the Office of the National Security Adviser, Nuhu Ribadu, in Yola on Thursday.
The meeting brought together security administrators and representatives from the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory to deliberate on security challenges affecting the country, particularly the North-East.

items.title: Bollywood Actor Tiger Shroff Targeted in Gun Attack in Mumbai
items.summary:
Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff escaped unharmed after multiple shots were fired at his vehicle in Mumbai’s Juhu area on Sunday evening.
The incident reportedly took place as Shroff was leaving a football ground near Pushpa Park in Juhu. A video of the incident later circulated on social media, showing panic in the area as gunshots could be heard.
Mumbai Police confirmed that a firing incident had taken place within the jurisdiction of Juhu Police Station. Officials said Shroff was safe and had not suffered any gunshot injuries.
Tiger Shroff’s Driver Injured
Reports said unidentified attackers opened fire at Shroff’s vehicle as he was leaving the ground.
His driver was injured in the shooting and received medical treatment. Some reports also said another person in the area suffered injuries during the incident.
Initial reports differ over the exact number of shots fired. Some accounts said three to four rounds were fired, while others reported as many as seven.
Police Launch Investigation

Mumbai Police have launched an investigation and formed multiple teams to identify and trace those responsible.
Investigators are reviewing CCTV footage from the surrounding area and questioning witnesses to establish the sequence of events.
A social media message later surfaced claiming responsibility for the attack in the name of the Lawrence Bishnoi gang. However, police had not immediately verified the authenticity of the claim or confirmed any link between the group and the shooting.
Authorities are continuing to investigate the motive behind the attack and the identities of those involved.

items.author: AHMAD MUKHTAR
items.content:
At dawn on a weekday that should have hummed with commerce, the GT Road and Motorway stand frozen. Multi-ton shipping containers, requisitioned overnight by relevant authorities and dropped onto thoroughfares like giant iron dominoes, choke the entry arteries to Islamabad. Barbed wire glints under streetlights, police vans idle with tear-gas launchers primed, and millions of workers across the urban corridor wake to severed cellular data networks and shuttered transit terminals.
This is the recurring anatomy of modern political agitation; the "Long March." Once conceived as a symbolic pilgrimage to air public grievances, the long march has mutated into an instrument of economic leverage. In contemporary power struggles, leverage is measured not merely by headcounts or speeches, but by the magnitude of paralysis an opposition can force, and the level of economic bleeding a government can endure before conceding ground.
Yet behind the rhetoric of constitutional rights and state sovereignty lies an unyielding ledger. In an economy operating on razor-thin fiscal margins, every day of political blockade, shuttered bazaar, and halted supply chain extracts an irreversible toll, one that strikes hardest not at the political elite negotiating in fortified compounds, but at the daily-wage labourer whose dinner depends on a single day's physical toil.
When national arteries are severed, the macroeconomic damage is immediate, severe, and compounding. According to official estimates compiled by the Ministry of Finance and economic research think tanks, a single day of nationwide disruption, strikes, and capital-bound long marches drains approximately Rs120 billion from national output.
A breakdown of this daily drain illustrates how comprehensively a modern strike metastasizes across sectors:
The services collapse (Rs86 billion/day): Wholesale trade, retail markets, banking clearing houses, urban transport and hospitality absorb over 70% of total output losses. When shopping districts lock their shutters and urban logistics freeze, transactions cannot simply be postponed; many vanish entirely. Industrial paralysis (Rs25 billion/day): Large-scale manufacturing plants grind to a halt as shifts fail to report, export consignments miss feeder vessels at regional ports and raw materials remain stranded inside locked transit corridors.
Agricultural wastage (Rs9 billion/day): Perishable agricultural goods – milk, vegetables, poultry and fresh fruit – rot in stranded trucks along provincial highways, inflicting direct capital losses on farmers and sparking localised food inflation in besieged urban centres.
Fiscal haemorrhage (Rs17 billion/day in lost revenue): The state exchequer suffers a direct blow in missed customs tariffs, sales taxes and withholding receipts. Concurrently, the state burns public funds on tear gas munitions, logistical support and security deployments costing upward of Rs5 to Rs10 billion per threat cycle.
When a march or sit-in stretches over a week or recurs across a volatile quarter, the cumulative shock shaves between 0.2% and 0.5% off the annual real GDP. For Pakistan, striving to transition from emergency stabilisation to sustainable growth under tight multilateral debt covenants, such losses are catastrophic. They wipe out fiscal headroom, suppress quarterly revenue targets and undermine sovereign credit ratings.
The contemporary fallout of street agitation extends far beyond blocked asphalt. In a bid to restrict coordination and quell unrest, authorities routinely deploy blanket mobile internet suspensions and bandwidth throttling. While state managers treat the digital "kill switch" as a low-cost security lever, the modern economy treats it as an unmitigated disaster. Over the past five years, freelance digital services, business process outsourcing (BPO) and software exports have emerged as rare bright spots for foreign exchange earnings.
Industry data indicates that prolonged connectivity disruptions during protest cycles cause software house billings and digital services exports to plunge by as much as 80% during outage windows. Global enterprise clients, operating on rigid Service Level Agreements (SLAs), do not accommodate geopolitical friction; an unrendered software patch or missed offshore support shift leads to cancelled retainers and blacklisted vendors. Similarly, physical exporters face prohibitive penalties. Textile mills, the backbone of export receipts, operate on unforgiving fashion calendar cycles. Stranded containers mean missed shipping windows, forcing manufacturers to charter emergency airfreight at five to eight times standard ocean transit costs, or face outright cancellation of seasonal purchase orders. Foreign buyers, observing chronic instability, quietly reallocate future supply chains to more predictable regional competitors in Vietnam, Bangladesh and India.
While macro figures outline national erosion, the human crisis plays out on the sidewalks. The most perverse reality of the protest economy is its regressive incidence: those who hold no stake in the political contest pay the highest price. In Pakistan's sprawling urban centres, between 70% and 80% of the non-agricultural labour force works within the informal economy. These are the pushcart vendors, port porters, auto-rickshaw drivers, construction day-labourers and loading dock coolies. They do not have remote-work contingencies, severance packages or salaried bank deposits. They live in a cash-in-hand ecosystem where missing a single shift means an empty cooking pot at night.
Beyond immediate transaction loss, repeated long marches inflict deep structural damage on the psychology of capital. Domestic businesses scale back capital expenditure, choosing cash preservation over modernisation or hiring. For foreign direct investors, predictable rule of law and unhindered movement of goods are non-negotiable prerequisites. When international headlines repeatedly broadcast images of capital encircled by freight containers, commercial confidence dissolves. Corporate planning horizons shrink from five-year capital deployments to 90-day survival tactics. The economy falls into a low-level equilibrium trap: investment stalls, job creation collapses, underemployment deepens and the resulting economic discontent fuels the very popular unrest that leaders mobilise for the next round of protests.
The right to peaceful assembly and free political expression is an indispensable pillar of any functioning democracy. No state can suppress political contestation without sliding into authoritarianism. Conversely, no fragile economy can survive a paradigm where every political disagreement is settled by weaponising public mobility and taking urban commerce hostage. Breaking this destructive feedback loop requires structural reform from both the political class and state managers. Following may be considered in this context.
First, to earmark the designated protest enclaves. Modern democracies channel large-scale demonstrations into dedicated rally grounds equipped with civic facilities, outside critical transit and commercial corridors. The politics of claiming "D-Chowk" or central business arteries must be replaced by structured conventions that allow political display without crippling logistics.
Second, ending the "Container Doctrine". Law enforcement's reflex to immobilise entire provinces with freight blockades and blanket telecommunications shutdowns often causes more economic damage than the marches themselves. Proportional policing, intelligence-led crowd management and targeted security must replace systemic paralysis. Third, institutionalising an Economic Red Line. Political actors must establish a cross-party "Charter of the Economy" – a formal consensus that critical infrastructure, digital connectivity, export supply chains and the livelihoods of informal labourers remain off-limits from partisan warfare.
When political movements measure their strength by how deeply they can paralyse a nation's pulse, victory is an illusion. The state loses revenue, businesses shed markets and democracy loses moral authority. But above all, it is the daily-wage worker, walking miles past cold shipping containers to an empty market, who quietly pays the ransom for political power.
THE WRITER IS AN INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIST

items.author: Shahbaz Khan
items.content:
Pakistan's power sector has been in crisis since 2004, when oil prices spiked by around 56% in a single year. The trend continued until 2008, when prices peaked at almost five times of their initial value in 2004. The country was then heavily dependent upon furnace oil for power generation. As a result, between 2004 and 2008, the annual energy import bill of Pakistan increased by around 2.5 times.
The government attempted to accommodate the impact on the power supply chain through subsidies. But the lack of required fiscal depth and the consequential delayed payments towards the independent power producers (IPPs) resulted in an acute crunch of working capital. This in turn gave birth to the venomous serpent we all know by the name of circular debt. The same pushed the country into the worst power crisis it has ever seen.
The new government in 2013, driven by highly ambitious growth targets and corresponding requirements of power on the grid, launched a new power policy and a massive plan for generation capacity augmentation. Consumption increased promisingly during the period but not as rapidly as capacity. The National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra)'s State of the Industry report of 2017 aptly forewarned about the fast-emerging monster of capacity charge due to the increasing gap between generation capacity and consumption.
As per the report, the capacity payments made in FY2015-16 and FY2016-17 were, respectively, Rs280 billion and Rs350 billion. In the same paragraph, it also tells us that for the value to remain at that of FY2015-16 in FY2018-19, the power sold was required to be 57% higher than its preceding year, ie 2017-18. However, the actual gain was even less than 2%.
Unfortunately, since 2019 till 2026, GDP growth has generally remained sluggish. The same in turn has continued to further increase the ratio of the capacity charge in the payments to the sellers. As a result, we have already paid around $40 billion in this respect during the period. This could, of course, have been largely avoided by incorporating informed and stringent qualifiers, for situations triggering capacity payments, in the "take or pay" clauses of the power purchase agreements (PPAs).
A major catalyst was the introduction of the Net Metering Regulations in September 2015, associated with solar power. Due to the economic benefits it offered, it virtually caused an exodus of users from the grid. For example, industrial power consumption from the grid was 29,885 gigawatt hours (GWh) in FY2020-21 and 29,114 GWh by 2024-25, despite a 7.5% increment in users in this category on the DISCO grid during the period.
To me, the magnitude of the impact solar ingress has caused in our economy is that out of its aggregate installed solar capacity, hardly 13% is integrated with the grid. After applying the commonly used capacity utilisation factor in the range of 18% to 22%, the estimated maximum net capacity of the off-grid system alone comes out to be above 10,000MW. The utilisation factor is primarily a function of a solar panel's efficiency, its exposure to sunlight hours and associated irradiance in each such hour. The above deduced capacity is already 42% of the average power demand which prevails on our grid in summers. Solar batteries are also improving this off-grid capacity further by keeping the power available from the same source even after sunset.
While the above transformation continues along with the augmentation of installed grid capacity, the utility bills of those on the grid continue to balloon with the impact of the increasing capacity charge. Yet the tariff structure still largely operates in the mode of power scarcity by charging higher per unit for higher consumption. Otherwise, widespread use of electricity for domestic and commercial cooking and heating may help a lot in this regard. Additionally, even partial diversion of the pertaining gas to industry can also reduce imports of expensive liquefied natural gas (LNG).
A highly encouraging development, though initiated under International Monetary Fund (IMF) pressure, is the effort which is under way since early last year to eliminate captive power and divert the associated load to the grid. This would, of course, also result in sparing around 280 million standard cubic feet per day (mmscfd) of processed gas for more efficient applications. Available data for the past fiscal year also indicates the effort is on the right track. However, its long-term success is largely conditional on the dependability of power supply to industrial units as per their stringent operational requirements.
The above measures can definitely go a long way in increasing the consumption of the grid's load and minimising capacity charge. However, I apprehend that the recent introduction of net-billing may not prove to be of much use. The fact that purchase of solar batteries in FY2025-26 increased by around 2.5 times compared with the preceding year rather indicates that even those partially on the grid now may soon be 100% off-grid.
This trend of opting for alternative avenues is visible in energy uses other than electricity too. For example, as per the Energy Yearbook 2025, the aggregate conventionally documented consumption of energy by the industrial sector experienced marked reduction of around 46% since 2020 till 2025. Solar ingress is not the only factor accounting for the entire gap. Higher utility costs have compelled industry to adopt alternative fuels like coal and wood too. As per a recent study, coal contributes 20% of the textile sector's energy mix. No wonder use of solid fuel boilers has increased considerably in recent years.
Similarly, the Energy Yearbook reports decline of 58% by volume in the use of coal since 2021 till 2025 in the brick-kilns industry. Probably, to accommodate economic factors, it is being used together with crop residues and in some cases even fuels like used tyres, lube oil, plastic and textile waste.
What is to be done
Based on the above, it is evident that we should be very cautious while intervening in solarisation. It has proven to be the biggest saviour for our economy. In addition to its contribution in savings in energy imports, the GDP it is annually shouldering is many times more. Secondly, the perennially open drain on the economy called capacity charge continues to widen. Therefore, there is a clear and urgent requirement for renegotiating the evidently pro-sellers' power purchase agreements and bringing the required balance to them.
Thirdly, we need to keep an eye on the changes in our energy fabric in the context of our carbon footprint and commitments to the United Nations regarding reduction in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.
THE WRITER IS A PETROLEUM ENGINEER AND AN OIL AND GAS MANAGEMENT PROFESSIONAL
