items.author: ZAFAR BHUTTA
items.content:
With plans underway to encourage the United States to invest in the mineral-rich Balochistan province, the government is going to organise the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum (PMIF) on November 12-13.
PMIF26 was originally scheduled to be held on April 8-9 in Islamabad but was rescheduled. During the last event, the US and its allies dominated the conference while Chinese participation was not much prominent. Later, a separate event was held for Chinese investors.
So far, no US company is operating in Balochistan but Pakistan is now urging Washington to lead investment in Balochistan's minerals despite security risks. Earlier, a Canadian firm delayed work on the Reko Diq copper and gold mining project due to the beginning of US-Iran war.
The last year's edition of the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum attracted 5,000 delegates from more than 50 countries. The event saw the signing of 16 memoranda of understanding (MoUs) and featured 18 panel discussions. For the upcoming event, Pakistan is desperately looking towards the US to invest in mineral resources in Balochistan.
Export-Import Bank of the US has already approved $1.25 billion in December 2025, which the US embassy said could unlock up to $2 billion in American mining equipment and services exports and support roughly 13,500 jobs in both countries. Reko Diq's first-year shipments, once operational, are projected to generate $2.8 billion in exports.
On September 8, 2025, Pakistan's Frontier Works Organisation and Missouri-based US Strategic Metals (USSM) signed two MoUs focusing on the development and processing of critical minerals, including rare-earth elements, and logistics services. The agreements establish a framework for collaboration in scores of critical minerals essential for defence, aerospace and technology industries.
According to the Prime Minister's Office, the partnership will begin immediately with the export of readily available minerals from Pakistan, including antimony, copper, gold, tungsten and rare-earth elements. This lays the foundation for scaling up towards establishing a USSM's highly flexible poly-metallic refinery in Pakistan.
The refinery will produce intermediate and finished products to meet the rapidly growing demand in the US market. The first phase is envisaged to result in an investment of $500 million in critical minerals. Next steps include forming dedicated teams to explore the full potential of Pakistan's vast resource base, identifying critical minerals for immediate export and building a strong base for long-term partnership in exploration, extraction and processing. Importantly, their cooperation will prioritise sustainability, profitability and environmental responsibility to ensure benefits for the people of both nations.
Pakistan's mineral reserves are estimated at around $8 trillion and spread over 600,000 square kilometres, according to the Institute of Cost and Management Accountants (ICMA). The vast mineral resources highlight the massive economic potential of the mining sector. The sector has historically contributed less than 3% to the gross domestic product (GDP), ICMA said. With strong governance and security, annual mineral exports could rise from about $3 billion to $8 billion and GDP growth could climb from roughly 3% to 6%.
The challenge, however, is to turn the geological potential into bankable projects, exports, jobs and industrial capacity. This requires more than mining and greater focus on exploration, geological data, modern technology, infrastructure, financing, predictable regulation, environmental safeguards and partnerships with international companies. Pakistan's policy direction is increasingly focused on building that ecosystem.
Reko Diq project
Reko Diq, located in Balochistan's Chagai district, has one of the world's largest undeveloped copper and gold deposits. The project is a joint venture between Barrick Mining, which holds a 50% stake, the Balochistan government with 25% shareholding and three federal state-owned enterprises having 25% interest. In February 2025, Barrick announced completion of the updated feasibility study for the project. Reko Diq will be a major contributor to Pakistan's economy and is also expected to have a transformative impact on Balochistan.
The updated study estimates a 37-year mine life, with total capital investment of $8.83 billion. The project will be developed in two phases, where phase-I requires around $5.6-$6 billion. Production is expected to begin by the end of 2028.
In phase-I, the project will process 45 million tonnes of ore annually, producing about 240,000 tonnes of copper and 297,000 ounces of gold. Phase-II, planned for 2034, will double the processing capacity to 90 million tonnes per year, raising average annual production to 460,000 tonnes of copper and 520,000 ounces of gold for first 10 years.
According to the feasibility study, Reko Diq has probable mineral reserves of around 3 billion tonnes, containing an estimated 15 million tonnes of copper and 26 million ounces of gold. Barrick estimates the project could generate $90 billion in operating cash flow and $70 billion in free cash flow over its mine life. Reko Diq is the largest foreign direct investment (FDI) project in Balochistan.
International lenders have assembled a financing package exceeding $2.6 billion. The Asian Development Bank approved $410 million in August 2025 – $300 million in loans and a $110 million guarantee for Balochistan's equity stake. The International Finance Corporation and World Bank approved a $700 million concessional loan in June 2025.
Global copper demand is forecast to grow 24% to reach 42.7 million tonnes a year by 2035, driven by electrification, according to Wood Mackenzie. The International Energy Agency has said electricity demand from AI-driven data centres will accelerate this further.

items.author: Our Correspondent
items.content:
Pakistan's short-term inflation remained in double digits at 11.38% year-on-year for the week ended October 15, 2026 as the fallout from the Middle East conflict continued to keep energy prices elevated, according to data released by the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS).
The Sensitive Price Indicator (SPI), which tracks 51 essential items from 50 markets in 17 cities, edged down 0.04% week-on-week. The combined index stood at 372.43 against 372.58 a week earlier and 334.39 in the corresponding week of last year.
The year-on-year reading has stayed above 10% for several consecutive weeks, driven mainly by sharp increases in fuel and related costs linked to the US-Iran war, disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi attacks affecting regional supply routes. Petrol was 49.60% higher than a year earlier, diesel rose 43.98% and LPG jumped 68.95%. Electricity charges for Q1 were up 58.59%.
Among food items, onions recorded the steepest annual increase of 75.19%, followed by wheat flour (35.13%) and chicken (20.77%). Mutton rose 14.90% and beef 12.27%. On the other hand, tomatoes were 63.65% cheaper year-on-year, potatoes fell 39.93%, sugar declined 23.20% and eggs were down 19.83%.
On a weekly basis, prices of 23 items (45.10%) increased, seven items (13.72%) decreased and 21 items (41.18%) remained unchanged. The biggest weekly drops came in tomatoes (23.05%), onions (4.90%), bananas (2.59%) and petrol (0.70%). Sugar and gur also eased slightly.
Weekly gains were led by gram pulse (4.97%), wheat flour (3.36%) and chicken (3.31%). Eggs, mash pulse, masoor pulse, firewood and diesel also registered modest increases.
Across consumption quintiles, the week-on-week decline ranged from 0.01% to 0.06%. The lowest expenditure group (Q1) saw a 0.06% weekly drop and an 8.19% year-on-year rise, while the highest group (Q5) recorded a 12.09% annual increase.
The SPI serves as a key short-term gauge of price pressures faced by households. Elevated energy costs continue to feed into transport, production and food prices, keeping inflationary pressures intact despite the modest weekly easing.

Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance said it welcomed competition from Elon Musk's Starlink and that its own satellite services were also ‌awaiting clearance, its first response to ‌accusations that ​Ambani was blocking Starlink's India launch.
Musk, the world's richest man, ​has repeatedly accused the Indian government ‌and Ambani of stalling Starlink's ​years-long efforts to launch in a market of more than a billion internet subscribers. India has denied any bias in its approval process.
The Friday statement, which did not name ⁠Musk, comes days before Reliance Industries' digital unit Jio Platforms seeks a $108 billion valuation in India's ‌largest IPO to date.
Read: Musk steps up attack on Ambani, shares reports on Reliance-linked BJP donations
Jio houses Reliance's telecom arm, which has over 530 million customers and is a potential competitor to Starlink in India's internet market.
"At Reliance, we have never feared competition," the conglomerate said ⁠on Friday, addressing "remarks about Reliance and the Indian market" in ⁠a statement it ​said was intended ‌to "place the facts on record".
Starlink responded on Friday, saying it had worked with Indian regulators and the industry for more than five years and had built dedicated systems, gateways and other infrastructure in the country with the required government approvals.
"Starlink is ready to connect India with high-speed internet," the company said on X.
In a separate post responding to Reliance, Musk said: "Much appreciated".
India’s long wait for satellite internet
Musk's posts on X have ranged from asking whether Ambani was the "real boss" of India to addressing ⁠him as "Prime Minister Ambani" and asking whether he would allow Starlink to compete.
The attacks mark a sharp turn for Musk, who has a warm public rapport with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and come as New Delhi courts foreign investment and negotiates a trade deal with Washington.
Also Read: Influential Hindu group urges India to block Starlink amid Musk-Ambani feud
India has licensed Starlink, Jio's satellite internet arm, and Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb to operate services, but none has the security clearance needed to launch.
Satellite broadband could help ⁠to connect hundreds of millions of Indians who remain offline, mostly ​in rural and remote areas.
Musk has said he would price Starlink affordably in India to take on Jio's low-cost internet plans.
Cheap data is how Jio built its presence in India, and Musk has used the same strategy in markets like Kenya to ​disrupt local telecom players.

items.author: editorial
items.content:
Pakistan, a perpetual recipient of assistance from the Washington-based lending institutions – the IMF and World Bank – has earned the unique honour of being named as the incoming chair of the Boards of Governors of the Fund and the World Bank Group for next year. It is the first time since 1953 that the developing country has secured this august seat. Pakistan has entered into 25 IMF programmes, and has also been a major recipient of assistance from ABD and other lending agencies. Ahad Khan Cheema, who is also Pakistan's governor to the World Bank, will shortly assume the position in Bangkok. It is a distinction, indeed, as Pakistan was chosen from among more than 15,000 participants across 191 countries.
Pakistan has been at the vanguard of advocating reforms to global organisations. At the United Nations, it has consistently advocated for abolishing the veto power, and opposed the expansion of the Security Council's permanent membership. Currently, it is serving a two-year term as an elected non-permanent member of the UN Security Council and holds the final presidency of the UN Conference on Disarmament for 2026. Islamabad, likewise, assumed the chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for the 2026–2027 and is also heading the Governing Council of the Borrowers' Platform for the 2026–2027 work plan. These credentials illustrate the country's positive role, amongside its efforts to mediate between Iran and the United States. The landmark Islamabad MoU, which the UN Secretary-General termed as the 'framework for permanent peace,' is a case in point.
With a leadership role at IMF and the World Bank, Pakistan will be better positioned to contribute to global economic and development discussions. Its intention has always been to facilitate constructive dialogue among member countries, strengthen South-South cooperation, and work against poverty and discrimination. As an ardent supporter of multilateralism, Pakistan believes in a just economic order in which the dominance of an elite group is reduced to give developing countries a greater say. This is essential to building stronger institutions and mobilising private capital to support sustainable and inclusive growth.

items.author: editorial
items.content:
The digital world has opened many doors for children all over the world to learn, connect, and imagine futures beyond their immediate surroundings. But in the wrong hands, the same technologies that empower them can be weaponised to harm them. In just one year, an estimated 1.5 million internet-using children in Pakistan between the ages of 12 and 17 experienced at least one form of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse. These are crisis-level numbers, and they are not being caused in some dark street corner or seedy hotel, but in the victims' own homes.
The Disrupting Harm in Pakistan report, a study of the issue backed by UNICEF and several other international organisations, features a brutal assessment of the situation. In most cases, the perpetrator was someone the child knew. Perhaps even worse is the fact that in almost two out of three cases, the child told no one. They stayed silent because they felt embarrassed or simply didn't know who to turn to. When an abused child is silenced by society, the entire society has collectively failed at one of its most basic duties.
The report underscores what many child protection experts have long warned: Pakistan's legal framework contains gaps that allow perpetrators to act with impunity, and survivors face daunting barriers to disclosure, reporting and justice. The National Commission on the Rights of the Child has previously called for legislative reforms that criminalise all forms of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation and abuse, and for child-centered, trauma-informed reporting and justice mechanisms. These are very realistic, common-sense suggestions.
But laws alone are meaningless. We need to break down the culture of silence and replace it with one where children can confidently talk to their parents and teachers about online safety without being shamed. We need schools that teach digital literacy alongside algebra. We need platforms that prioritise child safety over profit. And we need a justice system that treats every child's testimony with urgency and dignity.

items.title: One nation, one foreclosure
items.summary:

items.author: Farrukh Khan Pitafi
items.content:
A pluralistic Indian state based on Ganga-Jamuni syncretic culture was always a transitory bargain, a holding pattern until the underlying reality asserted itself. Ambedkar's Constitution was as alien to the casteist realities of India as he was to the religion of his birth. It was merely a face-saving arrangement for a Westernised elite to prepare the world for India's eventual descent into prejudiced madness. Fundamentally, this secular republic was a loan underwritten by the real owners of the land: the businessmen whose panic over Liaquat Ali Khan's 1947 tax-heavy budget helped dictate the borders of partition. The so-called Brahmin-Bania alliance, if you will. Today, that debt is being collected with interest.
What is this underlying reality? In his foundational 1966 text, "Bunch of Thoughts", the second supremo of the RSS, MS Golwalkar, laid out the blueprint. The goal, he wrote, was clear: "The most important and effective step will be to bury deep for good all talk of a federal structure of our country's Constitution, to sweep away the existence of all 'autonomous' or semi-autonomous 'states' within the one State viz., Bharat and proclaim 'One Country, One State, One Legislature, One Executive'." A long journey which begins with One Nation, One Election.
But to what end? On 30 November 1949, just four days after the Constituent Assembly adopted the document, the RSS mouthpiece Organiser openly lamented that it ignored the caste-based hierarchies of ancient India: "To this day his (Manu's) laws as enunciated in the Manusmriti excite the admiration of the world and elicit spontaneous obedience and conformity. But to our constitutional pundits that means nothing."
See how the Manusmriti excites this admiration: Chapter 8, Verse 417: "A Brahmana may confidently seize the goods of Sudra (the lowest varna, mostly today's OBCs); for, as that (slave) can have no property, his master may take his possessions." Chapter 10, Verse 129: "No collection of wealth must be made by a Sudra, even though he be able (to do it); for a Sudra who has acquired wealth, gives pain to Brahmanas." Chapter 10, Verse 51: "But the dwellings of the Kandalas and Svapakas (Dalits) shall be outside the village; they must be made Apapatras (permanently dispossessed), and their wealth (shall be) dogs and donkeys." Chapter 10, Verse 52: "Their dress (shall be) the garments of the dead, (they shall eat) their food from broken dishes, black iron (shall be) their ornaments, and they must always wander from place to place." This attitude towards property rights will become abundantly clear shortly.
You may argue India's complexity makes such regression impossible. For evidence, look at the current regime. The incumbent recently had his cabinet declare him the longest-serving prime minister in history, a fiction achieved by erasing Jawaharlal Nehru's first five years from the records. Despite tanking the economy and carrying the shadow of the Gujarat massacres, his grip remains absolute. He rules with unyielding centralisation, reducing even the mighty RSS to a subservient echo chamber.
Institutional independence is now purely decorative. The state machinery is captured. Unsurprisingly, the ruling establishment is the world's richest political party, bankrolled by a handful of billionaires. The system is entirely compromised to ensure these tycoons face no federal hurdles.
The final stumbling block is the South. The Dravidian states, with their entrenched pluralism and secularism, represent everything the new order must destroy. To neutralise them, the establishment deployed two Trojan horses: "One Nation, One Election" and a looming delimitation exercise. Both are designed to permanently disenfranchise the southern opposition and reduce autonomous states to modern-day apapatras.
When a compromised election commission holds simultaneous elections, it produces magical results. But the case of delimitation is even more surgical.
For decades, parliamentary representation remained frozen to reward southern states for controlling their populations. To break this freeze, the establishment deployed a brilliant Trojan horse: the Women's Reservation Bill. By inserting Article 334A into the 106th Amendment, the government hardwired the 33 per cent gender quota to take effect only after a post-2026 delimitation exercise. Oppose the redrawing of the electoral map to save federalism, and you are anti-women.
Once that trap springs, the mathematics of an expanded 848-seat Lok Sabha is ruthlessly stark. Uttar Pradesh is projected to gain up to 63 new seats and Bihar 39. Two states alone will capture over 100 new seats, permanently anchoring national power in the cow belt, which is keener on Modi than others. Conversely, the Dravidian states, rewarded for their governance success, will see their parliamentary share slashed from 24 per cent to about 20 per cent. This political erasure cements an economic one. Tamil Nadu receives roughly 29 paise back for every rupee it sends to the Centre, whereas Uttar Pradesh receives nearly 3 rupees back.
Once the South's voice is made irrelevant and the establishment captures a two-thirds majority in both houses of Parliament, the constitutional fiction can be discarded, and a Hindu Rashtra formally proclaimed. In practical terms, this means the country's overwhelming majority will lose their constitutional protections and, eventually, their property rights. This targets lower castes like Shudras or OBCs at roughly 60 per cent of the population, Dalits and Scheduled Castes at 16.6 per cent, and Adivasis and Scheduled Tribes at 8.6 per cent. The ongoing protests by marginalised communities against massive land acquisitions by regime-aligned billionaires like Adani are proof of the concept. They are the blueprint in action. Foreclosure at last.
I am often asked how this domestic restructuring is relevant to Pakistan or the broader region. The Hindu Rashtra project is intrinsically linked to the geographical fantasy of Akhand Bharat. Once the new state successfully renegotiates India's internal social contract, it plans to export this model to the neighbourhood. This expansion will not rely on conventional military invasions. Instead, the blueprint involves dismantling a target country's political and social order from within, engineering a collapse so complete that dismemberment and absorption into India appear as voluntary choices. Here too, property matters more than people.
Through state-promoted cinema like the Dhurandhar duology, the establishment is already making the exceptional claim that its operatives are permanently embedded within the power structures of neighbouring states. Even if entirely fictional, this broadcasts their ultimate ambition.

items.author: Imtiaz Gul
items.content:
Can I respond to this question over lunch in private?
This evasive, though light-veined, response by Dinesh Trivedi, the Indian High Commissioner, represented the catch 22 situation that both India and Bangladesh are trapped in over the issue of ex-PM Sheikh Hasina.
When pressed harder by several locals on Dhaka's request for Hasina's extradition, Trivedi referenced the "well-structured legal process currently underway in New Delhi" to extricate himself from the extremely uncomfortable situation during the recent Bay of Bengal Conversations 2026.
In a typical deflective way, the Indian envoy held the Bangladesh Army responsible for flying Hasina to India with an innocent qualification; as neighbours it was our duty to accept the situation on that day (August 5, 2024).
Such postulations, nevertheless, can hardly disguise a bitter reality; Bangladesh's political spectrum remains deeply divided over the fate of Sheikh Hasina. For many Bangladeshis, she must face justice for the murder and maiming of thousands of opposition activists, students during the July 2024 uprising. For them, Hasina's 15 year rule embodied brute repression and a foreign policy beholden to India at the cost of broader national interest.
Even the International Crimes Tribunal sentenced Hasina to death for crimes against humanity (on 17 November 2025). This verdict came on the back of raging public sentiment over the Hasina era.
Since Sheikh Hasina's 15-year era was marked by enforced disappearances (up to 4000, though figures vary), extrajudicial killings, arbitrary arrests, torture, politically motivated criminal cases and the use of administrative and legal mechanisms to marginalise and silence opposition parties, the younger generation seems unforgiving. The calls for bringing the former PM to justice resonate almost everywhere.
Between 2009 and 2024, the security establishment, intelligence agencies in particular, were used indiscriminately to abuse, harass and punish the political rivals. And hence the popular demand to hold her accountable.
Yet, for India, the former prime minister still counts as a "treasured guest" and hence New Delhi's nearly flat refusal to hand her over.
The issues also exposes limitations of any government in Dhaka; Bangladesh is almost surrounded by Indian territory, with the Bay of Bengal to its south and a short border with Myanmar to its southeast. Its land border with India extends roughly 4,096 kilometres. This makes India an unavoidable neighbour in Bangladesh's security, economic and diplomatic calculations – also called the "tyranny of geography" by Ali Riaz, a Bangladesh-origin Distinguished Professor at the University of Illinois.
Geography – a powerful structural factor – clearly imposes limits to Bangladesh's relations with India. No surprise that a recent speech Prime Minister Tarique Rahman delivered at the Bay of Bengal conference betrayed a deliberate shift towards diplomatic moderation, economic pragmatism and regional engagement. Though Rehman focused mostly on democratic transparency, accountability and indiscriminate rule of law, he did allude to the inevitability of normal relations with all neighbours.
That's why conscious transition from emotional vows of revenge to guarded rational positive messaging is clearly discernible in the government's narratives, possibly in view of the limits that inescapable geography and the Hasina legacy – deeply entrenched loyalists, supporters within civil-military hierarchies – place on the government.
Additionally, 15 years of Hasina's rule changed the institutional, political and economic landscape, and those networks, habits and loyalties cannot disappear with one electoral transition. At the same time, India's unusually close relationship with Hasina created a structural Indian stake in Bangladesh that complicates Rahman's effort to reform the state and redefine foreign policy.
While pursuing democratic ideals, Bangladesh also wants relations based on mutual respect and equality, Rehman underlined. The language of dialogue, partnership and mutual respect a clear signal, amplified also by Andaleeve Rahman, Rehman's information minister.
We are determined to take on the multitude of challenges that are upon our head and hence not interested in bloc politics. We want to stay clear of big power rivalries to be able to focus on internal economic development, improving governance and ensuring stability, the minister explained, in what appeared to be an indirect message to India.
Both the PM and the Information Minister as well as a number of Bangladeshi participants at the Bay of Bengal Conversation appeared to project their country as a pivotal access to maritime trade, regional supply chains and potentially more efficient transport links between India, Nepal, Bhutan and the Bay of Bengal.
Rahman's speech explicitly identified shipping, fisheries, tourism, energy and regional supply chains as areas of opportunity, without detailing the steps being taken to address the public anxiety over the injustice and oppression perpetrated under Hasina. Will he be able to deliver justice without turning accountability into another instrument of political revenge – as is the norm in South Asia and many African countries? This requires investigating disappearances, prosecuting those credibly implicated in abuses, providing redress to victims and ensuring fair trials regardless of political affiliation.
Rehman's predicament also shows that repression and autocratic regimes deeply scar the society, making it difficult for the victims and those at the receiving end to get over it. High-handed politics – rough treatment of the opposition, enforced disappearances, etc – subvert the rule of law to the extent that turns correction an arduous job – a double edged sword.
That is why the critical test that lies ahead for Rahman is whether he will be able to normalise relations with India on the one hand, and whether the pressing circumstances would allow him to break with the methods of the past or reproduce them under a different political leadership wrapped in a self-serving lingo.

items.author: M Zeb Khan
items.content:
For generations, the Pathans have been handed two compliments that should perhaps have made us suspicious long ago: "Pathans are very brave" and "Pathans are very devout Muslims." As a Pathan and a practising Muslim, I increasingly wonder whether we should politely return both compliments. Not because Pathans lack courage. Not because Islam matters any less to us. But because courage is not encoded in Pakhtun blood nor does any ethnicity hold a monopoly over religious devotion. Brave people and sincere believers exist in every society.
The more interesting question is therefore not whether these descriptions are true. It is: why has it been so important to keep telling Pathans that they are exceptionally brave and exceptionally religious? History provides uncomfortable clues. The stereotype of the Pakhtun as an inherently martial people did not begin with the Afghan jihad. Colonial representations routinely portrayed frontier Pathans as warriors, violent tribesmen and members of a "martial race". Academic research suggests that such ideas outlived colonialism and continued influencing state perceptions of the tribal areas.
Then came Afghanistan. By 1979, rebellion was already under way against Afghanistan's communist government. Declassified American records show Pakistan supporting Afghan insurgents before the Soviet invasion of December that year; subsequently, the US, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan built an enormous covert pipeline of money and weapons for the Afghan resistance, much of it operating through Pakistan. Resistance to foreign occupation was real, and Afghans possessed their own reasons and agency for fighting.
But geopolitics requires mobilisation, and mobilisation works best when it speaks the language people already associate with themselves. For Pathans, two buttons were particularly easy to press. You are brave; therefore, you do not retreat. You do not fear death. You are a true Muslim; therefore, when war is presented as jihad, questioning it can begin to feel like questioning one's faith. During General Zia-ul-Haq's rule, state Islamisation and the Afghan jihad became deeply intertwined.
Human beings possess agency but agency is never exercised in a vacuum. If, from childhood, a man is repeatedly told that courage defines his ethnic worth, refusing to fight carries a psychological price. If faith is added to the equation, refusal may appear simultaneously cowardly, culturally dishonourable and religiously suspect. The person may still choose. But somebody has already helped construct the menu from which he chooses. And eventually the narrative becomes self-fulfilling. This is how the Pathans have been conditioned and which has caused much of their suffering.
Afghanistan became one of the great displacement tragedies of modern history. UNHCR records that the refugee population in Pakistan and Iran reached around six million during the 1980s. War mutated into civil war, Taliban rule, international intervention, insurgency and renewed Taliban rule. On the Pakistani side, the vocabulary changed from jihad to militancy, extremism, counterterrorism and military operations. The geography changed much less. Swat, Waziristan, Bajaur and other Pakhtun areas repeatedly became theatres of conflict.
After nearly half a century, perhaps Pathans should ask a brutally simple question: What have these flattering titles of bravery and faithfulness done for us? Where is it written that our children must inherit extraordinary courage rather than ordinary childhoods? Why must the Pakhtun continuously prove that he is fearless? Why must his religious sincerity be certified through political causes chosen by others? Perhaps the most revolutionary demand Pathans can now make is surprisingly modest: the right to be ordinary.
The right to send children to school rather than to ideological battlefields. The right to admire a scientist as much, if not more, as a warrior. The right to build businesses, labs, universities and tech companies. The right to question a cleric without surrendering Islam. The right to refuse someone else's war without surrendering honour. And the right to live without constantly demonstrating that we are braver or more religious than everyone else. In a nutshell, they should be allowed to say no to "exceptionalism".

Pakistan Telecommunication Company Limited (PTCL) has earned two prestigious honors at the Dragons of Asia Awards 2026, with its social impact initiative, Dil Se Ba-Ikhtiar winning a Bronze Dragon in the Best in Digital category, while its Mother’s Day campaign received a Black Dragon in Marketing Discipline.
The recognition reflects the company’s efforts to leverage communications and digital technology to advance meaningful social causes, and contribute to a more inclusive and empowered society. It also underscores PTCL’s broader ambition to create value beyond connectivity by supporting initiatives that address real societal needs and enable individuals and communities to realize their full potential.
PTCL’s Dil Se Ba-Ikhtiar initiative mirrors the company’s commitment to women’s socioeconomic empowerment through digital inclusion, skills development and entrepreneurial opportunity. Ba-Ikhtiar, now spanning 22 flood affected districts nationwide, demonstrates how digital access and skills development can help create pathways towards greater economic independence.
PTCL’s ‘Mother’s Day: More Support for Mothers’ campaign similarly reflects the company’s belief that meaningful communication should extend beyond awareness to encourage tangible support for people and causes that matter. The campaign sought to encourage a more empathetic and supportive approach to motherhood, particularly with regards to new mothers’ fight against post-partum depression.
Commenting on the achievement, Amad Khan, Chief Marketing Officer, PTCL, said,

The Mishkaham Bokkos, Jatau Yohanna Samkwar, has reportedly died after suspected gunmen shot him at his residence in Daffo, Bokkos local government area of Plateau State.
The community leader was reportedly shot in the leg on October 13 after which he was rushed to the hospital in Mangu but died hours later.
Bulus Dabit, National President of Mwaghavul Development Association, confirmed the incident, adding that the deceased was attacked at his residence.
He said “The Mwaghavul people again mourns the murder of Mishkaham Yohanna Jatau Samkwar the Community Leader of Mwaghavul people in Bokkos LGA.who was attacked by unknown gunmen last night the 13th October 2026 at his residence at Daffor, in Bokkos LGA. He died at the cottage hospital Mangu following gun injuries he sustained from the attack.”
Tinubu appoints 4 INEC National Commissioners, 2 RECs
‘Nigerians living in lawless country’, PRP tackles Tinubu over insecurity
The President recalled that the deceased’s son, Zuhumnan Nanle, was kidnapped on 03/10/2026, at Daffo , adding that “his son was released on the 12 October, 2026. This release was followed immediately by an attack on the family during which the Mishkaham was shot on the evening of 13 October 2026. It is very clear that the recent attackers are the kidnappers.”
The Mwaghavul Development Association therefore condemned what it described as “terror and warns the attackers of dire consequences and demand justice for the decease by the immediate arrest and prosecution of the suspects by relevant security agencies and the judiciary respectively. We demand an immediate stopage of the selective killing of our people.”
Chairman of the Community Peace Observers in Bokkos LGA, Kefas Mallai, also confirmed the incident, expressing concern over the prevailing security situation in the area.
Mallai said, “They came to his house at night and shot him in the leg. He was rushed to a hospital in Daffo, but he was later referred to another hospital. Unfortunately, he died.”
He disclosed that the traditional ruler’s son had allegedly been kidnapped earlier but was released on Sunday, before the attackers reportedly returned to the residence and shot his father.
Mallai lamented that repeated attacks and killings had become a source of concern in Bokkos, adding that residents continued with their daily activities despite the prevailing security challenges.
He said, “The incidents are too many in Bokkos. Almost every day, somebody is killed or something happens. The situation is becoming normalised to the extent that people no longer report every incident because they have become used to hearing about killings.”
“People are still moving about, markets are open and businesses are going on. People cannot stop running their businesses because of fear, even though the security situation remains a concern,” he added.

items.author: Anadolu Agency
items.content:
Morocco announced a new cabinet on Friday, ushering in a historic era with the country’s first female prime minister leading a four-party coalition.
According to state-run Maghreb Arabe Presse, King Mohammed VI received members of the new cabinet, led by Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, and presided over their appointment ceremony at the Royal Palace in the capital, Rabat.
Fatima is the first Moroccan woman to hold the country’s top government post.
Read: Morocco's king appoints first woman prime minister following election
She will lead a new government formed by a four-party coalition comprising her Authenticity and Modernity Party, the Istiqlal Party, the Socialist Union of Popular Forces and the Party of Progress and Socialism.
The new government includes seven women, including Fatima, compared with six in the previous government led by Aziz Akhannouch.
The new government comprises 32 members, including ministers and ministers-delegate, according to official figures.
Abdelouafi Laftit kept his post as interior minister, alongside Nasser Bourita as foreign minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi as justice minister and Ahmed Toufiq as minister of Islamic affairs and endowments.
The new cabinet also established a Ministry of Artificial Intelligence, Digital Transformation and Administrative Reform, headed by Ahmed Rahhou.
On Monday, the Authenticity and Modernity Party, Istiqlal Party, Socialist Union of Popular Forces and Party of Progress and Socialism announced in a joint statement that they had formed the governing majority following the conclusion of the second round of consultations on forming a government, which began on September 30.
On September 29, King Mohammed VI tasked Fatima with forming a government after her party, the Authenticity and Modernity Party, came first in the September 23 elections with 97 seats.

items.author: Reuters
items.content:
Tencent said on ​Friday that AI agents used to evaluate third-party models displayed web-browsing behaviour not intended ‌by the tech giant, in what appears to be the first known incident of rogue agent actions acknowledged by a major Chinese company.
The statement followed a report by AI-safety research group Swarmchasers on Wednesday, which said "rogue" agents running on ​infrastructure it linked to Tencent Cloud made repeated attempts between September 28 and October 8 ​to retrieve information from Alibaba's Amap, China's equivalent to Google Maps.
Tencent Hunyuan, the ⁠company's artificial intelligence unit, said in a post on X that the activity did not originate ​from its Hunyuan models. Its review found no evidence of deliberate targeting or coordination, it said.
The Swarmchasers ​researchers said the agents sought information such as the commonly used entrances at Chinese parks, museums and zoos.
The actions are not as egregious as those disclosed by US AI companies, which include the hack of open-source platform Hugging Face by ​an OpenAI agent and the lodging of a fake homicide tip by an Anthropic agent.
Read: OpenAI's rogue agents probed Hugging Face for weaknesses two months before major hack
But the disclosure underscores research ​that shows Chinese AI agents can also misrepresent their identity, conceal failures and try to circumvent testing controls.
Tencent said ‌it ⁠took the findings very seriously and was strengthening network access controls and agent monitoring.
Hunyuan is one of China's leading AI model developers, competing with in-house teams at rivals such as Alibaba and ByteDance. ByteDance this week announced the creation of a new unit focused on AI model and agent safety.
Swarmchasers said it used ​the word "rogue" to describe agents ​taking actions outside ⁠their intended scope or completing a task in unintended ways.
Read More: As AI agents act in unexpected ways, is ‘rogue AI’ really here?
After routine automated requests were blocked, the agents tried other methods, including public web tools that could ​open pages and run code, routing requests through other websites and using ​Amap keys ⁠and security codes found in publicly available software code.
Swarmchasers said it found no evidence that the agents breached Amap's main anti-bot safeguards. Most of the 2,818 attempts it recorded either failed or returned anti-bot pages, login ⁠screens, ​or blank results.
Some requests returned information through cached pages and intermediary ​services, including data on visitor arrivals at Chengdu Zoo, Swarmchasers said. The researchers said they could not determine whether an agent ​read the result or completed its task.
Alibaba declined to comment.

items.author: Anne Florentyna
items.content:
Markets regulator SEBI has given its go-ahead to gym chain Cult.fit’s ₹950 Cr IPO about three months after it filed draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) with the regulator.
As per SEBI’s latest processing status, the regulator issued its final observation on the offer documents of Cult.fit on October 12. In SEBI parlance, the issuance of final observations signals the regulator’s go-ahead for a company to proceed with its public issue.
Cult.fit filed its DRHP in July this year. The company’s IPO will comprise a fresh issue of shares worth up to ₹950 Cr and an offer for sale of up to 17.86 Cr shares. As per sources, The total IPO size is likely to be around ₹4,000 Cr.
Early investors like Temasek Holdings, via MacRitchie Investments, Schroders Capital, German fitness operator LifeFit Group, Accel, Tata Digital and cofounder Mukesh Bansal are among the shareholders who plan to offload shares via the OFS.
Cult.fit plans to utilise the funds raised through the fresh issue towards setting up new gym centres, expenditure toward leasing, renting and licensing of existing identified fitness centres, repayment and prepayment of certain borrowings, setting up new exclusive brand outlets, marketing and promotional activities and general corporate purposes.
Axis Capital, Goldman Sachs, Jefferies India, JM Financial and Morgan Stanley India are the book running lead managers (BRLMs) to the issue.
Founded in 2016, Cult.fit operates a chain of gyms and fitness centres and offers online classes for physical and mental wellbeing.
It operated 708 fitness centres across 77 cities in India and had more than ​9.87 Lakh ​paid members as of March 31, 2026. Out of these, 218 centres are owned and operated by the company. The rest are owned or operated by franchises (288 centres) or by independent owners (202 centres).
Cult.fit managed to narrow its net loss for the fiscal year FY26 to ₹251.8 Cr from ₹480.8 Cr in FY25. It posted an operating revenue of ₹1,720.6 Cr, up 41.5% from ₹1,215.5 Cr in FY25. The business benefits from a diversified revenue profile, with fitness services contributing roughly 70% of revenues and the fitness products business accounting for the remaining 30%.
Cult.fit has raised over $800 Mn to date from investors like Zomato, Accel, Kalaari Capital, Chiratae Ventures, South Park Commons, among others.

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
Amid intense competition in the quick home services market, Snabbit incurred a net loss of ₹167.8 Cr in the financial year ended March 31, 2026 (FY26) as against a loss of ₹5.7 Cr in FY25.
Important to note that FY26 was Snabbit’s first full financial year of operations following its service launch in August 2024. Thus, comparability of the two fiscals is limited.
Snabbit posted an operating revenue of ₹12.2 Cr in FY26 compared to ₹26.3 Lakh in FY25. Platform services generated ₹10.8 Cr in revenue, while uniform sales to service professionals contributed the remaining ₹1.4 Cr. The startup recognises platform service revenue net of discounts it bears.
Including other income of ₹14.8 Cr, the startup’s total income for the fiscal stood at ₹27 Cr. Interest on bank deposits contributed ₹14.1 Cr, with the remainder largely coming from gains on mutual fund sales.
Snabbit held ₹292.2 Cr in cash and bank balances and ₹26.6 Cr in mutual fund investments, totalling ₹318.9 Cr. This balance predates its $56 Mn Series D funding round in April.
Founded in 2024 by former Zepto executive Aayush Agarwal, Snabbit connects users with trained domestic help for cleaning, dishwashing, and other household chores, promising arrivals within 10-15 minutes.
The April funding round took the startup’s total funding to $112 Mn. It is backed by the likes of Susquehanna Venture Capital, Mirae Asset Venture Investments, Bertelsmann India Investments, Nexus Venture Partners, Lightspeed Ventures, among others.
Snabbit currently operates in five cities, including Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Pune and Hyderabad. It intends to expand its operations to 10 cities, with Kolkata and Chennai as priorities.
The startup is focusing on penetrating deep into a handful of existing markets, rather than aggressive geographical expansion. Even within cities, it is doubling down on ‘micro-markets’, or certain neighbourhoods where it can ensure quick delivery, rather than the whole city.
It was present in 140 micromarkets by May this year, and had onboarded 40,000 professionals on its platforms, with an average order value of ₹169-₹199.
Where Did Snabbit Spend In FY26?
Snabbit’s total expenses rose to ₹194.8 Cr from ₹6.8 Cr in FY25.
Employee Benefit Expenses: These rose to ₹46 Cr from ₹3.3 Cr, including salaries and wages, provident fund contributions, employee stock options, and staff welfare expenses.
Expert Service Cost: Its largest expense head stood at ₹63.1 Cr, compared with ₹27 Lakh in FY25.
Marketing Expenses: Spending on marketing increased to ₹48.7 Cr from ₹82.1 Lakh in the previous year.
Service Fulfillment Expenses: Spending under this head stood at ₹23.8 Cr compared with ₹84.5 Lakh in FY25.
Snabbit’s Loss Per Job Falls Below ₹200
In a statement issued today, Snabbit’s CEO Agarwal said the startup closed FY26 with a run rate of 35,000 daily jobs, up 70X from around 500 jobs a day at the beginning of the fiscal year. It acquired nearly 10 Lakh customers and onboarded more than 20,000 service professionals during the year. He attributed the growth to investments in customer acquisition, workforce training, technology, infrastructure and geographical expansion.
Agarwal said the startup deliberately invested ahead to scale into the competitive quick home services category. The startup said it closed the fiscal with approximately ₹319 Cr in cash and investments, zero borrowings and a net worth of ₹312.4 Cr. He also argued that its annual financial statements do not fully reflect the underlying economics or maturity of the business.
In a separate statement, Snabbit claimed that its losses per job declined from approximately ₹1,500 at the beginning of FY26 to below ₹200 in September 2026, indicating an improvement in unit economics as its operations scaled.
Its Q2 FY27 metrics show that the platform completed 64.5 Lakh jobs, up 61% QoQ, and recorded a net transaction value (NTV) of ₹73 Cr, up 34%.
House help accounted for 64 Lakh jobs, while more recently launched verticals — home cooking and home salon services — accounted for 50,000 and 10,000 jobs, respectively, in the fiscal. The startup reported an EBITDA loss of ₹145 Cr, equivalent to 199% of NTV.
Snabbit also claimed to be the largest high-frequency home services platform by jobs completed and NTV, and the most capital-efficient at the job level. Its strategy centres on building density within fewer cities and micromarkets rather than expanding its geographical footprint aggressively.
Competition Heats Up In Quick Home Services
Snabbit competes with Pronto and listed home services company Urban Company’s InstaHelp in the instant household assistance market.
Pronto closed its $45 Mn Series B round in May at a $200 Mn valuation, adding to the capital flowing into the segment. However, profitability remains a challenge: all three platforms are loss-making due to intense competition, deep discounting, and rising operational costs.
Urban Company posted a ₹174 Cr EBITDA loss from InstaHelp in Q2 FY27, over 4X jump from ₹44 Cr in the same quarter last year. InstaHelp fulfilled 6.2 Mn orders, marking a 63% QoQ increase, while its net transaction value (NTV) rose 34% to ₹71 Cr. However, net order value declined to ₹114 from ₹138 in the previous quarter, which it attributed to competitive intensity and introductory pricing for new users.
In the past, Urban Company has claimed that it does not expect InstaHelp to meaningfully contribute to its bottom line over the next 4-5 years.
The quick home services segment also faces scrutiny over working conditions. Inc42’s reporting documented workers’ concerns about earnings, strict logged-in hour requirements, and inadequate access to waiting areas and washrooms.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) has intensified its nationwide monitoring efforts to improve mobile network coverage, call quality, and internet services. The regulator has directed telecom operators to address identified service issues within the specified deadlines.
According to an official statement issued on October 16, 2026, PTA conducted several monitoring and service improvement activities through its 10 Zonal Offices between October 8 and 14.
The latest initiative is part of the authority’s ongoing efforts to improve network performance and address connectivity problems faced by telecom consumers across Pakistan.
PTA Conducts Telecom Network Monitoring Across Pakistan
During the monitoring period, PTA’s zonal teams visited different areas of Thatta, Dera Ghazi Khan, Mandi Bahauddin, Quetta, Faisalabad, and Gilgit-Baltistan to assess the quality of telecom services.
The monitoring activities focused on identifying issues related to mobile network coverage, voice call quality, and internet connectivity. Following these assessments, PTA directed the concerned telecom operators to resolve the identified problems within the stipulated timeframe.
One of the notable developments was the successful resolution of a telecom site closure issue in Faisalabad. However, the authority did not disclose the reasons behind the closure or identify the telecom operator involved.
PTA conducted these activities in coordination with relevant stakeholders and local administrations to address service deficiencies affecting consumers.
The authority did not provide details regarding the total number of telecom sites inspected, specific network performance measurements, or any penalties imposed on operators during the monitoring period.
PTA Directs Operators to Ensure Better Telecom Services
PTA has reiterated its commitment to improving telecom services through continued monitoring, regulatory oversight, and coordination with mobile network operators.
The regulator is working closely with relevant organizations and local administrations to ensure that issues affecting network coverage, voice quality, and internet services are addressed promptly.
While these monitoring activities demonstrate PTA’s continued focus on telecom service quality, their actual impact will depend on how effectively operators resolve the identified problems.
Reliable mobile networks and internet connectivity remain essential for millions of Pakistanis who depend on telecom services for communication, education, business activities, and digital transactions.
PTA has maintained that it will continue its nationwide monitoring and service improvement efforts to ensure better and more reliable telecom services for consumers across the country.

items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif on Friday brushed aside online criticism after being mocked for responding to an AI-generated image of Hollywood icon Marilyn Monroe, saying he personally operated his social media account and saw nothing unusual about his response.
Speaking on private television channel programme Naya Pakistan, the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz stalwart was asked about the post and whether he managed his account on X himself.
“200% I operate it myself,” Asif said, adding that he led an ordinary life despite holding a prominent government position.
“I have a personal life and a normal life. I am a normal human being; there is nothing special about me,” he said, stressing he had no airs about him.
Read: Khawaja Asif trolled over Marilyn Monroe AI puzzle on X
The controversy began on Tuesday when Asif responded to an AI-generated image depicting Monroe, which challenged social media users to identify an object that would have been out of place in the 1950s.
Resharing the image on X, the defence minister identified the smartwatch worn by Monroe as the anachronism. The original post shared by Asif has since been deleted.
Addressing the criticism, Asif defended his response, arguing that he had simply answered the question posed in the post.
“They presented a riddle asking about what was amiss with the photo [of Monroe], asking what should not have been present in 1956, and that was a smartwatch, so I wrote ‘watch’. What is non-serious about this?” he said.
Asif maintained that being the defence minister did not mean he had to give up his personality or refrain from engaging with light-hearted content on social media.
He said he operated his account himself and used it “for fun”, questioning why his position should prevent him from expressing himself like any other individual.
“Am I not Khawaja Asif? If I am the defence minister, should I let go of my identity? Whether it be good or bad?” he asked.

Original | October 16, 2026 15:02 IST
B2B manufacturing company Zetwerk’s ₹5,012.3 Cr IPO was subscribed 27% on the second day of bidding today. Investors placed bids for 4.95 Cr shares against 18.51 Cr shares on offer as of 14:39 IST, according to BSE data.
Non-institutional investors (NIIs) bid for 67.85 Lakh shares against 5.13 Cr shares reserved for them, subscribing to 13% of their quota. Within the NII category, the portions for bids above ₹2 Lakh and up to ₹10 Lakh, and those above ₹10 Lakh, were each subscribed 13%.
Qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) subscribed to 32% of their allocation, placing bids for 3.13 Cr shares against 9.89 Cr shares on offer.
The retail portion was also subscribed 32%, with bids for 1.11 Cr shares against an allocation of 3.42 Cr shares.
Meanwhile, employees bid for 2.95 Lakh shares against 7 Lakh shares reserved for them, subscribing to 42% of their quota.
Zetwerk’s IPO opened yesterday and closes on October 19. The company has set a price band of ₹143-₹151 per share, implying a valuation of around ₹25,583 Cr (about $2.7 Bn) at the upper end.
The IPO comprises a fresh issue of ₹2,830 Cr and an OFS of up to 14.45 Cr shares, worth ₹2,182.3 Cr at the upper end.
Ahead of the issue, Zetwerk raised ₹2,251.2 Cr from anchor investors. Domestic mutual funds, including SBI Mutual Fund and ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund, accounted for around 46% of the anchor book. Global institutional investors, including Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, and ADIA, also participated.
Founded in 2018, Zetwerk operates a full-stack manufacturing platform serving businesses across industrial and consumer goods categories.
It combines capacity from third-party suppliers and its own facilities to manage manufacturing orders across sectors including renewable energy, consumer electronics, aerospace, defence, oil and gas, and industrial automation.
The company has raised over $900 Mn in funding to date from investors like Peak XV Partners, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Accel India, Greenoaks Capital Partners, and D1 Capital Partners.
On the financial front, operating revenue from continuing operations rose 55.4% to ₹4,117.9 Cr from ₹2,649.4 Cr in Q1 FY26. Net loss narrowed 46.4% to ₹733 Cr from ₹1,368.5 Cr in the year-ago period.
Of the latest quarterly loss, ₹668.9 Cr came from discontinued operations, while continuing operations accounted for ₹64.1 Cr. The year-ago quarter included ₹803.2 Cr in exceptional charges from continuing operations and the ₹453 Cr impairment charge in the discontinued business.

While developers can build prototypes faster, testing, verification and other stages of taking a product to market continue to require human involvement.
When AI Costs Start To Bite
As AI eats into SaaS revenue, it is also making software more expensive to run. Every AI query requires computing power, adding to operating costs. At the same time, growing demand for AI infrastructure is driving up hardware prices, making it more expensive for companies to run their software.
According to ICONIQ’s 2026 data, AI products have an average gross margin of around 52%, compared with the 80% benchmark for traditional SaaS. For established SaaS companies adding AI features, gross margins can fall by 12-17 percentage points, depending on how efficiently they manage AI computing costs.
The pressure is also forcing software companies to reconsider how much profitability they are willing to sacrifice to build AI products.
On October 15, 2026, SaaS giant Figma’s CFO, Praveer Melwani, said the design software company might not return to its previous gross margins of over 90% as it invests in AI features. Its margins were in the mid-80% range, with the company prioritising long-term growth and competitiveness over an immediate return to earlier profitability levels, according to Reuters.
Meanwhile, rather than treating every decline as a problem to be eliminated, some software companies are accepting higher costs, expecting AI features will attract more users, strengthen their products and create future revenue opportunities. Similarly, some are adding more capabilities without proportionately increasing subscription prices.
Krish Ramineni, cofounder and CEO of Fireflies, said that the company has not raised its subscription pricing in the five to six years since launching its meeting note-taking product. It is now expanding beyond meeting notes into tasks such as summarising emails, responding to workplace messages and preparing users for meetings, while aiming to include more tools within a single subscription.
The Push To Rein In AI Spending
The pressure to manage AI expenditure is also showing up in the financial results of Indian companies. Groww, for example, reported a 28% year-on-year increase in total expenses to ₹556 Cr in Q2 FY27, even as revenue from operations grew 47% to ₹1,501 Cr.
In its shareholder letter, the company identified inflation in compute costs due to AI adoption as one factor behind higher serving costs. Cofounder and CFO Ishan Bansal said AI-related costs began rising as the company increased its focus on AI, alongside higher compute usage on trading days and a one-off operational expense. Groww expects inflation-driven costs to remain part of its operational baseline going forward.
This is prompting companies to re-evaluate their technology investments. Instead of relying entirely on large, general-purpose models, some are fine-tuning smaller models for specific tasks, optimising infrastructure and using more expensive models only when necessary.
Perfios, a financial technology company serving banks and other financial institutions, is taking this approach to manage the cost of deploying AI.
Sumit Nigam, chief technology officer at Perfios, said the company is fine-tuning smaller language models and optimising model and GPU architecture to make specific workloads cheaper to run. According to him, GPU utilisation costs for some use cases have become significantly lower than the cost of relying on external models such as Google’s Gemini or Anthropic’s Claude.
Companies are also looking to improve visibility into how AI expenditure builds up across teams, applications and workflows. On October 12, US-based software company Freshworks signed an agreement to acquire Torii, a software management platform. The deal is intended to extend Freshworks’ Freshservice product into software management and AI spend governance.
Torii tracks software applications, licences and AI consumption and attributes spending to the people and teams driving it. The platform is designed to help IT and finance teams understand what is being used, identify cost spikes, set limits and forecast expenditure.
Perfios, meanwhile, is combining cost optimisation with closer scrutiny of business returns. Sridhar Narayan, chief business officer at Perfios, said the company tracks profitability at both the product and customer levels. The focus is on optimising costs and directing spending towards areas where it can deliver better business outcomes, rather than cutting expenditure indiscriminately.
These approaches point to two parts of AI cost management: making usage visible and controllable, and reducing the cost of delivering each AI-powered task.
While AI is making software cheaper to build, the real value lies in data, workflows, integrations and the ability to run business processes reliably at scale.
Adapting To A New AI Reality
As Indian technology companies head into 2027, they face a two-sided challenge: customers are demanding more productivity from AI, while companies must figure out how to earn sustainable revenues.
For IT services firms, this is changing how clients pay for work. A Reuters report found that AI is pushing clients to link payments to productivity gains rather than the hours billed by IT services companies, forcing the industry to rethink its pricing models.
For SaaS companies, the challenge is different. As AI makes software easier and cheaper to build, products with limited differentiation risk becoming easier to replace.
According to Prashant Singh, the cofounder and COO of LeadSquared, “If AI makes software cheaper to build, then software that was only ever an interface over a database becomes harder to defend. That pressure is real.”
But Singh believes the threat is not uniform across the industry. “What is being commoditised is the ability to build an application, not the ability to run a business process reliably at scale,” he said. Proprietary data, integrations and industry-specific workflows will continue to help companies retain their competitive edge.
Going into 2027, the challenge for Indian tech companies will be to adapt to AI-driven changes in pricing and customer expectations while protecting their margins.

items.author: Gaurav Bagur
items.content:
Urban Company’s board today approved a proposal to raise up to ₹2,500 Cr, alongside approving its financial performance for the September quarter. The proposed funding could involve issuance of equity shares, warrants, fully convertible debentures and convertible preference shares.
The fundraise will be executed in one or more tranches via preferential allotment, private placement or one or more qualified institutional placements (QIPs), subject to shareholder approval. The final issue pricing and structure is yet to be determined.
“The business is materially larger than at listing, growth has stepped up, and we now operate three businesses at scale with proven economics. The proposed raise of up to ₹2,500 Cr is about flexibility: it lets us invest with conviction across each of them, cement leadership in InstaHelp, and pursue inorganic opportunities selectively, without trading off one for another,” Urban Company said in a letter to shareholders.
The fundraise proposal comes at a time when Urban Company’s quick home services vertical InstaHelp is facing tough competition from the likes of Snabbit and Pronto, resulting in the prospect of a war for market share fuelled by cash burn.
Hefty investments in powering the quick home services vertical is also creating a dent in Urban Company’s bottom line. For the September quarter, Urban Company’s net loss more than tripled YoY to ₹182.5 Cr, while operating revenue jumped 41% YoY to ₹537.29 Cr.
Separately, the board also granted in-principle approval to explore residential air conditioners as a new business category under its product brand Native. This would be subject to further evaluations and final board clearances.
“This category represents a large market in which the Company already services millions of units annually, providing it with first-hand insights into the existing product gaps and customer needs,” noted UC’s board.
Urban Company made its debut on the bourses just around one year ago. Hence, its proposed fundraise puts it among the ranks of several new-age tech companies like Kissht, Swiggy, Ather Energy, and Ola Electric that have sought to return to the public markets for fresh capital soon after their IPOs.
On a quarterly basis, its net loss nearly doubled from ₹92.1 Cr. Operating revenue remained nearly flat compared with ₹528.3 Cr in Q1 FY27.
The company’s adjusted EBITDA loss for the quarter widened to ₹144 Cr, due to a “deliberate” ₹174 Cr investment in InstaHelp. The company also gave a timeline to improve its bottom line performance in the near future.
“We remain on track for Adjusted EBITDA breakeven by Q3 FY28 and Adjusted EBITDA of ₹1,000 Cr by FY31,” it said.

items.author: Team Inc42
items.content:
Ethnic wear brand Libas is opening nine exclusive brand outlets (EBOs) across five Indian cities during Navratri, expanding its retail footprint during a key festive shopping period.
The rollout spans high-street locations and shopping malls in Bengaluru, Jaipur, Kanpur, Noida, and Jabalpur. With these nine new openings, Libas now operates 55+ stores across India. The brand plans to add more than 50 stores in FY27, following 28 openings in FY26 and 10 in FY25.
The homegrown brand offers women’s ethnic and fusion wear, including kurtas, suit sets, sarees, lehengas and contemporary Indian outfits. Its portfolio covers both everyday and occasion wear, catering to a range of wardrobes and celebrations.
In the women’s ethnic and fusion wear segment, Libas competes with brands such as Biba, Aurelia, W for Woman and Soch.
The new outlets are bringing Libas’ collections closer to shoppers, allowing them to explore styles, fabrics and fits in person while extending the brand’s reach beyond its digital sales channel.
A Faster Push Into Offline Retail
Bengaluru accounts for four of the nine planned outlets at Airport Road, Jayanagar, Commercial Street, and Mantri Mall.
In Jaipur, Libas is opening stores at Pacific Mall and Vaishali Nagar. The remaining three outlets are at Z Square Mall in Kanpur, H&S Mall in Noida, and South Avenue Mall in Jabalpur.
Sidhant Keshwani, founder and CEO of Libas, said, “As Libas enters its next phase of growth, offline retail will be an important lever in expanding our consumer reach and strengthening our presence across markets. Our focus is on building a retail network that allows us to scale efficiently, respond to local demand and deliver a consistent brand experience.”
The company said it crossed an annualised revenue run rate (ARR) of ₹1,000 Cr in March 2026 and is targeting ₹1,000 crore in revenue in FY27.
With the nine openings forming part of its broader FY27 rollout, offline retail is set to play a larger role in Libas’ next phase of growth.

items.title: How LeadSquared’s Chandra Sahal Is Turning Finance Into A Real-Time Decision Engine
items.summary:

LeadSquared, a SaaS platform focused on sales execution and marketing automation,
items.author: Anirudh Trivedi
items.content:
For a long time, the finance function in organisations has been a back-office job — close the books, stay compliant, keep enough cash in the bank to survive the quarter. The job rewarded accuracy over foresight, and a CFO’s standing was measured by how few surprises were brought to the table.
The job description no longer holds today, particularly for SaaS businesses, where a small dip in quarterly retention can snowball into a much larger problem.
The role has grown to include almost everything under its ambit, from market research to product R&D and even deciding pricing of products or services, once exclusive to the CEO’s role.
Simply put: finance leaders are today involved in deciding which market deserves more investment, which product line is worth the losses, and whether a pricing model could open doors to the next big opportunity. In all odds, the CFO today is an organisation’s sounding board.
LeadSquared, a SaaS platform focused on sales execution and marketing automation, is also witnessing this shift under the aegis of its CFO, Chandra Sahal, who joined the company in November 2025 after a 12-year stint at Wipro as its head of finance.
Prior to joining Wipro, Sahal held key finance positions at Infosys, CRISIL, Vee Healthtek and GOAT Brand Labs.
In the 11 months since joining LeadSquared, Sahal has helped the company transition its finance department from a paper pusher (closing books and preparing for audits) to a strategic business partner, where it now has a say in building product roadmaps and driving AI investment decisions.
For Inc42’s latest initiative, The CFO Code, we spoke with Sahal about LeadSquared’s finance function, his take on AI, and how finance leaders can become the CEO’s guiding light towards growth and profitability.
Assuring Real-Time Visibility Into LeadSquared’s Financial Health
Finance teams have long relied on month-end reports to comprehend the financial health of their respective businesses. Sahal has always been obsessed with changing this. At traditional companies, he found it quite difficult to renovate systems that had been embedded for years and brought no benefit.
He saw an opportunity at LeadSquared to build systems and processes agile enough to scrutinise the business on the go. For this, he researched and experimented extensively, eventually zeroing in on using SAP, a leading ERP platform, for core financial records, alongside a CRM to track sales and an in-house system to manage the process from order placement to billing and payment.
On top of these three layers, he built an internal analytics cum audit system that compiles relevant data to give management a real-time view of what’s happening underneath.
“When an invoice is received, it is then looked at by the controller from a revenue recognition perspective and used by the financial team for reporting. All of this happens in real time. We do not wait until month-end to figure out what the revenue is going to look like,” Sahal said.
With this, management gets a view into roughly 30% of the month’s revenue in just week 1, 50% by week 2 and 75% by week 3. Therefore, the final week can be spent checking unusual cases and following up with the sales team, instead of trying to scrap the entire month’s numbers, which could be a process prone to errors. Scrapping numbers at the eleventh hour could also jeopardise the finance team’s productivity and create mockery of everyone’s efforts before the CEO.
“By month-end, our systems give over 95% visibility into what the final numbers are going to be. This near-real-time reporting assists us in closing books much earlier and getting the management information report (MIS) ready by the eighth of the month,” Sahal said.
From Letting AI Do The Grunt Work To Calling The Shots
Speaking about how AI has helped Sahal streamline his operations, he shared that everything that is finance at LeadSquared, including reconciliations, identification of journal-entry gaps, variance analysis and budgeting, now has AI behind the wheel.
This has helped Sahal do a rolling forecast for the full year by the 10th of every month “So, when I enter a board meeting, I have 80-85% visibility into full year numbers,” he said.
So, as someone who keeps an eye on every penny spent in the organisation, how does he analyse the ROI on the company’s AI investments?
Sahal has a simple thesis: the return should show up in the team’s productivity. “Faster deployment, faster code checks, quicker product launches and reducing the time spent collecting and reconciling information is where I feel the real ROI lies,” Sahal said.
At a time when most organisations think it is a good idea to hire specialised AI talent while bloating token costs, Sahal begs to differ. “The more practical approach here is to train existing employees by investing in their upskilling, be it AI or any other technologies. We, at LeadSquared, have the industry’s best token optimisation practices,” said Sahal.
Amid all the AI brouhaha, Sahal does not see AI as a magic bullet but a tool to speed up routine finance work. Tasks that once took days, he said, can now be completed in hours. Similarly, a board presentation that previously took about three days can now be prepared in a few hours.
But the bigger shift, according to Sahal, is the unclogged bandwidth his team uses to interpret numbers, challenge assumptions, and focus on decisions that move the needle.
Over more than a decade in finance, he has seen several tech cycles emerge and perish. But one thing remains: CFOs need to stay ahead of the tech learning curve. A tech-savvy CFO is a guiding force many organisations lack and don’t even know about.
“It is the endeavour of such [tech-savvy] finance leaders that the finance function today has a say at the table,” he said, while illustrating his role as a tech-savvy CFO in the organisation.
And ever since the arrival of AI, tracking token usage, the technology stack and utilisation across teams has also become a diligent part of CFOs’ job role, something nobody would have fathomed would be the case a few years ago, according to Sahal.
Becoming CEO’s Guiding Force To Defend Margins
All said and done, the last 11 months have been anything but a walk in the park for Sahal. He said that when he joined LeadSquared, the company was ailing with challenges that were only patched and never really got solved.
Like any other startup, LeadSquared’s focus was centred around growth at all costs. Somewhere along the way, the balance between growth and profitability went for a toss.
While such a growth strategy can work for a wide array of startups, the problem is that these fads are hardly sustainable.
“Any dollar of new revenue that costs $3 to acquire and churns in a year is not growth. It’s a subscription to losing money,” Sahal said, suggesting the Rule of 40 as a useful gut check for whether a company’s growth rate and profit margin together still make sense.
According to the Rule of 40, a company’s combined annual revenue growth rate and profit margin should equal or exceed 40%
The second major challenge, he noted, sat outside the company’s control. Sahal shared that LeadSquared was once too exposed to geopolitical unpredictability, which often made its decision-making uncertain while investing in a particular market.
“A case in point is our US operations that are averse to rupee volatility. With the INR inching closer to the 100 mark, the onus to defend margins falls on us,” said Sahal.
To combat such uncertainties in regional compliance, Sahal has helped LeadSquared partner with vendors that either operate locally in those regions or are based in India with expertise in specific markets. This helps the company cut compliance and other expenses, offsetting INR depreciation in many cases.
CFO As A Strategic Business Partner
When asked about the mistakes that startups on a hyper-growth path often make, Sahal said that for today’s new-age businesses, an integrated tech stack connecting ERP, CRM, order-to-cash, and an analytics layer is a must.
Without an integrated stack connecting the ERP, CRM, order-to-cash, and analytics layers, a new invoice flow could derail projections and create chaos.
So, does that mean businesses should build a highly stacked finance function from day one? Sahal argued that early stage startups, with a single product and one geography, have the legroom to operate comfortably on Excel and Tally for a couple of years.
“The trigger for upgrading should be complexity, whether that comes from multiple entities, products or geographies,” he added.
Finally, when we asked what the future holds for CFOs, especially in this time and age of AI, Sahal said the role is undergoing a churn and has become too demanding. Finance leaders who can act and play as strategic business partners will define the next phase of finance.
The era of just reporting numbers is over, and finance leaders’ new job is to chart the best course for the CEO.
