items.content:
The International Monetary Fund on Tuesday flagged significant growth and financial stability risks from a potential end to the AI investment boom, growing debt levels ‌and a prolonged Middle East conflict.
The IMF forecast global growth at 3.1% for 2026, a slight uptick from a 3.0% forecast in July as still-strong AI infrastructure investment offset higher oil prices caused by the war in the Middle East.
The latest World Economic Outlook report, released in Bangkok during the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank, also predicts 3.4% growth in 2027, but that is based on assumptions that the Strait of Hormuz reopens by March and shipping conditions ​return to the pre-war situation by October 2027.
A more protracted war that kept oil prices above $130 through the first quarter of 2027 would cut growth next year by half a ​percentage point, the IMF said.
AI correction
In another downside scenario, the IMF said that a steep drop in AI investment could lead to a sharp fall ⁠in asset prices, ultimately cutting global GDP by 1.1% by 2028, including a 1.8% drop in US output.
Also Read: Finance Minister Aurangzeb vows to strengthen collective influence of G-24
"We now have an economy that is standing on one leg, the AI leg," IMF Managing ​Director Kristalina Georgieva told a Bretton Woods Committee event. "What if it wobbles? What if there is disappointment and that leads to potentially a more difficult environment?"
The IMF emphasised similar risks in its separate Global Financial ​Stability Report, warning policymakers needed to avoid "complacency" in guarding against a potential pullback in AI investment and stock valuations.
"If there are questions about the monetisation of AI, the equity investments will deplete in value, the debt may be difficult to service, and the revenue commitments in the future may not materialise," Jason Wu, assistant director of the IMF's Global Markets Analysis Division, told a press conference at the Bangkok meetings.
An ensuing AI market correction would feed back through ​the real economy, dragging down broader asset prices and overall demand through a wealth effect reduction, said Athanasios Vamvakidis, deputy director of the IMF's Monetary and Capital Markets Department.
It would also lead to ​reduced trade, IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro said. Trade in AI goods grew 29% between 2023 and 2025, more than triple the 8.3% growth rate of global trade over the same period. Without the AI trade, overall ‌growth in ⁠trade would have been only 4.6%, she said.
The concerns highlighted in Bangkok also include AI-driven cybersecurity risks. They come as banking regulators step up efforts to contain AI-related risks, with Reuters reporting that major US regulators are quizzing banks on their use of advanced AI models and European regulators are pressing banks to boost recovery plans.
Recession unlikely
But even the steep drop in output seen under the worst-case AI risk scenario was not likely to reduce growth to levels consistent with a global recession, IMF deputy research director Petya Koeva Brooks told Reuters in an interview.
Fiscal, bond woes
The IMF reports and meeting participants also highlighted ​risks from elevated public debt levels and rising ​bond yields that may be driven higher still ⁠by war-driven inflation pressures, eating up budgets to service debts and sapping growth.
Georgieva warned against complacency in "systemically important" advanced economies that are "negligent about their fiscal position" and failing to rein in debts like developing economies have been forced to do.
Developing countries must cut spending despite war shock
The IMF also warned that while low-income developing countries were dealing with the disproportionate impacts of the Iran war-fuelled energy shock, many had "no choice" but to cut spending or potentially face debt restructuring.
Speaking to AFP on the sidelines of the organisation's Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Brooks said heavily indebted, oil-importing countries were facing the worst of the energy shock, and had difficult choices in helping their citizens through the crisis.
"Unfortunately, after years of the global economy being hit (by) shock after shock, debt levels have increased quite a lot, and at the same time, inflation has become a problem," she said.
"For those countries that are most vulnerable, this is where the consumption basket is heavily weighted towards energy and food, and so indeed it is much much more difficult," she added.
Read More: IMF raises inflation forecast to 9.9%
The debt vulnerabilities of many developing economies are a "major barrier" to ​inclusive growth, said Nigerian Finance Minister Taiwo Oyedele, who chairs the Group of 24 developing nations, warning that member governments were increasingly contending with mounting ​debt burdens.
Oyedele said estimates showed ⁠that developing countries were paying $500 billion more for their debt than developed countries, even as they contend with growing deficits.
The IMF this week is urging countries to begin politically painful steps to bring budgets under control. It singled out Britain for praise as the only major advanced economy to have set out clear plans to reduce government borrowing over the coming years, but urged it to stay the course just weeks before the ⁠new UK ​government unveils budget plans.
Few governments are listening to the IMF's calls to shrink borrowing, said Josh Lipsky, vice president of ​international economics at the Atlantic Council, who is attending the Bangkok meetings.
"France, Germany, the US all need to do fiscal consolidation, but they're moving in the opposite direction," Lipsky said. "I'm afraid that it's going to take some kind of crisis to wake ​up and realise that this is what has to be done."

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
Amid a potential fire sale on the horizon, ecommerce unicorn DealShare’s CEO Kamaldeep Singh has stepped down from his role to join electric mobility solutions provider Indofast Energy as its CEO. Singh took to LinkedIn to make the announcement but didn’t specify the reason behind his exit.
Singh had joined DealShare in December 2022 as its president, before transitioning to the role of CEO in January 2024 to spearhead the struggling startup as it revives its value-commerce business. He had a near 15 year long stint with Big Bazaar prior to DealShare, where he served as the CEO for more than a year.
“After more than 25 years of building and transforming consumer businesses, I am stepping into an industry that is itself going through a fundamental transformation. Mobility is being reimagined. I believe the winners in this transformation will be those who put customer experience at the core and technology at the backbone,” Singh said.
For context, Indofast Energy operates a fast charging battery-as-a-service network for EVs across India. It is a joint venture between Indian Oil Corporation and SUN Mobility. The company is planning to invest over $1 Bn over the next three years to deploy more than 10,000 battery-swapping stations across 50-plus cities.
Singh intends to lead Indofast Energy’s next phase of growth, accelerating business expansion, strengthening its market presence and building a scalable and sustainable energy and mobility ecosystem across India.
What This Exit Means For DealShare
The exit comes about a month after Inc42 reported that Singh was serving his notice period, while CFO Ashish Shah was also looking to exit the startup. As of now, the ecommerce startup is yet to announce its replacement.
The CEO exit comes amid ongoing questions around DealShare’s business model and future ownership. The startup’s founding team — Sourjyendu Medda, Vineet Rao, Sankar Bora and Rajat Shikhar — all exited by 2024.
DealShare, which is known for online grocery delivery catering to middle and lower income “Bharat” households in tier-II and tier-III cities, has seen mounting competition pressure in the ecommerce landscape.
DealShare began scaling back its online operations in April 2026 and eventually stopped fulfilling orders from its warehouses, effectively shutting down its two-hour delivery model.
While the app remains available, its online business has dwindled to “next to zero”, Inc42 reported in September. The startup continues to operate physical stores, although further offline expansion has been put on hold.
Amid all this, the startup is now reportedly in advanced discussions with online pharmacy Truemeds for a potential acquisition through a share-swap transaction that could value DealShare at just over $90 Mn, a 95% drop from its peak unicorn valuation. Westbridge is a common investor in both startups, holding roughly 18.4% of DealShare.
Notably, the transaction is yet to materialise, with Truemeds’ existing investors not necessarily aligned with the deal. DealShare is also in talks with other potential buyers, according to sources Inc42 spoke to earlier.
It has raised nearly $400 Mn to date from investors such as WestBridge Capital, Z47, Tiger Global, and Alpha Wave Global. It reached a peak valuation of $1.7 Bn in 2022.
On the financial front, DealShare’s revenue from operations fell to 13.3% YoY₹432.4 Cr in FY25 from ₹499 Cr in FY24, while its net loss narrowed 91% to ₹87.7 Cr from ₹167.7 Cr.
The post DealShare CEO Kamaldeep Singh Steps Down Amid Acquisition Talks appeared first on Inc42 Media.

items.content:
President Asif Ali Zardari reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to regional peace and stability under the Makkah Defence Alliance (MDA) in a meeting with Lieutenant General (Rtd) Nauman Mahmood on Tuesday in Islamabad.
On August 7, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye formalised their longstanding strategic relationship through the newly signed Makkah pact, a trilateral security framework that its proponents describe as a defensive arrangement aimed at strengthening collective deterrence, enhancing military cooperation and promoting regional stability.
In a post on X, the office of the president stated that Lieutenant General (Rtd) Nauman Mahmood, the first secretary general of the MDA, formerly called the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA), called on President Zardari at Aiwan-e-Sadr.
Read: Lt Gen (retd) Nauman Mahmood appointed first secretary general of Makkah pact
"The president expressed confidence that the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, signed by Pakistan, Türkiye and Saudi Arabia on August 7, 2026, would strengthen regional peace and stability through defensive cooperation guided by the principles of the UN Charter and international law," it added.
President Reaffirms Pakistan’s Commitment to Regional Peace and Defensive Cooperation Under Makkah Accord
Lieutenant General (Rtd.) Nauman Mahmood, the first Secretary General pursuant to Makkah Joint Defence Agreement called on President Asif Ali Zardari at Aiwan-e-Sadr today.… pic.twitter.com/9anJjovXdc
— The President of Pakistan (@PresOfPakistan) October 13, 2026
The president further underscored that the accord was "purely defensive in nature and not directed against any country, nor it constituted the formation of a new bloc".
The statement emphasised that Pakistan remained committed to the peaceful resolution of conflicts and enhanced regional and multilateral cooperation to address emerging challenges.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi was also present during the meeting.
Who is Lt Gen Nauman Mahmood?
Lt Gen (retd) Mahmood is a former senior Pakistan Army commander with experience in military operations, intelligence, professional military education and strategic affairs.
He was in the race for the army chief when the government was looking for the successor of General (retired) Qamar Javed Bajwa in November 2022. He was known as one of the most non-controversial army generals with an impeccable career and apolitical approach.
Read More: Ex-army officer to head Makkah pact secretariat
A member of the Baloch Regiment, he was commissioned into the army on September 11, 1987.
During his military career, he served in command and instructional appointments, including assignments with an infantry formation and at the Command and Staff College. As a major general, he commanded an infantry division in North Waziristan.
He also served in the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), including as director general of its Analysis Directorate, where his responsibilities involved assessment of regional and international developments.
After his promotion to lieutenant general, Naumam served at General Headquarters as inspector general for Communications and Information Technology.
He was promoted to lieutenant general in April 2019 and subsequently appointed commander of XI Corps, commonly known as Peshawar Corps, in December that year.
He remained in command of the corps until November 2021, during a period when Afghanistan was undergoing a major political and security transition following the US military withdrawal.
Nauman was then appointed president of the National Defence University (NDU), Islamabad, becoming the institution's 35th president. He served in that position until April 2023, when he retired from the army.
He has attended professional military courses in Pakistan and abroad, including at the Command and Staff College in Egypt, and is a graduate of the NDU.
On September 23, the government appointed Lt Gen Mahmood as the first secretary general of the MJDA.
The appointment was the first major institutional development since Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye signed the pact, and his appointment gives Pakistan the responsibility of establishing and leading the alliance's first secretariat during its formative three-year period.
The decision was taken at the inaugural meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee, held under the MJDA, which brought together the foreign and defence ministers and military chiefs of the three countries in Istanbul on August 31.
Under the arrangement agreed in Istanbul, the secretary general would head the alliance's General Secretariat, based in the Saudi capital and tasked with overseeing implementation of the agreement, coordinating joint activities among the three militaries and supporting expanded defence-industrial cooperation.
For Islamabad, the role also provides an opportunity to shape the working structure of the new defence arrangement as Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye move from the political commitment announced in Makkah towards a more organised mechanism for defence coordination.
Significance of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement
The Makkah pact was the latest step in longstanding military and strategic cooperation between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye. Signed in Makkah, the pact established a framework for collective deterrence and stipulated that an armed attack on any one of the three countries would be considered an attack on all three, while providing for wider cooperation across defence.
Also Read: Makkah defence alliance agrees to 'rapid force deployment' in Saudi Arabia: FO
The agreement followed nearly a year of negotiations and came amid heightened instability across the Middle East. Turkiye and Pakistan had sought closer regional security cooperation, while Saudi Arabia had faced growing security concerns as conflicts spread across the region, threatening its territory, energy infrastructure and ambitious economic development plans.
For Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, the trilateral pact is built on their Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement signed in September 2025. That agreement stated that “any aggression against either country shall be considered an aggression against both” and committed the two sides to strengthening defence cooperation and joint deterrence.
The three countries already had extensive military links. Pakistan had provided training and technical assistance to Saudi forces for decades, while Islamabad and Ankara had maintained close defence ties through military training, naval cooperation and defence equipment. In 2023, Saudi Arabia agreed to purchase Turkish drones in what Ankara described as its largest defence export contract.
The signing in Makkah, Islam’s holiest city, added symbolic weight to an agreement that brought together three countries with significant military and strategic capabilities. It also came as Pakistan sought to avoid becoming directly involved in the Iran conflict, instead pursuing diplomatic efforts to mediate, while strengthening its broader regional security partnerships.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) is considering dedicated regulations for ecommerce platforms, including quick commerce players, and cloud kitchens to tighten food safety compliance and product disclosures.
The proposed rules would require online food listings to display manufacturing and expiry dates and batch numbers, and hold platforms accountable for misleading claims made by manufacturers, Bloomberg reported. The regulator is also considering mandatory disclosure of cloud kitchen photographs and addresses
FSSAI CEO Rajit Punhani told ET that the regulator has held consultations with ecommerce and quick commerce companies and started inspecting dark stores and cloud kitchens.
“We’re planning to amend the regulation so that consumers know the manufacturing date, expiry date and batch number of products they’re ordering,” he said.
The regulator is also considering stricter checks on dark store storage conditions, including the handling of frozen products, as per the Bloomberg report.
The proposed changes come amid increased scrutiny of quick commerce platforms such as Blinkit, Zepto, and Swiggy Instamart over their failure to display essential product information, including expiry, best-before and use-by dates.
While platforms often mention a product’s shelf life, consumers may not know its actual expiry date or batch number before placing an order.
The proposed ecommerce rules are part of the FSSAI’s broader crackdown on food safety and labelling violations. Prosecutions involving ecommerce companies have risen at least five- to sixfold over the past year, Punhani said, adding that platforms were improving compliance but not at the expected pace.
Wider Food Safety Crackdown
The scrutiny extends to food manufacturers and their labelling practices. The FSSAI has issued notices to more than 150 food and beverage makers, including Nestle, PepsiCo, Dabur, ITC, Ferrero, Danone, Red Bull, and Abbott, over allegedly incorrect or misleading ingredient claims and other labelling violations.
“We are doing nothing wrong; we are just implementing the regulations,” Punhani said, adding that large companies should lead by example and avoid misleading claims and advertisements.
Alongside action over existing labelling requirements, the FSSAI is pursuing front-of-pack warning labels for packaged foods. The regulator proposed red, hexagonal labels displaying the amounts of nutrients such as sugar, salt, and saturated fat in an affidavit filed with the Supreme Court.
Separately, PepsiCo, Reliance Consumer Products, and Monster Beverage have challenged the FSSAI notices in court. The companies recently secured procedural relief after a court found that they had not been given adequate opportunity to respond or present their cases to the regulator.
Punhani expressed confidence in the FSSAI’s position, telling Bloomberg, “They are resisting but we are far stronger and we have consumer support.”
The regulator is also scrutinising supplements and nutraceuticals sold online. It is reviewing approvals granted three to five years ago to determine whether companies are making claims beyond those cleared by it. It plans to issue notices and suspend licences where it finds violations.

items.author: Gaurav Bagur
items.content:
Ex-Fundamentum’s cofounder Ashish Kumar’s VC firm Fundamentum Frontier Advisors (F2A) has marked the first close of its growth-stage AI and deeptech fund at ₹3,000 Cr, India’s largest fund in the sector.
Additionally, F2A said its LPs have approved plans to increase the size of the fund to ₹3,500 Cr, given the investor demand beyond the current capacity.
The fund has raised capital from both domestic and overseas investors and will divide the funds across two vehicles. It plans to deploy the corpus into 12-15 companies over the next 2-3 years, writing cheques in the range of ₹100-200 Cr each.
It claims to be in the advanced stages of closing three investments within the upcoming quarter.
“More Indian companies are now building deeptech products for global markets, with India as their engineering and commercial base. Having worked with such companies from their early years, I have seen how much the right capital matters once the technology is validated and customers start to scale. We believe that is the stage at which F2A can help them become category leaders,” said general partner Debraj Banerjee.
F2A was founded by Fundamentum Partnership partner and cofounder Ashish Kumar earlier this year. Kumar, Banerjee and Vivek Singla are F2A’s general partners while Fundamentum’s former general partner Nandan Nilekani is the anchor investor for the fund.
The VC investor’s strategy focuses on three sectors: consumer business leveraging AI and frontier technologies, enterprise software, deeptech infrastructure and engineered systems. It targets India-domiciled companies earning revenue from India as well as globally.
Despite the common involvement of team members including Kumar and Nilekani between Fundamentum and F2A, the two are separate legal entities.
Notably, Fundamentum has itself launched its new fund this year – its third fund with a target corpus of ₹2,200 Cr.
Deeptech is the latest investor darling as funding for the sector nearly tripled to $290 Mn across 28 deals in the quarter ending September 2026, as against $105 Mn across 29 deals a year ago, per Inc42’s ‘Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026’ report.
The likes of South Korean gaming giant KRAFTON, global VC investor Accel, and Mumbai-based early-stage VC AUM Ventures have all mentioned plans to bet on this space in the past few months.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has deferred the introduction of merchant discount rate (MDR) on select UPI person-to-merchant (P2M) transactions until immediately after Diwali, pushing back the October 15 rollout.
The NPCI said its UPI and Services Steering Committee took the decision keeping the festive season in mind. The revised implementation date will be notified separately.
The announcement confirms a delay in the rollout but does not set January 1, 2027, as the new deadline, as earlier reports had suggested.
Under the proposed framework UPI MDR, merchants would be charged an MDR of 0.40% on eligible P2M UPI transactions above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300 per transaction.
The move had faced significant push back from retail traders’ associations. The committee was also reportedly considering exempting businesses with an annual turnover of up to ₹40 Lakh from the proposed fee.
The new framework marks a shift from the zero-MDR regime. Transactions up to ₹2,000, person-to-person (P2P) transfers and eligible small-merchant transactions would remain exempt.
The All India Mobile Retailers Association (AIMRA) and the All India Consumer Products Distributors Federation (AICPDF) had called for a ‘No UPI Day’ on October 2 to protest the proposed charges. They withdrew the planned protest after meeting Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman on September 30.
AIMRA had sought a fixed, nominal charge for digital transactions instead of the proposed 0.40% MDR. The AICPDF, meanwhile, has estimated that the fee could add ₹7,000 Cr-₹9,000 Cr in annual costs across the FMCG distribution and retail ecosystem.
Recently, the Supreme Court refused to stay the Centre’s implementation of MDR charges on select UPI transactions. However, it directed the Centre and other respondents to file their counter-affidavits within four weeks, observing that the issue was “less legal and more technical”.
UPI Monetisation And The Cost Of Payments
Earlier this month, NPCI MD and CEO Dilip Asbe defended the proposed MDR framework, saying a market-driven economic model for UPI is necessary to fund rising cybersecurity, scalability and infrastructure costs.
Asbe said banks and payment companies would need to invest continuously in AI to strengthen security and maintain user trust.
“The ability and the tools with the hackers are really very powerful compared to what we could actually use inside,” he said, adding that AI was expensive to deploy and would require sustained investment to protect payment systems.
Meanwhile, UPI continued to see double-digit year-on-year (YoY) growth in volume and value last month, despite a marginal month-on-month (MoM) decline. UPI processed 24.07 Bn transactions worth ₹29.37 Lakh Cr in September, down 1.8% and 1.5%, respectively, from 24.51 Bn transactions worth ₹29.82 Lakh Cr in August.
On a YoY basis, transaction volume grew 23%, while transaction value rose 18%. Average daily transactions increased to 802 Mn in September from 791 Mn in August, while the average daily transaction value climbed to ₹97,913 Cr from ₹96,205 Cr.

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
Electric two-wheeler maker e-Sprinto has entered the business-to-consumer (B2C) market with the launch of its G1 family electric scooter, priced at ₹89,999 onwards, as the startup looks to expand beyond its business-to-business (B2B) fleet operations.
The G1 is available in three variants priced at ₹89,999, ₹94,999 and ₹99,999, respectively, with all prices ex-showroom Delhi. The variants offer battery options of 2 kWh, 2.5 kWh and 3 kWh, with claimed ranges of up to 80 km, 100 km and 130 km on a single charge, respectively.
The scooter features three riding modes, Eco, City and Sport, with maximum speeds of 30 kmph, 40 kmph and 50 kmph, respectively. Developed over nearly two years of research and development, the G1 has been designed for families and everyday commuters, the startup said. Customer deliveries are scheduled to begin from January 1, 2027.
e-Sprinto is targeting sales of around 5,000 G1 units by March 2027, cofounders Atul Gupta and Shalu Gupta told Inc42.
The launch comes amid a broader push by electric two-wheeler makers to tap the family scooter segment, traditionally dominated by petrol-powered scooters. While Ather Energy has its family-focused Rizta range, Simple Energy entered the segment with its Wave scooter in 2026, priced from ₹1.09 lakh.
Ola Electric, meanwhile, has expanded its S1 portfolio across price points, including scooters below the ₹1 Lakh price point.
The trend points to EV makers looking beyond performance-led models and early adopters to reach households and everyday commuters, making affordability, comfort, storage, reliability and after-sales service key areas of competition.
From Fleet Operations To Consumer Mobility
Founded in 2022 by Vinod Gupta, Atul Gupta, and Shalu Gupta, e-Sprinto has built its business around electric two-wheelers for commercial and fleet customers. The startup says it has more than 70,000 vehicles on Indian roads, supported by three manufacturing facilities with a combined annual production capacity of 1.5 Lakh units.
Its B2B customer ecosystem includes mobility and fleet operators such as Zypp Electric, Hala Mobility, Ride EV, Bike Bazaar, Shadowfax, among others. The startup also works with delivery and quick commerce businesses through its partners.
e-Sprinto’s B2C foray comes following a 1,564% month-on-month jump in its monthly escooter registrations to 1,997 units in September, according to Vahan data. The cofounders attributed the growth partly to festive demand and the commissioning of a third manufacturing facility in July, which doubled production capacity and helped the startup fulfill pending orders.
The cofounders claimed that the startup typically sells twice as many scooters as are recorded on the Vahan portal, as its portfolio also includes low-speed scooters that do not require registration.
According to the cofounders, e-Sprinto’s vehicles deployed in commercial operations have an uptime of over 97%. They said operating in demanding fleet environments has helped the startup understand vehicle reliability, servicing requirements, and performance across geographies.
The G1 differs from its fleet-oriented products in both battery configuration and vehicle design. While e-Sprinto’s B2B scooters use swappable batteries, the G1 has a fixed battery, larger 12-inch tyres, and seating designed for families.
The cofounders said the B2C foray aims to diversify the startup’s customer base and reduce its dependence on fleet demand. While commercial customers drive volumes, the dealership network will help it reach individual buyers.
However, dealer margins and the cost of building a retail network could weigh on profitability initially. The cofounders expect unit economics to improve with higher sales volumes and plan to use the startup’s existing manufacturing and service capabilities to support the expansion.
They said e-Sprinto is bootstrapped and EBITDA profitable, with no plans to raise external capital in the near term. The startup expects its revenue to double YoY in FY27 but didn’t give its FY26 revenue number. It is also targeting a double-digit EBITDA margin.
Dealership Expansion & Growth Plans
To support its B2C push, e-Sprinto plans to add around 10 dealers a month, targeting approximately 150 dealerships by FY28. These will be standalone outlets, with expansion initially focused on northern India, followed by western and southern markets. The startup plans to enter eastern India in a later phase.
It will fund the expansion through internal accruals and promoter capital. Alongside the dealership rollout, e-Sprinto is investing in R&D and hiring more employees. Its workforce has grown from around 10 in its first year to approximately 260, according to the cofounders.
The expansion comes amid growth in India’s E2W market. Registrations rose 12.2% MoM to 2.07 Lakh units in September, with TVS and Bajaj together accounting for half the market.
The sector has also attracted investor funding in recent months. In Q3 2026, River raised $120 Mn, Yulu secured $93 Mn, and Ultraviolette raised $85 Mn.

También señaló las estafas y el frau
items.author: Albert Cuesta
items.content:
La junta directiva de la GSMA ha fijado las prioridades de conectividad del sector. Ha reclamado medidas sobre la asequibilidad de los smartphones, las estafas en internet y la inversión en redes, y ha respaldado una cooperación internacional más estrecha en los futuros estándares 6G.
Tras una reunión de la junta en Nueva Delhi (India), la asociación del sector ha indicado que, aunque el 97 % de la población mundial tiene cobertura de banda ancha móvil, 3400 millones de personas siguen sin acceso a internet móvil.
El coste de los dispositivos continúa siendo una barrera: un teléfono móvil básico con conexión a internet equivale al 44 % del ingreso mensual medio del 20 % más pobre de la población en países de ingresos bajos y medios.
La GSMA planteó posibles medidas para mejorar la asequibilidad, como planes de financiación, rebajas fiscales específicas y una cooperación más estrecha entre los fabricantes de dispositivos y los proveedores de memoria.
También señaló las estafas y el fraude como una amenaza creciente. Advirtió de que, aunque el sector móvil sigue reforzando sus herramientas de detección en red y de ciberdefensa, «ningún sector puede afrontar la amenaza por sí solo».
Añadió que los contenidos generados con IA y los deepfakes aumentan los riesgos para los consumidores, la confianza pública y los objetivos de los gobiernos, e instó al sector a «unir fuerzas para contrarrestar las estafas con soluciones prácticas».
Inversión sostenida
La GSMA subrayó también la necesidad de invertir en redes y de contar con políticas de apoyo para acelerar el crecimiento de la conectividad. Según sus conclusiones, las tecnologías y los servicios móviles aportaron un valor económico de 6 billones de dólares (unos 5,2 billones de euros) en 2025, el 6,4 % del PIB mundial.
Se prevé que esa cifra alcance los 11,3 billones de dólares (unos 9,7 billones de euros) en 2030.
Además, se estima que los operadores invertirán 1,2 billones de dólares (algo más de un billón de euros) en gastos de capital entre 2025 y 2030 para ampliar y modernizar las redes, y que el 57 % de las conexiones móviles utilizará 5G a finales de la década.
El director general de la GSMA, Vivek Badrinath, afirmó que la próxima prioridad del sector debe ser convertir la expansión de la 5G en valor real y garantizar que más personas puedan participar en la economía digital.
«Esto requerirá inversión sostenida, políticas favorables y colaboración en todo el ecosistema», recalcó.
De cara al futuro, la asociación reiteró su apoyo a los estándares globales y a la armonización del espectro radioeléctrico a medida que avanza el desarrollo de la 6G.
Señaló que países que suman más del 80 % de la población mundial respaldan el uso móvil de la banda superior de 6 GHz, que podría proporcionar los anchos de banda de canal de entre 200 MHz y 400 MHz que se prevé que necesitará el 6G.
El presidente de la GSMA, Gopal Vittal, afirmó que, «trabajando con estándares globales y colaborando entre mercados, podemos acelerar la innovación y reforzar la confianza y la resiliencia», a medida que el sector desarrolla la próxima generación de conectividad.
Con información de Amiya Johar.

Pakistan Expands Fiber Infrastructure to Support 5G

items.author: Usama Anjum
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Pakistan is close to finalizing its regulatory framework for satellite internet services, Federal Minister for Information Technology and Telecommunication Shaza Fatima Khawaja said while addressing an Asia-Pacific Telecommunity symposium.
The minister said work on the Fixed Satellite Services (FSS) framework had entered its final stages and that the rules would be finalized following consultations with the relevant institutions. She added that the government aimed to provide a supportive business environment for companies seeking to invest in Pakistan’s satellite internet market.
The development could pave the way for greater participation by satellite broadband providers, particularly in areas where conventional fixed-line infrastructure remains limited. However, the minister did not announce a launch date or confirm approvals for any individual operator.
Pakistan Expands Fiber Infrastructure to Support 5G
Highlighting efforts to improve internet connectivity, Khawaja said three new submarine internet cables had landed in Pakistan during the past two and a half years, while work on alternative international connectivity routes and additional cable links was continuing.
She said more than 17,000 kilometers of optical fiber had been deployed through the Universal Service Fund (USF). Meanwhile, the number of homes passed by fiber broadband networks had increased from fewer than three million in 2024 to more than five million.
According to the minister, the share of mobile towers connected through fiber had also risen from below 15% to more than 19%. The government is targeting a fiberization rate of at least 60%, as fiber connections are essential to provide reliable capacity and performance for 5G services.
Khawaja said Pakistan had introduced 5G technology following the auction of 480 MHz of spectrum in March 2026. She added that the government was exploring new business models and district-level connectivity licenses, including CVAS licenses, to help local entrepreneurs provide internet services in rural communities.
The minister said Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif reviewed progress on the National Connectivity Plan every two weeks.
Digital Inclusion and Public Services Remain Key Priorities
The minister also highlighted progress in narrowing Pakistan’s gender gap in mobile internet usage, saying it had declined from 38% to 8%. Citing GSMA findings, she said Pakistan had recorded the world’s fastest progress in reducing the gap over the past two years.
On the use of digital technology in public services, she said more than 10 million people had benefited from a technology-enabled fuel subsidy program. A smartphone was not required to access the assistance, she noted, to ensure that eligible citizens were not excluded.
Khawaja said around 2.2 billion people globally remained offline, while approximately 48% of the population in the Asia-Pacific region lacked internet access. These figures, she said, underlined the need to make digital connectivity more affordable and inclusive.
She stressed that technology should improve the lives of ordinary citizens rather than serve as an end in itself. Access to the internet, she added, had become essential for education, healthcare, disaster response, economic development, and national security.

Co-hosted by the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication (MoITT) and USF Pakistan, in collaboration with the APT Secretariat, the high-level international forum brings together ministers, telecom regulators, industry executives, and delegates from across the Asia-Pacific region.

Federal IT Minister Announces $1 Billion USF Milestone
Delivering the Chief Guest inaugural address, Honourable Federal Minister for IT
items.author: Press Release
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The landmark Asia-Pacific Telecommunity (APT) Symposium on Digital Transformation and Universal Service Fund (USF) officially opened today at the Islamabad. Co-hosted by the Ministry of Information Technology and Telecommunication (MoITT) and USF Pakistan, in collaboration with the APT Secretariat, the high-level international forum brings together ministers, telecom regulators, industry executives, and delegates from across the Asia-Pacific region.
The three-day symposium establishes a forward-looking operational blueprint to modernize universal service mandates across member states—pivoting from traditional coverage and voice subsidies toward gigabit fiberization, non-terrestrial satellite networks, smartphone device financing, and localized rural Artificial Intelligence (AI) infrastructure.
Federal IT Minister Announces $1 Billion USF Milestone
Delivering the Chief Guest inaugural address, Honourable Federal Minister for IT & Telecommunication, Shaza Fatima Khawaja, emphasized Pakistan’s commitment to building an inclusive, secure, and future-proof digital economy, while announcing a monumental achievement for the national telecom sector:
“True digital transformation requires bridging the usage gap just as aggressively as the coverage gap. In driving meaningful connectivity, we treat digital access as an indispensable engine of economic empowerment and social mobility. Under the APT Tokyo Statement 2025 guidelines, Pakistan is modernizing its policy landscape to empower rural communities with high-speed Fiber backhaul, smartphone affordability, and localized AI compute capabilities.”
“I am proud to announce a landmark milestone today: USF Pakistan has officially crossed the threshold of over $1 Billion ($1.054 Billion) in deployed contracted subsidies, playing a vital, historic role in advancing digital transformation across the country.”
Regional Leadership Calls for Next-Generation USF Models
In his inaugural address Dr. Masanori Kondo, Secretary General of the Asia-Pacific Telecommunity (APT) said;
“Digital transformation is changing our economies and societies—reshaping how governments deliver public services, how businesses operate, and how people learn, work, and communicate. As the Asia-Pacific advances rapidly into the age of 5G, satellite constellations, and artificial intelligence, the risk of digital exclusion has shifted from a lack of physical coverage to a lack of quality, capability, and digital readiness. Universal Service Funds must evolve into agile, outcome-oriented frameworks. Regional cooperation and harmonized regulatory approaches are key to ensuring that no country, island, or remote community is left behind.”
Highlighting the Organizational performance and APT Symposium sessions in his welcome address Ch. Mudassar Naveed, Chief Executive Officer, USF Pakistan said that;
“For decades, USFs were measured by tower counts in remote regions. Today, meaningful connectivity demands high-speed fiberization, active infrastructure sharing, and demand-side inclusion. USF Pakistan is proud to lead discussions on co-creating Buy-Now-Pay-Later (BNPL) device-financing frameworks, low-cost Right-of-Way (ROW) policies, and resilient middle-mile networks that bridge both economic and geographic divides.
“Aligned with the Prime Minister’s Digital Pakistan Vision and under the guidance of the Honourable Federal Minister, our mission focuses on extending connectivity where commercial viability falls short. To date, we have completed 158 out of 185 awarded projects, utilizing over PKR 169 Billion in subsidies and directly benefiting more than 38.4 million people.
The event was attended by a distinguished lineup of senior leadership, international delegates, and telecom pioneers. Prominent attendees included Ms. Palwasha Khan, Chairperson, Senate Standing Committee; Ms. Sabheen Ghoury, Parliamentary Secretary, MoITT; Mr. Rafique Ahmed Buriro, Additional Secretary, MoITT; Mr. Masanori Kondo, Secretary-General, APT; and Maj. Gen. (R) Hafeez Ur Rehman, Chairman, PTA.
The regulatory body and the Ministry were further represented by PTA Members Mr. Muhammad Naveed and Dr. Khawar Siddique Khokhar, along with MoITT Members Mr. Asfandyar Khan, Member DET, and Mr. Muhammad Jahanzeb Rahim, Member Telecom.
Global delegates included Mr. Moshiur Rahman (Bangladesh), Mr. Warren Suti (Papua New Guinea), Ms. Tshering Dema (Bhutan), Mr. Mohd Akmal Radzuan (Malaysia), and Ms. Cecily Jemaima Iakopo (Samoa).Industry leadership was strongly featured through Mr. Naveed Khalid Butt (PTCL), Mr. Shan Ul Haq (PTML), Mr. Shahid Razzaq (CMPak/Zong), Mr. Ahmed Bilal Masudand deputy CEO Huawei other sector executives.
Building on the Tokyo Statement 2025 and the APT Strategic Plan, the symposium repositions Universal Service Funds as drivers of socio-economic development across four pillars:
Accelerating Gigabit Broadband: Expanding Fiber backhaul and last-mile connectivity to unserved and low-income areas.
Integrating Emerging Technologies: Leveraging AI, LEO satellites, 5G/6G, cloud, and IoT to bridge the digital divide.
Sustainable Funding & Governance: Advancing transparent BNPL device financing streamlined ROW frameworks, and long-term fund sustainability.
Multi-Stakeholder Collaboration: Aligning governments, regulators, USF administrators, operators, vendors, and local communities.

NCCIA Investigating Alleged Misuse of AI

The incident brings renewed attention to how law enforcement agencies assess potentially threatening online communications involving generative AI. The case concerns the alleged actions and intentions of a user, while the investigation and any subsequent court proceedings will determine the legal outcome.

items.author: Meha Agarwal
items.content:
With winter almost here, it’s almost time to reopen those trunks and suitcases holding the family’s woolen and warm clothes. The sweaters, shawls and jackets go through trials before being rolled out for the season.
This is a familiar routine for anyone who lives in a city or town with a winter to speak of, and every season brings the same challenges of keeping up with the trends and the changing needs of everyone in the family.
For everyday wear, keeping an old favourite sweater or cardigan makes sense, but going on a holiday or dressing up for an occasion in winter changes things. Plus, if you live in Mumbai or Chennai or any other temperate city with no real cold months, buying winter wear for that occasional trip to the mountains or cold cities means spending on things you will barely touch once you’re back home.
Take a casual look at the online aisles of winter wear on Myntra or AJIO or any fashion platform. The total expense adds up rather quickly and grows quite large when the whole family needs new winter clothes.
For instance, Decathlon lists a snow jacket somewhere at ₹5,999 and a winter parka at ₹6,999. And those are some of the less pricey options out there when it comes to gear that keeps you warm in true cold.
Beyond the price, there’s the responsibility of cleaning, storing and maintaining it until the next use. For many, this is simply not worth the hassle. So can rental change the game?
Mumbai-based winter apparel and thermo-layer brand Kosha is offering winter wear rentals with a good number of options starting at ₹990 for seven days. Bengaluru’s SharePal is renting a wide assortment of products at rates as low as ₹50 per day, while Mumbai-based Roamwear has packaged winter wear into its travel wardrobe rental for women.
Rentals are not a new idea in India. We touched upon the circular fashion economy earlier and Gen Z’s interest in thrifting and value-conscious shopping is being seen in winter wardrobes too. Just like in wedding wear and designer fashion earlier.
Unsurprisingly, the market for winter rentals is quite large in markets where winter travel is a major tourist attraction. But players such as Finland-based Winterent, Sweden’s SkiStar, Austria’s SkiGala and Japan’s Soranoshita offer outdoor winter clothing near ski retreats. These largely target tourists and not individuals in the region.
That’s the key difference between these players and the Indian startups we spoke to. In India, winter wear rental is undoubtedly an experiment. The question is: is the market big enough for the startups to scale?
Where’s The Ceiling?
Rishav Jain, managing director, Alvarez & Marsal India, says the idea of creating a shared economy matters more than which category is being targeted. Anything with a high average selling price and low usage can move into the rental or shared economy game, especially in a market like India.
Kosha founder Yuktie Jhangiani Verma believes that traction is inevitable even though the category is small today.
“This is a brand new space. It is still too early to define its absolute ceiling, the growth momentum is undeniable. Exciting shifts are happening across consumer behaviour every single month,” she added.
One of the key differences between renting and direct sales is that the former targets premium products that are not widely available or are out of reach of individuals due to their price.
This is why rental for winter wear as a business is positioned and linked with travel. Startups are targeting customers that are booking ski trips, treks or their next European winter holiday. This makes rental a small add-on cost to the overall travel budget.
“Fashion renting works when the item costs above roughly ₹6,000-8,000 and you expect two or fewer trips. Rental typically prices at 10-20% of retail per rental period, so a ₹10,000 jacket at ₹1,490 a week is a clear saving, compared to another jacket that sells for ₹3,299, where that rental price will be 45% of directly buying one. In the latter case, most customers would prefer to buy the jacket than rent it,” TDV Partners’ founder and managing partner Ujwal Sutaria said.
For instance, a published comparison by Indiahikes’ Crosstrek says renting a full set of trekking gear comes up to ₹2,435 for six days, compared to ₹18,250 for buying that same gear. This includes trekking shoes, a padded jacket, rain jacket, backpack and accessories. These are indicative prices rather than what a typical customer might end up spending if they take their time researching the options in the market but not everyone has the time for that.
Sutaria said that as more and more Indians make international trips, the market for rentals is growing. India reported 32.71 Mn overseas departures in 2025, and Japan alone went from 233K to 315K+ Indian visitors between 2024 and 2025. The market for Indian tourists to Northern European destinations like Sweden, Iceland and Norway has grown tremendously in the past two years.
“Viable categories are heavy parkas, ski and snow suits, snow boots and trek gear. Frequency is the ceiling, because by the third trip the customer buys,” he added.
But purely depending on customers planning travel can end up becoming a paradox for rental platforms. More travel plans means more rental opportunities, but it means customers are also more likely to purchase rather than rent every time.
Which is why rental platforms cannot just market the affordability; it’s also about keeping up with the latest styles, materials and trends. Even a short weekend trip can be a window for rental platforms. Some are targeting customers that change their wardrobe with the destination rather than using their existing winter wardrobe.
“When you rent, you have the flexibility of a changing wardrobe with every itinerary. You get a sleek trench for a city break, a technical parka for sub-zero trips, and a vibrant ski jacket for the slopes, all at a fraction of the retail cost,” Kosha’s Verma told Inc42.
Small factors like holiday photographs and social media posts influence choices too. Customers who want a different look on each trip may keep renting even when they can afford to buy. The stigma around rented clothing is disappearing fast among metro users.
So what can brands do in this space to scale? According to Sutaria, customer experience and discovery are the critical levers here. Distribution also matters because the category is sensitive to other parts of the economy i.e. travel.
Founders in this space added that resale of retired rental stock is a second revenue line but that requires a captive audience base as well.
The next demand signal is therefore whether customers return for another itinerary, and whether those orders extend beyond the same short travel season. And that dictates the whole economic model for rental platforms.
Going Beyond The Rental Season
Once the holiday is over and the heavy winter coat comes back to the platform, the startup has to prepare it for another paying customer.
So maintenance and upkeep is a central challenge and can skew unit economics. Any company in this space has to provide for reverse pickup without which the rental proposition does not work.
The dry cleaning and storage is managed by platforms to limit the exposure to costs and to maintain high quality of products. At Kosha, Verma said, clothes go through a 10-point checklist before being rented out again.
So the key metric here would be rentals-per-SKU. The margins are baked into the rental fee, so the actual growth should be seen in the number of rentals for every jacket, coat or sweater in the inventory.
This is just like the RentoMojo or Furlenco business model, and it’s a parallel for which we have numbers too.
As per recently listed RentoMojo’s disclosures, the company had 8.51 Lakh items as of March 2026, of which 83.34% were out on rent. Items purchased nearly ten years ago had already earned 5.12X their original cost by this point in time.
More than 56% of the assets added in 2017 and 60.92% of those added in 2018 were still generating revenue in FY26. These are metrics that even rental platforms have to track, and the shelf life of a wool sweater may be much shorter than that of a hardwood table or other items that Rentomojo offers on rent.
In other words, the business for fashion rental platforms — which includes winter wear — depends on how much of the stock is out on rent, how long each item lasts and how much it costs to put it back into circulation.
For winter wear, the peak demand sits in a short travel season, so the share of stock out on rent across the full year is also another number to watch when assessing startups and their operations.
As of now, none of the companies we have spoken to have hit the kind of scale to speak meaningfully about these metrics and their revenue in detail. That itself gives us a clue as to how winter wear startups are still figuring their way around the economic models of this business. Perhaps the end of this winter season may give us an idea of where this is headed.
SPOTLIGHT | HOW UPLIANCE.AI IS MAKING HOME COOKING SMARTER
Bengaluru-based Upliance.ai builds AI-powered kitchen appliances designed to simplify everyday cooking. Its flagship device automates chopping, stirring, grinding and heating through a smart jar, built-in weighing scale and touchscreen-guided recipes.
The appliance offers more than 750 guided recipes across 34 cuisines, covering everything from Indian curries and biryanis to pasta, soups and desserts. Users follow step-by-step instructions on the screen, while the device manages cooking temperature, timing and stirring.
Upliance.ai is expanding beyond its cooking assistant into smart air fryers powered by its UpAI technology. The fryers let users turn food photos, recipe reels and YouTube recipes into cooking settings. The startup reports more than 6.6 Lakh meal sessions since November 2022 and sales crossing 7,500.
THE DEEP DIVE
ECOMMERCE BUZZ
Nat Habit Raises ₹142 Cr: The personal care brand’s Series C round was led by Trident Growth Partners, with existing investors participating. Nat Habit plans to expand its retail network tenfold to two lakh stores, enter modern trade, strengthen quick commerce and launch sunscreens and serums.
Bewakoof’s FY26 Net Loss Jumps 19%: The D2C fashion brand’s operating revenue grew 40.6% YoY to ₹243.1 Cr in FY26, while net loss widened from ₹73.2 Cr. Total expenses rose 35.4% to ₹335.6 Cr, even as its EBITDA loss narrowed marginally.
KISAH Bags ₹35.9 Cr To Scale Men’s Fashion: The ethnicwear brand raised its first institutional round, led by Fireside Ventures at a ₹211 Cr post-money valuation. KISAH plans to expand beyond its 12 stores, targeting 100 outlets and ₹500 Cr in revenue while remaining profitable.
DailyObjects Secures ₹332 Cr For Offline Expansion: The lifestyle accessories startup’s Series C round was co-led by Xponentia Capital Partners, Anicut Capital and Axiom Asia Private Capital, valuing it at ₹1,050 Cr. DailyObjects plans to expand to 150 exclusive brand outlets, strengthen product development and explore international markets.
Swish Pilots Restaurant Food Delivery: The quick food delivery startup is testing Swish Go in select Bengaluru pincodes, sourcing orders from third-party restaurants and cloud kitchens. The service advertises zero packaging and platform fees, marking a shift from Swish’s own-kitchen model to compete with Swiggy’s Toing and Rapido’s Ownly.
Lumio Secures Series A: The consumer electronics brand raised $12 Mn in a Series A round led by Blume Ventures, with participation from Stellaris Venture Partners and 3one4 Capital. Lumio plans to expand its product portfolio, strengthen software and after-sales support, and build an offline retail presence.
Beyond Appliances Raises ₹110 Cr: The smart kitchen startup raised ₹110 Cr in a Series B round led by Fireside Ventures. Beyond Appliances plans to establish a new manufacturing facility in South or West India and launch ovens within 9–12 months, expanding beyond smart chimneys and hobs.

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
MakeO, the parent of clear aligner brand Toothsi, has raised ₹90 Cr (about $9.4 Mn) in a funding round led by Singularity AMC, with participation from DSP family office, Genesis, and Unispace Ventures.
The Mumbai-based startup will use the fresh capital to expand its offline presence across India and Southeast Asia and strengthen its manufacturing operations. It will also invest in consumer experience, clinical centres, and backend technology.
MakeO is also evaluating acquisitions of dental and aligner businesses across India and Southeast Asia as part of its offline expansion
The fundraise follows its acquisition of Singapore-headquartered Zenyum, which expanded its presence across Southeast Asia. MakeO had announced an agreement to acquire Zenyum in February.
In 2025, it also acquired Apple Dental for ₹10.9 Cr in a cash-and-stock deal. The chain operates 20 clinics across Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, extending MakeO’s offline presence beyond major Indian cities.
Following the Zenyum acquisition, the combined group has a network of around 1,100 partner dentists across 10 countries. It also operates more than 60 offline clinical centres and has served over 4 Lakh consumers, according to the startup.
Founded in 2018 by Arpi Mehta, Pravin Shetty, Manjul Jain and Anirudh Kal, makeO initially offered teeth aligners under the brand toothsi. In 2022, it merged its brands toothsi and skinnsi under makeO to offer dental, skin and hair treatments on one platform.
MakeO had raised over $100 Mn before the latest round from investors including Eight Roads Ventures, 360 ONE Asset, and Paramark Ventures. Its earlier fundraises include ₹100 Cr in June last year and a $16 Mn round led by 360 ONE Asset and the investment office of Ashish Kacholia in January 2024.
MakeO said its combined business has crossed ₹500 Cr in revenue and turned EBITDA profitable earlier this year. It aims to double revenue over the next two to three years.
The startup’s expansion plans come amid projected growth in India’s clear aligner market. According to Market Research Future, the market is projected to grow from $466.99 Mn in 2025 to $2.83 Bn by 2035, at a CAGR of 19.74%.

items.content:
African technologists and entrepreneurs are applying blockchain in innovative ways, creating a new financial infrastructure for the continent with wide-ranging benefits, including for the humanitarian sector.
Through its Blockchain Ventures investment programme – supported by Ethereum Foundation and GSR Foundation – UNICEF Office of Innovation provides funding and technical assistance to emerging market startups building innovative blockchain-based solutions.
Unreliable and expensive internet access locks millions out of the digital economy, but as XMesh founder Benjamin Yan explains, blockchain could help equip ordinary people to act as a hyper-local connectivity provider and earn an income from their unused bandwidth.
What problem were you trying to solve when you came up with XOneFi?
I love adventure travelling and I use Starlink in remote areas. I was paying a fair amount of money for that service and I’d find that people around me also wanted to get online, but there was no way to share the connection and there was no way to charge people who want to use my internet, so that’s when I began thinking about a usage-based solution for sharing the internet.
How does XOneFi work?
Anyone with an internet connection can become a provider. They purchase their upstream connection, and then install an XOneFi-enabled router, set their rate and they are good to go.
Nearby customers can use their phones or computers to discover the network, purchase internet access by time or data usage, and the XOneFi firmware meters the session and automatically sends the payment from the customer to the provider.
Where does blockchain come in, and why is it essential?
The blockchain is valuable because we are facing an open network with many independent providers and customers who don’t know the infrastructure owners.
Blockchain is fully transparent, offers tamper-resistant usage accounting – so that providers and customers cannot cheat– and automated micro payments. If a customer is paying $4 a month, maybe every hour you are only paying several cents, which is a very small amount of money, and without blockchain we really cannot transact that.
How are prices set so they work for providers and customers?
We provide a default rate, but providers can adjust it based on their own payment for the internet. When the customer connects they see how much they need to pay and, if they agree, they click, and the transaction starts.
How does the connectivity gap you are bridging affect children and schools?
School administrators tell us connectivity issues are really a big problem: their internet is not reliable, the data rate is very low. Sometimes they cannot sustain a Zoom call or YouTube video, and you can’t even talk about coding or using AI. It is really a missed opportunity for the kids to get a better education, to get the opportunities that they want.
Why did you choose Nigeria to test XOneFi?
Nigeria is a growing economy with big cities and a large population of young people looking for opportunities. They want to utilise the digital economy to improve their living standards.
What is happening on the ground now?
We are running a pilot project at two Nigerian schools and planning to expand to community centres and business centres. Our chief financial officer and our director – both are women – are really moving things forward and identifying and solving challenges on the ground.
Looking ahead, what is your vision for connectivity and local digital economies?
The ultimate vision is that a child or any other user does not need to know where the connection comes from – whether it’s fibre, cellular, satellite or any other technology – but will be able to find an affordable network that they can use. For providers, they can operate their own access points, earn income and reinvest in the hardware to get a better connection. So, everyone has the opportunity to become a mini, hyper-local provider of connectivity, and everyone can get affordable and reliable internet.

Pick up a slim phone and you already know the catch. Thin has always meant less: less room, less battery, less of the day before the charger comes out. TECNO is about to bring a phone to Pakistan that claims the catch is gone.
The upcoming POVA Curve 2 5G is positioned as the slimmest phone in its segment, and it carries the POVA name, a name built on staying power. Those two things are not supposed to fit in the same body. TECNO has not said how it made them fit, which leaves one question hanging over this launch: how much power can a phone this slim actually hold?
The rule every slim phone has obeyed
The pattern is familiar. Day one is a delight: light in the pocket, easy in the hand. Then the afternoon arrives, the percentage starts falling, and the hunt for a charger or a power bank begins. Thinness and battery life have long been treated as opposites, because every millimetre shaved off a phone is space the battery used to have.
Pakistan punishes that trade-off harder than most places. Long commutes, load-shedding, hours of social media, video calls and mobile gaming drain a phone quickly. A phone that turns heads at breakfast and dies by mid-afternoon is not much of a phone.
The phone that refuses to choose
The POVA Curve 2 5G walks straight into that problem. The “Curve” in its name points to the design: softer lines and a shape made to sit comfortably in the hand. The “slimmest in segment” claim is the bolder part, and putting it on a POVA suggests TECNO believes the old trade-off has been beaten.
TECNO is framing the phone as Beauty and Beast. The Beauty is in plain sight: the slim, curved body. The Beast is the part nobody has seen yet, the power packed inside it, and TECNO is holding that back for the reveal. If the early signals are right, the answer may be far bigger than a phone this thin has any right to give.
Three questions before launch day
Until TECNO lifts the curtain, these are the questions worth asking:
How does it feel in the hand? Slim phones live or die on comfort and grip, and a curved body should count in its favour.
How long does it last? This is the test every slim phone eventually fails, and the one TECNO seems most eager to take. The number behind that confidence could be the headline of the launch.
How does the segment respond? If a slim phone can match or beat its thicker rivals on stamina, every other phone in the segment has some explaining to do.
The POVA Curve 2 5G arrives in Pakistan on October 15. Until then the question stays open, and TECNO seems to be enjoying the suspense: how much power can the segment’s slimmest phone hold?

items.author: Rizwana Omer
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
The Higher Education Commission (HEC) and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA) have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to set up digital degree verification between their attestation systems. The aim is to let HEC-attested academic credentials be checked directly through a secure link between the two bodies.
The MoU is an agreement of intent. It does not say when the connection will go live.
What the MoU says
According to HEC, the MoU provides for secure, API-based integration between the attestation systems of the two institutions. An API (application programming interface) lets one software system ask another a question and get an answer without a person in between. In this case, the question is whether a degree carries a valid HEC attestation.
Executive Director HEC Prof Dr Zia Ul Haq and Foreign Secretary Asim Iftikhar Ahmad signed the document. Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar and HEC Chairman Prof Dr Niaz Ahmad Akhtar witnessed the signing, along with senior representatives of both organisations.
Where the two offices sit in the process
HEC has recently moved its own side online. It now runs a fully online, paperless degree attestation system that removes the need to visit HEC offices or submit original documents. Under that process, the applicant’s details are checked against NADRA records, the university verifies the credentials against its own records, and HEC issues an e-Attestation Certificate after a final review.
MoFA’s role comes after that step. One applicant, writing publicly, says MoFA requires university degrees to be HEC-attested before they go through its authentication and apostille process. That is a user’s account, not an official statement, but it matches how the two offices are generally understood to work together.
Stage
Body
Current form
Institutional verification
University or HEI
Checks records, reports to HEC
Attestation
HEC
Online, issues e-Attestation Certificate
Authentication for external use
MoFA
Requires HEC attestation first
Link between HEC and MoFA
Both
MoU signed; API integration planned
Why the link matters
A credential passes through several offices before an employer or university abroad accepts it. If each office checks the previous one by looking at a stamped document, every stage depends on paper or PDFs that can be altered or lost. A direct system-to-system query lets MoFA check the status against HEC’s own record instead of trusting the copy in front of it.
For Pakistani graduates applying for jobs, study places or residency overseas, the practical gain would be fewer chances for a document to be rejected or delayed over a doubt about its origin. That outcome depends on how the integration is built, which the announcement does not describe.
This is also not HEC’s only recent data link. In July, HEC signed an MoU with the Pakistan Software Export Board to connect its degree verification system to a planned national digital workforce platform and a verified digital talent repository of students and IT professionals. Taken together, HEC’s attestation record is being wired into more systems, each with its own audience: employers in one case, the foreign service in the other.
What the announcement leaves open
HEC’s statement does not say several things. It gives no launch date. It does not say whether foreign embassies, employers or universities will be able to query the system, or only MoFA. It does not cover fees or how personal data will be protected when two government systems exchange it.
There is also a question about older records. The applicant quoted above asks why a degree already attested under the old system should have to go through verification again after the move to digital. That is one person’s complaint, and HEC has not responded to it in the material reviewed. It does point to a gap the MoU’s authors may need to address: how legacy attestations are carried into the new setup.
What to watch
Attestation works as a chain of custody, and each stamp is only as strong as the link before it. Replacing paper hand-offs with an API strengthens that link but adds new points of failure. System downtime, mismatched records and unclear rules on who can query what would all become policy problems, not just technical ones.
The test of this MoU is simple. If an applicant needs fewer steps and fewer repeat payments after the integration, it has worked. If the same documents are still requested at each counter, the API will exist, and the process will not have changed. The agreement is a necessary first step, and the details that follow will decide whether it delivers.

items.author: Arooj Fatima
items.content:
Jhang is set to host its first-ever Desert Rally 2026 alongside a three-day cultural festival from October 16 to 18 in the Thal Desert at Rehmat Abad, Tehsil 18-Hazari.
Deputy Commissioner (DC) Jhang Babar Sahib Din announced the event during a press conference in Lahore, saying it is being organized under the vision of Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz Sharif to promote tourism, highlight regional culture and introduce Jhang’s attractions to national and international audiences.
The rally will feature a 95-kilometer off-road racing track, with around 100 drivers and riders from across Pakistan expected to participate, including female jeep racers. Renowned racer Nadir Magsi is also among the leading competitors expected to take part.
Sahibzada Sultan Muhammad Ali, founder and leader of the off-road racing team Team Sultan, confirmed his participation and invited motorsport enthusiasts to attend the event.
He said the rally would provide an opportunity to showcase racing talent and establish a new sporting tradition in Jhang. He expressed confidence that participation from leading national and international racers would help make the first edition successful and one of the district’s most memorable sporting events.
The event’s main sponsor, Mukarram Waheed Sheikh, also encouraged tourists and sports enthusiasts to visit Jhang and experience its landscape, hospitality and cultural heritage.
Alongside the desert racing competition, the three-day festival will feature traditional sports, adventure activities and family entertainment. Planned attractions include tent pegging, horseback archery, kabaddi, volleyball and paragliding.
Sheikh particularly highlighted tent pegging and horseback archery as major attractions expected to generate public interest.
MPA Col. (R) Ghazanfar Abbas Qureshi, former MPA Faisal Hayat Jaboana, Ameer Abbas Sial and other participants at the press conference also expressed support for efforts to promote tourism, preserve local culture and encourage recreational activities.
Organizers expect between 50,000 and 100,000 visitors during the three-day event, although actual attendance will depend on public response and event arrangements.
By bringing together desert racing, traditional equestrian sports and cultural activities, organizers aim to establish Jhang as an emerging adventure tourism destination while showcasing the heritage and hospitality of southern Punjab.

items.author: Rizwana Omer
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Pakistani advertisers are moving money toward social media creators, and they are changing how they pay them. A Retail News Asia analysis describes a market where flat sponsorship fees are giving way to commissions tied to sales.
Influencer marketing in Pakistan now rests on a large audience. The more useful question for brands is what a post actually sells.
A large audience, with a caveat attached
DataReportal counted 79.9 million social media user identities in Pakistan in October 2025, equal to 31.2 percent of the population. A user identity is an account, not a unique person, so one individual can account for several.
TikTok’s advertising reach is close to 80 million adults, YouTube at about 54 million and Instagram at about 22 million. Other trackers give different numbers. A TikTok agency guide citing DataReportal puts TikTok at 66.9 million adult users in early 2026. NapoleonCat counted 25.6 million Instagram users in Pakistan in September 2026.
The gaps come from dates and methods, but they also point to a real distinction. Ad reach estimates the audience an ad tool may be able to reach, which is different from active users. It is a planning figure, not a count of people who watch or buy.
The report also lists creators with audiences large enough to rival broadcasters:
Creator
Platform
Followers (as reported)
Jannat Mirza
TikTok
Over 25 million
Hania Aamir
Instagram
Over 20 million
Ducky Bhai
YouTube
Over 10 million subscribers
Rajab Butt
Not specified
Around 9 million
Flat fees give way to commissions
According to the report, deals are moving from flat fees to direct affiliate commissions. Smaller creators often accept free merchandise or modest cash retainers. Top celebrities still charge premium rates.
Retailers are handing out trackable discount codes and custom referral links. A merchant that gives unique codes to 100 creators can see within days which accounts produce orders.
For consumer startups and domestic cosmetic lines, this offers distribution without the upfront cost of a television run. The creator is paid when the sale happens, so the brand carries less risk before it knows what works.
Relevance over follower count
The analysis argues that fit now matters more than size. Its example is a specialist account with 50,000 motorcycle enthusiasts, which it says regularly converts better for vehicle parts suppliers than an entertainment channel with five million subscribers.
The report compares this to live-stream selling in Southeast Asia and China, where a product demonstration leads straight to payment and delivery. It says Pakistan has similar conditions: growing smartphone use, digital payment systems and a young urban population used to buying on mobile.
Authenticity and measurement problems
Growth has brought disputes over audience quality. The report names synthetic engagement, bought followers and unclear commercial disclosures as risks. It says they are most serious in regulated sectors such as consumer health and financial services.
Marketing teams are responding by judging creator deals on customer acquisition cost, basket size and repeat orders. The report says this demand is supporting talent agencies, affiliate platforms and analytics firms in Karachi and Lahore.
Promo codes have their own weakness, and the report does not address it. A code proves a sale happened. It does not prove which post caused it. Codes also spread to coupon sites and group chats, so a buyer may use a code from a creator they never watched. Brands comparing 100 creators on code redemptions will be comparing noisy numbers.
What to watch next
Billboards, print and television still draw institutional budgets, the report says, but broadcasters no longer control consumer reach. Its closing expectation is that budgets will follow verified checkouts and that brands will watch whether creator live streams deliver steady sales through the coming festive shopping cycles.
That season is the practical test. A creator-led campaign that tracks well but sells poorly will look different against year-end sales pressure than it does in a pilot.
The commission model also moves risk around. Under flat fees, the brand pays whether or not the post works. Under commissions, the creator carries the conversion risk, and the brand carries the tracking risk. The side with better data will have the stronger position in the next negotiation, and for now that is more often the brand. Creators and agencies that can show buyer-level results, not just reach, are likely to command the better terms.

Dan melalui OnePlus 16, aspek performa benar-benar dibuat lebih serius, lewat tambahan fitur hardware maupun software.
Lewat acara peluncuran yang berlangsung luring, OnePlus 16 juga dirilis bersamaan dengan sejumlah aksesori pelengkap yang tidak kalah menarik. Mulai dari power bank 10.000 mAh yang mendukung pengisian daya 67W, hingga pendingin berbasis hardware dengan mekanisme magnetik. Memberikan kemampuan smartphone agar bisa terus berperforma kencang dalam waktu lebih lama.
Baca juga: OPPO Reno X Dirumorkan Usung Layar 16:9, Lebar Bodi Capai 85 mm
Aspek Performa OnePlus 16 Dibuat Maksimal
Bisa dibilang desain OnePlus 16 masih terlihat identik dibandingkan generasi sebelumnya, dengan semua sudut dibuat flat, lengkap dengan bentuk modul kameranya. Hanya saja kini tersedia dalam opsi warna berbeda, yakni Starlight, Dark Forest, serta Martian Masterpiece—di mana salah satu opsi warnanya memberikan corak LED khusus pada sisi bodi belakangnya.
Namun sisi depan smartphone tidak kalah spesial, di mana layar OnePlus 16 mengusung panel BOE X4 versi kustom berukuran 6,78 inci, dan diklaim menjadi smartphone pertama dengan “global refresh rate” hingga 165Hz. Tak sampai di situ, layar smartphone bisa naik ke 185Hz untuk memberikan pengalaman gaming 185fps pada sejumlah judul game tertentu.
Tepi bezelnya sangat tipis, hanya 1,15mm saja. Sementara pada sektor hardware, selain cip Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, OnePlus 16 juga membawa P4 display chip tambahan, G3 eSports chip, hingga T3 touch chip—semuanya hadir untuk memberikan pengalaman gaming yang lebih optimal. OnePlus janjikan akan ada setidaknya 23 judul game populer yang bisa berjalan hingga 185fps, dengan pengalaman lebih imersif lewat giroskop yang lebih presisi.
Baterai OnePlus 16 juga tergolong andalan, karena kini berkapasitas 9000 mAh, dengan dukungan fast charging hingga 100W. Menariknya, smartphone ini juga bisa mengisi daya perangkat lain, hingga 27W. Tentunya opsi seperti bypass charging juga ikut hadir.
Kamera Lebih Andal, Harga Mulai Rp16 Jutaan
Umumnya smartphone rilisan OnePlus membawa setup kamera yang lebih inferior dibandingkan flagship lainnya. Kabar baiknya, setup kamera OnePlus 16 sudah ditingkatkan. Sensor utamanya kini beresolusi 200MP, mengusung sensor Samsung HPE berukuran 1/1,4 inci. Dan sensor tersebut dipasangkan bersama telefoto 50MP 1/1,95 inci 3x optical zoom, dan 50MP ultra-wide yang juga mendukung autofokus.
Pada sisi depan, juga disematkan sensor kamera 50MP yang mendukung autofokus. Harga OnePlus 16 dibanderol mulai CNY5999 atau sekitar Rp16 jutaan untuk kapasitas 12+256GB. Namun untuk varian tertinggi dengan kapasitas 16GB+1TB, mencapai CNY8499 atau sekitar Rp22,7 jutaan. Sayangnya, smartphone OnePlus sudah lama absen secara resmi di Indonesia.
