items.author: Ankush Das
items.content:
For years, enterprises hired thousands of human executives to sell loans, answer customer queries and recover abandoned sales. Yet, even with massive teams, many high-value client interactions would slip through the cracks every single day.
While some prospects were lost due to poor agent training, others were lost to long support queues. As a result, businesses consistently struggled to reach every lead on their lists.
The common assumption was that companies simply needed better training for human agents or simply more calling executives. However, Arrowhead’s founders saw things differently.
According to them, the core issue was that human-driven phone processes struggle to function effectively at enterprise scale. The realisation could not have come at a more opportune time.
With rapid improvements in AI voice technology, they saw the future clearly – improving human-led call centres would soon matter far less than automating them entirely. This single realisation changed the direction of the startup.
Founded in 2022 by Devyani Gupta and Vengadanathan Srinivasan, Arrowhead is building voice AI agents primarily for enterprises. It claims to power autonomous voice systems for many leading banks, NBFCs, ecommerce platforms and healthcare providers.
The startup claims that its conversational agents automate everything, from loan sales and customer queries to abandoned cart recovery and collections.
In January 2026, the startup raised $3 Mn in its seed funding round led by Stellaris Venture Partners. It claims to work with over 50 BFSI clients, including Tata 1mg, Bank of Baroda Cards, IndiaMART, Aditya Birla Capital, Paytm, Turtlemint, Kissht, InsuranceDekho and others.
Yet, Arrowhead did not start with the technology it uses today. The startup’s pivot to enterprise voice AI was the result of a calculated gamble, which forced its team to rethink everything they had built.
When Analysing Human Calls Was No Longer Enough
Arrowhead didn’t start in voice automation. The startup’s initial product was a conversation intelligence tool. Drawing on her experience at BCG across continents, cofounder and CEO Gupta initially built Arrowhead to identify mis-selling and compliance violations on recorded sales calls. Early clients, such as edtech platform upGrad, used the tool to pinpoint bad sales pitches that resulted in refunds.
Then came the GenAI boom of 2023 and 2024, and the founders reached an uncomfortable conclusion.
“We quickly realised that if we continued analysing just human sales calls, we would soon be analysing something that would potentially go extinct,” Gupta told Inc42.
Recognising that human-driven call centres were on borrowed time, Arrowhead pivoted sharply to AI in late 2024. Rather than competing on building another chatbot, the startup focused almost entirely on voice-first enterprise workflows.
Arrowhead initially targeted banks and financial institutions, where large calling operations remain critical for loan sales, collections and customer engagement. But, in a stroke of fate, many enterprises that originally bought Arrowhead’s analytics software returned as buyers for its autonomous voice agents – this time, to replace their manual calling queues altogether.
To scale its voice stack, Arrowhead quickly realised that off-the-shelf software simply would not cut it. The founders needed to control every layer of its underlying engine.
Building A Voice AI Stack From Ground Up
Instead of relying entirely on third-party API providers, Arrowhead has gradually built much of its voice AI infrastructure in-house. The startup recently launched internally fine-tuned small language models (SLMs), engineered specifically for live enterprise conversations. Rather than optimising purely for lower inference costs, the founders claim that the platform prioritises latency and conversational quality.
According to the startup, its latest deployments have achieved response latency below 500 milliseconds, allowing conversations to feel significantly more natural during live phone calls. For context, even small delays in voice interactions can disrupt the flow of conversation, making latency a much bigger challenge than traditional text-based AI systems.
To complement its language models, Arrowhead has also developed its own text-to-speech (TTS) models, powered by thousands of hours of custom speech recordings. The startup hired voice artists across specialised agencies to record speech across multiple Indian languages and emotional contexts.
This primary data, instead of generic public datasets, enables Arrowhead’s AI models to master subtle human nuances, such as empathy, hesitation, filler words and natural speech rhythms, which generic TTS systems typically miss.
Overall, its underlying AI stack also includes:
Fine-tuned SLMs built on open-source foundation models such as Gemma and Qwen
Proprietary TTS models trained using custom primary speech datasets
Emotion-aware speech synthesis systems capable of responding with empathy and contextual tone
Optimised inference infrastructure for sub-500 millisecond voice responses
Support for multiple Indian languages, including Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam
Enterprise deployments designed around data residency, privacy and single-tenant architecture for regulated industries
Voice orchestration systems capable of integrating with multiple enterprise APIs during live conversations
Speaking with Inc42, cofounder and CTO Srinivasan said that hosting proprietary language models provides cost savings, predictable latency and superior conversational quality while ensuring sensitive customer data stays safely within India for regulated industries such as banking.
On the back of its in-house AI stack, the founders claim that over 90% of users cannot distinguish Arrowhead’s voice agents from human representatives unless explicitly told that they are speaking with an AI agent.
This conversational fluidity has enabled the startup to move beyond pilots to deploying its agents directly into critical, revenue-generating operations.
Arrowhead’s BFSI Strength
On the business front, financial services remain Arrowhead’s biggest market. Around 80% of the company’s revenue comes from banks, NBFCs and fintech companies, although it has also started expanding into sectors such as healthcare, ecommerce and edtech. Overall, Arrowhead’s voice AI platform is currently being deployed across three major enterprise workflows.
The first is outbound loan sales, where its AI agents move far beyond basic lead qualification to complete much of the loan application journey. During a live call, the agent addresses customer objections, collects required documents, runs OCR-based verification and hands over fully completed files straight to underwriting.
The second core area for Arrowhead is inbound customer support. Here, its AI agents first determine customer intent before tapping into the enterprise database to answer complex policy questions, fetch real-time loan statuses and retrieve account-specific records. This drastically cuts manual workload for enterprises that handle tens of thousands of support hours each month.
The third area is abandoned cart recovery. For ecommerce platforms, Arrowhead’s AI agents contact customers shortly after they leave without completing a purchase. During the conversation, the system can modify cart items, apply discount codes, update shipping details, and process transactions without ever transferring to a human representative.
The startup recently disclosed that its deployment with Tata 1mg generated conversion rates around 15% higher than human agents during abandoned cart recovery campaigns.
But with healthy market traction and product-market-fit (PMF) in its kitty, how is Arrowhead monetising its customer base?
How Arrowhead Makes Money
Arrowhead employs a hybrid pricing strategy that blends traditional SaaS usage with performance-based monetisation. A portion of revenue is generated through per-minute billing, while another component depends on business outcomes delivered through AI deployments.
The founders believe that outcome-based pricing creates stronger alignment with enterprise customers while reducing the long-term impact of declining AI infrastructure costs.
While the founders did not disclose Arrowhead’s revenue figures, they said that usage-based contracts drive the majority of revenue and yield gross margins between 25% and 30%. They added that profitability varies depending on customer scale and committed call volumes.
That said, the startup, despite operating with a lean team, has scaled rapidly to partner with most of the country’s top banks, NBFCs, and fintechs.
For the founders, replacing traditional call centres is just the opening move. Their bigger bet is that enterprise voice AI platforms will become completely autonomous, capable of completing entire business workflows on their own.
But the road ahead may not be easy. The voice AI space in India is peppered with deep-pocketed homegrown startups such as Observe AI, Bolna, and Gnani.ai, among others. On top of this, unit economics also remains a real challenge, as LLM reasoning and TTS together can be an expensive purchase for early stage startups.
Infrastructure and UX challenges also persist, particularly around mobile voice navigation and integration with existing enterprise systems. So, as India’s AI ecosystem matures and voice AI infrastructure turns into a commodity, Arrowhead is tasked with maintaining its tech edge to thrive in the long haul.
The post How Arrowhead Is Using Voice AI To Fix The Gaps In Enterprise Sales And Support appeared first on Inc42 Media.

items.summary:

The train was travelling towards Agege when the collision occurred, involving the Honda, with registration number EKY 902 JT.
Operatives of the Lagos State Traffic Management Authority (LASTMA) and security personnel swiftly rescued the driver and removed the wrecked vehicle from the railway track, enabling the train to resume its journey.
No casualty was reported in the incident.

items.author: Christopher Louis
items.content:
NetApp memperkenalkan Novus, arsitektur penyimpanan yang dirancang untuk mendukung operasional AI factory berskala besar. Solusi ini menyasar penyedia infrastruktur AI, termasuk perusahaan neocloud dan layanan GPU-as-a-Service, yang membutuhkan pasokan data berkecepatan tinggi untuk menjalankan beban kerja kecerdasan buatan.
Menurut NetApp, salah satu tantangan dalam pembangunan AI factory adalah kemampuan sistem penyimpanan memasok data secara konsisten ke GPU. Ketika pasokan data tidak mencukupi, pemanfaatan GPU dapat turun di bawah 30 persen. Kondisi tersebut berpotensi meningkatkan biaya operasional karena infrastruktur komputasi yang mahal tidak digunakan secara optimal.
Melalui Novus, NetApp menargetkan throughput agregat lebih dari 100 TB per detik. Namun, angka tersebut merupakan kemampuan yang dituju oleh arsitektur ini, bukan jaminan bahwa setiap penerapan akan langsung mencapai performa serupa. Hasil akhirnya tetap bergantung pada konfigurasi infrastruktur dan kebutuhan beban kerja.
Baca Juga: ChatGPT dan Gemini Palsu Dipakai untuk Curi Password serta Kode MFA
Pisahkan Metadata untuk Mengurangi Hambatan Penyimpanan
NetApp Novus menggunakan pendekatan yang memisahkan pengelolaan metadata dari jalur data. Dengan desain ini, performa, kapasitas, dan konkurensi dapat ditingkatkan secara independen dalam satu namespace melalui protokol NFS. Pendekatan tersebut ditujukan untuk menangani pertumbuhan dataset AI tanpa harus membagi penyimpanan menjadi banyak sistem terpisah.
Pada tahap awal, Novus menggabungkan NetApp Novus Data Director yang berjalan pada infrastruktur Supermicro terkualifikasi dengan layanan data NetApp ONTAP melalui sistem AFF A90. NetApp menyatakan arsitektur tersebut dapat dipesan saat ini dan dirancang untuk lingkungan cloud serta multi-tenant. Perusahaan juga menyiapkan jalur menuju implementasi berbasis perangkat lunak pada masa mendatang.
Skalabilitas Jadi Fokus, Efektivitas Tetap Perlu Diuji
NetApp mengklaim Novus dapat membantu operator meningkatkan pemanfaatan GPU sekaligus mengurangi kebutuhan ruang, daya, dan infrastruktur tambahan. Kemampuan meningkatkan kapasitas serta bandwidth secara terpisah juga berpotensi membantu penyedia layanan menyesuaikan sumber daya dengan kebutuhan masing-masing beban kerja.
Meski demikian, klaim performanya perlu dilihat dalam konteks pengujian dan penerapan nyata. Omdia menyebut pengujiannya menunjukkan skalabilitas yang mendekati linear dan memproyeksikan kemampuan baca sekuensial hingga 100 TBps dengan kapasitas efektif puluhan exabyte atau lebih. Angka tersebut merupakan proyeksi berdasarkan pemodelan, bukan hasil yang otomatis berlaku untuk semua konfigurasi. Bagi penyedia AI, manfaat Novus pada akhirnya akan ditentukan oleh kemampuan meningkatkan efisiensi GPU tanpa menambah kompleksitas dan biaya operasional secara berlebihan.

items.title: Anti-Apartheid South African who condemned Gaza Genocide wins 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
items.summary:
The Norwegian Nobel Committee has award the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, who fought Apartheid and called out Israel over Gaza genocide.
In a statement, the Nobel Prize Committee described Navi Pillay as one of the great defenders of international legal principles.
The committee added that this year’s laureate had been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.
According to the committee, “Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.”

The Norwegian Nobel Committee has award the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, who fought Apartheid and called out Israel over Gaza genocide.
In a statement, the Nobel Prize Committee described Navi Pillay as one of the great defenders of international legal principles.
The committee added that this year’s laureate had been instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted.
According to the committee, “Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.”

The statement said that the Nobel Peace Prize for 2026 went to a person who with exceptional courage and integrity has led the way towards a more comprehensive global legal order.
“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career.”
“Pillay has shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence. Navi Pillay has also contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law. Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time.
“In awarding this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, the Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently. Peace requires justice.
“History has shown that a world operating without the rule of law is unjust, unwise and inhumane. The judges – those who guard the thin red line between order and chaos – are therefore highly deserving of our praise. But today, as these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked, we need people of courage, vision and determination – qualities that Navi Pillay demonstrates in her work on the bench.
“Navi Pillay has held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict. In all the positions she has held, she has stressed the responsibility of individuals and states to comply with the rule of law.
“She has also helped define the relevant norms and legal principles. When the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda established that rape and sexual violence could constitute a crime against humanity – as well as genocide – her influence was a significant factor.
“In the same case, Ms Pillay was instrumental in a separate legal breakthrough: for the first time, a defendant faced charges of incitement to commit genocide purely on the basis of spreading propaganda.”
Who is Navanethem “Navi” Pillay?
Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin under apartheid in Durban, South Africa, Pillay became a lawyer and legal pioneer, confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation and exclusion.
A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time.
She has served as a judge on the High Court in South Africa, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court.
She was the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and, until recently, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
Pillay is now a judge on the International Court of Justice in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide.

items.title: Preparations complete, ball in K-P govt's court on emergency imposition: Tariq Fazal
items.summary:
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry on Friday said the federal government had completed its preparations for imposing governor’s rule or an emergency in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, adding that it was now up to the provincial government to decide what role it would play in the proposed measures.
Speaking on a private television programme, Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Sath, the minister said the federal government and law enforcement agencies had to eliminate terrorism in K-P at all costs, and it would be better for the provincial government to cooperate and participate in the fight.
“If the provincial government stays away from this effort, the other option would be to impose an emergency and eliminate terrorism and terrorists from the province once and for all,” he said, clarifying that an emergency would be imposed across the entire province, not just in 12 districts.
Read More: PTI warns of quitting assemblies if governor's rule imposed in K-P
Chaudhry categoric
items.author: Web Desk
items.content:
Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry on Friday said the federal government had completed its preparations for imposing governor’s rule or an emergency in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, adding that it was now up to the provincial government to decide what role it would play in the proposed measures.
Speaking on a private television programme, Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Sath, the minister said the federal government and law enforcement agencies had to eliminate terrorism in K-P at all costs, and it would be better for the provincial government to cooperate and participate in the fight.
“If the provincial government stays away from this effort, the other option would be to impose an emergency and eliminate terrorism and terrorists from the province once and for all,” he said, clarifying that an emergency would be imposed across the entire province, not just in 12 districts.
Read More: PTI warns of quitting assemblies if governor's rule imposed in K-P
Chaudhry categorically stated that the proposed emergency had nothing to do with the PTI’s planned long march.
He said the government had dealt with longer marches towards Islamabad in the past and stopped them, adding that preparations had been completed to prevent the planned march as well.
“We know how to deal with this long march. This long march is neither a threat nor a problem,” he said.
The minister refrained from giving a date for the imposition of an emergency but said the federal government had now concluded, both mentally and practically, that further delay was not possible.
“I cannot give you a day or date, but a final decision has been made that decisive action to eliminate terrorists in K-P is inevitable,” he said.
Asked whether there was still a chance of negotiations, particularly with Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman emerging as a possible mediator, the minister said the door to dialogue was never closed in political affairs.
However, he blamed PTI for a lack of consensus within its own ranks on whether to authorise Maulana Fazl to mediate.
“When I said the ball was in the Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa government’s court, the option of Maulana Fazlur Rehman was also on the table,” he said.
He added that if the PTI did not authorise Maulana Fazl to mediate or was unwilling to appoint him as an intermediary, it would be difficult to move the dialogue process forward.
Chaudhry said the PTI leadership would have to provide assurances that it would cooperate in the fight against terrorism if it wanted meaningful and effective negotiations.
“That assurance is the foundation of any lasting solution,” he concluded.
Sanaullah links K-P governor’s rule to counterterrorism cooperation
Earlier, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah said that the proposed governor’s rule or emergency in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa was related to the matter of counterterrorism cooperation, not the PTI’s planned long march, and could be resolved if the provincial government stood alongside the federal government and law enforcement agencies.
Speaking on a private television programme, Naya Pakistan, Sanaullah said the negotiations appeared to be heading towards a dead end as the PTI did not seem willing to abandon its plan for a long march and accept the offer of talks.
Linking the possibility of governor’s rule or an emergency in K-P to the PTI leadership and provincial government’s commitment to the fight against terrorism, he said the matter could be resolved if PTI leaders and Chief Minister Sohail Afridi declared their support for the federal government and law enforcement agencies in the fight against terrorism.
Read: CM Afridi says PTI to unveil ‘final plan’ in Swabi as long march enters 6th day, heads to Charsadda
He stressed that the proposed imposition of governor’s rule had nothing to do with the long march.
“If they do not make this commitment, then whether they hold the long march all the way to Islamabad or keep it short of Islamabad will make no difference,” he said.
The PML-N leader said that, over the past three or four days, the K-P chief minister had stated that no military operation would be allowed in the province.
Sanaullah said there would be no need to displace people or evacuate valleys, as the proposed measures would involve intelligence-based operations.
“Imposing an emergency certainly does not mean that those districts will be evacuated and people turned into internally displaced persons (IDPs). Rather, intelligence-based operations will be conducted within the territorial jurisdiction,” he said.
During the same program, K-P Law Minister Aftab Alam expressed surprise at what he described as ambiguity in statements by federal ministers on the proposed measures.
“One minister says that if the long march is not called off, an emergency will be imposed, while another says that the government wants to impose an emergency or governor’s rule because the provincial government is not cooperating with the federation on terrorism-related matters,” he said.
Alam said he believed a narrative was being built against the K-P government as part of what he called a “nefarious conspiracy”.
“God forbid, it is being suggested that we are somehow on the side of someone else in these matters. However, our stance is clear: this war is ours even before it is the federation’s,” he said.
Also Read: Govt trying to avoid ‘last option’ but may consider governor’s rule in K-P if no alternative remains: Khawaja Asif
He maintained that the PTI and the K-P government stood with law enforcement agencies in the fight against terrorism, adding that the provincial government had strengthened the police.
“Our mission is very clear, and it is being deliberately made controversial,” he said.
The issue of Governor’s Rule has become a major point of contention between the federal and K-P government. On September 21, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi said the government was consulting the law ministry on legal options for the province, including Governor’s Rule, if the PTI proceeded with its long march. Two days later, however, Information Minister Atta Tarar ruled out any plan to impose Governor’s Rule, saying the federal government had no intention of removing the PTI administration.
Some federal ministers publicly raised the possibility of federal intervention in K-P. Federal Minister for Kashmir Affairs Amir Muqam said consultations were under way on the "constitutional and legal option" of imposing Governors' Rule.
Afridi, however, rejected the warnings and said he would not retreat from his position because of threats of Governors' Rule or an emergency. He also said PTI supporters could take to the streets at short notice if an attempt was made to remove him.
However, amid the speculation, just days before the PTI’s planned long march, the prime minister and the president formed a committee last week to negotiate with the PTI and other opposition parties over the march, while expressing concern over the province’s deteriorating law and order situation.
The government and opposition parties held negotiations over two days, and the talks initially appeared to be bearing fruit. However, just as the two sides were nearing agreement on most of the contentious issues, a deadlock emerged, bringing the negotiation process to a halt.
The government blamed the K-P government, particularly Afridi, for the deadlock and failure of the negotiations. The PTI, however, claimed that the talks broke down over its demand for a meeting with the party’s founder, which the government refused to accept.
Read More: Bilawal urges PTI to return to political engagement, says governor's rule in K-P would be 'atomic bomb'
As the negotiation process collapsed, CM Afridi began his long march towards Islamabad, further escalating tensions between the two sides, with both sides continuing to trade allegations.
As tensions peaked, PM Shehbaz once again entered the fray and extended an olive branch to the PTI, saying the government was prepared to engage with the opposition if the party ended its long march and sit-ins.
The PTI, however, rejected the offer as its march continued towards Islamabad, entering its sixth day on Friday. The convoy moved towards Charsadda, with CM Afridi leading the procession.

items.summary:

"That is ​why
items.author: Reuters
items.content:
US President Donald Trump's ​administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize, putting Washington on ‌a diplomatic collision course with European allies.
The ICC's deputy prosecutor, Nazhat Shameem Khan, condemned the sanctions and said they would not halt the tribunal's work.
The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges. Friday's move would go far further by potentially punishing companies that provide services to the ​court itself.
Read: Trump administration prepares sanctions against International Criminal Court, sources say
"President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement, first published by Reuters.
"That is ​why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off its resources and crippling its ability to operate."
Today, the Trump Administration is sanctioning the ICC.
This action should encourage our Allies within the Court to work for solutions to end this threat to U.S. sovereignty forever. pic.twitter.com/D86dCqLUaZ
— Secretary Marco Rubio (@SecRubio) October 9, 2026
ICC Deputy Prosecutor Khan told Reuters the sanctions "must be condemned".
"The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work ​that an independent judicial institution is doing," Khan said. "Our work will continue across all our situations, our investigations and our prosecutions."
US sanctions on the ICC “must be condemned” as they intend to undermine rule of law internationally and will not stop the court’s investigations and prosecutions across all situations, says ICC deputy prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan pic.twitter.com/fDaXrcDL88
— TRT World Now (@TRTWorldNow) October 9, 2026
Washington has denounced the ICC over arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials, including ​Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC has since closed.
The court counts 125 countries as member states, including all EU countries and all members of the NATO alliance apart from the United States and Turkiye. It has received strong public backing in the past from member countries including major US allies, and is based in the Netherlands, an EU and ​NATO member.
Navi Pillay, the South African jurist who won the Nobel Peace Prize earlier on Friday, had served as a judge on the ICC's Appeals Chamber from 2003-2008. The prize committee ​said in its citation that in naming her it had sought to "issue a reminder" at a time when "judges and institutions of international law are under political attack".
Read More: Navi Pillay: Nobel laureate who led UN inquiry that found genocide in Gaza
"An international legal system in which war criminals are ‌held to account ⁠, and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world," the prize committee said.
Rubio said the sanctions had been structured to give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns.
Washington immediately allowed some exemptions. Shortly after the sanctions were announced, the US Treasury issued four general licenses, which would allow some transactions for ICC telecommunications, software and pension payments, and transactions linked to ICC detainees.
US expects allies to 'rein in the court'
US sanctions typically bar all US-based companies from any work with a sanctioned organisation, ​forcing banks to shut accounts, insurers to end ​coverage and software companies to halt ⁠cooperation.
The Trump administration previously imposed targeted sanctions on court officials during his first term, which were rescinded under President Joe Biden. Washington announced new sanctions just days after Trump returned to office in January 2025.
Court officials have been preparing for months for the prospect of sanctions ​on the court itself, shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open-source equivalents and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance.
The court's registrar, ​Osvaldo Zavala Giler, called ⁠earlier this week for the EU to be prepared to use a so-called "blocking mechanism" that lets it shield European countries from the extraterritorial effects of sanctions.
In his statement, Rubio said the United States had delayed its sanctions hoping that the ICC and the countries party to its founding Rome Statute would address US concerns, but they had failed to do so.
The Trump administration imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), potentially cutting off its banking, insurance and software services.
The move comes amid U.S. anger over ICC arrest warrants for Israeli officials, including Netanyahu, and a previous… pic.twitter.com/CJfJMbxbwL
— Clash Report (@clashreport) October 9, 2026
"Either the ICC will ⁠end its ​threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ​ICC and that rely on American service members for their defence, to rein in the court," Rubio said.
"We have structured this action to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address our ​concerns. If these efforts do not bear fruit, we will continue to adjust accordingly," Rubio said.
UN chief condemns sanctions against ICC, warns of 'serious blow' to justice
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned US sanctions against the ICC on Friday, warning that the measures could undermine its work and deal "a serious blow" to international efforts to ensure accountability for grave crimes.
"Today's decision marks a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar. Accountability for international crimes and delivery of justice to victims are central to our global commitment to peace, security, human rights and fundamental freedoms," said a statement issued by his spokesperson, Stephane Dujarric.
UN Secretary-General @antonioguterres condemns the announcement of the imposition by the United States of sanctions against the International Criminal Court as an institution.
Full statement: https://t.co/4tZzdbfcsz pic.twitter.com/hGVDlEII3y
— UN News (@UN_News_Centre) October 9, 2026
Guterres was "deeply alarmed" by the expected impact of the sanctions on the court as a whole, particularly its ability to carry out its mandate, the statement said.
The UN chief also reiterated his support for the court's independence and called on countries to uphold their obligations under international law.
US sanctions draw opposition as countries warn of impact on its work
Meanwhile, six European countries, Canada and Japan, expressed regret over the US announcement of sanctions against the ICC, warning that the measures could significantly affect its operations, staff and their families.
In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands and the UK, along with their Canadian and Japanese counterparts, said they "strongly disagree" with Washington's announcement.
"We, the undersigned States Parties to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC), reaffirm our continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC," the statement said.
Foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, Netherlands and UK issue joint statement on ICC:
- We reaffirm our continued and unwavering support for independence, impartiality, and integrity of ICC
- We regret and strongly disagree with announcement of… pic.twitter.com/WL1O4gEkjp
— TRT World Now (@TRTWorldNow) October 9, 2026
The ministers welcomed the court's preparations to respond to potential sanctions, saying the measures would help it continue carrying out its mandate under the Rome Statute.
"Nevertheless, if put into effect, these sanctions will have a significant impact on the Court's work, its dedicated staff and their families," they warned.
The eight countries also pledged to pursue "constructive and inclusive dialogue" with countries that were not parties to the Rome Statute ahead of the Assembly of States Parties scheduled for December.
"We will continue to work together to support the Court's vital work, uphold the rules-based international system, and advance accountability," the statement said.

Microsoft’s Xbox division is expanding its presence in the entertainment industry with a new initiative aimed at turning more video games into movies, television series, merchandise, and live experiences. The company announced a new division called XP on October 8, 2026, following the success of A Minecraft Movie and the Fallout television series.
The move comes as Xbox looks for new ways to grow its business beyond gaming consoles and traditional video games. Through XP, the company plans to bring its popular gaming brands to a wider audience and create new opportunities across the entertainment industry.
Xbox Launches New XP Division to Turn More Games Into Movies and TV Shows
Xbox has a large collection of games, but only a small number have received major film or television adaptations. The new division will help the company expand these efforts and explore opportunities for more of its franchises.
Xbox XP Division Will Have Four Departments
The new XP division takes its name from “experience points,” a familiar term in video games. It will operate through four departments, each focusing on a different area of entertainment and brand development.
Xbox Pictures will focus on producing movies and television adaptations based on Xbox games. The department aims to bring more gaming franchises to film and television audiences.
Xbox Products will manage licensing and merchandise, allowing the company to expand its brands through products connected to its popular games.
Xbox Places will focus on live experiences and events. These could include activities at theme parks and other venues, as well as broadcast events that bring gaming communities together.
Xbox Partnerships will work with creators and other brands to develop new experiences based on Xbox properties.
Together, these departments will help Xbox explore opportunities beyond game development and reach consumers through different forms of entertainment.
Success of Minecraft and Fallout Inspired the Move
The success of A Minecraft Movie and the Fallout television series has demonstrated the potential of adapting video game franchises for other entertainment formats.
A Minecraft Movie generated approximately $961.2 million in worldwide box office revenue, making it a major commercial success. Its popularity also helped increase interest in the Minecraft game itself.
Following the movie’s release in 2025, Minecraft recorded a 75% increase in weekly active users, according to the reported figures. The results showed how a successful film adaptation can encourage viewers to explore the original game.
The Fallout television series also delivered positive results for the franchise. During the show’s first season on Prime Video, the number of hours players spent across Fallout games increased fivefold.
These results have strengthened the case for expanding established gaming franchises into movies and television. Such projects can introduce familiar characters and fictional worlds to people who may never have played the original games.
Kayleen Walters Appointed President of XP
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has appointed Kayleen Walters as president of the new XP division.
Walters previously served as an executive producer on A Minecraft Movie and is also working as a producer on its sequel, A Minecraft Movie Squared. The sequel is scheduled to arrive in cinemas on July 23, 2027.
Before joining Mojang Studios in February 2025, Walters spent 13 years at Lucasfilm, where she led global marketing campaigns for the Star Wars franchise.
Her experience in film production and entertainment marketing could help Xbox identify gaming properties with the strongest potential for adaptation.
Sharma also announced that Maria Angelidou-Smith, a former Meta vice president and Reddit chief product officer, will become CEO of Mojang and Minecraft.
Xbox Looks Beyond Its Gaming Business
The XP announcement comes during a challenging period for Xbox. The company’s gaming business has faced revenue declines, layoffs, and major organizational changes.
Xbox hardware revenue fell by approximately $1.7 billion, or 7%, during the 2026 fiscal year, which ran from July 2025 through June 2026.
In July 2026, Sharma announced a major restructuring plan that included plans to lay off 3,200 employees by mid-2027 and move four studios out of Xbox and under new management.
Expanding into entertainment could help the company diversify its revenue sources while making its gaming brands more recognizable outside the gaming community.
Streaming services and film studios may also benefit from working with Xbox because established game franchises already have recognizable characters, storylines, and fan bases.
Not Every Xbox Game Will Become a Movie
Industry analyst Dan Rayburn believes the expansion makes sense because Xbox needs to reach audiences beyond its core gaming market. However, he also cautioned that not every game will translate successfully into a film or television series.
Some franchises may appeal mainly to gamers, while others could attract a much broader audience. Xbox will need to select its projects carefully and work with experienced entertainment professionals to develop adaptations that connect with viewers.
The company’s existing successes provide a strong starting point, but future projects will need to demonstrate their own appeal.
With XP, Xbox is taking a more organized approach to expanding its intellectual property across entertainment formats. If the strategy succeeds, more of its gaming franchises could eventually appear on cinema screens, streaming platforms, merchandise shelves, and at live events.

items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
A new malware campaign called Midnight Mimosa has raised security concerns after researchers discovered that malicious software was pre-installed on some cheap Android smartphones. The threat is particularly concerning because the malware is built into the device’s firmware, meaning it can be present before users even turn on their new phones.
According to security researchers at Bitdefender, Midnight Mimosa is linked to a campaign involving disguised applications, fraudulent advertising activities, and system-level access. Unlike ordinary malicious apps, users cannot simply uninstall the malware through their phone’s settings.
Midnight Mimosa Malware Targets Cheap Android Smartphones in 150 Countries
The discovery highlights the risks associated with buying inexpensive smartphones from unknown brands or unauthorized sellers, particularly when the devices may contain modified or compromised software.
How Midnight Mimosa Malware Works
Midnight Mimosa operates through a persistent system application integrated into a smartphone’s firmware. This gives the malware elevated privileges that regular Android applications do not normally have.
With these privileges, the malicious software can install and remove applications, download additional code from remote servers, and grant permissions to other apps. These capabilities allow it to carry out activities without the user’s knowledge or approval.
Researchers also identified 32 disguised applications associated with the operation. These apps reportedly support advertising fraud by generating fake impressions and clicks, allowing the operators to benefit from fraudulent advertising activity.
Another concerning feature is the malware’s ability to temporarily disable the Google Play Store while executing certain malicious operations. It can restore the Play Store after completing these activities.
This technique may help the malware avoid detection by Google Play Protect during particular stages of its operation. It also makes the threat harder for ordinary users to identify because the phone may appear to work normally.
Cheap Android Phones Are the Main Target
The Midnight Mimosa campaign has primarily affected low-cost Android smartphones from multiple brands, particularly devices built on MediaTek platforms.
Although many affected models come from lesser-known manufacturers, the campaign reportedly reaches users in more than 150 countries. This suggests that the threat extends beyond a single market or region.
Researchers have also found that some affected devices are counterfeit copies of premium smartphones, including models designed to resemble the Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra and Galaxy S26 Ultra.
However, genuine Samsung smartphones are not affected by this campaign, according to the report. The presence of counterfeit devices highlights the importance of checking a phone’s authenticity before purchasing it.
The complete list of affected smartphone models remains unknown. Therefore, buyers should not assume that every inexpensive Android phone is infected, but they should exercise caution when purchasing devices from unfamiliar sellers.
Researchers Find More Suspicious Apps
The investigation also uncovered 13 Google Play applications that communicated with the same infrastructure used by Midnight Mimosa.
This finding suggests that the campaign may extend beyond smartphones carrying the pre-installed malware. Applications communicating with the same infrastructure could represent another part of the broader operation, although their precise role requires further investigation.
The discovery also demonstrates why checking individual apps may not be enough to protect a device when the underlying firmware itself has been compromised.
Can Users Remove Midnight Mimosa?
Removing Midnight Mimosa may be difficult because the malware is integrated into the phone’s firmware rather than installed as a normal application.
Users generally cannot eliminate such threats by uninstalling an app or clearing the device’s storage. A factory reset may also fail to remove malware that resides in the firmware.
If a phone is suspected of carrying Midnight Mimosa, users should avoid entering sensitive information, including banking credentials and passwords, until the device’s security has been assessed. They should contact the manufacturer or a qualified security professional for guidance.
If the malware cannot be safely removed, replacing the device with a trusted, genuine smartphone may be the most practical option.
How to Avoid Pre-Installed Malware
The Midnight Mimosa discovery serves as a reminder to check a smartphone’s source before making a purchase. Buying from authorized retailers and established manufacturers can reduce the risk of receiving counterfeit or compromised devices.
Consumers should also be cautious of smartphones offered at unusually low prices, particularly models that imitate premium devices from well-known brands.
Keeping Android and installed applications updated is important for general security, but software updates may not resolve malware embedded in compromised firmware.
Ultimately, Midnight Mimosa shows that smartphone security risks can begin before a user installs their first application. Choosing a genuine device from a reliable seller remains one of the most effective ways to reduce the risk of buying a phone that already contains malicious software.

The biggest saving comes every time you drive.
Fuel has become one of the biggest ongoing costs of owning a car in Pakistan. With petrol prices approaching PKR 400 per litre, a comparable petrol car averaging around 8 km/l can consume approximately PKR 100,000 in fuel every month for a 2,000-kilometre monthly drive, translating into nearly PKR 1 million in fuel costs over 20,000 km.
This is Fuel Anxiety: the cost and uncertainty that comes with every kilometre driven.
The Chery Tiggo 8 Super Hybrid offers a different way forward. Powered by Chery Super Hybrid (CSH), its plug-in hybrid system combines electric driving for everyday mobility with petrol flexibility for longer journeys, allowing customers to reduce fuel dependency without giving up the SUV they want.
With up to 90 kilometres of pure electric range and a combined range of around 1,200 kilometres, the Chery Tiggo 8 Super Hybrid operates as an electric-priority vehicle, enabling most daily driving without fuel while retaining the flexibility needed for longer journeys. And for customers with solar at home, the energy already being generated on their rooftop can power their everyday electric driving, turning their solar investment into mobility.
As Pakistan’s only 7-seater plug-in hybrid D-SUV, it brings three full rows of seating into the PHEV category, giving customers the space to bring the whole family along in one car, without needing an additional vehicle and another fuel bill.
Its performance matches its capability, with 496 horsepower, 735 Nm of torque and 0–100 km/h in just 6.8 seconds, making it one of the most powerful SUVs in the D segment.
Inside, the Chery Tiggo 8 Super Hybrid is one of the most feature-rich SUVs in its class, with a Queen Co-Pilot zero-gravity massage seat, heated and ventilated front seats, 15.6-inch HD infotainment display, digital instrument cluster, 12-speaker Sony premium audio system and immersive ambient lighting.
Chery ranks No. 1 among Chinese brands in J.D. Power in Quality. The Tiggo 8 Super Hybrid also carries a 5-star global safety rating, with 10 airbags, 23+ active safety features and Level 2 ADAS, alongside Euro 6B compliance.
You don’t have to give up the SUV you want to escape the fuel bill. You can change what powers it.
Introduced through Master Auto Engineering, part of Master Group, in partnership with Chery Automobile, China’s No. 1 automotive exporter for 23 consecutive years.
Backed by Master Group’s 60+ years of legacy and 40+ years in automotive, Chery Master Pakistan is building the next chapter of New Energy mobility in Pakistan. items.author: Debarghya Sil
items.content:
AI emerged as the defining theme in the Indian startup ecosystem in the July-September quarter, with startups in the segment raising their highest-ever-recorded quarterly funding.
According to Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, AI startup funding surged 265% year-on-year to $438 Mn. The number of deals rose 35% to 35 from 26 in Q3 2025. The momentum builds on a strong first half of the year.
Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn across 57 deals in H1 2026, more than four times the $162 Mn raised in the corresponding period last year. With another $438 Mn raised in Q3, the sector’s funding for the first nine months of 2026 stood at $1.1 Bn+.
The surge stands out against a relatively subdued funding environment. Indian startups collectively raised $2.2 Bn across 210 deals in Q3, up just 5% YoY, even as the deal count fell 13%. Quarterly funding also remained below the $3.4 Bn raised in Q3 2024 and the eight-quarter average of about $2.7 Bn.
AI was not the only segment to record a significant increase in investor interest during Q3. Cleantech startups raised $433 Mn, up 267% YoY, while funding for advanced hardware and technology startups, including robotics, semiconductors and aerial vehicles, rose 176% to $290 Mn. Meanwhile, fintech funding fell 11% YoY to $249 Mn, while ecommerce funding declined 31% to $245 Mn.
The divergence suggests that AI is attracting a growing share of investor capital even as funding across the wider startup ecosystem remains under pressure. But with valuations under scrutiny and large funding rounds driving the headline numbers, the question is whether AI can sustain its momentum in the coming quarters.
Investors Want More Than AI Exposure
Inc42’s Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, based on responses from more than 85 institutional investors, found that about 63% of investors see some degree of froth in Indian AI startup valuations.
About half of the investors who see valuation froth expect a correction within the next 18 months. Another 31% see mild froth but believe valuations are supported by real revenue.
Pranav Obhrai, founding and managing partner at Atrium Ventures, said the rise in AI valuations is part of a global trend, particularly in the US. At the pre-seed stage, he said, valuations are often shaped more by capital requirements, future potential and acceptable founder dilution than by revenue or profitability multiples.
For instance, a startup raising $3 Mn at 20% dilution would imply a $15 Mn post-money valuation, assuming the investor agrees to that price.
Beyond valuations, investors are also becoming more selective about the AI applications they expect to create the most value.
Vertical AI applications across sectors such as BFSI, healthcare, defence and agriculture emerged as the top choice in Inc42’s survey, with 39% of investors expecting this segment to capture the most value over the next five years.
AI hardware and semiconductors followed at 23%, while AI-led IT and business services accounted for 18%. Indian-language and sovereign foundation models received 14% of investor votes. Data, tooling and evaluation, and AI infrastructure and compute received 3% each.
Obhrai said foundation models and AI infrastructure typically have longer gestation periods than venture investors prefer. Vertical AI, by contrast, offers a clearer path towards building a defensible business through distribution.
“Distribution becomes the moat, especially in India, where technology alone offers limited protection against global competition,” he said.
An investor who requested anonymity made a similar distinction, pointing to the capital required to scale foundation models and model-routing infrastructure.
Such businesses may have to operate at nil or negative gross margins for extended periods, a commitment that Indian venture capital firms find difficult to sustain given their smaller asset bases compared with their US counterparts.
The investor added that application-layer businesses could offer more durable revenue opportunities than model-routing or foundation-model companies. While some investors are backing small language models and task-specific model developers, the capital required to build and scale the underlying technology remains a constraint.
The findings suggest that rising AI funding is not translating into an indiscriminate appetite for the sector. Investors are increasingly distinguishing between businesses that can use AI to solve specific problems and those that need substantial capital to develop the underlying technology.
Can AI Sustain The Funding Momentum?
The scale of the funding increase raises questions about how much of the momentum reflects a broad-based expansion in investor activity and how much is attributable to large growth-stage rounds.
The investor who requested anonymity said funding figures need to be assessed after accounting for sizable Series B and Series C transactions, including rounds raised by companies such as Emergent.
“One would have to normalise by excluding large Series B or Series C cheques,” the investor said, adding that, in their assessment, absolute AI funding had not moved significantly after accounting for these larger rounds.
This distinction matters because a small number of large transactions can lift aggregate funding without necessarily signalling that more investors are deploying capital across the sector.
Obhrai expects AI to retain a strong share of startup funding, even if capital flows fluctuate between quarters. However, he warned that a broader global AI bubble bursting could trigger a correction, given what he described as arguably inflated valuations of companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic.
Several structural factors could continue to support investment in Indian AI startups. In its H1 report, Inc42 highlighted the transition of enterprise AI adoption from pilots to production, global hyperscalers’ investments in Indian AI infrastructure, and efforts to build sovereign AI infrastructure and foundation models as drivers of the sector.
However, India’s AI funding pool remains much smaller than the capital being deployed globally. The H1 report noted that Indian AI startup funding was still a fraction of global investment, even as companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic raised multi-billion-dollar rounds during the same period.
For Indian startups, this gap presents both an opportunity and a constraint. Growing enterprise adoption and demand for specialised applications could support further investment, but businesses requiring substantial capital to develop foundational technology may find it harder to compete with better-funded global peers.
The Q3 numbers establish AI as one of the biggest drivers of Indian startup funding in 2026. Whether that momentum continues will depend on more than the size of the next funding round: investors will be watching for sustainable revenue, defensible applications and valuations that can withstand a potential correction in the global AI market.
Edited By Akshit Pushkarna
Creatives: Abhyam Gusai

The Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) has proposed expanding the scope of income tax rules from YouTube to all social media platforms, potentially bringing a wider range of online content creators and digital platforms within the existing tax framework.
The FBR has drafted notifications proposing amendments to the Income Tax Rules, 2002, replacing the word “YouTube” with “social media platforms” in two separate provisions dealing with income tax.
Under the first proposed amendment, the FBR seeks to revise clause (d) of sub-rule (1) of rule 13ZP in Chapter IIA of the Income Tax Rules, 2002. The amendment is being proposed under section 99C, read with sub-section (1) of section 237 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.
The second draft notification proposes a similar change in clause (d) of sub-rule (1) of rule 19R in Chapter VA of the Income Tax Rules, 2002. This amendment is proposed under section 99C, read with clause (b) of sub-section (3B) of section 101 and sub-section (1) of section 237 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.
By replacing the platform-specific reference to YouTube with the broader term “social media platforms”, the proposed changes could extend the relevant provisions beyond YouTube to other social media services.
The FBR has invited objections and suggestions from all persons likely to be affected by the proposed amendments. Stakeholders have been given seven days from publication of the draft notifications in the official Gazette to submit their feedback for consideration by the Board.
The notifications state that objections and suggestions received within the prescribed period will be considered by the FBR before proceeding further. The proposed amendments remain at the draft stage and do not, by themselves, establish that the changes have been finalised or brought into force.

items.author: Tom Jackson
items.content:
Kenyan digital bank Cloud9, which enables cross-border payments and borderless banking for African consumers and businesses, has secured an undisclosed investment from crypto and fintech accelerator Alliance, taking the startup’s total funding to date to US$1 million.
Disrupt Africa reported in late-2025 Tesh Mbaabu and Mesongo Sibuti were to launch a new digital banking platform called Cloud9.
Mbaabu and Sibuti are best known as founders of MarketForce, which began life in 2018 as a sales force automation software company, but soon pivoted to operate a B2B retail marketplace, RejaReja, where informal merchants in Africa could source, order and pay for inventory digitally and conveniently, as well as other things.
The startup was selected into Y Combinator, raised a US$2 million seed round, and followed that up with what was in theory a US$40 million Series A in 2022. MarketForce, however, was forced to close down RejaReja in 2024, after failing to adequately scale it given the global “funding winter”. The pair pivoted to a new joint venture, Chpter, which provides AI-powered chat automation tools for businesses on platforms like WhatsApp and Instagram, before launching Cloud9, a newer version of an old venture.
Cloud9 is targeting the gap faced by Kenyan entrepreneurs who import more than US$20 billion worth of goods a year, much of it from China, Dubai and India. Moving money across borders remains slow and expensive for these businesses, with banks taking up to two weeks to open business accounts and days to settle each wire transfer, while informal agents offer speed but no record or recourse. Mobile money, meanwhile, does not work across borders.
Built on stablecoin rails, Cloud9 gives entrepreneurs a single mobile account to hold, send, receive, save and invest money across currencies and borders. Users can hold Kenyan shillings, US dollars, euros, pounds and yuan, pay suppliers in more than 100 countries within minutes, receive payments from overseas clients through dedicated virtual accounts, and cash out to mobile money.
Businesses can also run payroll, bulk payments and team approvals from a single dashboard, while the startup’s Cloud9 Wealth product gives Kenyans access to savings vaults and global stock markets.
“Kenya already skipped the bank branch once. Mobile money became how the country pays for almost everything, but only within its borders,” said Mbaabu. “With Cloud9, a merchant in Nairobi should be able to pay a supplier in Guangzhou as easily as they pay a vendor down the street.”
Cloud9 went live in early 2026, and has since seen more than 25,000 accounts created. The startup says its transaction volume is growing by more than 15 per cent week-on-week.
“Stablecoins are becoming the settlement layer for global trade, and Africa is where that shift matters most,” said Imran Khan, general partner at Alliance. “Tesh has built for African merchants at scale before, and Cloud9 is turning stablecoin rails into an everyday bank account for the entrepreneurs who need it most.”
Cloud9 will use the new funding to expand its cross-border payment corridors, improve its product experience, launch virtual and physical cards, and grow its user base.

items.author: Anjali Jain
items.content:
MSME-focused lending platform NeoGrowth has secured ₹85 Cr ($8.8 Mn) in a mix of debt and equity round led by Dutch development bank FMO, with participation from LeapFrog Investments.
The startup is planning to use the fresh capital to scale its digital lending capabilities, deepen market presence across India and expand access to credit for MSMEs.
Founded in 2012 by brothers Dhruv and Piyush Khaitan, NeoGrowth offers loans to MSMEs across more than 75 business segments, targeting small businesses that often have difficulty accessing credit. Its lending model also includes daily repayment options and multiple repayment channels.
The fresh capital will aid the NBFC in scaling and supporting more MSMEs with timely and accessible formal credit, “enabling more small business owners to pursue their growth aspirations through our financially inclusive lending solutions,” managing director and CEO Arun Nayyar said.
The Mumbai-based startup uses its proprietary AI initiatives to strengthen underwriting, portfolio monitoring and risk management.
It offers collateral-free loans in the range of ₹5-75 Lakh, through products including NeoCash, NeoCash Insta, NeoCash Express, which cater to different business scales and segments.
NeoGrowth manages assets under management (AUM) of nearly ₹2,000 Cr and has engaged with more than 4 Lakh businesses. It has disbursed over ₹16,000 Cr in loans to date.
During FY26, NeoGrowth added 17 branches, taking its total branch network to 46 locations in India.
NeoGrowth last raised ₹300 Cr in equity funding 2022, with FMO footing over half the round. Its existing investors also include Omidyar Network, Lightrock, Khosla Impact, Accion Frontier Inclusion Fund–Quona Capital and 360 ONE Asset. The lender has also raised nearly ₹2,000 Cr in debt from 18 lenders between April 2025 and July 2026.
The fresh round comes as digital lenders increase focus on MSMEs, which often have difficulty in raising formal credit despite being the country’s second largest employer.
New-age NBFCs like Indifi Capital, Techfino, Lendingkart, FlexiLoans, Aye Finance, among others, are leveraging technology to address this issue and provide credit to MSMEs.
As the ecosystem evolves, many NBFCs are also taking the public markets route to raise capital for their lending operations. In the past year, those that have hit the bourses include Aye Finance, Kissht, Moneyview, Tata Capital and Northern Arc, among others.
Meanwhile, those in the IPO pipeline include Fibe, InCred, Avanse and Muthoot, reflecting broadening maturity of the sector, with total NBFC AUM expected to reach ₹50 Lakh Cr by FY27 end.
Notably, NBFC credit accounted for nearly 26% of the country’s GDP in 2026, as they step in to expand credit access for those not covered by traditional banking.

items.author: Amiya Johar
items.content:
Mobile World Live (MWL) brings you our top three picks of the week as Indian authorities rejected Elon Musk’s allegations about Starlink’s regulatory roadblocks, BT rescued TalkTalk in a £400 million deal and Deutsche Telekom (DT) looked to capitalise on sovereign AI demand.
India hits back at Musk over Starlink oligarch claims
What happened: India’s Ministry of Communications rebuked Elon Musk’s accusation that Indian oligarchs were blocking Starlink’s launch in the country and seeking to preserve a “monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people”, stressing its satellite communications framework is “fair and non-discriminatory”.
Why it matters: The watchdog explained Starlink, along with Indian telecom incumbents Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel, are all at the same stage of the regulatory process. Each operator must complete security assessments before they can seek spectrum, with final clearances pending. Musk has previously clashed with Reliance Jio owner Mukesh Ambani over satellite spectrum access in the country. Starlink’s protracted approval process in India has lasted four years, with security requirements and spectrum access among key issues. Its presence in the country has also been complicated by reports that Starlink equipment was recovered across parts of the country, claims Musk said do not indicate an illegal active service in India.
Manas Mody, founder of business consultancy FX & Float, said the regulatory debate was “broader than a contest between Musk and operators” because “there could be legitimate regulatory and security considerations behind the resistance”, adding India “has done considerable work to secure its critical digital infrastructure”. “While Musk’s concerns may have some merit, I believe there’s likely more to this than just a conspiracy involving oligarchs,” he argued, adding Starlink is “unlikely to make a significant dent in India’s consumer telecom market” at its planned pricing as its “real opportunity lies in improving connectivity in underserved regions and remote hubs”.
India hits back at Musk over Starlink oligarch claims
BT strikes £400M deal for TalkTalk
What happened: BT Group agreed a £400 million deal to acquire TalkTalk’s consumer and wholesale businesses out of administration, bringing 2.5 million customers and around 900 employees under its ownership.
Why it matters: The acquisition prevents the UK broadband provider from folding and potentially disrupting services for millions of customers. TalkTalk reported £1.2 billion in revenue in the past 12 months but was loss-making following a prolonged, unsuccessful sales process. BT CEO Allison Kirkby called the situation “genuinely unprecedented”, warning millions of citizens, businesses and public services were at risk if TalkTalk collapsed. She said the acquisition was “the only viable option to keep millions of customers connected and supported”, with the BT adding the business can become value accretive if it is stabilised.
Kester Mann, director of consumer and connectivity at FDM CCS Insight, said the deal “will inevitably also evoke scrutiny from regulators keen to ensure a fair and competitive playing field”, given BT’s “strong position in the broadband market”. He added that this was particularly relevant after competition authorities raised concerns over Nexfibre’s planned acquisition of fellow broadband player Netomnia.
For TalkTalk, Mann said the deal “cements a painful decline” as the company “failed to respond sufficiently to a fast-changing and increasingly competitive market”. Its demise, he warned, should be “a stark warning to any value-focused telecom provider”.
BT strikes £400M deal for TalkTalk
DT eyes sovereign AI revenue bump
What happened: DT set out plans to turn rising demand for sovereign AI into a new revenue stream, targeting around €250 million in non-US AI-related revenue this year and approximately €800 million by 2030.
Why it matters: The German operator noted European businesses and public institutions seeking AI capabilities while retaining control of data and operations presented a key opportunity, describing sovereign AI as a “growth business”.To that end, DT said it is developing an automation platform for SMEs and expanding AI customer service offerings. CEO Timotheus Hoettges stressed it is crucial AI “delivers measurable value” across the business.
Jamie Escott, account director at Vodafone Business Security Enhanced, said DT’s projected €2.5 billion reduction in indirect costs by 2030 highlights “the growing importance of AI moving beyond experimentation and into large-scale operational deployment”. He added organisations are increasingly focusing on “measurable outcomes such as productivity, efficiency and service quality”. Meanwhile, Jean-Philippe Romieu, executive director for cloud and AI professional services at Microsoft Germany, described DT’s strategy as a “telco blueprint”, pointing to use cases included network integrated AI, autonomous infrastructure and AI-assisted operations. However, he flagged issues including volatile compute costs and market adoption, warning DT’s success “relies heavily on European enterprises prioritising data localisation over hyperscaler pricing and performance”.
DT eyes sovereign AI revenue bump

items.author: Usama Anjum
items.content:
Copyright protected content copied from PhoneWorld website.
Pakistan Telecom Mobile Limited (PTML) has challenged the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority’s (PTA) decision to suspend the commercial operations of its digital telecom brand ONIC, escalating a dispute over the service’s regulatory status.
The PTA had directed PTML to immediately halt new ONIC SIM and eSIM sales, activations, subscriptions, marketing, and other commercial activities, ruling that the service falls within the Mobile Virtual Network Operator (MVNO) framework and requires separate regulatory authorization.
The regulator has allowed PTML three months to migrate existing ONIC subscribers to PTML to avoid service disruption. However, it clarified that the transition period does not permit ONIC to continue commercial operations or acquire new customers.
PTML has contested the ruling, maintaining that ONIC is a digital brand operating under its existing Mobile Network Operator (MNO) license rather than an independent virtual network operator.
Why PTA Wants ONIC’s Operations Suspended
The dispute centers on ONIC’s business model and its commercial relationship with Digital Technology Management Services (DTMS), a separate entity responsible for several customer-facing operations.
According to the PTA, ONIC operates through separate billing and customer management systems, dedicated digital platforms, and customized packages. DTMS also handles key functions, including marketing, customer acquisition, SIM distribution, and customer support.
The regulator highlighted a Build-Operate Services Agreement under which DTMS receives 55% of relevant revenue during the initial three years, with the share declining subsequently.
PTA maintained that these arrangements give ONIC the characteristics of an MVNO, despite the brand operating on PTML’s existing network infrastructure.
PTML, however, argues that its arrangement with DTMS is an outsourcing agreement and does not change ONIC’s status as a digital brand. The company insists that spectrum, numbering resources, subscribers, and regulatory responsibility remain under PTML.
The regulator also raised concerns over subscriber data management, SIM verification, billing systems, lawful interception and compliance with telecom security requirements.
Legal Dispute Dates Back to 2023
The regulatory disagreement began in June 2023, when PTML informed the PTA of plans to introduce ONIC as an app-based mobile service targeting major Pakistani cities.
In August 2023, the regulator instructed PTML not to launch the service until its operational structure had been reviewed. PTML subsequently challenged the directive before the Islamabad High Court.
In February 2026, the court referred the matter back to the PTA for a reasoned decision. Following a hearing, the regulator concluded that ONIC’s operating arrangements fell within the MVNO framework.
Under its latest order, the PTA has given PTML two options: restructure ONIC as a product operating entirely under its existing telecom license or obtain the necessary MVNO authorization.
The latest legal challenge has placed ONIC’s operating future under renewed uncertainty, with the court’s decision potentially influencing how digital telecom brands and third-party service arrangements are regulated in Pakistan.
For existing ONIC customers, the immediate concern is the regulator-directed migration process, while restrictions on new customer acquisition remain central to the dispute. The available information does not establish whether the court has granted any interim relief.
Also read:
PTA Orders ONIC to Stop New Sales, Rules Service Falls Under MVNO Framework

items.author: Shrishti Bisht
items.content:
The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) may introduce its proposed insurance commission caps as early as January 2027, amid opposition from brokers over potential revenue losses and job cuts.
The regulator is considering January 1 and April 1, 2027 as possible implementation dates for its distribution reforms, Girija Subramanian, whole-time member (distribution) at IRDAI, told Bloomberg in an interview.
The proposals seek to curb distribution costs through product-wise commission caps and tighter limits on insurers’ overall expenses. IRDAI has argued that commissions have risen faster than premiums since rules were relaxed in 2023, without a corresponding increase in insurance coverage.
Subramanian said commission caps should take effect sooner, arguing that phased reductions could encourage distributors to rush sales and increase the risk of mis-selling. Separately, IRDAI’s consultation paper proposes a five-year transition to lower expense limits for insurers, with the first interim milestone in FY29.
“There is an earlier-the-better case, but getting the reforms right is more important than getting them early,” she told Bloomberg.
The proposals have implications for listed insurance distributors such as Policybazaar parent PB Fintech and Turtlemint, whose businesses depend on commissions from insurance sales. Shares of PB Fintech and Turtlemint have slumped over 47% each since IRDAI proposed the commission caps on September 23.
However, the framework is still under consultation. Stakeholders have until October 25 to submit comments, after which IRDAI will review the feedback and publish draft regulations for another round of consultation before issuing the final rules.
Brokers Flag Revenue, Employment Risks
The Insurance Brokers Association of India (IBAI) has warned that the proposed norms could cut broking sector revenues by 60–70% and result in the loss of up to 10 Lakh jobs across insurance distribution.
At a press briefing, the association’s representatives said the distribution sector employs more than 83 Lakh people. While supporting IRDAI’s objective of making insurance more affordable and accessible, they argued that the proposed changes threaten small businesses and MSMEs.
The resulting job losses could affect insurance awareness, policy renewals, assistance to policyholders, and insurance penetration among underserved communities, they added.
The association has sought an extension of the feedback deadline to December-end from October 25 and submitted letters to the Prime Minister’s Office and the finance ministry.
The IBAI also disputed IRDAI’s interpretation of data showing that general insurance premiums sourced through brokers grew 37%, while commission payouts rose 173%. It argued that the increase in commissions since FY23 largely reflected the reclassification of previously off-book marketing expenses following regularisation, rather than inflationary pressures on insurance consumers.
The association claimed that general insurers’ operating expenses averaged around 26.5% of gross premiums, below the mandated 30% limit. It also said policyholders received ₹84.4 in non-life insurance claim payouts for every ₹100 of premiums paid over five years, compared with a global average of 72–75%.
The representatives said the association was ready to work with IRDAI to address specific market anomalies, including mis-selling and disproportionate remuneration.
IRDAI Backs Wider Distribution
IRDAI, meanwhile, has pointed to rising expenses at private insurers. Expenses at private life insurers increased to about 22% of total premiums from 16% in FY21, while those at private general insurers rose to roughly 32% from 25% in FY19. Additional rewards have also pushed distributor remuneration 30–60% above base commissions in some cases.
Subramanian rejected concerns over large-scale job losses, arguing that the reforms would create employment by widening the distribution network and lowering entry barriers.
To encourage expansion beyond major cities, IRDAI has proposed allowing distributors to earn an additional 10% of the applicable commission limit on business generated in towns with populations below 10 Lakh. This would rise to 20% for areas with fewer than 50,000 residents.
Other proposals include allowing distributors to undertake financial and non-financial activities beyond insurance.
