items.content:
…Foundation engages campus journalists on IPO
By Udeme Akpan
University students across Nigeria have welcomed the Aliko Dangote Foundation’s Student Share Grant Initiative, describing it as an opportunity to participate in wealth creation and gain practical investment experience through the ongoing Initial Public Offering, IPO, of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals FZE, DPRP.
As part of efforts to raise awareness and deepen financial literacy among young Nigerians, the Foundation, over the weekend, held an online engagement with campus journalists from tertiary institutions across the country.
The session focused on the Dangote Refinery IPO, the importance of financial education, responsible investing and opportunities available through Nigeria’s capital market.
Under the Student Share Grant Initiative, eligible students aged 18 and above in public and private tertiary institutions can receive free DPRP shares after purchasing a minimum of 10 shares through the dedicated platform, ipo.alikodangotefoundation.org. For every qualifying subscription, the Foundation provides an additional 10 shares at no extra cost to the student.
The programme is designed to introduce young Nigerians to investing early in life while promoting financial literacy, ownership and long-term wealth creation.
The initiative has generated interest across campuses, with students describing it as an opportunity to become shareholders in one of Africa’s major industrial projects while gaining practical knowledge of investment.
Speaking on the initiative, Amaechi Rosemary, a student of the University of Ibadan, said the programme had made investing more accessible to students.
“Many students hear about shares and investments but never imagine they can become shareholders while still in school. This initiative removes that barrier and gives us an opportunity to learn about wealth creation through practical participation,” she said.
Emmanuel Ndah, also of the University of Ibadan, described the initiative as both educational and empowering.
“Owning shares in a world-class refinery is exciting. Beyond the additional shares, the programme teaches us important lessons about investing and financial responsibility. It is encouraging to see young people being included in Nigeria’s economic growth story,” he said.
Similarly, Moshood Muheeb of Usmanu Danfodiyo University, Sokoto, said the initiative demonstrated confidence in the ability of Nigerian youths to build wealth responsibly.
“This programme sends a strong message that students are not too young to invest. The support provided by the Foundation makes the opportunity even more attractive and encourages young people to start planning for their financial future,” he said.
Esther Olatunji of Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife, said the initiative could encourage students to take investing and financial planning more seriously.
“This is more than a share offer. It is an opportunity to learn about ownership, financial discipline and long-term wealth creation. Programmes like this can inspire students to develop healthy investment habits that will benefit them throughout their lives,” she said.
The students also noted that the initiative had generated conversations around investing, saving and asset ownership on campuses, potentially broadening awareness of financial planning among young Nigerians.
Eligible students enrolled in recognised tertiary institutions can visit the Foundation’s dedicated platform to complete the verification process. Following successful verification, participants can subscribe for a minimum of 10 DPRP shares and qualify for an additional 10 shares funded by the Aliko Dangote Foundation.
According to the Foundation, the initiative is a stand-alone programme designed to encourage investment participation among Nigerian youths and help develop a generation of financially informed investors with a stake in the country’s economic future.
Chairman of the Aliko Dangote Foundation, Alhaji Aliko Dangote, said the initiative aligned with the Foundation’s commitment to empowering young people beyond traditional educational support.
“Supporting young people goes beyond access to education. It also involves providing opportunities that enable them to participate meaningfully in economic growth and wealth creation. Through this initiative, we want students to understand the value of saving, investing wisely and building wealth through ownership,” he said.
Dangote said exposing young people to investment opportunities early could positively influence their financial decisions and encourage greater participation in the formal economy.
“When young people understand ownership and investing from an early stage, they are better equipped to make sound financial decisions, build wealth responsibly and contribute to national development,” he added.
Chief Executive Officer of the Aliko Dangote Foundation, Mrs Zouera Youssoufou, said the programme combined financial education with practical investment experience.
“Financial literacy becomes more meaningful when individuals can apply what they learn. This initiative enables students to experience the investment process firsthand, from verification and subscription to share ownership, while reinforcing the importance of responsible participation in the capital market,” she said.
Youssoufou added that the Foundation’s objective extended beyond the current IPO.
“We hope to inspire a lifelong interest in investing, financial literacy and asset ownership among young Nigerians. The experience and knowledge gained through this programme can serve as a foundation for sound financial decision-making throughout their lives,” she said.
The Student Share Grant Initiative forms part of the Foundation’s broader youth empowerment and economic inclusion efforts, encouraging students to embrace saving, investing, entrepreneurship and long-term wealth creation.

items.author: efosataiwo@vanguardngr.com
items.content:
Portugal superstar Cristiano Ronaldo can return to the squad if he wishes, despite walking out on his team-mates, said national team coach Jorge Jesus on Sunday.
Jesus said Ronaldo can come back into the fold “if he wants to” after the team beat Norway without the veteran attacker to reach the Nations League quarter-finals.
The dispute began last week when Jesus left 41-year-old Ronaldo on the bench for Portugal’s first win over Norway. Ronaldo subsequently walked out on the squad on Wednesday after learning he would not start against Denmark.
“For me, Cris, in the next call-up, if he’s playing at Al-Nassr, he’ll be a player who can be called up,” Jesus told reporters, referring to Ronaldo’s Saudi club side. “If he wants to, he’ll return to the national team.”
The coach said if Ronaldo wishes to speak to him before Portugal’s next matches in November, that would happen.
“If he wants to, as we did before this call-up, we talked before the call-up, we can talk before the next call-up,” continued Jesus. “But Cris is the one who’s going to decide.”
Former Real Madrid and Manchester United attacker Ronaldo is Portugal’s all-time leading scorer and most-capped player.
Jesus said he had told Ronaldo he needed him in the squad for his first games at the helm after replacing Roberto Martinez following the 2026 World Cup.
“Cristiano should end his time in the national team the way he wants, he’s the one who will decide how he wants it,” said Jesus.
“That’s how we talked, the two of us — I said, ‘I need you’. In my first call-up, I said, ‘I need you, I need you to be close to me, playing or not playing, I need you’. And now I’m saying the same thing.”
Ronaldo, who made his Portugal debut in 2003 at the age of 18, has said this will “probably” be his final year in football.
The forward has been a fixture of the national team for more than two decades and has played at six World Cups.
In Ronaldo’s absence Portugal became the first team to secure a place in the quarter-finals, with two group games still to play.
Ronaldo’s long-time rival for the title of the world’s best player, Lionel Messi, will play his final match for Argentina in a friendly against Benin in Buenos Aires on Tuesday.

items.content:
President Bola Tinubu on Sunday paid a courtesy visit to the Oba of Lagos, Oba Rilwan Akiolu, at Iga Idunganran Palace, Lagos Island.
The visit provided an opportunity for the President to receive royal prayers and counsel from the traditional ruler for his administration.
Tinubu was received at the palace by members of the royal household and enthusiastic residents who gathered to welcome him.
Supporters, All Progressives Congress (APC) members and well-wishers lined the streets around Marina and Isale Eko as the President’s motorcade approached.
The gathering created a festive atmosphere, with residents cheering the President and expressing enthusiasm over his presence on Lagos Island.
The royal father offered prayers for Tinubu, his administration and the nation, seeking divine guidance and continued peace and prosperity.
Oba Akiolu also offered counsel to the President on matters concerning the country and the wellbeing of Nigerians.
The meeting underscored the traditional institution’s role in maintaining dialogue with the Federal Government and supporting national development.
Tinubu was accompanied by Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu, and President’s Chief of Staff, Femi Gbajabiamila.
Also accompanying the President were APC stalwarts, political associates and other dignitaries who joined him during the visit.
The President’s visit formed part of his engagements with prominent Nigerians, traditional rulers and other stakeholders since his return to Lagos.
Tinubu returned to Lagos from his working vacation and has continued meetings with important personalities and stakeholders across different sectors.
The engagements have provided opportunities for the President to interact with influential figures and exchange views on national and state-level developments.
His meeting with Oba Akiolu further strengthened the longstanding relationship between the presidency and traditional institutions in Lagos.
The Oba of Lagos, as a prominent traditional authority, remains an influential voice on issues affecting Lagos State and the country.

items.author: efosataiwo@vanguardngr.com
items.content:
Portugal defeated Norway 2-1 without sulking superstar striker Cristiano Ronaldo on Sunday to qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals.
Goncalo Ramos secured a comeback victory for Jorge Jesus’s Portugal in the Group A4 clash after Joao Cancelo’s rocket levelled Kristoffer Ajer’s stunning opener for Norway.
Portugal played out the final minutes with 10 men after Francisco Conceicao was dismissed for two yellow cards in the space of a few seconds for dissent after he appealed for a penalty unsuccessfully.
Former Real Madrid and Manchester United striker Ronaldo walked out on the squad on Wednesday ahead of the previous game against Denmark, after Portugal’s all-time top goalscorer learned he would not start.
Portugal are now guaranteed to finish in the top two spots in the group with two matches to spare, thus becoming the first team to reach the last eight in March 2027.
“Cristiano is our captain, the best player Portugal has ever had,” Cancelo told RTP.
“Things will certainly end in the best way (with Ronaldo) but the important thing is the four victories.”
Norway took the lead in Porto against the run of play with a stunning effort from Brentford defender Ajer after 36 minutes.
The Norwegian met a bouncing ball on the edge of the box perfectly to bend it into the top corner.
However two minutes later Barcelona defender Cancelo scored a similarly superb goal, rifling home from around 20 yards.
Manchester City striker Erling Haaland fired across the face of goal after an hour and was replaced by Jorgen Strand Larsen a few minutes later.
Nations League holders and two-time record champions Portugal nosed in front when AC Milan striker Ramos, starting in place of Ronaldo, tucked home from close range.
Ramos was teed up by Joao Felix, who reached Vitinha’s lofted pass and put it on a plate for the forward.
Ramos scored for a third consecutive game, and helped Portugal seal back-to-back wins since 41-year-old forward Ronaldo left the squad.
Conceicao’s foolish dismissal left Jesus’s team in a tough spot for the final few minutes. The Juventus winger was about to be replaced by Pedro Neto but his complaints led to a red card before the substitution could happen.
Portugal held on to triumph for the fourth time in four games in the group, completing a successful first international window for 72-year-old coach Jesus, despite the Ronaldo controversy.
“Any player who comes to the national team is welcome, obviously. If Cris returns, we’ll be here to receive him with open arms,” said Portugal defender Nuno Mendes.

items.author: efosataiwo@vanguardngr.com
items.content:
Brazilians waited anxiously Sunday for the results of a tight election race between President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro that will determine if the Latin American powerhouse joins a regional swing to the right championed by US President Donald Trump.
From the Amazon rainforest to the agricultural heartlands in the south and sprawling urban favelas, Brazilians queued to cast their vote, many of them fed-up with familiar choices.
Lula, almost 81, is seeking a fourth term in an election which he has branded a battle between democracy and “barbarism,” warning voters that Brazil’s sovereignty is at stake in the face of US pressure.
He is facing a tough battle against right-wing senator Bolsonaro, 45, eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup after his failed 2022 re-election bid.
Little known until a few months ago, Flavio Bolsonaro, who describes himself as more moderate than his firebrand father, has vowed to “rescue” Brazil from Lula, corruption, high taxes and crime.
Oscarina de Oliveira, a 62-year-old caregiver, told AFP she had planned to vote for Lula, as she always has. But “when I got there, I switched to Bolsonaro. Just to see what happens, to see if anything changes.”
Results are expected within a few hours after polls closed, due to the vast nation’s electronic voting system.
Opinion surveys show neither Lula or Bolsonaro were likely to score more than 50 percent — the threshold required to win in the first round. They and are neck-and-neck if the vote goes to a runoff on October 25.
Both candidates have extremely high rejection rates in the deeply polarized nation where a bitter election campaign featured more scandals and mud-slinging than policy and promises.
While all eyes are on the presidential race, Brazilians are also electing lawmakers, senators and governors.
– ‘Flaws and all’ –
Lula is more popular in Brazil’s poor northeast, among low-income voters, Catholics, and women.
“Lula is the only one doing anything for us — at least for us working-class people — flaws and all,” said Sabrina, 34, selling drinks in Rio de Janeiro.
Revered for social welfare programs that lifted millions out of poverty, Lula made a dramatic comeback to office in the 2022 elections after being jailed on a corruption conviction that was later thrown out on procedural grounds.
Riots in Brasilia and the botched coup attempt after his election allowed him to cast himself as guardian of Brazil’s democracy.
In his third term he has overseen a drop in inflation and unemployment, but voters complain about a high cost of living.
Lula has also sharply curbed deforestation in the Amazon, while backing oil exploration.
Despite a growing number of extreme weather events in Brazil, climate change has been absent from the campaign.
“It is important to elect a candidate who defends our territory, who defends nature,” said Tainara da Costa Cruz, 22, who lives along the banks of the Rio Negro in Amazonas state and voted for Lula.
– Trump watching –
Buoyed by his father’s legacy, Bolsonaro leads in the south, among wealthier voters and evangelical Christians.
In a cascade of scandals that dominated the campaign, it emerged that Bolsonaro was under investigation for corruption over the financing of the biopic “Dark Horse” about his father.
For many voters, this did little to move the needle.
“Things are truly terrible. As far as I’m concerned, the left just doesn’t work anymore,” said tech worker Joao Batista, 36, in the Rocinha favela, saying he was fed up with the “horrible” expense of basic goods.
Bolsonaro’s rallies featured massive US flags and images of Trump, who has said he is “very closely” watching the election, but did not endorse the candidate.
The US president has wielded tariffs and sanctions to pressure Brasilia over complaints ranging from the trial against his ally Jair Bolsonaro to alleged unfair trade practices.
Lula repeatedly warned him not to “meddle” in the elections.
He also argued that Brazil would retain control over the development of its vast reserves of rare earths, which have attracted interest from Washington and other foreign powers.
Flavio Bolsonaro has pitched Brazil as a “solution” to ease US dependence on China for these critical minerals.
“I support Lula because he stands up for the poor. Flavio will sell our Brazil off to foreigners,” said Victor Jorge Martins, a 25-year-old event planner.

items.content:
Family Homes Funds Limited (FHFL), in partnership with Post-Service Housing Development Limited (PHDL) and the National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure (NASENI), has commissioned 50 two-bedroom detached, energy-efficient homes for the spouses of Nigeria’s fallen military personnel in Idi-Ape, Akobo, Lagelu Local Government Area of Oyo State.
The commissioning brought together government representatives, military authorities, development partners and other stakeholders to mark the completion of a housing intervention dedicated to families of fallen heroes. The development provides beneficiaries with secure and dignified homes while advancing a housing model that brings together affordability, sustainability, and social impact.
FHFL’s commitment to the beneficiaries extends beyond the provision of homes. Representing the Managing Director/CEO of FHFL, Abdul Mutallab Mukhtar, the Executive Director, Operations, Dr. Henry Inegbu stated: “This initiative is about providing the wives of our fallen heroes with the security and stability that comes with having a home of their own. Their husbands gave their lives in service to Nigeria, and we have a responsibility to ensure that the families they left behind receive meaningful support. Beyond the homes we are delivering today, we are committed to supporting the widows with skills development and livelihood opportunities that can strengthen their capacity for self-sustainability.”
This project aligns with FHFL’s mandate to expand access to housing that improves lives and responds to real needs by combining affordable housing delivery with sustainability and social impact. 
Speaking on the importance of partnerships in providing affordable housing and creating impact, Dr. Nnegbu stated: “For these families, the homes provide a stable and dignified environment in which they can build their future, while honouring the sacrifice of the men who served our country. We remain committed to working with credible partners to deliver housing solutions that create lasting value for beneficiaries and communities.”
The housing units were formally commissioned on behalf of the Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, by the General Officer Commanding, 2 Division, Nigerian Army, Major General Auwalu Mahmuda.
Representing the Chief of Army Staff, Major General Mahmuda reaffirms the Nigerian Army’s commitment to initiatives that provide housing and other forms of assistance to the families of fallen personnel: “The Nigerian Army remains committed to supporting initiatives that provide housing and other forms of assistance to the families of our fallen heroes, in recognition of their patriotic service and sacrifice to the nation. We appreciate FHFL for bringing this intervention together with its partners and for providing these families with homes that offer greater security, stability, and dignity. The welfare of the families of our fallen personnel remains an important responsibility, and partnerships of this nature provide practical support to those who have made significant sacrifices for Nigeria.”
The commissioning featured the presentation of keys to the beneficiaries, with the wives of the fallen heroes receiving their homes amid visible excitement and appreciation. For the families, the homes provide a greater sense of security, stability, and hope as they move forward.
The project reinforces FHFL’s commitment to reducing Nigeria’s housing deficit and expanding access to quality, affordable and sustainable housing, particularly for vulnerable households. Through partnerships with institutions across the housing and development ecosystem, FHFL continues to deliver interventions that connect housing provision with broader social and economic outcomes.

items.content:
Professor Anthony Kila has rejected reports describing him as a “fake professor”, saying the characterisation was inaccurate, misleading and damaging to his reputation and professional standing.
Kila, in a statement responding to a publication dated October 3, 2026, said he remained a professor and stood by the academic and professional credentials on which his professorial title was based.
“For the avoidance of doubt, I am a professor, and I stand by the title and the professional and academic credentials on which it is based,” he said.
He argued that the report was based on what he described as an incomplete understanding of the nature, origin and institutional basis of his professorship.
According to him, the matter should be assessed on the basis of the relevant facts and supporting documentation.
Kila, who is Pro-Chancellor of Michael and Cecilia Ibru University, Delta State, and Director of the Commonwealth Institute of Advanced and Professional Studies (CIAPS), said he was prepared to make the relevant facts and documents concerning his professorial status available.
He particularly objected to the description “fake professor”, arguing that the phrase was presented as a factual conclusion that required evidence and carried serious implications for his reputation.
While acknowledging the role of journalism in scrutinising the credentials of people occupying positions of responsibility, Kila said such scrutiny should be conducted fairly and with a proper understanding of the facts.
He said he was “baffled” by the level of attention directed at him, noting that he neither holds political office nor is seeking one, and is not a government official.
Kila also thanked colleagues, friends, students and members of the public who contacted him after the publication to express confidence in his academic and professional credentials.
He disclosed that he had instructed his lawyers to review the publication and any subsequent dissemination of the allegations and advise him on appropriate legal steps to protect his reputation and professional standing.
“The facts and documentation will speak for themselves,” Kila said.

items.author: Nwafor
items.content:
…..Council boss says structure was built under high-tension wire, insists action not politically motivated
By Efe Onodjae
Ambassador Tobore Alex Agbah, organiser of the 10,000-man march for the National Democratic Congress, NDC, in Ughelli, Delta State, has alleged that the Ughelli North Local Government Council Chairman, Olorogun Jaro Egbo, sealed his property following the political rally.
Agbah, who disclosed this in an interview with Vanguard on Sunday, alleged that the action was politically motivated and linked to his role in organising the NDC awareness march held on Saturday.
He said the march, organised by his group, Team Agbah, was aimed at sensitising residents and mobilising support for the NDC and its aspirants.
According to him, the march attracted a huge turnout, which he described as an “organic” mobilisation.
Agbah said he was informed by his wife during the march that officials were coming to inspect his property and possibly demolish it.
He said: “While we were on the march, my wife called me that they were coming to see my property and demolish it. We thought it was a joke.
“But this afternoon, as I was coming from church, before I could get to my house, they called me that the local government chairman had sealed my property.”
Asked whether he was aware of any breach of law that could have led to the sealing, Agbah attributed the action to his political activities.
He said: “The reason is the 10,000-man march against APC. It is political.
“There was no notice. The property has been there for decades. All the local government chairmen who have come and gone have met the property there without any issue.
“Yesterday was Saturday and we did the march. Today, Sunday, they brought a notice and sealed the place.”
Agbah further alleged that the council chairman had threatened to frustrate him because of his political activities.
He appealed to the Federal Government and relevant authorities to intervene, saying political differences should not result in victimisation.
“I am calling on the Federal Government to call the local government chairman to desist from politics of bitterness.
“Politics is not a game of enmity; it is a game of interest. We are not doing politics to hurt ourselves.
“I have known him before now. We have been in the same political struggle before. So why is it that because I am in NDC, he is trying to frustrate me?
“He told my wife openly that I am fighting this party and that, as a result, he would make sure they frustrate me.
“I don’t deserve such treatment just because I led a 10,000-man march for NDC.”
However, reacting to the allegation, Egbo said the property was sealed because it was allegedly built under a high-tension electricity line and that the action had nothing to do with Agbah’s political affiliation.
The council chairman said his officials had written to Agbah several times over the alleged violation of environmental regulations, but that he failed to comply.
Egbo said the council had, since he assumed office, carried out more than 30 demolitions involving structures allegedly obstructing waterways or built under high-tension lines.
He said: “The particular sealed property was built under high-tension wire. As a matter of fact, my officials told me that they have written to him several times, but he refused to obey simple environmental regulations.
“Since I took office, we have carried out over 30 demolitions from those who block waterways and those who build under high tension, like this particular illegal structure.
“Let me reiterate that being in opposition does not make you above the law. Let your man bring his approval for the illegal structure.”
On allegations that the action was connected to the NDC march, Egbo dismissed the claim, insisting that the enforcement was based on alleged regulatory violations.
He also accused Agbah of branding a vehicle without paying the prescribed mobile advertising fee.
Egbo said: “On the branded bus, he branded the vehicle without paying for mobile advert. By the grace of God, I am the Chairman of the Governing Board of Delta State Advertising Agency, DESSAA.”
He warned that the council would enforce the law if Agbah failed to produce approval for the structure or pay the prescribed advertising fees.
“If he fails to bring the approval for the illegal structure or fails to pay the prescribed fees, the law will take its course and heaven will not fall,” Egbo added.

“Our troops are now closer to vulnerable communities in these areas, strengthening our ability to respond swiftly and decisively when our people are threatened,” he said.

“As we demand more from our men and women in uniform, we must do more to support them and their families,” he said.

“Every deployment is a sacrifice made by a family too,” he said.

“As our Armed Forces stand watch over Nigeria, my duty as Commander-in-Chief is to ensure they have the resources and support to do their job, and that Nigeria stands firmly behind the families waiting for them at home,” he said.

items.content:
By Golok Nanmwa
JOS — Gunmen on Sunday evening opened fire on traders returning from the Kara Bukuru Livestock Market in Jos South Local Government Area of Plateau State, killing one person and injuring seven others.
The victim was identified as Musa Abubakar.
The incident occurred at about 7pm around the Bukuru Low-Cost area, according to sources who spoke to our correspondent.
The Plateau State chapter of the Miyetti Allah Cattle Breeders Association of Nigeria, MACBAN, confirmed and condemned the attack, calling on security agencies to investigate the incident and bring those responsible to justice.
In a statement signed by its chairman, Alhaji Ibrahim Yusuf Babayo, MACBAN described the incident as disturbing, saying the victims were returning from their lawful business activities.
“This unfortunate incident is deeply disturbing and represents yet another attack against innocent herders who were peacefully returning from their lawful business activities,” Babayo said.
He urged the Nigeria Police Force, Operation Safe Haven, the Department of State Services, DSS, and other security agencies to conduct a thorough investigation into the incident.
Babayo recalled that five herders were reportedly killed on September 20, 2026, around Kassa in Barkin Ladi Local Government Area while returning from the same Kara Bukuru Livestock Market.
He also recalled that traders were attacked near the Conoil Filling Station in December last year while returning from the market.
According to him, the recurrence of such incidents had heightened fear and insecurity among pastoralists and traders who depend on the market for their livelihoods.
“No Nigerian should be attacked or killed because of his or her ethnic background or occupation,” he said.
The MACBAN chairman called on the Plateau State Government and security agencies to strengthen security along the Kara Bukuru market route and take measures to prevent further attacks.
He also appealed to members of the association to remain calm and law-abiding and refrain from any form of retaliation.
Babayo said MACBAN remained committed to peaceful coexistence with communities across Plateau State, stressing that lasting peace could only be achieved through justice, fairness and equal protection of citizens irrespective of ethnicity or occupation.

By Henry Umoru
ABUJA — The presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, Peter Obi, has called for the immediate and safe rescue of about 20 prospective members of the National Youth Service Corps, NYSC, reportedly abducted while travelling to their orientation camp.
Obi, in a post on his official social media page on Sunday, described the reported abduction as another indication of what he called worsening insecurity in the country, warning that Nigerians should not accept insecurity as a normal part of everyday life.
The former Anambra State governor said the victims were young Nigerians travelling to serve their country but were unable to complete their journey safely because of insecurity on the nation’s roads.
He said the incident had also heightened anxiety among families whose loved ones travel across the country for work, education and national assignments.
“The abduction of approximately 20 prospective NYSC members travelling to their orientation camp is yet another distressing indication of the worsening insecurity in our country.
“These young Nigerians were preparing to serve their nation, but they were unable to travel safely on our roads. Families are increasingly burdened by the fear that their loved ones could fall victim to kidnapping,” Obi said.
The 2023 presidential candidate of the Labour Party, LP, said protecting lives and property remained a primary responsibility of government.
He urged security agencies to intensify efforts to prevent attacks and respond promptly to threats rather than waiting until lives had been disrupted.
“Protecting lives and property is the government’s foremost responsibility. We cannot continue to regard insecurity as an ordinary occurrence or act only after people’s lives have been disrupted,” he said.
Obi called on security agencies to intensify efforts to locate and rescue the abducted prospective corps members and apprehend those responsible for the attack.
“I call for the immediate and safe rescue of all the abducted corps members and the arrest of those responsible. Nigeria must become a country where young people can travel, work, and serve their nation without fear,” he said.
The reported abduction has renewed concerns over the safety of travellers on Nigerian highways, particularly young Nigerians travelling to unfamiliar locations for national assignments.
The NYSC, established in 1973, was designed, among other objectives, to promote national integration by deploying graduates to states outside their states of origin for one year of national service.
However, recurring reports of kidnappings and attacks on major highways have continued to raise concerns about the safety of corps members and other travellers across the country.

items.author: Akinbayo Wahab
items.content:
Minister of Works, David Umahi, has dismissed claims linking the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway to flooding in communities along its corridor, blaming the situation on climate change and global warming.
Umahi said the flooding in the affected areas predated the highway’s construction, arguing that the project should not be held responsible for a problem he described as a consequence of changing weather patterns.
The minister spoke on Sunday during an interview on Channels Television, where he also criticised social media users for making claims about the project without adequate technical knowledge.
“The Coastal Highway has nothing to do with flooding,” Umahi said, adding that infrastructure built decades ago had not been designed to accommodate the effects of climate change and global warming.
He explained that unusual flooding was not peculiar to Nigeria, citing his experience in Paris, France, where he said some buildings had experienced severe flooding, forcing occupants to relocate their ground-floor activities to higher levels.
“At the coastal highway corridor, the premises were built below the unexpected flood level occasioned by global warming, the climate change,” he said.
Umahi argued that flooding had occurred in communities along the highway corridor before construction began, insisting that the project was not the cause of the problem.
“Before the construction of Coastal Highway, was there flooding within that premises? The answer is yes,” he said.
The minister challenged critics to consider the impact of climate change and the occurrence of unusual flooding across the country before attributing the problem to the highway.
He also questioned why flooding was being reported in areas on both sides of the coastal road if the project was responsible for the situation.
“The Coastal Highway has nothing to do with the flooding. Otherwise, if it is what is causing the flooding, why is there flooding left and right of the Coastal Highway?” he asked.
Umahi described the highway as a significant infrastructure project and took aim at critics he accused of commenting on its impact without sufficient technical understanding.
“It’s a beauty to behold, and so people just started counselling without knowledge. You see that there are emergency engineers these days, people just talk on social media anyhow,” he said.

items.author: Khadim Afridi
items.content:
In the picturesque Kalash Valley of Lower Chitral in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, a place long celebrated for its unique civilisation, ancient traditions, natural beauty and cultural heritage, climate change, deforestation, erratic rainfall, flash floods, water shortages and declining agricultural yields are confronting local communities with new environmental and economic challenges.
Residents of Bamboret, Rumbur and Birir valleys report marked shifts in weather patterns over recent years. Snowfall has become shorter and lighter in winter, summers hotter, rains more unpredictable and sudden flash floods more frequent. These changes are damaging farmland and crops while also destroying roads, houses, irrigation systems and other basic infrastructure.
Daniel Feroz, a resident and social activist of the Kalash Valley, told The Express Tribune that the effects of climate change have grown more visible over the past decade. Repeated floods, he said, have severely disrupted daily life, agriculture and infrastructure.
"Flash floods damage people's agricultural land and crops, and in several places houses have also been affected," Feroz said. The main road leading into the valley as well as internal link roads are regularly hit, creating difficulties for both residents and tourists.
The impact is not limited to flooding. Natural water sources are under strain, with many springs showing reduced flow.
Agriculture in the Kalash Valley depends heavily on springs and rainfall. According to Feroz, several springs have seen declining water levels and some have dried up completely. Lands that once supported regular crops are now suffering.
Maize and wheat remain the main crops, but water shortages and unreliable rains are cutting yields. Wheat, in particular, relies on timely rainfall; if adequate rain fails at critical stages, production falls, directly affecting household food security and income.
A major environmental stressor is the community's reliance on forests. With no natural gas supply, residents use wood year-round for cooking, heating homes in winter and other household needs. Wood is also central to traditional construction of houses, livestock shelters and other structures.
While permits are sometimes required for timber used in building, the continuous demand for fuelwood keeps pressure on forests high.
Local journalist Sameer said that dependence on wood is a long-standing issue across parts of Chitral. Both construction and domestic fuel needs drive the demand. He noted that some people extract more timber than permitted and that collecting firewood further strains forests. Providing alternative energy sources that take local needs into account is essential for forest conservation, he said.
Livestock rearing adds another layer of pressure. Large numbers of goats are taken into forests and mountain pastures, where they browse young shoots and saplings, hindering natural regeneration.
"On one hand mature trees continue to be cut; on the other, new plants struggle to grow," Feroz said. Over time this can reduce both the area and density of forests.
Yet goats remain deeply embedded in Kalash society and culture. They feature in social and religious rituals, particularly funeral and mourning ceremonies in which large numbers are sacrificed.
Feroz observed that winter snowfall has also altered. In the past, regular snow fell in December, January and other cold months. In recent years the timing, quantity and consistency of snowfall have changed. Reduced winter snow coincides with hotter summers and more unpredictable rains, further disrupting local life.
In mountain regions forests play a critical role in preventing soil erosion, maintaining natural water systems and stabilising slopes. Their decline, combined with intense rains and weakened hillsides, can increase landslides, debris flows into streams and the destructive power of flash floods.
Residents report that monsoon streams now frequently carry large boulders and debris, damaging roads and disrupting irrigation channels. The Forest Department maintains a presence, Feroz said, but the number of field staff and forest guards is small relative to the vast forested areas. Effective monitoring, transparent permit systems and alternative fuel supplies at the local level could ease pressure on the forests.
Social activist Log Rahmat stressed that Kalash culture cannot be separated from its natural surroundings. Traditions, religious rituals, farming, livestock rearing, water sources and forests are deeply interwoven.

items.title: Thai youth still fight for dissent 50 years after massacre
items.summary:
Fifty years after a student demonstration against dictatorship ended in a massacre, Thailand's latest generation of protesters say they still face threats including prosecution, jail or exile.
Nutthanit Duangmusit, 24, spent several months in pre-trial detention before being convicted under Thailand's strict royal defamation law, among almost 300 people charged under so-called lese majeste since 2020.
She is currently on bail while she appeals against her conviction and has been helping organise commemorations for Tuesday's anniversary of the October 6, 1976, killings at Thammasat University.

items.content:
Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs' centre-right party emerged as the victor on Sunday from Latvia's parliamentary election, and he will now set about forming a coalition to maintain his pro-European and pro-Ukrainian course.
Populist parties, boosted by support from Latvia's Russian-speaking minority, also had a good night after an election campaign dominated by fears over neighbouring Russia, the cost of living and other social issues.
Kulbergs' United List party won 42 seats in the 100-seat parliament -- an unprecedented result in the former Soviet republic's post-independence history.
After exit polls hinted at the magnitude of his party's victory, Kulbergs said it was a wider margin than he had expected.
"That means people truly want change," he said, which he said meant "economic growth" and a future for the country's children.
Kulbergs, a former manager in the telecoms and automotive sectors, took over as prime minister in May at the head of a centre-right coalition.
He will be forced to change partners after the election, as one of his members failed to clear the five-percent hurdle to get into parliament.
'Strong border'
Security remains central to political debate in Latvia, more than four years after Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Latvia, a member of NATO and the European Union since 2004, views Russia as its principal security threat and has significantly increased defence spending in response.
"Because we are the external border of Europe, we must have a strong economy... a strong border region," Kulbergs said.
"That is the main task."
But rising living costs, low wages, strains on the healthcare system and long-term population decline all featured prominently in campaign debates.
While most parties expected to enter parliament back both high military spending and maintaining aid to Kyiv, the right-wing Sovereign Power party has broken ranks.
It has opposed military aid to Ukraine and further increases to defence spending. It looked set for a third-place finish, with 15 MPs, after focusing on cost of living issues.
Right-wing populist parties
Soverign Power has been tarred pro-Russian by its detractors and most major parties have ruled out working with it.
Latvia First, a conservative party run by a property magnate often compared toh US President Donald Trump, came second in the poll and took 17 seats.
Both populist parties benefitted from changes in voting patterns among the Russian-speaking minority, who make up a third of the population.
They had long rallied around Harmony, which was at one time the country's biggest party.
But Harmony was broadly seen as pro-Kremlin and its support collapsed dramatically in the last election, held shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

items.title: Maui $1.35M lot fight: $7M judgment vacated after 32 years
items.summary: In 1994, Don Williams paid $1.35 million for 1.137 acres near Maui’s Maʻalaea Harbor. More than three decades later, Hawaiʻi’s Intermediate Court of Appeals vacated a Circuit Court judgment awarding $7 million in his long-running eminent-domain case. The appellate court found competing valuation evidence created factual disputes requiring further proceedings over just compensation.

items.title: Your silence on abduction of corps members worrisome, APM tells Tinubu
items.summary:
The Makinde-Daura Presidential Campaign Organization (MDPCO) under the platform of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM) has charged President Bola Ahmed Tinubu to immediately rescue the prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members abducted in Imo state.
The campaign council also demanded that President Tinubu take a decisive step to securing the “unconditional release and safe return of other Nigerians abducted in Niger, Kwara, Kaduna, Zamfara, Sokoto, Katsina, Borno and other parts of the country”.
In a statement, Richard Ihediwa, Director of Strategic Communications of the campaign, said “notwithstanding the fact that Nigerians are determined to vote out the President, it is still unpardonable that four days after the abduction of the corps members and despite the public outcry, President Tinubu has remained silent while the abducted corps members languish in misery in their captors’ den.”

items.content:
Eight members of the Zamfara State House of Assembly have resigned from the All Progressives Congress (APC).
The lawmakers, including an ally of former Governor Abdul’aziz, said they decided to leave the party over insecurity, alleged injustice and other issues affecting the wellbeing of the people.
In a statement announcing their decision, the lawmakers said they could no longer remain in a political party which, according to them, had failed to provide adequate security for citizens.
They expressed dissatisfaction with what they described as the party’s inability to address challenges confronting the state, particularly the worsening security situation.
Why Nigerians Don’t Trust Government Institutions — Islamic Scholar
2027: Muslims Charged To Obtain PVC, Vote Responsible Leaders
The lawmakers who resigned include Hon. Aliyu Ango Kagara, representing Talata Mafara South; Hon. Ibrahim Tukur Bakura, representing Bakura; Hon. Faruk Musa Dosara, representing Maradun I; and Hon. Barrister Bashir Abubakar Masama, representing Bukkuyum North.
Others are Hon. Muktaru Nasiru Kaura (Kaura North), Hon. Nasiru Abdullahi (Maru North), Hon. Bashar Bello (Bungudu West), and Hon. Bashar Aliyu (Gummi I).
Their resignation adds to the growing political developments within Zamfara APC, where internal disagreements and realignments have continued to shape the political landscape ahead of the 2027 general elections.
The lawmakers did not immediately disclose their next political destination.
When contacted, the state APC publicity secretary, Hon. Ibrahim Danmadamin Birnin Magaji, said the party at the state level was yet to be officially notified.
“We are still waiting for their correspondence from their respective political wards after reaching their local government executives, which would later be forwarded to us,” Danmadamin said.
He added that the party had only seen the resignation letters on social media platforms like other members of the public.
“We all saw it on social media platforms, but whenever we receive the copies officially, we would communicate with you on our stand,” the party publicity secretary said.
Responding to questions on whether the development was linked to an internal crisis within the party, Danmadami said the APC was not aware of any grievances until it received copies of the resignation letters.
On their part, the resigned lawmakers accused Governor Dauda Lawal’s administration of failing to give adequate attention to insecurity affecting rural communities.
Kagara further said they decided to leave the APC because the party had failed to properly address insecurity and had allegedly turned down their earlier agreements.
“What we are challenging Governor Lawal’s administration about is even worse now compared to previous times, so we have seen no reason to continue remaining in the APC.
“Our constituents in rural areas who voted us into power to address their security concerns were not being given any attention,” Kagara said.
He also alleged that the lawmakers had gone for 32 months without receiving salaries, allowances and other benefits due to them as elected members of the state House of Assembly.
“This is our 32 months without salary, allowances and other entitlements as honourable members, and the people of Zamfara; the ball is in their court. Whether they enjoy what is happening or not, they are in the best position to take action and they need not to be told,” Kagara said.
Meanwhile, a party official who spoke with Daily Trust on condition of anonymity said he did not blame the lawmakers for leaving the APC, alleging that Governor Lawal had chosen to work with others instead of reconciling with some members.
“I don’t blame them, and they did the right thing, as the governor chose not to reconcile with them despite all efforts to ensure they remained in the APC,” he said.
The governor has not reacted to the allegation. But Daily Trust understands that the lawmakers were on suspension before they left the APC.
They were suspended for allegedly trying to impeach the speaker about a year ago.

items.content:
An Islamic scholar and Chief Imam of Olabisi Onabanjo University (OOU), Ago-Iwoye, Ogun State, Professor Abdulhakeem Adebayo Akanni, on Sunday attributed the low level of trust Nigerians have in government institutions to perceived exclusion, unequal development, political patronage and what he described as the denial of citizens’ rights.
Akanni stated this in Abeokuta while delivering the 19th Annual State Lecture of the Muslim Congress (TMC), Ogun State, titled “National Cohesion, Sustainable Security and Civil Trust: From Policy to Performance.”
The lecture was part of the week-long activities that commenced with the organisation’s Quarterly Public Lecture, Free Medical Outreach and Fire-Fighting Enlightenment Programme at the Olowu Palace, Owu, Abeokuta.
This was followed by humanitarian visits to HOB Medical Centre and Lekfad Medical Centre, while TMC structures at various local government levels across Ogun State have also carried out similar humanitarian activities, including visits to patrons, hospitals, correctional centres, homes for motherless and vulnerable children, and old people’s homes.
Benue boat mishap: 5 bodies recovered, 6 still missing
Insecurity: Imams seek divine intervention
Delivering his address, the Islamic scholar said Nigeria had enough policies designed to promote national cohesion, security and public trust, but that the major challenge was translating those policies into the everyday experiences of citizens.
According to him, the gap between government policies and citizens’ lived experiences has contributed to weak national identification and declining trust in public institutions.
Akanni cited a study which, he said, found that only 48.8 per cent of Nigerians identified primarily as Nigerians, while many continued to place greater emphasis on their ethnic identities.
The scholar said government initiatives and institutions such as the Federal Character Commission, the National Youth Service Corps, the National Orientation Agency and national symbols had not been sufficient to build strong national cohesion.
“Despite efforts by the Nigerian government to ensure national cohesion, with various policies… Nigerians still do not trust themselves. They do not believe in one another. Nigerians do not see themselves as Nigerians,” he said.
He identified “denying their rights on the basis of merits, indignity, unequal development, political patronage, and perception of exclusion” among the factors responsible for the lack of trust.
On insecurity, Akanni said Nigeria was facing different security challenges across its regions, including banditry and kidnapping in the North-West, terrorism in the North-East, farmer-herder clashes in the North-Central, separatist agitation in the South-East, and cultism in parts of the South-South and South-West.
He said although some of these challenges are more pronounced in particular parts of the country, their consequences were being felt nationwide.
“Every part of the country is feeling the consequences,” he said, citing kidnapping on interstate routes as an example.
Akanni further argued that citizens’ distrust extended to political and security institutions because many Nigerians did not believe such institutions could adequately protect their rights or provide security.
He cited a 2026 survey by the African Polling Institute, saying only 28 per cent of respondents expressed trust in the Federal Government, while 23 per cent believed the National Assembly would provide for their needs and 24 per cent believed the police would protect them.
In contrast, he said, 45 per cent expressed trust in traditional institutions and 51 per cent in religious leaders.

PMDC President Prof. Dr. Rizwan Taj said the initiative is aimed at identifying people experiencing emotional distress or other mental-health problems and providing support before their condition worsens or leads to self-harm.

items.content:
The Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC) has ordered annual mental health screening for 22,500 medical and dental students, as well as faculty and staff, to identify psychological distress and suicide risk at an early stage.
PMDC President Prof. Dr. Rizwan Taj said the initiative is aimed at identifying people experiencing emotional distress or other mental-health problems and providing support before their condition worsens or leads to self-harm.
He made the remarks at the Pakistan Global Mental Health Summit 2026, where Federal Health Minister Syed Mustafa Kamal launched the National Mental Health Policy 2026-2035.
Prof. Taj said mental health has also been made an independent and compulsory subject in undergraduate medical and dental education.
The council has increased mental-health teaching from 50 to 175 hours and plans to raise it further to 200 hours to better prepare future doctors and dentists to recognize and respond to mental-health conditions.
Medical and dental colleges have also been directed to establish primary mental-health care centers to provide support and referral services for students, staff and others who need assistance.
The measures come as Pakistan’s first nationally representative psychiatric survey found that 32.3 percent of adults, or nearly one in three Pakistanis, were living with a diagnosable mental or behavioral disorder.
The study also found that 6.2 percent of participants had experienced suicidal thoughts or behavior during the previous month, while 1.1 percent reported having attempted suicide at some point in their lives.
Prof. Dr. Mohammad Iqbal Afridi, professor emeritus of psychiatry and a co-author of the study, said the findings should help guide policymaking, workforce planning and the expansion of community-based mental-health services.

items.author: ProPK Staff
items.content:
Canada has updated its immigration processing times tool to give some work permit applicants personalized estimates based on the date they submitted their applications.
The new feature applies to applicants seeking work permit extensions from inside Canada and international graduates applying for their first post-graduation work permit (PGWP).
Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) added the personalized estimates to its processing times webpage in late September 2026.
Applicants Can Now Check Remaining Wait Times
Applicants visiting the government’s processing times webpage can select “Temporary residence” as the application type.
They can then choose the new “Work permit extension in Canada” option.
The system shows an estimated remaining processing time in weeks based on the applicant’s submission date.
It also displays how many work permit applications are ahead of the applicant and the total number of cases currently waiting for decisions.
According to the latest available figures, around 202,900 applicants were awaiting decisions as of September 26, 2026.
People who have not yet submitted an application can also use the tool. In that case, it shows an estimated processing time based on applying on the date of the lookup.
Who Can Use the Personalized Estimate?
The application-date-based estimate is available only to certain applicants applying from within Canada.
It covers people extending an existing work permit. It also applies to international student graduates submitting their first PGWP application.
The work permit extension category also includes people already holding Canadian work permits who are applying to change the conditions attached to their existing permits.
Previously, the processing times webpage offered only one relevant selection called “Work permit in Canada.”
That option showed a general processing estimate based on the date someone checked the website rather than when they had actually submitted their application.
The “Work permit in Canada” option remains available. However, it now applies only to non-PGWP applicants submitting their first work permit application from within Canada.
Work Permit Applicants May Benefit From Maintained Status
Work permit holders who submit an extension application before their existing permit expires may qualify for maintained status.
Maintained status allows eligible applicants to continue working under the conditions of their existing work permit while IRCC processes the extension application.
The system was previously known as “implied status.”
In practice, it can allow an applicant to remain legally authorized to work in Canada even after the existing permit expires, provided the extension application was submitted on time and the person remains in Canada.
Temporary Relief for Provincial Nominees
Canada also introduced a temporary measure on June 9, 2026, to help many provincial nominees whose work permits are approaching expiry.
The measure applies to some permanent residence applicants under the base Provincial Nominee Program (PNP).
It allows eligible applicants to seek a bridging open work permit (BOWP) earlier than under the normal process.
Typically, applicants must first receive an acknowledgement of receipt for their permanent residence application before becoming eligible for a BOWP.
Under the temporary measure, eligible provincial nominees can apply without first receiving that acknowledgement.
The policy is scheduled to remain in effect until December 31, 2026.
Canada Expands Personalized Immigration Processing Estimates
The latest change is part of a broader effort by IRCC to provide applicants with more individualized processing information.
The immigration department first introduced personalized processing times for citizenship and permanent residence applicants in October 2025.
With the latest update, work permit extension and PGWP applicants can now get a more relevant estimate based on when they actually applied instead of relying only on a general processing-time figure.

EMOTO OTOX DIMEN Specifications
The EMOTO OTOX DIMEN is the more performance-focused model in the new lineup.
It uses a motorcycle-style design and comes with a motor rated at 3,000W. Peak output reaches 6,300W.
EMOTO claims the DIMEN can reach a top speed of up to 95 km/h.
The bike also supports both single- and dual-battery configurations. Buyers can use one battery for lighter daily use or install two removable 72V 38Ah NCM battery packs for longer journeys.
With the dual-battery setup, EMOTO claims a range of 130 to 150 km.
With a single battery, the company quotes a range of 70 to 90 km under ideal conditions when riding at 45 km/h.

Super Power has positioned it primarily as an urban mobility option for city riders.

items.author: SHAMSUL ISLAM KHAN
items.content:
Pakistan's recurring wheat and sugar crises are not simply the result of poor harvests. They stem from weak planning, flawed policies, administrative failures, market manipulation and political influence of vested interests that have shaped these sectors for decades. Successive governments have spent trillions of rupees on subsidies, procurement and market interventions, yet farmers hue and cry that they remain underpaid, and consumers continue to face price spikes.
Wheat has been heavily regulated since the 1960s and sugar since the 1970s. These policies were meant to protect growers, increase production, and benefit consumers, but in practice they have often benefited flour millers, sugar barons, middlemen and politically connected groups. Several influential political families hold significant interests in the sugar industry, while many flour mills are linked to politicians, their relatives or cronies. The result is a system that socialises losses while allowing private players to capture profits.
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif assumed office first in April 2022 and again in March 2024. Throughout both tenures, the government repeatedly assured the public that wheat and sugar stocks were sufficient and that prices would remain stable. Yet market realities frequently contradicted these claims. Artificial shortages, abrupt shifts from exports to imports, weak oversight and speculative hoarding have repeatedly disrupted supply over the past four years.
Official data show that wheat production increased by 4.3% to 29.605 million tons, rice by 2.8% to 9.998 million tons, and sugarcane by 6.2% to 89.45 million tons. Despite these increases, flour prices have continued to rise, suggesting that the latest wheat shortage is driven less by production constraints and more by market manipulation and speculative behaviours of hoarders. Pakistanis are not consuming wheat only; they eat rice, nearly 4 million tons, corn, millet and sorghum too; hence per capita consumption of 124 kg is exaggerated.
Pakistan has also paid a heavy price for inefficient wheat imports in the recent past. The government spent more than $1 billion importing wheat, much of which remained in warehouses, got rotten and/or was stolen, and huge stocks were stolen over time, burdening the national exchequer. The country has repeatedly imported wheat and sugar when global prices were historically high and exported them when international prices were relatively low; an approach that reflects poor timing and inefficient policy.
The IMF has long argued that Pakistan's agricultural markets suffer from excessive protectionism, distorted pricing mechanisms, costly subsidies and inefficient state intervention. In September 2024, Pakistan agreed with the IMF to phase out government market intervention and support prices in agriculture – wheat during fiscal year 2024-25 and sugar by June 2026.
The government moved quickly on wheat by announcing the discontinuation of official procurement and support prices. It also formally committed to deregulating the sugar sector by June 2026, including the removal of minimum support prices of sugarcane and trading restrictions. On paper, these reforms promise greater efficiency, fiscal savings, private investment and more competitive markets. In reality, however, deregulating Pakistan's two most politically sensitive food commodities may prove "mission impossible" for the current coalition government's political partners.
The central question is not whether deregulation is economically desirable. It is whether Pakistan's political economy is capable of implementing it in its true spirit. For decades, the government controlled nearly every aspect of the wheat economy: support prices, procurement targets, public storage and strategic reserves. These measures were intended to ensure food security, but they also created inefficiencies, corruption and opportunities for rent-seeking.
The sugar sector has been similarly regulated since the 1970s. Governments fixed sugarcane prices, restricted the production of jaggery and raw sugar, approved imports and exports, imposed stock limits and frequently intervened through the state-owned entity Trading Corporation of Pakistan whenever shortages or public outrage emerged. These policies often favoured mill owners rather than farmers or consumers.
The IMF-backed reforms seek to end this interventionist model. The government plans to withdraw from wheat procurement, shut down Passco, maintain only emergency strategic reserves and allow prices to be determined largely by market forces. In sugar, minimum support prices, zoning restrictions, mill licensing and trading controls are expected to be liberalised. This would represent the most significant transformation of Pakistan's agricultural markets in generations.
From an economic perspective, deregulation has strong arguments in its favour. Artificial prices distort production decisions, encourage inefficiency, burden public finances and create opportunities for rent-seeking. Every year, the government spends billions managing procurement, storage, subsidies and emergency imports, yet artificial shortages and engineered price spikes persist. A competitive market could improve efficiency, attract investment, modernise storage infrastructure and allocate resources more rationally.
But markets do not become competitive simply because the government role exists. Pakistan's agricultural marketing system remains fragmented and dominated by middlemen (Arthis) hoarders, weak logistics, inadequate old-fashioned warehousing and limited access to commodity financing. Without modern market institutions, deregulation could merely transfer market power from government agencies to private cartels unless free import/export is allowed.
Ending public wheat procurement would transfer price risk directly to farmers. Large commercial producers may adapt, but small farmers often depend on guaranteed procurement to recover production costs and repay seasonal loans borrowed from Arthis.
On the consumer side, wheat is Pakistan's staple food. Even modest increases in flour prices immediately feed into inflation, poverty and political unrest. A more practical approach would be to build a mandatory strategic stockpile through private-sector participation. Licensed traders, flour mills, exporters, and importers with approved storage facilities could be required to maintain 10% of their stocks in government-designated warehouses involving zero investment of government. In an emergency, the government could purchase these reserves at verified purchase cost price and release them into the market to stabilise prices. Such a system would reduce the fiscal burden while preserving food-security safeguards.
If wheat deregulation is difficult, sugar liberalisation is politically explosive. The sugar industry has long been associated with powerful business interests, policy reversals and recurring market controversies. Nearly every year, Pakistan witnesses disputes over actual sugar stocks, exports, imports, shortages, subsidies or fixation of retail prices. Allowing prices to be determined entirely by market forces may improve efficiency, but only if genuine competition exists. This requires a liberal import-export policy for raw and refined sugar, no unnecessary restrictions on new entrants and transparent stock reporting.
Without strong competition laws and effective action against collusion, consumers could remain vulnerable to coordinated pricing by dominant market players. Removing regulations without strengthening regulators is not deregulation; it is merely replacing public control with private cartelization and concentration.
This is where economics collides with politics. The IMF expects Pakistan to reduce fiscal costs and minimise state intervention to reduce losses. Governments, however, survive on public confidence, and nothing erodes that confidence faster than rising food prices. Whenever wheat or sugar prices surge, political pressure inevitably forces governments to intervene through imports, subsidies, export bans or administrative price controls. Pakistan's history is full of such reversals. This makes complete and sustained deregulation extraordinarily difficult.
Successful deregulation requires far more than withdrawing government notifications. Pakistan must first build competitive commodity markets supported by modern storage facilities, warehouse financing, reliable market intelligence, efficient logistics, digital futures trading platforms, crop insurance and robust competition enforcement.
THE WRITER IS A FORMER VICE PRESIDENT OF KCCI, FORMER BOARD MEMBER OF REAP AND AN INTERNATIONAL TRADE EXPERT

items.author: Naeem Ahmad
items.content:
Pakistan's export-oriented textile sector is facing a defining energy challenge as the country moves towards a more competitive power market while global buyers impose increasingly stringent requirements for sustainability, traceability and environmental performance. Industry faces the challenge of balancing reliable, affordable energy with pressure to improve efficiency, integrate renewables and cut emissions.
These issues came under discussion at a multi-stakeholder dialogue titled "Threads of Accountability: Traceability and Energy Policy for Textile Competitiveness", which brought together textile manufacturers, power-sector professionals, sustainability and verification specialists, business representatives and renewable-energy stakeholders.
The central question was how Pakistan's textile industry can participate in a transforming power market while maintaining reliable energy supplies and meeting increasingly demanding global sustainability standards.
Participants stressed that successful energy transition would require more than simply opening the electricity market or increasing renewable-energy capacity. Transparent pricing, reliable networks, commercially workable market mechanisms, credible environmental data, appropriate risk allocation and stronger coordination among industry, regulators, utilities, financiers and international buyers would all be necessary.
A major focus of the dialogue was Pakistan's emerging Competitive Trading Bilateral Contract Market (CTBCM) and its implications for industrial consumers. Muhammad Usman Bin Ahmed, Energy Transition Officer at Alternate Development Services (ADS), examined the practical requirements for industrial participation, including eligibility, competitive procurement, bilateral contracting and wheeling.
He also highlighted several commercial and operational issues associated with the emerging market, including the Use of System Charges (UoSC), security and performance guarantees, SMP exposure, balancing and settlement, hybrid bulk power-consumer arrangements and firm capacity requirements for renewable-energy supply. He presented a CTBCM readiness toolkit to help industrial consumers understand the requirements and practical considerations of participating in the competitive market.
The commercial viability of wheeling emerged as a key concern. Analysis presented at the dialogue noted that Nepra's September 2026 determination places effective UoSC at Rs9.46 per kWh for B-3 consumers and Rs12.32 per kWh for B-4 consumers, including Rs3.23 per kWh in distribution-of-subsidy surcharge. Participants noted that such charges would be an important consideration for industries evaluating alternative electricity procurement arrangements.
A power-market panel featuring Syed Iftikhar Ali, power-sector professional, Saham Qamar, Director of Power Matrix, and Hasnat Khan, Senior Vice Chairman of the Pakistan Solar Association, examined network capability, metering and settlement infrastructure, transmission constraints, UoSC and the predictability required by industrial consumers.
The discussion highlighted that industrial participation in a competitive market would require not only a regulatory framework allowing consumers to participate but also adequate infrastructure and commercial certainty to make such participation practical.
The wider cost structure of Pakistan's power sector was also examined. Rehan Javed, Head of the Energy Advisory Committee at FPCCI, highlighted major cost pressures within the country's generation portfolio, citing a combined Rs2.899 trillion increase in the disclosed costs of five major hydropower projects. Individual project cost overruns ranged from 21% to 285%. Dasu was cited as an example, with its approved cost of Rs486 billion compared with the current cost of Rs1.737 trillion, representing a 257% increase.
For the textile industry, the energy challenge extends beyond electricity. Asim Riaz, Energy Adviser at Aptma, linked power-market reform with the sector's wider competitiveness challenges, discussing changing national and global energy markets, gas-market liberalisation, captive generation, energy efficiency, renewable integration and the economics of industrial energy supply. His intervention highlighted that decisions involving renewable energy, captive generation, efficiency and electrification must ultimately make economic sense for manufacturers.
Energy costs and reliability are directly linked with textile production and export competitiveness. Higher electricity or gas costs can affect manufacturing margins, while unreliable supplies can disrupt production and increase the cost of maintaining alternative sources of power.
At the same time, global textile markets are increasingly demanding evidence of sustainable production, credible carbon information and traceable supply chains. ESG compliance, traceability and measurement, reporting and verification are therefore becoming important elements of export competitiveness.
Participants identified fragmented environmental data, limited verification capacity and inconsistencies in reporting as persistent challenges. They stressed the need to connect factory-level operational information with credible sustainability claims made by textile exporters.
This means that energy management is increasingly connected with access to international markets because manufacturers must be able to demonstrate the environmental benefits of efficiency measures and renewable-energy investments through credible data and documentation.
ADS Chief Executive Amjad Nazeer calls for moving beyond compliance-only relationships towards shared investment, technical assistance, long-term procurement arrangements and credible monitoring and reporting mechanisms.
Participants also stressed that decarbonisation should begin with measurement, energy efficiency and process optimisation, including waste-heat recovery, before industries move towards electrification, renewable generation and storage, where appropriate. Improving efficiency can simultaneously reduce energy costs and emissions while strengthening the economic case for future renewable-energy and storage investments.
The dialogue concluded that Pakistan's textile sector needs more than access to new electricity procurement models and renewable-energy options. Transparent pricing, reliable networks, credible data, appropriate risk allocation, storage and firm-capacity solutions, and stronger institutional coordination would all be required to make the transition commercially sustainable.
The discussion ultimately connected Pakistan's energy policy with its export strategy. Power-market reform that fails to provide reliable and competitively priced energy could undermine industrial competitiveness, while a renewable-energy transition without adequate storage, network planning, market mechanisms and credible data could create additional technical and financial challenges for manufacturers.
The writer is a freelance journalist
